Atomic writes
The thread pool limit, restated for fs specifically
Default 4. Four concurrent fs operations, then everything queues.
The symptom is specific: fast under light load, clustered under burst. Latency is not a smooth function of load; it is a step function at 4× concurrency.
A createReadStream holds a pool slot per in-flight chunk read, so four pool threads means four chunks in flight *in total*, not four files.
Measure by setting the pool to 1 and comparing throughput. If throughput is unchanged, the pool was never the bottleneck.
The env var must be set before the process starts; assigning process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE in application code is a no-op.
Watch: the API that lies
fs/promises costs a promise allocation per call, and a FileHandle in the handle form. For very hot paths, fs.read with a reused buffer avoids the allocation.

topics.title: Cluster module
topics.description: Both mechanisms give you more than one core, and they differ in what is shared. worker_threads gives N V8 isolates inside one process, communicating over a fast message channel with transferable memory. cluster gives N processes, forked by a master, fronted by a shared listening socket.
keyConcepts: The comparison, stated as a table
Worker threads: the pool, done properly
Message passing: copy vs transfer vs share
cluster, and its one genuine advantage
Modern Node note
Workers add a serialisation boundary to every call, plus a queue and a failure mode. A worker that returns a rejected promise must be accounted for or callers hang.
Workers and the main thread do not share JavaScript objects. SharedArrayBuffer shares *bytes*, not structure, and you then need Atomics or accept data races.
cluster costs memory linearly and pays JIT warm-up N times. For a service with a small working set, N processes can be *slower* than one until the load justifies them.
Both need explicit lifecycle management: worker.terminate(), cluster disconnect, and the shutdown path in 5.1.11.
Size the pool to availableParallelism(), not os.cpus().length — inside a container, cpus() reports the *host* and you will oversubscribe. This is a very common production bug.
The main thread must stay free to accept and respond to requests while workers run. If you dispatch work synchronously in a burst, you have simply moved the blocking.
Monitor worker health: a worker that died and respawned loses its caches and its warm JIT, which looks like a latency spike with no code change.

topics.title: process.nextTick vs setImmediate
topics.description: Four ways to defer work, with three distinct positions in the tick and one genuinely different mechanism (nextTick is a Node-specific queue drained ahead of everything, not a libuv phase).
keyConcepts: The one table to memorise
nextTick vs a promise, on the question of stacks
To schedule application work. It is a V8-adjacent ordering tool, not a scheduler.
Inside a library that runs in someone else's process. nextTick runs before the *caller's* continuation, which will surprise them.
To "yield". It does not yield to I/O. If you want to yield, you want setImmediate or setTimeout(0).
In a EventEmitter handler or a request handler, process.nextTick work happens before the current request's response can be flushed — that is the *point*, and also the risk if the work is heavy.
Never use nextTick to schedule a retry with a backoff; use setTimeout (or a real queue). A microtask "retry" against a condition that is still false produces a permanent 100% CPU spin.
setTimeout in Node returns a Timeout object with unref()/ref(). unref()'d timers do not keep the process alive — useful for keep-alive probes in a CLI, dangerous for a business timer.
Under load, "check phase runs every tick" means setImmediate callbacks can be starved by a poll phase that always has work. There is no fairness guarantee between phases.

"Order these six callbacks, and tell me which ordering is guaranteed and which is a race." The guaranteed set is: sync code → all nextTick → all promises → then *one* of timer/immediate. Saying that precisely is the whole answer.
"Why did Node deprecate recursive nextTick and then un-deprecate it?" — starvation vs the recursive-promise memory footprint.
"How do you schedule a function after the current I/O batch but before the next timers phase?" — setImmediate.
commonMistakes: process.nextTick(() => reject(e)) inside an async function, where the function's own rejection already covers it. Now you have an unhandled rejection and a double-settle.
Using setTimeout(fn, 0) and claiming it runs "before promises".
Assuming nextTick and queueMicrotask are interchangeable. They are ordered differently, and libraries depend on the difference.
Using queueMicrotask to spawn concurrent work: microtasks run *before* the promise you returned is even observed, so a caller can never get control between them.

topics.title: libuv and thread pool
topics.description: libuv is the C event-loop and cross-platform I/O library under Node's core. It provides the loop, the async I/O primitives (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), the thread pool, and cross-platform abstractions. Node's JavaScript runs on one thread; the actual blocking work happens in the pool.
keyConcepts: The pool
The knob, and its classic bug
Sizing the pool, honestly
The default of 4 is conservative and appropriate for a service that is mostly *network*-bound: most of a typical service's "async" work is socket I/O, which does not touch the pool at all.
Raise it when you can *measure* pool saturation. Raising it costs memory (each thread has a stack and a libuv request) and adds contention.
Never raise it as a substitute for moving the work out of the process. If compression or PBKDF2 is saturating the pool, the answer is a worker thread or a different architecture, not 64 pool threads.
Measure with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 as a diagnostic: if throughput barely changes, the pool was not your bottleneck, and you have saved yourself a tuning mistake.
zlib is the most common hidden pool consumer. compression and sharp/sharp-adjacent pipelines and brotli all land here. If you gzip, prefer doing it once at a proxy, or accept the pool cost knowingly.

crypto.pbkdf2/scrypt are the most dangerous, because the work factor is attacker-controllable in the sense that a login endpoint *always* runs them. Node 18+ and the WebCrypto API give you off-thread variants; a dedicated worker or an async KDF in a separate process is the robust answer for high login rates.

dns.lookup vs dns.resolve is a real production footgun: lookup is getaddrinfo, which is in the pool, and a slow DNS server then stalls unrelated fs calls. Use dns.resolve4/resolveAny (c-ares, loop-based) for high-volume outbound calls, or set dns.setDefaultResultOrder('ipv4first') to reduce the A+AAAA double lookup.
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE must be set before anything requires libuv — setting it in application code after boot is a no-op. Put it in the Dockerfile ENV or the process manager's environment.
"Which of these 10 fs/network/zlib operations use the thread pool?" — expect you to classify all ten.
commonMistakes: Believing sockets use the thread pool. They do not.
Believing fs.promises means "not the thread pool". It means "the pool, but with a promise instead of a callback".
"We raised UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 64 and p99 got worse" — plausible: more context switches, more memory, and more contention on the same data structures.
Using fs.readFileSync in a migration script that runs concurrently with serving traffic.
Assuming async crypto/zlib work does not block. It blocks *the pool*, which is a shared, finite resource — a different kind of blocking, with a different blast radius.

topics.title: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O
topics.description: Blocking I/O stops execution until the operation completes; non-blocking I/O returns immediately and delivers completion later via a callback/promise/stream event. Node is a *non-blocking by design* runtime, which means every synchronous operation you write is a bug waiting for traffic.
keyConcepts: The trap, stated precisely
The three correct fixes, and what each costs
The classification rule interviewers like
I/O-bound (waiting on a socket, disk, DNS, a queue): async/await, keep the work on the main thread, and let the loop overlap it with other requests. Concurrency comes free.

CPU-bound (parsing a 40 MB payload, image transforms, crypto on large buffers, JSON stringify of a giant graph, a tight loop): a worker thread or a process, plus backpressure so the queue does not become its own outage.

Ambiguous (a database query: network I/O, but the *driver* may block): assume the driver is async, but verify. Some drivers do synchronous DNS or synchronous certificate validation. Check the driver's await coverage and its connection-pool behaviour before you claim a route is non-blocking.
When NOT to reach for a worker thread
The work is under about 1 ms. Message-passing overhead and structured-clone/transfer cost exceed the work itself.
The work is a "blocking" library call you can replace with an async one. fs.readFileSync → fs.promises.readFile is nearly always better than wrapping readFileSync in a worker.
You can push the work downstream: an image resize belongs in a job queue, not in the API request.
Every synchronous API in the standard library has a rule: sync in the *startup* path, async in the *request* path. readFileSync for config at boot is idiomatic and correct.
--max-old-space-size does not make main-thread compute faster; it only delays the OOM. Treat a raised heap limit as a symptom, not a fix.
commonMistakes: Marking a function async and believing that made it non-blocking. It changed the *signature*, not the *execution*.
Awaiting a promise chain that never actually suspends (1000 iterations of await Promise.resolve(1)) and calling it "concurrent". It is 1000 microtasks and zero overlap.
Reading a 20 MB file into memory per request with readFile, then JSON.parseing it — two main-thread stalls per request.
Using a while loop to poll for a condition instead of a timer or an event, producing a 100%-CPU spin.
Assuming a rate limiter or a queue in front of a CPU-bound endpoint makes the CPU work cheaper. It only makes the queue longer.

topics.title: Graceful shutdown
topics.description: Graceful shutdown is the sequence between "the orchestrator sent SIGTERM" and "the process exited": stop accepting new work, tell the load balancer to stop routing to you, finish or abandon in-flight work within a deadline, flush durable state, then exit. Without it, every deploy drops requests.
keyConcepts: The signal vocabulary
The full pattern
The keep-alive problem, which is where most real shutdowns fail
The deadline arithmetic, stated as the operational rule
What must be flushed, in order
The "process will not exit" checklist
Draining perfectly costs you a long shutdown (deploys are slower) and risks exceeding the grace period. Draining fast loses in-flight work. The answer is a deadline, not a choice.
process.exit(0) in the handler is the pragmatic hammer; it can truncate stdout writes and skip flushes you forgot. Prefer letting the loop empty, with process.exit only as the final backstop.
Retry the whole thing on the next instance: for idempotent requests, a 502 during a deploy is cheaper than a slow deploy. Knowing when to accept that is a senior judgement.
Do not put a long sleep in a signal handler. A handler that awaits a 30 s timer *will* be SIGKILLed, and the timer is not needed — the loop stays alive as long as handles exist.

Liveness and readiness must be different endpoints with different meanings (see PHASE 8 → Health checks). Liveness must stay green for the whole drain or the orchestrator kills you at 50% drained. Readiness flips first.
Log the drain with counts (in-flight, open sockets, queue depth) so a slow drain is diagnosable in the log rather than inferred.

topics.title: Memory profiling and leaks
topics.description: A memory leak in Node is *reachable* memory that never gets collected. It is not a bug in the collector; it is your code holding a reference it should have dropped. Finding it is a matter of comparing two heap snapshots and reading the retainer path.
keyConcepts: The four numbers, and what each one tells you
The diagnostic rule that saves hours
The heap snapshot workflow — the one you must be able to describe
--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit, and the allocation-rate tools
The seven leak shapes you will actually find
GC tuning: mostly a mistake, occasionally a necessity
--max-old-space-size — a *limit*, not a target. Raising it delays the OOM and increases the time between OOMs and the visible symptom (GC thrashing). It never fixes a leak.

--max-semi-space-size — the size of the young generation. Raise it if your workload allocates a few very large short-lived objects (big Buffers, large JSON) and you are seeing excessive scavenges. This is the one tuning knob with a plausible use case.
--max-semi-space-size too high, or a large young gen, causes *promotion* of short-lived objects into old space, which increases fragmentation. Bigger is not always better.
v8.setFlagsFromString for memory flags is unreliable; set them in the command line or the NODE_OPTIONS env var.
RSS that is not a leak
V8 does not return freed memory to the OS promptly; heapTotal staying high after a spike is normal and is *not* a leak.

topics.title: async_hooks
topics.description: async_hooks gives you a low-level view of every asynchronous resource: its asyncId, its triggerAsyncId (what created it), and its type, plus hooks for init, before, after, destroy, promiseResolve, and resolve. It is the mechanism that powers AsyncLocalStorage, request context, APM tracing, and async-stack-trace reconstruction.
keyConcepts: The four ideas, in the order you need them
A complete, working async_hooks trace
Reconstructing an async stack trace, by hand
AsyncLocalStorage: what you actually use day to day
What the diagnostics module gives you for free
Performance: the honest numbers
init/destroy are the expensive ones. before/after only fire for resources that actually execute.
Never do expensive work (string building, allocation, an HTTP call) inside a hook — you are on every async operation in the process, including ones you did not create.
Keep hook state in a Map keyed by asyncId and delete on destroy. Unbounded growth here is a guaranteed leak.
Measure before shipping: AsyncLocalStorage is designed to be cheap precisely because the naive async_hooks approach is not.

AsyncLocalStorage is per-*context*, not per-request-thread. With worker_threads each worker has its own store; a context set in the main thread does not exist in the worker, so you must pass it explicitly in the message payload.

The store is a reference: putting a large object in it makes that object reachable from every async resource in the chain, which is a (bounded, usually small) memory cost and a potential retention risk.

topics.title: Node vs Bun vs Deno
topics.description: Three runtimes that execute the same language with different defaults: Node (V8 + libuv + npm, the incumbent), Bun (JavaScriptCore + a bundled toolchain, prioritising startup time and built-ins), Deno (V8 + Rust + deno-native permissions, prioritising a secure-by-default web runtime).
keyConcepts: The comparison, on the axes that actually decide it
Where each genuinely wins
The migration cost, stated honestly

Node → Bun: usually "works", with four recurring costs. (1) Some node: built-ins are shimmed with different semantics (dns, net TLS options, child_process signals). (2) N-API addons generally work but must be rebuilt for Bun's platform target. (3) Bun's event loop has a "should we await this?" heuristic that changes performance characteristics for certain sync/async mixes, and it is not bug-free. (4) The production runbook — your APM, your log shipper, your crash reporter — may not have a Bun integration.

Node → Deno: the node: compat layer covers a lot, but node: coverage is not complete and the differences around streams, Buffer, and error cause semantics bite. The bigger cost is ecosystem: most of your dependencies are distributed for node_modules.
Both: you lose the LTS guarantee and the LTS conversation. In a regulated or large-organisation setting, "what is your support plan" is a procurement question, not an engineering one.
When to choose what — the honest heuristic

Bun's headline number is startup time and bundling speed. Both matter enormously for CLIs and serverless, and not at all for a long-running service, where steady-state throughput and ecosystem integration dominate. Saying "Bun is faster" without qualifying *what* is the mistake.

Deno's permissions are a real security improvement and a real operational cost: every new capability is a prompt or a flag, and flags are easy to over-broaden (--allow-all is the default in some tooling and the exact thing you did not want).
Node's "boring" is an asset. Predictable semantics, LTS, an enormous body of production knowledge, and no surprises at 3 a.m.
Every runtime's TypeScript story is a *transpile-only* story except Deno's deno check; neither Node nor Bun type-checks by default, and neither will catch a type error that exists only in types.

Benchmark your actual workload, not a synthetic one. Startup time, p99 under a realistic request mix, and a memory profile are three different numbers and Bun's advantage is concentrated in the first.

topics.title: Package management and package.json
topics.description: package.json is both a manifest (name, version, entry points, dependencies) and a set of executable contracts with the tooling — the exports/imports maps, type, engines, sideEffects, files. The fields that bite production incidents are almost never dependencies.
keyConcepts: The fields that matter, and what each one actually does
The module system, in one table

exports is a hard wall. require('mypkg/src/internal') fails with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED once exports exists. That is a feature: it is how you can refactor internals without a breaking release. It is also why "just import the deep path" is a bug report waiting to happen.

exports also controls types. A package with a types condition inside exports gives TypeScript the right declaration; one with only a top-level types field breaks under moduleResolution: "bundler"/"node16".
"imports" with # is not optional. A bare "#db" key or a non-# key is invalid and the resolution fails at load time, not install time.
Dependencies, correctly

dependencies should be exact or caret-minus, but the lockfile is the real pin. Commit package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml and use npm ci (or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile) in CI. npm install in CI can silently change versions, which is how "it worked yesterday" incidents happen.

peerDependencies means "the host must provide this", which is right for React plugins and wrong for libraries that just want a version range. Getting this wrong produces a *nested duplicate* of a singleton library, and duplicate singletons are a real bug class (see PHASE 4 → micro-frontends).
optionalDependencies is a genuine "best effort": a platform-specific binary that must not break the install on the wrong OS. It is also the standard way to ship fsevents.
A runtime dependency imported inside a try in an optional code path is still a hard dependency for bundlers. If a package is truly optional, do not import it statically.

```dockerfile
FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app

FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
```

topics.title: The event loop: phases, microtask vs macrotask ordering
topics.description: The event loop is libuv's scheduler: a fixed sequence of *phases* that run once per "tick", with a microtask queue drained completely between every single phase, and between every individual callback. Node's own process.nextTick queue is drained *before* the microtask queue.
keyConcepts: The phases, in order, one tick
The two drain queues, and their exact relationship
The canonical demonstration, and how to read it
What the poll phase actually blocks on

Microtask (await, queueMicrotask): work that must happen *before* the program does anything else observable — unwinding a chain of state updates, writing a value that the next synchronous reader must see, batching within one turn. It is the default for "sequence-dependent continuation".

Timer (setTimeout(fn, 0)): deliberately yielding to the event loop so *other* work (I/O, other callbacks) can proceed. A zero-delay timer is not "immediately"; it is "after at least one turn of the loop, and in practice no sooner than 1 ms".

A common mistake that is also a common pattern: awaiting a resolved promise in a loop that awaits other promises. Each await is a microtask, so the whole chain drains before any I/O, even if the loop body is I/O-shaped. If you *need* to let I/O interleave, you need a macrotask boundary (setImmediate).

Microtasks give ordering guarantees but are un-preemptible; a runaway microtask chain starves the loop, and the loop is the only place your I/O completions can be delivered. There is no "interrupt" in JavaScript.
Timers give fairness but are imprecise (clamped, and never earlier than the requested delay) and cost a bit more per scheduling.
setImmediate is the correct tool for "do this after the current I/O batch, before yielding to timers", e.g. kicking off work right after draining a socket.

Never schedule a timer to represent "a duration in the future" if a single long timer would do (setTimeout(fn, 3600_000) vs 3,600,000 one-second timers). A large timer list is real memory and a real epoll bookkeeping cost.
Timers are not cancelled by garbage collection if a reference remains. clearTimeout in the teardown path of long-lived objects (request handlers, subscriptions) is not optional.
commonMistakes: Claiming setTimeout(0) always fires before setImmediate. It does not, at the top level of a module.
Claiming process.nextTick and promises interleave. They do not; nextTick fully drains first.
Using queueMicrotask for a heavy loop and calling it "async". It blocks the loop exactly like a for loop, with fewer debugging tools.
Assuming a pending timer keeps the process alive. Only the *unref'd* case is subtle: timer.unref() lets the process exit even though the timer is registered.

"Order these six callbacks, and tell me which ordering is guaranteed and which is a race." The guaranteed set is: sync code → all nextTick → all promises → then *one* of timer/immediate. Saying that precisely is the whole answer.
"Why did Node deprecate recursive nextTick and then un-deprecate it?" — starvation vs the recursive-promise memory footprint.
"How do you schedule a function after the current I/O batch but before the next timers phase?" — setImmediate.
commonMistakes: process.nextTick(() => reject(e)) inside an async function, where the function's own rejection already covers it. Now you have an unhandled rejection and a double-settle.
Using setTimeout(fn, 0) and claiming it runs "before promises".
Assuming nextTick and queueMicrotask are interchangeable. They are ordered differently, and libraries depend on the difference.
Using queueMicrotask to spawn concurrent work: microtasks run *before* the promise you returned is even observed, so a caller can never get control between them.

topics.title: libuv and the thread pool: what runs off the main thread
topics.description: libuv is the C event-loop and cross-platform I/O library under Node's core. It provides the loop, the async I/O primitives (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), the thread pool, and cross-platform abstractions. Node's JavaScript runs on one thread; the actual blocking work happens in the pool.
keyConcepts: The pool
The knob, and its classic bug
Sizing the pool, honestly
The default of 4 is conservative and appropriate for a service that is mostly *network*-bound: most of a typical service's "async" work is socket I/O, which does not touch the pool at all.
Raise it when you can *measure* pool saturation. Raising it costs memory (each thread has a stack and a libuv request) and adds contention.
Never raise it as a substitute for moving the work out of the process. If compression or PBKDF2 is saturating the pool, the answer is a worker thread or a different architecture, not 64 pool threads.
Measure with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 as a diagnostic: if throughput barely changes, the pool was not your bottleneck, and you have saved yourself a tuning mistake.
zlib is the most common hidden pool consumer. compression and sharp/sharp-adjacent pipelines and brotli all land here. If you gzip, prefer doing it once at a proxy, or accept the pool cost knowingly.

crypto.pbkdf2/scrypt are the most dangerous, because the work factor is attacker-controllable in the sense that a login endpoint *always* runs them. Node 18+ and the WebCrypto API give you off-thread variants; a dedicated worker or an async KDF in a separate process is the robust answer for high login rates.

dns.lookup vs dns.resolve is a real production footgun: lookup is getaddrinfo, which is in the pool, and a slow DNS server then stalls unrelated fs calls. Use dns.resolve4/resolveAny (c-ares, loop-based) for high-volume outbound calls, or set dns.setDefaultResultOrder('ipv4first') to reduce the A+AAAA double lookup.
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE must be set before anything requires libuv — setting it in application code after boot is a no-op. Put it in the Dockerfile ENV or the process manager's environment.
"Which of these 10 fs/network/zlib operations use the thread pool?" — expect you to classify all ten.
commonMistakes: Believing sockets use the thread pool. They do not.
Believing fs.promises means "not the thread pool". It means "the pool, but with a promise instead of a callback".
"We raised UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 64 and p99 got worse" — plausible: more context switches, more memory, and more contention on the same data structures.
Using fs.readFileSync in a migration script that runs concurrently with serving traffic.
Assuming async crypto/zlib work does not block. It blocks *the pool*, which is a shared, finite resource — a different kind of blocking, with a different blast radius.

topics.title: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O, and the CPU-bound trap
topics.description: Blocking I/O stops execution until the operation completes; non-blocking I/O returns immediately and delivers completion later via a callback/promise/stream event. Node is a *non-blocking by design* runtime, which means every synchronous operation you write is a bug waiting for traffic.
keyConcepts: The trap, stated precisely
The three correct fixes, and what each costs
The classification rule interviewers like
I/O-bound (waiting on a socket, disk, DNS, a queue): async/await, keep the work on the main thread, and let the loop overlap it with other requests. Concurrency comes free.

CPU-bound (parsing a 40 MB payload, image transforms, crypto on large buffers, JSON stringify of a giant graph, a tight loop): a worker thread or a process, plus backpressure so the queue does not become its own outage.

Ambiguous (a database query: network I/O, but the *driver* may block): assume the driver is async, but verify. Some drivers do synchronous DNS or synchronous certificate validation. Check the driver's await coverage and its connection-pool behaviour before you claim a route is non-blocking.
When NOT to reach for a worker thread
The work is under about 1 ms. Message-passing overhead and structured-clone/transfer cost exceed the work itself.
The work is a "blocking" library call you can replace with an async one. fs.readFileSync → fs.promises.readFile is nearly always better than wrapping readFileSync in a worker.
You can push the work downstream: an image resize belongs in a job queue, not in the API request.
Every synchronous API in the standard library has a rule: sync in the *startup* path, async in the *request* path. readFileSync for config at boot is idiomatic and correct.
--max-old-space-size does not make main-thread compute faster; it only delays the OOM. Treat a raised heap limit as a symptom, not a fix.
commonMistakes: Marking a function async and believing that made it non-blocking. It changed the *signature*, not the *execution*.
Awaiting a promise chain that never actually suspends (1000 iterations of await Promise.resolve(1)) and calling it "concurrent". It is 1000 microtasks and zero overlap.
Reading a 20 MB file into memory per request with readFile, then JSON.parseing it — two main-thread stalls per request.
Using a while loop to poll for a condition instead of a timer or an event, producing a 100%-CPU spin.
Assuming a rate limiter or a queue in front of a CPU-bound endpoint makes the CPU work cheaper. It only makes the queue longer.

topics.title: Buffers, encoding, and binary data
topics.description: A Buffer is Node's view over a chunk of raw memory, a fixed-length byte array backed by an off-heap allocation. It is how Node represents binary data, and it is deliberately *not* a JavaScript string: strings are UTF-16 code-unit sequences, which cannot represent arbitrary bytes.
keyConcepts: The mental model: bytes vs characters
Allocating and reading
The pool slab, subarray vs slice, and mutation
Reading: three methods, three meanings
Encoding choice matters for the wire
Streams of bytes: the Buffer → Stream relationship
Buffer: file I/O, network frames, crypto input, anything you will hand to a native API.
String: text you are parsing, printing, or putting in JSON. Convert at the boundary, not in the middle of logic.
Stream: size unknown, or you want constant memory while processing.

Uint8Array / DataView: when you share memory with a worker via transfer, or when interoperating with a browser-side buffer, or when you want explicit endianness control. Buffer is a Uint8Array subclass, so it interoperates, but Buffer allocates from the slab.

Strings are convenient and universally understood by libraries; Buffers are exact and allocation-cheap. Converting between them costs a copy every time. Pick one representation per layer and convert at the boundary.

latin1 is 1 byte per char and lossless for bytes, which makes it a fast intermediate for binary parsing — but the moment you toString('utf8') it you are decoding, and a mis-split multi-byte sequence becomes U+FFFD. Parse *bytes*, then decode the field.
commonMistakes: buf.toString('utf8', 0, len) where len was computed from a string's .length — string length is UTF-16 units, buffer length is bytes.
Treating a truncated multi-byte sequence as a bug in the data when it is a bug in the framing.
Buffer.from(str) (no encoding) instead of Buffer.from(str, 'utf8') — identical for ASCII, and a trap the moment the string is not ASCII.
Using base64 for a token that goes in a URL (should be base64url, or the +// and = get percent-encoded or rejected).
Mutating a Buffer you received from a stream chunk and being surprised when the source's data changes.

topics.title: Streams: readable, writable, duplex, transform, backpressure
topics.description: A stream is a partial input or output: an object over which data arrives or leaves incrementally, with an internal buffer and an explicit contract about how much it will accept before telling you to stop. Streams are Node's answer to "I do not know the size, and I refuse to hold it all in memory."
keyConcepts: The four types
The flow control problem, stated as arithmetic
The right way: pipeline
highWaterMark — the knob that decides your memory ceiling

Readable highWaterMark (default 16 KB for file streams, 64 KB for net.Socket): the amount the stream buffers *per read* before pushing back. It is a *threshold*, not a cap — nothing stops a _read implementation from pushing more.
Writable highWaterMark (default 16 KB): the buffer level at which write() starts returning false.
objectMode: true makes the unit "one object" and sets the HWM to 16 objects. Handy for object pipelines; a memory hazard for large objects.
Object mode, and the encoder/decoder you actually want
The final/destroy contract — how a Transform signals "I am done"
cb() after this.push(...) means "I processed this chunk, give me more".
cb(err) aborts the pipeline with an error.
push(null) signals end-of-stream. Never push() after push(null).
commonMistakes: .pipe() without an error handler on the destination.
Ignoring write()'s false in a manual loop, and losing data or growing unboundedly.
objectMode everywhere "for convenience" — every object is a heap allocation, and HWM 16 objects of 10 MB each is 160 MB.
Forgetting flush(cb) in a Transform that buffers a tail, so the last line is silently dropped and the stream never ends.
Converting every chunk with chunk.toString() in a text transform, corrupting characters split across chunk boundaries.

topics.title: fs and the file system: async, streams, and the thread pool limit
topics.description: node:fs exposes the file system in four shapes — the callback API, the promise API (fs/promises), the synchronous API, and the streaming API. Choosing between them is mostly a question of size, and the two facts people miss are that the async forms still use the thread pool, and that "async" readFile still loads the whole file into memory.
keyConcepts: The four shapes and what each actually does
Why fs.promises.readFile is a memory hazard, not a performance win
The fs API surface worth knowing precisely
Atomic writes
The thread pool limit, restated for fs specifically
Default 4. Four concurrent fs operations, then everything queues.
The symptom is specific: fast under light load, clustered under burst. Latency is not a smooth function of load; it is a step function at 4× concurrency.
A createReadStream holds a pool slot per in-flight chunk read, so four pool threads means four chunks in flight *in total*, not four files.
Measure by setting the pool to 1 and comparing throughput. If throughput is unchanged, the pool was never the bottleneck.
The env var must be set before the process starts; assigning process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE in application code is a no-op.
Watch: the API that lies
fs/promises costs a promise allocation per call, and a FileHandle in the handle form. For very hot paths, fs.read with a reused buffer avoids the allocation.

topics.title: Worker threads and the cluster module, and when each applies
topics.description: Both mechanisms give you more than one core, and they differ in what is shared. worker_threads gives N V8 isolates inside one process, communicating over a fast message channel with transferable memory. cluster gives N processes, forked by a master, fronted by a shared listening socket.
keyConcepts: The comparison, stated as a table
Worker threads: the pool, done properly
Message passing: copy vs transfer vs share
cluster, and its one genuine advantage
Modern Node note
Workers add a serialisation boundary to every call, plus a queue and a failure mode. A worker that returns a rejected promise must be accounted for or callers hang.
Workers and the main thread do not share JavaScript objects. SharedArrayBuffer shares *bytes*, not structure, and you then need Atomics or accept data races.
cluster costs memory linearly and pays JIT warm-up N times. For a service with a small working set, N processes can be *slower* than one until the load justifies them.
Both need explicit lifecycle management: worker.terminate(), cluster disconnect, and the shutdown path in 5.1.11.
Size the pool to availableParallelism(), not os.cpus().length — inside a container, cpus() reports the *host* and you will oversubscribe. This is a very common production bug.
The main thread must stay free to accept and respond to requests while workers run. If you dispatch work synchronously in a burst, you have simply moved the blocking.
Monitor worker health: a worker that died and respawned loses its caches and its warm JIT, which looks like a latency spike with no code change.

topics.title: Child processes and IPC
topics.description: A child process is a separate OS process. Node gives you spawn (streams), execFile/exec (buffered output through a shell or not), fork (a Node process with an IPC channel), and spawnSync/execFileSync. The choice determines your IPC model, your security exposure, and your ability to stream.
keyConcepts: The four ways to create one
Why exec is a security problem and execFile is not
IPC, and the three channels available
Buffering vs streaming is the decision that matters most here
Security posture for child processes
spawn + streams: the most control, the most code, the only option for large output.
execFile + buffer: simple, with a timeout and maxBuffer; fine for short outputs, dangerous without the cap.
fork: Node-to-Node only, structured messages, easy; adds a process and a protocol.
cluster (5.1.8) is fork plus load balancing plus respawn, and it is not for untrusted work.

Long-lived children are stateful, which means restart logic, version skew between parent and child, and a place for state to diverge. A fresh spawn per job is simpler to reason about and usually correct for batch work.
Always set timeout and maxBuffer on buffered exec. Both defaults are effectively "wait forever" and "grow until OOM".
Kill the child when the client disconnects, and use SIGKILL for processes you cannot reason about.

topics.title: The event emitter: error events, once, and listener leaks
topics.description: EventEmitter is Node's pub/sub primitive, and the base of nearly every Node API you use: streams, HTTP request/response objects, the process object, most libraries. It is synchronous, unbounded, and it has one special rule: emitting 'error' with no listener throws.
keyConcepts: The API, and the three parts everyone forgets

once is implemented as on plus a wrapper. off(evt, originalFn) will not remove it, because the registered function is a wrapper, not your function. You must call off(evt, wrapper) or use removeListener with the same wrapper. This is why once handlers leak in code that "obviously" unsubscribes.
removeListener removes the most recently added matching listener, not the first. With duplicate registrations this surprises people.

Emitting inside a listener is a snapshot iteration. Listeners added during an emit do not run for that emit; listeners removed during an emit after their turn has passed do not run at all. This is deliberate and it is how once guarantees "exactly once" even under re-entrancy.
The 'error' rule, precisely
Listener leaks: the two shapes and how to prove each
Detection, in order of directness
The one-shot API, and why it is usually the right answer to a leak
Async iterators: the leak-free subscription
Cross-process or cross-service. An emitter is in-process, in-memory, fire-and-forget, and has no durability. If a message must survive a crash, use a queue (Background Processing).
As a substitute for a return value. If the caller needs the result, return the result. Emitters are for *additional* observers.
As a job queue. A long chain of .on() handlers is a workflow engine with no backpressure, no retry and no visibility.

topics.title: Graceful shutdown: draining, timeouts, and SIGTERM handling
topics.description: Graceful shutdown is the sequence between "the orchestrator sent SIGTERM" and "the process exited": stop accepting new work, tell the load balancer to stop routing to you, finish or abandon in-flight work within a deadline, flush durable state, then exit. Without it, every deploy drops requests.
keyConcepts: The signal vocabulary
The full pattern
The keep-alive problem, which is where most real shutdowns fail
The deadline arithmetic, stated as the operational rule
What must be flushed, in order
The "process will not exit" checklist
Draining perfectly costs you a long shutdown (deploys are slower) and risks exceeding the grace period. Draining fast loses in-flight work. The answer is a deadline, not a choice.
process.exit(0) in the handler is the pragmatic hammer; it can truncate stdout writes and skip flushes you forgot. Prefer letting the loop empty, with process.exit only as the final backstop.
Retry the whole thing on the next instance: for idempotent requests, a 502 during a deploy is cheaper than a slow deploy. Knowing when to accept that is a senior judgement.
Do not put a long sleep in a signal handler. A handler that awaits a 30 s timer *will* be SIGKILLed, and the timer is not needed — the loop stays alive as long as handles exist.

Liveness and readiness must be different endpoints with different meanings (see PHASE 8 → Health checks). Liveness must stay green for the whole drain or the orchestrator kills you at 50% drained. Readiness flips first.
Log the drain with counts (in-flight, open sockets, queue depth) so a slow drain is diagnosable in the log rather than inferred.

topics.title: Memory profiling, heap vs RSS, and finding leaks
topics.description: A memory leak in Node is *reachable* memory that never gets collected. It is not a bug in the collector; it is your code holding a reference it should have dropped. Finding it is a matter of comparing two heap snapshots and reading the retainer path.
keyConcepts: The four numbers, and what each one tells you
The diagnostic rule that saves hours
The heap snapshot workflow — the one you must be able to describe
--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit, and the allocation-rate tools
The seven leak shapes you will actually find
GC tuning: mostly a mistake, occasionally a necessity
--max-old-space-size — a *limit*, not a target. Raising it delays the OOM and increases the time between OOMs and the visible symptom (GC thrashing). It never fixes a leak.

--max-semi-space-size — the size of the young generation. Raise it if your workload allocates a few very large short-lived objects (big Buffers, large JSON) and you are seeing excessive scavenges. This is the one tuning knob with a plausible use case.
--max-semi-space-size too high, or a large young gen, causes *promotion* of short-lived objects into old space, which increases fragmentation. Bigger is not always better.
v8.setFlagsFromString for memory flags is unreliable; set them in the command line or the NODE_OPTIONS env var.
RSS that is not a leak
V8 does not return freed memory to the OS promptly; heapTotal staying high after a spike is normal and is *not* a leak.

topics.title: async_hooks, diagnostics, and async context
topics.description: async_hooks gives you a low-level view of every asynchronous resource: its asyncId, its triggerAsyncId (what created it), and its type, plus hooks for init, before, after, destroy, promiseResolve, and resolve. It is the mechanism that powers AsyncLocalStorage, request context, APM tracing, and async-stack-trace reconstruction.
keyConcepts: The four ideas, in the order you need them
A complete, working async_hooks trace
Reconstructing an async stack trace, by hand
AsyncLocalStorage: what you actually use day to day
What the diagnostics module gives you for free
Performance: the honest numbers
init/destroy are the expensive ones. before/after only fire for resources that actually execute.
Never do expensive work (string building, allocation, an HTTP call) inside a hook — you are on every async operation in the process, including ones you did not create.
Keep hook state in a Map keyed by asyncId and delete on destroy. Unbounded growth here is a guaranteed leak.
Measure before shipping: AsyncLocalStorage is designed to be cheap precisely because the naive async_hooks approach is not.

AsyncLocalStorage is per-*context*, not per-request-thread. With worker_threads each worker has its own store; a context set in the main thread does not exist in the worker, so you must pass it explicitly in the message payload.

The store is a reference: putting a large object in it makes that object reachable from every async resource in the chain, which is a (bounded, usually small) memory cost and a potential retention risk.

topics.title: Package management and package.json semantics
topics.description: package.json is both a manifest (name, version, entry points, dependencies) and a set of executable contracts with the tooling — the exports/imports maps, type, engines, sideEffects, files. The fields that bite production incidents are almost never dependencies.
keyConcepts: The fields that matter, and what each one actually does
The module system, in one table

exports is a hard wall. require('mypkg/src/internal') fails with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED once exports exists. That is a feature: it is how you can refactor internals without a breaking release. It is also why "just import the deep path" is a bug report waiting to happen.

exports also controls types. A package with a types condition inside exports gives TypeScript the right declaration; one with only a top-level types field breaks under moduleResolution: "bundler"/"node16".
"imports" with # is not optional. A bare "#db" key or a non-# key is invalid and the resolution fails at load time, not install time.
Dependencies, correctly

dependencies should be exact or caret-minus, but the lockfile is the real pin. Commit package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml and use npm ci (or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile) in CI. npm install in CI can silently change versions, which is how "it worked yesterday" incidents happen.

peerDependencies means "the host must provide this", which is right for React plugins and wrong for libraries that just want a version range. Getting this wrong produces a *nested duplicate* of a singleton library, and duplicate singletons are a real bug class (see PHASE 4 → micro-frontends).
optionalDependencies is a genuine "best effort": a platform-specific binary that must not break the install on the wrong OS. It is also the standard way to ship fsevents.
A runtime dependency imported inside a try in an optional code path is still a hard dependency for bundlers. If a package is truly optional, do not import it statically.
Lockfiles and reproducibility
Publishing and install artefacts
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```jsonc
{
  "type": "module",            // .js is ESM. Use .mjs/.cjs to override per file.
  "main": "./dist/index.cjs",   // CJS entry
  "module": "./dist/index.js",  // bundler hint (not a Node contract)
  "exports": {                 // THE public API. Nothing outside is importable.
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "import": "./dist/index.js",     // ESM consumers
      "require": "./dist/index.cjs",   // CJS consumers
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    },
    "./package.json": "./package.json",  // required for tools that read the manifest
    "./sub": "./dist/sub.js"
  },
  "imports": {                 // YOUR package's internal aliases. '#' prefix is mandatory.
    "#db": "./src/db/index.js",
    "#config": { "node": "./src/config.node.js", "default": "./src/config.js" }
  },
  "files": ["dist", "README.md"],
  "sideEffects": ["**/*.css", "./src/polyfills.js"],
  "engines": { "node": ">=20.11" },
  "packageManager": "pnpm@9.12.0"
}
```

```jsonc
{
  "dependencies":    { "pg": "8.13.1" },                     // exact: you control it
  "devDependencies": { "typescript": "^5.6.3" },             // range: you tolerate churn
  "peerDependencies": { "react": "^18 || ^19" },
  "optionalDependencies": { "fsevents": "^2.3.3" }          // failure is tolerated
}
```

```bash
npm ci                       # CI: exact, from the lockfile, fails if the lock is stale
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
yarn install --immutable
node -p "process.versions"    # what you actually run

# Audit and provenance
npm audit --omit=dev         # production tree only; dev vulns rarely matter at runtime
npm ls --all                 # who is pulling in lodash 3?
npm explain express
npm outdated --long
```

```bash
npm publish --dry-run         # shows exactly what goes in the tarball
npm pack --dry-run            # same, tarball form
npm pkg get name version      # read manifest fields via the CLI
npx node-gyp rebuild          # native addon, if it is yours
```

```dockerfile
# Multi-stage, and the install step is the one people get wrong.
FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # deps only, no build tools needed

FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci                         # dev deps needed to build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20.11-bookworm-slim
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps  /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json ./
USER node                            # never run as root
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]         # no npm/npx in the entrypoint: PID 1 signal delivery
```

topics.title: V8 and the JavaScript engine: hidden classes, JIT tiers, and what that means for you
topics.description: V8 compiles JavaScript in stages, using runtime feedback. The practical consequences for a Node engineer are: object *shape* determines property access speed, monomorphism beats polymorphism, and a function's speed changes over its lifetime (which is why a "slow" function can become fast and a fast one can become slow).
keyConcepts: The pipeline, and why "it got slower" happens

Warm-up is real. A serverless function that runs 200 ms is mostly running interpreted bytecode. A long-running service is JIT-compiled after seconds. *This is why a microbenchmark and a production service disagree.*

Deoptimization is real. When a function optimised on assumption A is called with a shape that violates A, V8 throws away the optimised code and drops back. In a monorepo this often looks like "the p99 got worse after deploy" when the real cause is one route hitting a code path the JIT had optimised away.

Polymorphism degrades property access. A property access compiles to a fixed offset if the object's shape is stable. Change the shape and the access becomes a dictionary lookup or a megamorphic stub — an order of magnitude slower, and it never gets fast again.
delete breaks hidden classes. Using delete obj.x transitions the object to dictionary mode permanently, for that object's shape.
Hidden classes (hidden classes / shapes / maps), demonstrated
The things that actually cost you in a Node service
Isolating GC, which is the other half
Scavenges are cheap and frequent. They are driven by allocation rate, not by live size.
Major GCs are expensive and grow with live data. A large live heap means longer mark and sweep.
GC pauses are the tail latency. This is the single most common cause of a Node service with a great average and a terrible p99.
Reducing allocation rate is usually the highest-leverage GC fix, and the tools are the allocation profile (--heap-prof) and --trace-gc.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
JavaScript source
   ↓  parse (lazy: only what's reached)
   ↓  Ignition  — bytecode interpreter. Everything starts here. Fast to start, slow to run.
   ↓  (feedback vector fills: which branches are taken, which types are seen)
   ↓
   ├─ Sparkplug (baseline, near-ignition speed) — cheap, no optimisation
   ↓  (function is hot: invocation count + bytecode budget crossed)
   ↓
   ├─ Maglev (mid-tier, mid-JIT, ~2-5× Sparkplug) — speculative, fast to compile
   ↓  (even hotter, and after enough OSR / idle time)
   ↓
   └─ TurboFan (top-tier, optimising, 10-100× Ignition) — the real deal
         ↓
         deoptimization (bailout) if a speculative assumption is violated
```

```js
// Shapes are created in insertion order, and the engine caches the offset.
function readA(p) { return p.name; }
const a = { id: 1, name: 'x' };
const b = { id: 2, name: 'y' };
for (let i = 0; i < 1e7; i++) readA(a);   // monomorphic: name is always at offset 1
console.log(readA(b));                     // still monomorphic — same shape

const c = { name: 'z', id: 3 };            // DIFFERENT insertion order → different shape
readA(c);                                  // polymorphic (2 shapes) — slightly slower
readA({ q: 1, name: 'w' });                // a third shape
readA({ r: 1, name: 'v' });                // a fourth: megamorphic, the slow generic path

// Consequences:
// 1. Create objects with the same properties in the same order.
// 2. Initialise every property in the constructor, even to undefined — an
//    absent property and an undefined property are different shapes.
// 3. Do not use `delete` on hot objects; set to undefined instead.
// 4. Do not add properties after creation in a hot loop.
```

```js
class Point { constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } }
// Do NOT do this: adds a third property post-construction, changing the shape
// for a subset of instances and making the access polymorphic.
p.z = 0;
```

```
Young generation (scavenge, ~1-16 ms, very fast, copies live objects)
  → survivors are promoted to old space
Old space (major GC / incremental marking + sweeping, 10-100s of ms, STW-ish pauses)
  → memory is compacted
```

```js
// Two allocation-rate offenders and their fixes.
// 1. String concatenation in a loop.
let s = '';
for (const part of parts) s += part;          // allocates a new string each time
const s2 = parts.join('');                    // one allocation

// 2. Intermediate objects in a hot transform.
const out = rows.map((r) => ({ ...r, total: r.qty * r.price }));   // new object per row
// If you only need numbers out, return a number:
//   rows.map((r) => r.qty * r.price)      // no object churn, no GC pressure
```

```bash
node --prof app.js && node --prof-process isolate-*.log > v8.txt
# What is the CPU actually doing? Includes GC time in the bottom-up view.
# The "GC" section at the top is the first thing to read.

node --cpu-prof app.js     # .cpuprofile, loads in DevTools or in speedscope
node --heap-prof app.js     # allocation sites, ranked by selfSize
```

topics.title: Middleware
topics.description: middleware.ts (or src/middleware.ts) runs before a matched request is handled — before pages, route handlers, and rewrites — on the Edge runtime by default.
keyConcepts: Ordering
What middleware can and cannot do
Auth in middleware: the pattern and its limits
The classic redirect loop
Broad matcher including /login. Fix: exclude auth routes explicitly (matcher regex or next.config).

Cookie present but invalid. Middleware checks presence only; the page's requireUser() sees an invalid session and redirects to /login; middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects to /dashboard; infinite loop. Fix: middleware must delete the cookie when it rejects, and the deep check must cookies().delete() on failure.

Param-aware routes. Middleware uses pathname only, so /login?next=/login or an i18n prefix mismatch loops. Fix: normalize with the same prefixes your routes use and validate next to prevent open redirects.
Trailing slash / case mismatch producing /Login which doesn't match your exclusion.
Rewrite loops: rewriting to a path that matches your own matcher again.
commonMistakes: doing DB authorization in Edge middleware; mutating req.nextUrl in place instead of cloning; matching everything and slowing every request; treating middleware as the only auth check; forgetting that middleware can run on RSC/prefetch requests and must be cheap; using redirect() in middleware when you meant an internal rewrite.
practiceTasks: implement middleware with a narrow matcher, a presence-only session gate, a safe next redirect parameter (validate it is a same-origin relative path), and a debug header x-mw: allowed|redirected. Then deliberately create each of the five loop causes above, observe the redirect chain with curl -I -L, and fix each by editing only middleware or requireUser(). Add a test asserting exactly one redirect for an invalid cookie.

interviewQuestions.text: When does middleware run in the request lifecycle?
What does the `config.matcher` do and why prefer it over pathname checks?
Can middleware do authorization? Why not?
What is the redirect loop bug and what causes it?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* A /dashboard route 307s to /login and the browser reports "too many redirects". *Decision.* Trace the two redirect sources as separate actors: the middleware gate and the data-layer session check, and find out which pair is disagreeing. *Reasoning.* The canonical cause is a split-brain: middleware validates *presence* of the session cookie while the page calls requireUser(), which validates the session *value*. When the session is expired, revoked, or signed with a rotated key, the cookie still exists. Middleware therefore admits the request, requireUser() rejects it and redirects to /login, middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects back to /dashboard. Neither component is wrong in isolation; the missing invariant is that the cookie's presence must imply its validity, or that rejection must clear the cookie. *Trade-offs.* Full verification in middleware (JWT signature check, session lookup) is cheap for stateless JWTs and expensive for database sessions on the Edge; verifying fully makes every request pay that cost and still leaves object-level authorization undone. *Failure scenario.* A key rotation invalidates all sessions; 100% of authenticated traffic 307-loops, error monitors fill with 3xx chains, and login itself appears broken. *Prevention.* Clear the cookie on rejection at every layer; make the matcher exclude /login and static assets; keep one requireUser() used by pages, handlers, and actions; add a synthetic check that requests a protected route with an invalid session cookie and asserts a single redirect to /login, plus a loop detector alert on repeated redirect chains.

topics.title: Error handling
topics.description: Error handling within Express Framework.
keyConcepts: Error types: syntax errors (can't parse), runtime errors (thrown while running), logic errors (wrong result, no exception, the hardest).

Operational vs programmer errors: operational ones are expected (network down, invalid input, file missing) and handled gracefully. Programmer ones are bugs (undefined is not a function) and are fixed, not caught and ignored.
try/catch/finally, throw, custom error classes, and error cause:
Async errors: try/catch works with await. Un-awaited promises produce unhandled rejections, which crash modern Node by default.

Principles: fail fast; don't swallow errors (catch {}); don't use exceptions for normal control flow; log with context; return meaningful errors to users without leaking internals (no stack traces to clients); validate at boundaries.
Alternatives: result types ({ok, value, error}), error codes.

interviewQuestions.answer: Always, even after a `return` or throw.

topics.description: Express itself does not parse bodies. req.body is populated by middleware — express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text(), express.raw() — and each one only activates for a matching Content-Type. The cors, helmet, pino-http and express "batteries" people think ship with it are separate packages.

express.json() is convenient and correct for most APIs; it is also a synchronous JSON.parse of the whole body, which is a main-thread stall proportional to size. For a 10 MB body that is tens of milliseconds of blocked loop.
qs gives you nested query objects for free and gives you its own attack surface and bundle weight. Most APIs do not need nesting.

Express's implicit status/body behaviour is convenient, and its implicitness is the risk: res.send('ok') gives text/html and a 200 whether or not that is what you meant. Being explicit costs a few characters and removes a class of review arguments.

topics.title: Middleware order
topics.description: Express executes its stack in registration order, first match first. Order is therefore a correctness property, not a style choice: moving one line can change a 401 into a 500, a 200 into a 403, or a working CORS preflight into a hard failure.
keyConcepts: The order rules, and the failure each one produces
A canonical, ordered app.js — and the reasoning in comments
The four order bugs that produce real incidents
A defence, not just a convention
app.use prefix matching, the order bug that hides inside it
When the framework can help

Fastify uses encapsulation (plugins register their own hooks, and sibling plugins cannot see each other's), which structurally prevents a whole class of order bugs. This is the strongest architectural argument for Fastify (5.2.15).
NestJS gives you explicit phases (middleware → guards → interceptors → pipes → handler → filters), so ordering is declared rather than positional. Also 5.3.
In plain Express, the discipline is: one app.js that registers everything in order, with no scattered app.use calls in feature files. Centralising registration is the actual fix.

A single ordered file is the easiest thing to review and the worst thing to scale to 50 people editing it; the compromise is a middleware/index.js that imports and registers named stacks in a documented order.
Splitting registration across modules means the order is determined by import order, which is invisible. Explicitly registering in one place removes a whole class of bug.
Preflight OPTIONS must not be rate-limited or authenticated. If your limiter runs first, browsers break during traffic spikes and the error looks like CORS.

topics.title: Helmet and CORS
topics.description: helmet sets a set of security-related HTTP response headers; the cors package implements the CORS protocol. Both are middleware, both are configuration, and both are easy to set to a value that either does nothing or breaks production.
keyConcepts: What helmet() actually sets (v7 defaults)
CORS, done correctly

CORS is browser-only. It is enforced by the browser, not the server. curl is unaffected. Every "CORS is not a security control" answer is correct, and it is *also* correct to say the browser-enforced list is the last line of defence for cookie-authenticated APIs.

credentials: true + origin: true (reflect-any) = vulnerability. The spec forbids * with credentials, and the cors package reflects the origin to satisfy that — which means every website can make authenticated requests to your API. This is the single most common real CORS vulnerability.
Vary: Origin must be set, or a shared cache serves one origin's response to another. The cors package does it for you when origin is a function; if you build headers yourself, do not forget.
Preflight must bypass auth and rate limiting. CORS middleware answers OPTIONS itself and ends the chain, so it must be before both (5.2.3).
Other headers worth setting by hand

helmet() defaults are deliberately strict and will break a site that uses inline scripts, third-party analytics, or cross-origin images. Turning headers off "to fix it" removes the protection; the correct sequence is report-only → fix → enforce.
HSTS with includeSubDomains is irreversible for months if you have a non-HTTPS subdomain. Start with a short max-age and no preload.
CORS allowlists require a deploy when you add an environment. A configuration-driven list from a validated env var (5.2.12) is the maintainable form.
crossOriginResourcePolicy: cross-origin weakens a real protection; set it only for the paths that genuinely serve cross-origin assets.
CSP connect-src must include your WebSocket origin in the wss:// form or real-time features break in a way that is very hard to debug from the server side.

topics.title: Logging (Morgan, Pino)
topics.description: morgan is a request/response access log — one line per completed request, format string configurable. pino is a general-purpose structured logger — fast, JSON by default, low-overhead, with child loggers. Most production Node services use both: pino for application logs, and either morgan-in-pino or a custom res.on('finish') hook for the access line.
keyConcepts: Morgan, precisely
It is an access log. It has no context, no error, no trace, and no structure you can query beyond the fields you hand it.
It logs on finish, so a request that never finishes is never logged. A hanging request is invisible in the access log. That is exactly when you need to see it.
It does not know your request id unless you add it, and it cannot add one (see below).
String formats are unqueryable. A grep over a text log is not a metric, and it is not an alert.
Pino, and why it is the default choice for app logs
Morgan + Pino, integrated properly: pino-http
Do you need morgan at all if you use pino-http?
Request ids, end to end
Log levels, and the discipline that makes them useful
Log events, not strings. log.info({ orderId, total, currency }, 'order created') is queryable; 'order created' is not. An event name is a schema — treat it like a database column.
Do not log the same failure twice. If the error handler logs it with full context, the catch site should not. Duplicate log lines are the main cause of alert fatigue.

topics.title: Fastify and Hono awareness
topics.description: Fastify is a Node HTTP framework built around encapsulation and schema-driven serialisation. Hono is a tiny, Web-standard router that runs on Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, and edge platforms. Both exist for the same underlying reason: Express's global middleware stack and untyped request/response are hard to reason about and hard to make fast.
keyConcepts: Fastify, and the three ideas that are actually different
Fastify plugins, and the encapsulation payoff
Hono, and the thing it optimises for
The honest comparison table
How to choose, in one sentence each

Express — the default, and the right answer unless you have a specific reason. The largest middleware ecosystem, the most documentation, the most hireable skill. If your team knows it, the cost of anything else is real.

Fastify — when JSON throughput, typed handlers, or *structural* correctness (encapsulation removes a whole bug class) justify a migration. The strongest "why not Express" answer, because it names mechanisms rather than benchmarks.
Hono — when you must run the same API on more than one runtime, including the edge, or when you want Web-standard types.
NestJS — when the coordination cost of many engineers and many modules exceeds the framework's tax (5.3.1).

Express → Fastify is a rewrite, not a refactor: handlers, middleware, error handling, and every plugin. The #fastify/express compatibility layer exists and it gets you started, but it is a first step, not a destination.

Fastify's JSON Schema validation and serialisation require writing schemas. That is a real cost on a codebase with dynamic shapes, and it is *also* the thing that makes it fast and type-safe. Teams that hate duplication love it; teams with a fast-moving internal API hate it.

Fastify's encapsulation is a feature and a constraint: a "global" middleware is a plugin with fastify-plugin, and a decorator declared in the wrong scope is a runtime error. It is learnable in an hour and it eliminates the ordering bugs of 5.2.3 permanently.

topics.title: Routing: methods, paths, params, and route ordering
topics.description: A route is a method + path pattern mapped to a stack of handlers. Express builds a layered router: an Express app *is* a middleware stack, and app.use() and app.METHOD() both append to it. First match wins, and matching is prefix-based for use, exact-by-default for routes.

Route ordering is the whole game
req.params, req.query, req.body — the three places data hides
router() for modularity
Named routes and URLs, which matter for redirects and form posts
HTTP method matching, and the traps
The 404 and the terminal handler

Express's router is a runtime regex match per layer. A stack of 200 middlewares and 60 routes means a lot of regex evaluation per request. This is measurable, and it is one of the honest reasons Fastify exists.

Path patterns are strings (or regexes) with no type checking, so a typo is a 404 in production, not an error at build time. A schema-validated router (Fastify) or a generated OpenAPI client catches it.

Express 5 fixes several Express 4 footguns (path syntax, req.query, promise rejection handling) but it is a breaking change: * → /*splat, no optional ? params, no regex inside a path string, and removed methods. Know both behaviours.
Order routes: literals → prefixed routers → parameterised routes → 404 → error handler. Put a 404 handler after routers and before the error handler.
Reject unknown query parameters at the validation layer (5.2.8) rather than ignoring them silently; a typo'd filter is a correctness bug that looks like "the filter doesn't work".

topics.description: Middleware is a function (req, res, next) in a stack. It receives the request and response, and next() hands control to the next layer. A realistic middleware stack, top to bottom
res.on middleware, the actually-correct request logger

Every layer costs a function call and, for app.use, a regex match against the path.
next() inside a for loop of asynchronous work is a classic bug: you must wait for all of it before calling next, or the request proceeds with partial data.
Short-circuiting is idiomatic and correct, but it makes the stack's behaviour path-dependent, which is exactly why order matters (5.2.3).
The error handler must be registered after all routes, and be a 4-arity function. Both are load-bearing.
Mount cors before authentication and before rate limiting, or preflight OPTIONS requests fail with 401/429 and browsers report a generic CORS error that hides the real problem.
Never next(err) after the response has started sending; Node will throw ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT. Guard with res.headersSent.

topics.title: Error handling: the 4-arity middleware, async errors, and error shapes
topics.description: An Express error is any value passed to next(err) or thrown synchronously inside a handler. Express routes it to the nearest 4-arity error-handling middleware that was registered after the throwing layer. The shape of that error — and whether the client sees it — is entirely your design decision.
keyConcepts: The routing rule, stated precisely
A production error handler, in full
RFC 9457 Problem Details is the right error shape
Domain errors, translated once at the boundary
The expect(err, 404) trap, and the correct alternative
Five error-handling mistakes, ranked by how often they bite
Three parameters instead of four. The handler is registered as normal middleware and never runs. Every error reaches Node's default HTML error page.
Registered before the routes. Same outcome, and no warning.
next(err) after a response was sent. ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT, and the *original* error is replaced by a confusing one.
Leaking internals. res.json({ error: err.message, stack: err.stack }) on a 500 leaks file paths, SQL, and library versions.
Catching everything and returning 200. try { … } catch { res.json({ ok: true }) } — the client believes the write happened. Never do this.

topics.title: Async error handling patterns in Express 4 vs Express 5
topics.description: In Express 4, a rejected promise in an async handler is not caught: the request hangs until the client times out, and the rejection becomes an unhandledRejection. Express 5 fixed this by making it forward rejections to next(err). Everything else about async error handling is the same in both.
keyConcepts: The Express 4 bug, demonstrated
Express 5 changes this
What Express 5 changed, exactly
The wrapper, done well, for a codebase that stays on Express 4
The next()-in-an-async-middleware trap
Timeouts, which are the async failure mode nobody handles
The wrapper is boilerplate, but it is one line per route and it removes an entire bug class. That is a good trade at any scale.
express-async-errors (or a 3-line local equivalent) achieves the same with zero per-route cost, and is the right answer for a large Express 4 codebase you do not want to touch.
Upgrading to Express 5 to get this is a bigger change than adding the wrapper. Pick the wrapper unless you want the other Express 5 fixes.

A global unhandledRejection handler is *not* a fix. It converts a silent hang into a log line; the request still hangs. Say this out loud, because "we added an unhandledRejection handler" is a very common and very wrong answer.
Every await on an external resource needs a timeout, and the timeouts must be ordered so the outer one fires first.
AbortSignal is the modern way: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) }), and it also lets you cancel the *request* when the client disconnects.

topics.description: Validation is the process of turning untrusted input into a value your domain can trust: rejecting the wrong type, the missing field, the out-of-range number, the unknown key, and the injected string. Zod and Joi are the two libraries you will be asked about; they have a genuinely different philosophy, and the *philosophy* is what an interviewer is probing.
