A reusable validation middleware, with the error shape mapped to HTTP
Joi, for the same job, so you can speak to both
The properties a good boundary schema has
Validating params and query — the two people forget
Environment validation, which is the other boundary
The performance note nobody mentions
Zod is 5-20× faster than Joi on typical schemas, which matters if you validate large arrays on a hot path.

Both validate the whole value even after the first error, so a 10,000-item array with .refine() per item is real CPU. For large collections, validate the *shape* with a cheap schema and the *items* with a capped per-item schema, or validate in a streaming transform.
z.coerce.number() on a huge numeric string is a Number() call — cheap, but it silently turns "1e999" into Infinity. Add .finite().
Compilation is not free but is negligible; do not try to hand-roll a faster validator.
Validate once, at the boundary, and pass the typed value inward. Do not re-validate in the service: it duplicates rules and it validates data your own code just constructed.

topics.title: Security headers with Helmet and CORS configuration
topics.description: helmet sets a set of security-related HTTP response headers; the cors package implements the CORS protocol. Both are middleware, both are configuration, and both are easy to set to a value that either does nothing or breaks production.
keyConcepts: What helmet() actually sets (v7 defaults)
CORS, done correctly

CORS is browser-only. It is enforced by the browser, not the server. curl is unaffected. Every "CORS is not a security control" answer is correct, and it is *also* correct to say the browser-enforced list is the last line of defence for cookie-authenticated APIs.

credentials: true + origin: true (reflect-any) = vulnerability. The spec forbids * with credentials, and the cors package reflects the origin to satisfy that — which means every website can make authenticated requests to your API. This is the single most common real CORS vulnerability.
Vary: Origin must be set, or a shared cache serves one origin's response to another. The cors package does it for you when origin is a function; if you build headers yourself, do not forget.
Preflight must bypass auth and rate limiting. CORS middleware answers OPTIONS itself and ends the chain, so it must be before both (5.2.3).
Other headers worth setting by hand

helmet() defaults are deliberately strict and will break a site that uses inline scripts, third-party analytics, or cross-origin images. Turning headers off "to fix it" removes the protection; the correct sequence is report-only → fix → enforce.
HSTS with includeSubDomains is irreversible for months if you have a non-HTTPS subdomain. Start with a short max-age and no preload.
CORS allowlists require a deploy when you add an environment. A configuration-driven list from a validated env var (5.2.12) is the maintainable form.
crossOriginResourcePolicy: cross-origin weakens a real protection; set it only for the paths that genuinely serve cross-origin assets.
CSP connect-src must include your WebSocket origin in the wss:// form or real-time features break in a way that is very hard to debug from the server side.

topics.title: Logging with Morgan and Pino, including request IDs
topics.description: morgan is a request/response access log — one line per completed request, format string configurable. pino is a general-purpose structured logger — fast, JSON by default, low-overhead, with child loggers. Most production Node services use both: pino for application logs, and either morgan-in-pino or a custom res.on('finish') hook for the access line.
keyConcepts: Morgan, precisely
It is an access log. It has no context, no error, no trace, and no structure you can query beyond the fields you hand it.
It logs on finish, so a request that never finishes is never logged. A hanging request is invisible in the access log. That is exactly when you need to see it.
It does not know your request id unless you add it, and it cannot add one (see below).
String formats are unqueryable. A grep over a text log is not a metric, and it is not an alert.
Pino, and why it is the default choice for app logs
Morgan + Pino, integrated properly: pino-http
Do you need morgan at all if you use pino-http?
Request ids, end to end
Log levels, and the discipline that makes them useful
Log events, not strings. log.info({ orderId, total, currency }, 'order created') is queryable; 'order created' is not. An event name is a schema — treat it like a database column.
Do not log the same failure twice. If the error handler logs it with full context, the catch site should not. Duplicate log lines are the main cause of alert fatigue.

topics.title: Configuration management and 12-factor environment config
topics.description: Configuration is everything that differs between environments: URLs, secrets, timeouts, feature flags, pool sizes. The twelve-factor rule is one sentence — store config in the environment, not in the code — and almost every production incident in this area is a violation of it or of the obvious follow-on: *validate it at boot, and fail fast.*
keyConcepts: The hierarchy, and why the order matters
Why parse at boot and not per use
A missing or malformed variable becomes a startup failure with the variable name, not a runtime error 3 hours into a deploy.
The failure is loud, immediate, and in the deploy log, where someone is watching.
env is a plain typed object, so a typo (env.DATABSE_URL) is a TypeScript error, not a silent undefined at runtime.
Sources of configuration, ranked
The secrets story, concretely
Config changes at runtime, and why they mostly should not happen
The twelve-factor rules, applied to a Node service

Env vars are excellent for scalars and awkward for structured config (nested, lists). A CORS origin list becomes a comma-separated string (as above), and a per-tenant rule set belongs in a file or a service.
Validating at boot means you cannot start without every variable, which is correct for a service and annoying for a CLI. Split the schema by entry point.

A secret manager at boot adds latency and a hard dependency. Cache aggressively, and consider that a secret manager outage should not take down an already-running process (it should not — only boot needs it).

topics.title: Compression and its pitfalls
topics.description: The compression middleware wraps res.write/res.end with a zlib transform and negotiates the encoding via Accept-Encoding. It reduces bytes on the wire at the cost of CPU — and, in Node, that CPU is spent in the libuv thread pool, so it is not merely a CPU cost: it is a shared, finite resource that your file I/O and your hashing also need.
keyConcepts: The configuration that matters
The Accept-Encoding negotiation, and the traps

The middleware adds Vary: Accept-Encoding itself, and that is essential: a shared cache that does not vary on it will serve gzipped bytes to a client that cannot read them, or vice versa. If you build the header yourself, you own Vary.

Accept-Encoding: br, gzip — compression only supports gzip and deflate. Brotli needs shrink-ray-current or a manual zlib.createBrotliCompress pipeline. Brotli is 15-25% smaller than gzip; it is also 5-10× more expensive to compress. That is usually a good trade at a CDN and a bad one in the app.
An empty Accept-Encoding (some old clients) means identity — correct, and the reason you must not assume a client wants gzip.
Never compress a 204/304. compression skips empty bodies, and you should verify it does in your version.
The six production pitfalls, with the fix for each
Sizing, the numbers worth knowing

Compression costs CPU and thread-pool slots, and buys bandwidth and latency for the *client*. It is worth it when the payload is large relative to the RTT (which is why it matters on mobile and for first-byte latency on text) and not worth it for a 2 KB JSON response on a LAN.

Moving compression to the proxy/CDN is almost always the right call for a Node service: you get brotli, more CPU, and zero cost to your event loop. The cost is that the app no longer controls the header, and a misconfigured proxy produces double compression.
Precompression is the best of both for static assets, at the cost of a build step and a manifest.
Per-response opt-out (res.set('Content-Encoding', 'identity') or a filter rule) is useful for already-compressed and secret-bearing responses.

topics.title: Templating engines and view rendering
topics.description: A template engine turns a template plus a data object into HTML. Express's res.render locates a file in views/, runs it through a registered engine, and sends the result. The security property that matters is escaping by default — because server-rendered HTML is the number-one XSS delivery path for a Node service.
keyConcepts: The engines you will be asked about
A working setup, both engines
Rendering, with the layout and locals that actually get used
XSS: the rules, and the exact mechanism
Performance, and the production settings that matter

res.render is synchronous in the template engine's execution (after the async file read when cache is off). A heavy template on a hot path is a main-thread block. Templates are usually cheap; a loop over 10,000 rows in a template is not.
With view cache off (development), every render reads the file. That is the point in dev and a throughput problem in production.

Precompile at build time (EJS: ejs --compile into a directory; Eta has a precompile API) and point the engine at the output. This removes both the file read and the runtime compile from the request path.
The architectural point worth making out loud
Templates keep everything in one language and one deploy, and the first paint needs no JavaScript. They lose on interactivity, on asset pipelines, and on reuse.
A template engine is not a security boundary on its own; it is a set of defaults. A single <%- in a codebase disables the protection for that value, and no linter you have will reliably catch it.
Layouts and partials are the engine's real ergonomic story. EJS's include is a synchronous file read per render unless the file is cached.

topics.title: Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
topics.description: Fastify is a Node HTTP framework built around encapsulation and schema-driven serialisation. Hono is a tiny, Web-standard router that runs on Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, and edge platforms. Both exist for the same underlying reason: Express's global middleware stack and untyped request/response are hard to reason about and hard to make fast.
keyConcepts: Fastify, and the three ideas that are actually different
Fastify plugins, and the encapsulation payoff
Hono, and the thing it optimises for
The honest comparison table
How to choose, in one sentence each

Express — the default, and the right answer unless you have a specific reason. The largest middleware ecosystem, the most documentation, the most hireable skill. If your team knows it, the cost of anything else is real.

Fastify — when JSON throughput, typed handlers, or *structural* correctness (encapsulation removes a whole bug class) justify a migration. The strongest "why not Express" answer, because it names mechanisms rather than benchmarks.
Hono — when you must run the same API on more than one runtime, including the edge, or when you want Web-standard types.
NestJS — when the coordination cost of many engineers and many modules exceeds the framework's tax (5.3.1).

Express → Fastify is a rewrite, not a refactor: handlers, middleware, error handling, and every plugin. The #fastify/express compatibility layer exists and it gets you started, but it is a first step, not a destination.

Fastify's JSON Schema validation and serialisation require writing schemas. That is a real cost on a codebase with dynamic shapes, and it is *also* the thing that makes it fast and type-safe. Teams that hate duplication love it; teams with a fast-moving internal API hate it.

Fastify's encapsulation is a feature and a constraint: a "global" middleware is a plugin with fastify-plugin, and a decorator declared in the wrong scope is a runtime error. It is learnable in an hour and it eliminates the ordering bugs of 5.2.3 permanently.

topics.title: Dependency injection
topics.description: Dependency Injection (DI) is supplying a class's collaborators from outside rather than constructing them inside. Inversion of Control (IoC) is the general principle; a container is one mechanism for achieving it. Critical distinction: DI does not require a container.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why DI
Fakes instead of mocks. A constructor parameter typed as an interface can be replaced with an in-memory implementation. A new inside a method cannot.

Determinism. Inject Clock, IdGenerator, Random, and your tests stop being flaky. A codebase that injects Clock has no jest.useFakeTimers; a codebase that calls Date.now() deep in a domain service has flaky tests forever.
Scope control. Whether something is a singleton, per-request, or per-test becomes a decision in the composition root rather than an accident of static.
Decoupling for change. Swapping a payment provider touches the composition root and the adapter, not the service.
The five kinds of injection, and which to use
An IoC container
Registration: bind(Foo).to(PostgresFoo), bind(Token).to(Impl).singleton(), bind(Foo).toFactory(...).
Resolution: the container walks the graph, resolving each constructor parameter by type token, recursively. This is why it must handle circular dependencies — and why it usually cannot.
Lifetimes: transient (new each time), singleton (one per container), scoped (one per request — the one you usually want), container (one per DI container in a modular system).
Wiring by type token: interfaces need a token (the interface type itself, or a symbol/string) since you cannot new an interface.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain the five kinds of injection, and which to use and when you would use it.
Explain an ioc container and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* you stop repeating new chains, you get lifetimes and scoping for free, you can swap bindings per environment. *Cost:* your dependency graph becomes runtime data. Debuggers cannot follow it, stack traces get a resolution frame, mistakes become startup-time "no registration for X" instead of compile-time errors, IDE "go to definition" breaks, and the graph can hide coupling that looks clean in the code. The worst outcome is a codebase where classes have no constructors at all and take everything from a service locator — that is DI without any of its benefits: still hidden dependencies, but now untyped.

topics.title: DTOs and validation
topics.description: A DTO is a class that describes the shape of an input at runtime. Because it is a class, class-validator decorators become real runtime constraints, and class-transformer can coerce and nest plain JSON into typed instances.
keyConcepts: Why a class and not a TypeScript interface
interface is erased at compile time — zero runtime information.

class emits both a runtime constructor and (with emitDecoratorMetadata) design-time type metadata (design:type), which is how @Type(() => OrderItemDto) can be applied automatically to nested properties.
DTO classes give you one place for OpenAPI metadata, validation rules, defaults, and documentation of what the client may send.

They give a compile-time type you can import in the controller signature *and* a runtime check — which is the whole point of "types are not validation" (see PHASE 1 TypeScript and 5.2's Zod discussion: Zod is the other valid answer, and a codebase should pick one).
Global pipe configuration

whitelist: true alone is the mass-assignment fix, because a property with no decorator is dropped. forbidNonWhitelisted: true turns "dropped silently" into a loud 400, which catches client bugs. Enable both; they are complementary.

transform: true is required for the handler to receive a CreateOrderDto instance, not a plain object, which matters as soon as you use class methods, nested @Type() conversion, or ClassSerializerInterceptor.

enableImplicitConversion will happily convert "true", "12", and — dangerously — anything truthy-looking. Prefer explicit @Type(() => Number) / @Type(() => Boolean) per field and leave implicit conversion off, then convert query DTOs explicitly.

Response validation exists too: new ValidationPipe({ ... }) on responses is opt-in per handler (@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe(...)) plus a response DTO class) and is mostly useful for preventing internal objects from leaking private fields.
Query DTOs need explicit conversion
Array pipes and other built-ins
commonMistakes: interfaces for DTOs; forgetting @Type(() => NestedDto); enableImplicitConversion on globally; @Expose() on a password field; echoing value back in validation errors; running an async validator per row in a loop (N+1 on validation); assuming the DTO's TS type protects the DB write.
practiceTasks: build a ValidationPipe configuration, then attack it: send role: 'admin', send an unknown field, send limit=99999999999999999999, send items as an object instead of an array, send items[] with 51 entries, and send totalCents with a string. Record the status code and body for each, and confirm none of them reaches the database. Then swap the stack to Zod and diff the two error shapes.

interviewQuestions.text: Why must a DTO be a class rather than an interface?
What do `whitelist` and `forbidNonWhitelisted` each do, and why both?
Why does nested validation need `@Type()`?
What breaks with `enableImplicitConversion: true`?
Explain the mass-assignment risk in three sentences.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a signup endpoint takes a JSON body, and a DTO that declares only email and password still carries whatever else the client sent. Decision: run a global ValidationPipe with whitelist: true and forbidNonWhitelisted: true on every body, and treat the DTO as the only thing allowed to reach the persistence layer. Reasoning: the request body is untrusted input, so every property that is not explicitly declared and validated must not exist. Without whitelisting, an attacker who guesses a field name — or reads it from the public JavaScript bundle — can set role: 'admin', orgId of another tenant, or an internal creditBalance, because data: req.body forwards all of it to the ORM. That is mass assignment, and it is a privilege-escalation bug, not a data-validation nit. Trade-offs: forbidNonWhitelisted turns silent drops into 400s, so older clients that send extra fields (a stale SDK sending nulls) start failing — which is a feature if you version the API, and an incident if you do not. Failure scenario: a mobile client version 3.2 sends a removed field for eight months because the store keeps old builds alive, and the fix is server-side leniency for known-old fields, not removing the whitelist. Alternative: derive the persistence input explicitly — create(dto) { return prisma.user.create({ data: pick(dto, ['email','passwordHash']) }) } — which protects you even if the pipe is misconfigured, and pair it with a schema library whose output type is derived from the validator (Zod) so the allowed keys are visible in the type."

interviewQuestions.text: When would you use Zod instead of class-validator?

topics.title: Comparison with Express and Fastify
topics.description: Comparison with Express and Fastify — part of NestJS and Backend Frameworks in Backend Foundations.

topics.title: Why a DI Framework, and When You Do Not Need One
topics.description: NestJS is a TypeScript framework built around decorators and a dependency injection container. It layers module boundaries, a lifecycle pipeline and conventions on top of an HTTP adapter (Express by default, Fastify as an alternative).
keyConcepts: What DI actually buys you

Substitutability without patching: constructor(private readonly repo: OrderRepository) can be replaced with a fake in a unit test without a mocking library, because the dependency is an explicit constructor parameter rather than a module-level import.
Startup wiring errors instead of runtime errors. An unresolvable provider fails at boot, not on the first request in production.
Decoupling across module boundaries. A service depends on an interface token, not on a concrete database module, so swapping Prisma for raw SQL touches one module.
One place for cross-cutting concerns: logging, auth, validation and error mapping are registered once, not copy-pasted into 40 route files.
A shared mental model for a large team. New engineers read the module list and know the shape of the system.
What it costs you

Reflection and metadata: DI resolution is runtime work driven by emitDecoratorMetadata. Startup and first-request cost go up, and the compiler needs experimentalDecorators plus emitDecoratorMetadata (or the newer standard decorators with metadata support).
Decorators obscure data flow. Ten stacked decorators on a controller method are harder to read than the equivalent Express handler plus two middleware calls.
Learning curve and vocabulary: modules, providers, tokens, scopes, dynamic modules, forwardRef, lifecycle hooks, interceptors, enhancers. A new hire needs days, not minutes.
The magic cost: when something does not work, "why is my guard not running" becomes a real debugging session (see debugging scenario #9).
Bundle and cold-start weight for serverless or edge deployments, where a full framework container is exactly the wrong shape.
commonMistakes: claiming NestJS is faster or "more scalable" than Express (it is strictly slower per request and the scalability ceiling is your process, not the framework); saying "you can't unit test without DI"; treating the framework as a substitute for domain design; forgetting that REQUEST-scoped providers and heavy enhancers can dominate the frame budget.
practiceTasks: take an Express app from 5.2 and rewrite it twice: once with hand-rolled dependency injection (a createApp(deps) composition root), once in NestJS. Count LOC, count lines needed to swap the repository for an in-memory fake, and measure p99 with autocannon before and after.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem does the NestJS DI container solve that Express middleware does not?
When would you deliberately *not* use NestJS?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a team of about ten engineers, four domains, and a rule that domain code must not import another domain's repository. Decision: I would start with layered Express, because 5.2's structure already gives me the seam I need and it has no framework tax. Reasoning: DI's real value is substitutability and boot-time validation, and both can be had with hand-rolled factory functions or TS interfaces plus a small composition root. Trade-offs: I lose decorator-driven validation pipelines and standardized enhancers, so I would hand-write one validation helper and one error wrapper. Failure scenario: the team grows to 30 people, three new domains appear per quarter, and the composition root becomes a 1,200-line file that nobody dares refactor. Alternative: that is precisely the trigger to introduce a DI container, and the migration is mechanical because the layers already exist — each layer becomes a module, each constructor parameter becomes a provider token."

interviewQuestions.text: What is the runtime cost of decorator metadata and where does it show up?
How do you migrate a working Express app to NestJS incrementally?

topics.title: Modules: Boundaries, imports/exports, Dynamic Modules
topics.description: A module is a container with four metadata lists — imports, controllers, providers, exports — and a scope that is the unit of both encapsulation and test setup.
keyConcepts: The visibility rule people get wrong
A module can use anything in its own providers and controllers.
A module can use providers exported by the modules in its imports array. Importing a module gives you only its exports, not its internals.
A provider that is not exported is invisible outside its module, even if the other module imports it.
export can export a provider class, a re-exported module (export { FooModule } re-exports its public surface), or a token.
Feature-first vs technical-first layout
Feature-first: src/orders/{orders.module.ts, orders.controller.ts, orders.service.ts, orders.repository.ts, dto/}. The folder tree mirrors the domain. This is the default and it scales with teams.
Technical-first: src/controllers/, src/services/, src/repositories/. Fine for one small service, and it breaks down as soon as two features touch the same service file.

Barrel files (index.ts) re-exporting everything are usually a mistake in a NestJS codebase: they flatten the tree, create import cycles that only show up in production builds, and make "who depends on this" unanswerable. Prefer explicit imports from the concrete file; use barrels only for genuinely public package entry points.
Global modules
Dynamic modules
forRoot() — configure once per application (root-level). Typically @Global().
commonMistakes: exporting everything ("it might be needed later"); using @Global() as a substitute for imports; assuming imports: [A, B] exposes A's and B's private providers; expecting forRoot to be enforced (it is a convention — the framework will happily let you call it twice and create two instances); barrel files in a feature folder.
practiceTasks: build a CacheModule with forRoot and forFeature over a shared Redis client, prove the client is a singleton (assert identity across two features), then deliberately create a cycle and fix it both with forwardRef and with extraction, comparing the number of edges in each graph.

interviewQuestions.text: Why does a module need `exports` at all?
What breaks if you mark a provider `@Global()`?
`forRoot` vs `forRootAsync` vs `forFeature`?
How do you break a circular dependency without `forwardRef`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: OrdersModule and FulfilmentModule import each other, because an order needs fulfilment state and a shipment needs the order. Decision: I would not use forwardRef; I would extract the shared concept. The thing both need is the order's identity and status, so that becomes a small OrderReadModel provider in a third module that both import — one-directional edges, and the cycle disappears. Reasoning: forwardRef only defers a resolution error to runtime; it keeps a cycle in the graph, which means the modules can never be tested or reasoned about independently, and it hides the real problem. Trade-offs: the extract costs a small refactor and possibly an extra query, and I have to pick the right seam once. Failure scenario: after two quarters the team adds a third mutual import, forwardRef calls spread to eight places, and a boot-time NullInjectorError appears only on the code path that lazy-loads a module. Alternative: if the cycle is genuinely unavoidable (an event listener that must call back into its own module), use ModuleRef.get with strict: false at call time so the dependency is resolved lazily, and document why the cycle exists."

interviewQuestions.text: Are barrel files harmless?

topics.title: Providers and DI: The Five Kinds, and Token-Based Injection
topics.description: A provider is anything the container can construct and inject: a class, a factory result, a value, an existing instance, or a token aliased to one of those.
keyConcepts: The five provider forms
Class tokens vs string/symbol tokens
Interface injection rule of thumb
Resolution order and failure modes
Nest resolves the dependency graph at bootstrap. A missing provider throws UnknownDependenciesException at boot, which is a feature.
Providers are singletons per module instance (unless a scope says otherwise), so a request mutating provider state is a data race.

ModuleRef is the escape hatch: moduleRef.get(Token), moduleRef.resolve(Token) (async, cross-module), moduleRef.create(Cls) (new instance, bypasses the container's reuse), and moduleRef.get(Token, { strict: false }) to search the whole app when the provider is not in an imports chain.
Lifecycle hooks
commonMistakes: confusing useClass (new instance) with useExisting (alias); using a string token that does not match the provider; doing async work in a module constructor; injecting ModuleRef everywhere as a shortcut around proper module boundaries; assuming moduleRef.get validates the module graph.
practiceTasks: build a REPOSITORY_FACTORY generic factory provider, register three entities through it, then write a unit test that overrides the token with overrideProvider and asserts the service used the fake. Count how many lines the same setup takes without the factory.

interviewQuestions.text: `useClass` vs `useExisting`?
When is a string token better than a class token?
What does `ModuleRef` buy you?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: the DI container is a strict graph resolver — a module can only see providers from modules in its imports, and only if those providers are exported. Decision: I use ModuleRef in exactly three situations: lazily resolving an optional provider that may not be registered, breaking an unavoidable cycle without forwardRef at constructor time, and building instances at runtime (an admin tool that creates a provider per tenant). Reasoning: it is an escape hatch, so each use needs a justification; if I can express the dependency in the module graph, the graph is the better source of truth because the boot-time validation covers it. Trade-offs: get() with strict: false silently searches the entire application, so a typo becomes a runtime UnknownElementException far from its cause instead of a boot failure. Failure scenario: someone uses moduleRef.get(OrdersService, { strict: false }) in twenty places, then a second OrdersModule is registered for a different database, and half the app silently reads the first database's module. Alternative: define an explicit optional provider ({ provide: X, useFactory: (m: ModuleRef) => ..., inject: [ModuleRef] }) so the failure mode is a documented undefined rather than a wrong-instance surprise."

interviewQuestions.text: Why does a missing provider fail at boot rather than at request time?
Where does module construction happen relative to DI?

topics.title: Injection Scopes: DEFAULT, REQUEST, TRANSIENT, and Bubbling
topics.description: The scope of a provider controls how many instances the container creates and how long they live.
keyConcepts: Bubbling is the part everyone is surprised by
What request scope costs
The rule
commonMistakes: assuming scopes are set per provider in isolation; injecting REQUEST in a widely used service; treating a constructor that opens a connection as fine in request scope; thinking transient providers are free; forgetting that a durable transient provider is a wrapper, not a different implementation.
practiceTasks: build the same feature three times — default scope, Scope.REQUEST, and AsyncLocalStorage. Inject the container into a benchmark loop, measure instance creation per 10,000 requests, and count how many providers became request-scoped in each variant. Then bubble a transient provider to the controller and observe the warning.

interviewQuestions.text: What are the three scopes and how do they differ in instance count?
What is scope bubbling and why is it dangerous?
How do you get the current user into a service without going request-scoped?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: forty services need the current user and tenant, and the DI container is in danger of being dragged into request scope. Decision: I keep every provider at default scope and put the request context in AsyncLocalStorage, injected as a singleton RequestContextService whose methods read from the store. Reasoning: the request context is ambient, cross-cutting data, not a construction-time dependency; binding it to the DI graph couples object lifetime to HTTP semantics, which is exactly the coupling that makes REQUEST scope bubble and turn a singleton cache into a per-request allocation. Trade-offs: AsyncLocalStorage is invisible in the type signature, so a service can be called outside a request context and get undefined — I mitigate that with a typed accessor that throws a clear error when the store is empty, plus a lint rule against accepting an ambient user where an explicit parameter would do. Failure scenario: someone injects REQUEST directly into the repository layer 'just to read the tenant id', the whole repository becomes request-scoped, the in-process memo cache stops working, and p99 latency doubles at 500 rps. Alternative: if the codebase already passes an explicit ctx: { userId, tenantId, traceId } first argument through every service method, that is equally good and fully type-checked — it is just more typing."

interviewQuestions.text: What is a durable transient provider for?
Why does NestJS warn at bootstrap about request-scoped providers?

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
REQUIRES_TRANSIENT / REQUEST-scoped Repo
        ▲
        │ bubbles
   Singleton Service          → becomes request-scoped
        ▲
   Request-scoped Controller   → every request pays container work
```

topics.title: Controllers: Routing Decorators and the @Res Caveat
topics.description: A controller is a class whose decorated methods map HTTP routes to handlers. It is deliberately thin: parse input, delegate, shape output.
keyConcepts: Handler rules that matter

Return a value, a Promise, an Observable (converted with lastValueFrom internally), or a StreamableFile/Buffer for downloads. Returning a promise is fully supported; you do not need async just to be safe, though async is clearer.
Route order matters. Static segments must be declared before parameter segments, otherwise search is matched as :idOrSlug. This is a common production bug.
@Body() with the app's body-parser limit, @Query(), @Param(), @Headers(), @Req(), @Ip(), @Session() (needs the session middleware) are the parameter decorators.

@Header('X-Request-Id', id), @Redirect(url, status), @Render(template), @HttpCode(status), @UseGuards, @UseInterceptors, @UsePipes, @UseFilters complete the set. @UseGuards/@UseInterceptors registered on a controller apply to every handler; registered on a method only to that one; app.useGlobalGuards to all.
Headers are case-insensitive; use @Headers('x-request-id').
The @Res() caveat — the single most common NestJS surprise
With @Res() (no passthrough): ClassSerializerInterceptor will not strip @Exclude()d fields, logging/timing interceptors will not see the result, and the route will hang if you forget to send/finish.
Nest's docs say to use @Res() only when you need a library that requires the raw object (@Res() + passthrough: true is the escape hatch that keeps the pipeline).
Streaming responses
commonMistakes: using @Res() "just to set a header"; expecting interceptors to run; returning a promise from a handler that also used @Res() without passthrough; declaring search after :id; putting business logic in the controller instead of the service; changing status codes in the service layer.
practiceTasks: build a controller with twelve routes, then add: a ListOrdersQueryDto, a route that returns a CSV stream, a route that returns a 204, and one route using @Res({ passthrough: true }) to set an ETag. Then inject a logging interceptor and prove the @Res() (non-passthrough) handler never logs — and fix it.

interviewQuestions.text: What do you lose when you use `@Res()` without `passthrough`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: someone injected @Res() to set a header and then wondered why their @Exclude()d password field appeared in the response. Decision: treat @Res() as an opt-out from the framework's response pipeline, and use it only when a third-party library needs the raw Express/Fastify object. Reasoning: the presence of the response object is how the framework knows you took over, so it stops doing the things it would otherwise do — running the response interceptors, applying class serialization, and finalising the response for you. With passthrough: true you get the best of both: you set headers yourself, Nest still awaits your return value and serialises it, and exceptions still reach the filters. Trade-offs: passthrough still means you are responsible for Content-Type and for not calling send() yourself, and mixing the two styles in one handler is a good way to produce a double-send bug. Failure scenario: a Stripe SDK integration calls res.raw in an interceptor; every response in that controller now skips the logging interceptor, and support cannot find the request id in logs. Alternative: put the library behind an adapter class that exposes a plain method, and keep the response object inside the adapter — the controller never touches it."

interviewQuestions.text: Why must static routes be declared before parameterized ones?
How do you stream a large file from a controller?
What is the default status code for `POST`, and how do you change it?
Controller or service: who decides the HTTP status code?

topics.title: Guards vs Middleware vs Interceptors vs Pipes vs Filters vs Decorators
topics.description: Six extension points in the NestJS request lifecycle. Confusing them is the single most common NestJS interview and debugging failure, so this section is a reference, not a summary.
keyConcepts: Execution order
Ordering rules worth memorising
Interceptors wrap in reverse order of declaration: the first-registered outermost interceptor's next() callback is entered first, and its post-processing runs last.
Global enhancers run *before* controller-level ones.
A guard returning false throws ForbiddenException automatically; a guard that throws its own exception can return any status.

Exception filters do not reliably catch errors thrown in app.use() middleware, because middleware runs before Nest's exception layer exists. Wrap middleware bodies in try/catch or add a platform-level error handler.
Worked example 1 — Guard (authorization)
Worked example 2 — Pipe (validation + transformation)
Worked example 3 — Interceptor (response envelope + timing + timeout)
The important limitation
Worked example 4 — Filter (uniform error body)
Worked example 5 — Custom decorator (metadata + behaviour)
commonMistakes: putting authorization in middleware (no DI, no route awareness); using a guard to transform the response; expecting @Res() handlers to pass through interceptors; assuming exception filters cover middleware; thinking decorators execute code (they mostly attach metadata); forgetting that interceptor post-processing runs in reverse order.
practiceTasks: build one of each — a guard, a pipe, an interceptor, a filter, a middleware and a custom decorator — on the same route. Then instrument the pipeline with a log line in each and hit the endpoint, so you can state the exact order from memory. Then deliberately throw an error inside a middleware and observe which filter (if any) catches it.

interviewQuestions.text: Put the six extension points in execution order and say what each can change.
Why can't middleware use DI?
What does a guard returning `false` do, and how do you return a custom status?
Why doesn't a timeout interceptor actually stop work?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a report endpoint started timing out at 30s, and after a few minutes the database showed hundreds of still-running queries, even though clients had already received 503. Decision: treat the timeout interceptor as a *client-facing* deadline and implement real cancellation separately. Reasoning: rxjs's timeout operator unsubscribes from the observable chain, but the handler is usually an async function whose promise is already executing inside the database driver. Unsubscribe does not send pg_cancel_backend or abort a fetch — the work continues and may commit after the client is gone, which is worse than slow: you get partial side effects with no client to receive the result. Trade-offs: real cancellation means threading an AbortSignal through the service and repository signatures, which touches a lot of code and needs driver support (node-postgres AbortSignal, pg cancellation, fetch's signal). Failure scenario: a batch job cancels 10,000 rows client-side and every cancellation still performed the write, so the retry logic double-charged customers. Alternative: two deadlines — a short timeout interceptor for the HTTP response, plus a long, enforced job-level timeout inside the worker that actually owns the work, with idempotent operations so an ambiguous outcome can be retried safely (see 5.4.4)."

interviewQuestions.text: Do exception filters catch errors thrown in middleware?
What's the difference between `@UseInterceptors(A, B)` and `@UseInterceptors(B, A)`?

topics.title: DTOs and Validation: The Actual Security Boundary
topics.description: A DTO is a class that describes the shape of an input at runtime. Because it is a class, class-validator decorators become real runtime constraints, and class-transformer can coerce and nest plain JSON into typed instances.
keyConcepts: Why a class and not a TypeScript interface
interface is erased at compile time — zero runtime information.

class emits both a runtime constructor and (with emitDecoratorMetadata) design-time type metadata (design:type), which is how @Type(() => OrderItemDto) can be applied automatically to nested properties.
DTO classes give you one place for OpenAPI metadata, validation rules, defaults, and documentation of what the client may send.

They give a compile-time type you can import in the controller signature *and* a runtime check — which is the whole point of "types are not validation" (see PHASE 1 TypeScript and 5.2's Zod discussion: Zod is the other valid answer, and a codebase should pick one).
Global pipe configuration

whitelist: true alone is the mass-assignment fix, because a property with no decorator is dropped. forbidNonWhitelisted: true turns "dropped silently" into a loud 400, which catches client bugs. Enable both; they are complementary.

transform: true is required for the handler to receive a CreateOrderDto instance, not a plain object, which matters as soon as you use class methods, nested @Type() conversion, or ClassSerializerInterceptor.

enableImplicitConversion will happily convert "true", "12", and — dangerously — anything truthy-looking. Prefer explicit @Type(() => Number) / @Type(() => Boolean) per field and leave implicit conversion off, then convert query DTOs explicitly.

Response validation exists too: new ValidationPipe({ ... }) on responses is opt-in per handler (@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe(...)) plus a response DTO class) and is mostly useful for preventing internal objects from leaking private fields.
Query DTOs need explicit conversion
Array pipes and other built-ins
commonMistakes: interfaces for DTOs; forgetting @Type(() => NestedDto); enableImplicitConversion on globally; @Expose() on a password field; echoing value back in validation errors; running an async validator per row in a loop (N+1 on validation); assuming the DTO's TS type protects the DB write.
practiceTasks: build a ValidationPipe configuration, then attack it: send role: 'admin', send an unknown field, send limit=99999999999999999999, send items as an object instead of an array, send items[] with 51 entries, and send totalCents with a string. Record the status code and body for each, and confirm none of them reaches the database. Then swap the stack to Zod and diff the two error shapes.

interviewQuestions.text: Why must a DTO be a class rather than an interface?
What do `whitelist` and `forbidNonWhitelisted` each do, and why both?
Why does nested validation need `@Type()`?
What breaks with `enableImplicitConversion: true`?
Explain the mass-assignment risk in three sentences.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a signup endpoint takes a JSON body, and a DTO that declares only email and password still carries whatever else the client sent. Decision: run a global ValidationPipe with whitelist: true and forbidNonWhitelisted: true on every body, and treat the DTO as the only thing allowed to reach the persistence layer. Reasoning: the request body is untrusted input, so every property that is not explicitly declared and validated must not exist. Without whitelisting, an attacker who guesses a field name — or reads it from the public JavaScript bundle — can set role: 'admin', orgId of another tenant, or an internal creditBalance, because data: req.body forwards all of it to the ORM. That is mass assignment, and it is a privilege-escalation bug, not a data-validation nit. Trade-offs: forbidNonWhitelisted turns silent drops into 400s, so older clients that send extra fields (a stale SDK sending nulls) start failing — which is a feature if you version the API, and an incident if you do not. Failure scenario: a mobile client version 3.2 sends a removed field for eight months because the store keeps old builds alive, and the fix is server-side leniency for known-old fields, not removing the whitelist. Alternative: derive the persistence input explicitly — create(dto) { return prisma.user.create({ data: pick(dto, ['email','passwordHash']) }) } — which protects you even if the pipe is misconfigured, and pair it with a schema library whose output type is derived from the validator (Zod) so the allowed keys are visible in the type."

interviewQuestions.text: When would you use Zod instead of class-validator?

topics.title: Interceptors: Logging, Envelopes, Timeouts, Caching
topics.description: An interceptor wraps handler execution. It receives the execution context and a next handle, and returns an RxJS Observable of the result — so it can transform the value, time it, swap it, or fail it.
keyConcepts: 1. Structured request logger
2. Response envelope
The honest opinion
3. Timeout
4. Caching interceptor (per-request memo, not a shared cache)
Caveats that make this mostly a teaching example
Composing them
commonMistakes: logging the request body or Authorization; ordering serializers after the envelope; caching non-GET or error responses; using a process-wide cache interceptor in a clustered deployment; returning of(value) synchronously for a slow value (it lies about duration); assuming interceptors see WebSocket/RPC contexts the same way.
practiceTasks: stack logging, timeout, envelope and serializer interceptors, hit five routes (including one with @Res() and one with a thrown HttpException), and log from inside each interceptor so you can draw the true order. Then swap the cache interceptor to request scope and re-measure a duplicate-heavy endpoint.

interviewQuestions.text: Why must a logger interceptor log on completion rather than on entry?
Why does `ClassSerializerInterceptor` have to be ordered before the envelope interceptor?
What does a per-request cache interceptor buy you, and what is unsafe about a process-wide one?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a controller fetches the same configuration row 40 times inside one request, because 40 branches of the request each need it. Decision: a request-lifetime memo, not a shared cache. Reasoning: within a single HTTP request the data cannot change underneath you if it was read once from the primary, so a Map keyed on the request gives you free deduplication with zero risk of staleness, invalidation or cross-tenant leakage — the failure modes that make process-wide or Redis caches dangerous. A process-wide interceptor is a different animal entirely: it is per-instance, so the same URL can return different data from different pods, it never expires, and unless the key includes the principal and tenant it will serve one user's data to another. Trade-offs: request scope means the memo has to be instantiated per request, which in NestJS means a request-scoped provider — precisely the scope that bubbles (5.3.4) — so the correct shape is a provider constructed in a middleware or created explicitly per request rather than a global singleton. Failure scenario: a singleton cache interceptor in a 20-pod deployment, a user updates their display name, and for up to the TTL (or forever) 19 of 20 pods serve the old name, so the bug is intermittent and looks like a replica-lag problem. Alternative: push the dedupe down to the query layer with a per-request identity map or a DataLoader, which gives batching as well as caching and keeps the cache lifetime tied to the request by construction."

interviewQuestions.text: Why is an envelope response format a debatable choice?
How do you skip an interceptor for one handler?

topics.title: Exception Filters: Mapping Domain Errors to HTTP
topics.description: An ExceptionFilter is the boundary where a thrown value becomes a status code and a body. Its job is to make every failure in the system look the same to a client, and to make sure internal details never leak.
keyConcepts: The three layers of error
Domain exceptions — OrderNotFound, PaymentDeclined, InsufficientInventory. They know nothing about HTTP. They are thrown from services and unit-tested without a server.

HTTP exceptions — HttpException and its subclasses (NotFoundException, ConflictException, ForbiddenException, UnauthorizedException, PayloadTooLargeException, UnprocessableEntityException, TooManyRequestsException, ServiceUnavailableException, ...). They carry a status and a response body.
Unknown errors — TypeError, driver errors, ECONNREFUSED, third-party SDK faults. They become 500 with a generic message and a trace id.
HttpException vs custom exceptions
Filter that uses the mapper and emits RFC 9457
Rules that keep error bodies consistent across services

Same media type and same shape everywhere: application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, instance, plus code and traceId. Generate it from one shared package so ten services cannot drift.
A stable machine-readable code (ORDER_NOT_FOUND) is the contract; detail is for humans and may change; title is a short human phrase. Clients branch on code (or status), never on detail.
5xx bodies are uniform and information-free: same type and title for every internal error, a traceId, and the real cause only in logs. Never return stack traces, SQL, file paths, or upstream URLs.
4xx bodies are specific and may include field-level errors, because the client can act on them.

A filter registered with app.useGlobalFilters(new X()) applies to unhandled routes too (it is registered as the platform's terminal error handler), but not to errors thrown in app.use() middleware — wrap those yourself.
commonMistakes: extending HttpException in domain services (couples the domain to HTTP and makes unit tests need HTTP types); using the exception message as the client contract; returning different shapes for 400 vs 500 vs exceptions; logging 4xx at error level (it destroys signal in the logs — 5xx and unhandled are errors, expected 4xx are info/debug); forgetting host.getType() !== 'http' in a hybrid app.
practiceTasks: write a DomainExceptionMapper covering ten domain errors and six database error codes, plus a global filter, and unit-test the whole table. Then deliberately leak a stack trace, run a linter/grep over your repo for res.json(e) patterns, and count how many you find.

interviewQuestions.text: Should a domain exception extend `HttpException`? Why or why not?
What is the single mapping point for error → status, and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: five services each hand-rolled catch (e) { res.status(500).json({ error: e.message }) }, so clients had to special-case each service. Decision: one tiny shared package exporting domainErrorToHttp(err) plus one problemFrom(status, ...) builder, and a global filter in every service that uses them. Reasoning: the mapping from a domain failure to an HTTP status is a *contract decision*, so it deserves tests and one owner, not five independent if chains. Centralizing it means the same INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY produces 422 with the same code and the same application/problem+json body in every service, so a client can write one error handler. It also lets me unit-test the entire mapping table — a pure function from error object to HTTP exception — with no HTTP, no database, and no framework, which is far stronger coverage than asserting on responses. Trade-offs: a shared package couples services together, so it must stay dependency-free and boring, and it must be versioned carefully because a status change is a breaking change for clients. Failure scenario: a new service skips the shared filter, and one 500 response leaks e.message containing a connection string with the password; the leak is discovered by a customer reading their own error body. Alternative: if you cannot run a shared package, generate the OpenAPI error schema per service and assert in CI that the emitted application/problem+json schema matches the reference — a spec-level contract that catches the same drift without a runtime dependency."

interviewQuestions.text: What must never appear in a 5xx body?
Where do validation errors fit in the error contract?
Do global filters handle errors thrown in middleware?
How do you test error mapping without starting a server?

topics.title: Configuration: @nestjs/config with Validation
topics.description: Configuration is external, typed, validated at boot, and per-environment. Reading process.env.DATABASE_URL in twenty files is the failure mode.
keyConcepts: Typed access
Per-environment config
.env.development checked in, .env.test in CI, production values only from the platform's secret store.

Secrets never in the image, never in git, never in logs. Load from the environment (or a mounted secret file), redact in the logger, and give each environment a distinct key so a production key leak does not unlock staging.
Feature flags belong in config too, but read them through a typed flag service so FEATURE_X is a union type, not a string compared with 'true' in nine places.
Never branch on NODE_ENV for behaviour that should be a flag. NODE_ENV is for error verbosity and optimizations, not product decisions.
Validation options
commonMistakes: reading process.env in feature code; config.get('KEY') with no default and no infer (silent undefined); committing .env; putting secrets in build args; using one giant APP_CONFIG object with everything any; branching on NODE_ENV for product behaviour.
practiceTasks: add a Zod-validated config to a NestJS app with six variables (two required in prod only), then write a script that boots the app with each variable missing/empty/wrong-type and confirms it exits with a non-zero code and a readable message. Type the config so a misspelled key is a compile error.

interviewQuestions.text: Why validate configuration at boot instead of lazily?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a service deployed with a missing REDIS_URL booted fine, served 200s for 40 minutes because Redis was only used by one feature, then failed every request that touched the cache. Decision: validate the entire environment against a schema in ConfigModule.forRoot({ validate }) so the process exits non-zero at boot. Reasoning: configuration is a dependency of the whole application, not of the code path that happens to read it. Lazy validation converts a deployment error into a partial, hard-to-diagnose runtime error, and it fails *late* and *intermittently*, which is the worst combination. Boot-time validation is also cheap insurance for the specific production failure that causes the most pain: an environment variable that was renamed in CI, is absent in the manifest, or has an invalid shape. Trade-offs: a strict schema means you cannot deploy with a partially new configuration, and adding an env var becomes a deploy-ordering concern since the old version must tolerate its absence; that is a real constraint but a good one, because it forces the migration order to be explicit. Failure scenario: the app validates fine locally because a developer's .env.local has a value CI never sets, so the first production deploy with the new schema fails after the migration has already been announced. Alternative: if a hard fail is unacceptable for a read-only replica or a worker that can degrade, split the schema into critical (must have, exit on failure) and optional (validated, warned, defaulted), and have the degraded paths check the parsed result rather than assuming it is present."

interviewQuestions.text: `registerAs` and namespaces — what problem do they solve?
How do you keep secrets out of logs and images?
When is `NODE_ENV` the wrong thing to branch on?
How do you type configuration so a typo is a compile error?

topics.title: Testing NestJS: Unit with Mocks, E2E with Supertest
topics.description: Two levels that matter. Unit tests instantiate a provider with hand-made or framework-provided fakes and assert behaviour. E2E tests boot the whole HTTP application in-process and assert the real contract: routing, pipes, guards, filters, serialization and the database.
keyConcepts: Unit test — no framework needed
TestingModule — when you need the container
overrideProvider(TOKEN).useValue(fake) and overrideProvider(TOKEN).useClass(Fake) are the standard overrides.
moduleRef.init() is required only if something in the graph calls onModuleInit.
.compile() and .resolve() return promises — forgetting await is the most common cause of a mysteriously empty test.
jest.resetModules() / per-test module creation causes Nest to warn about duplicate module instances; create the module once in beforeAll, or use testingModule.get() inside each test.
E2E — the real contract
What to test where
commonMistakes: testing only services and never HTTP; new NestFactory in tests instead of the module; forgetting await app.init() before getHttpServer(); not closing the app (open handles hang CI); mocking repositories in e2e; asserting on res.body shapes that come from an interceptor that e2e never registered.
practiceTasks: write three unit tests with hand-rolled fakes, one TestingModule integration test for a module's wiring, and four supertest e2e tests covering 201, 400-whitelist, 404 problem details, and idempotent replay. Extract configureApp() so the global pipe cannot be forgotten, and prove it by deleting the pipe registration and watching two tests fail.

interviewQuestions.text: When do you need `TestingModule` rather than `new Service(fake)`?
Why must the E2E test apply the same global pipes as `main.ts`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an e2e test for POST /users asserted a 400 for an oversized payload and passed — but only because a route-level pipe was set in the test module. The controller had no @UsePipes, and the global pipe was only ever registered in main.ts, which the test never ran. Decision: extract the entire bootstrap into a configureApp(app: INestApplication) function that both main.ts and the e2e test call, and forbid any app.useGlobalX call outside that function. Reasoning: an e2e test that builds a differently-configured application is not testing the application's contract, it is testing a convenient fiction. Every global concern — the ValidationPipe with whitelisting, the exception filter, the global prefix, versioning, CORS, and body-parser limits — is part of the observable API, so all of it must be present in the test. Centralising the configuration also means a new global concern cannot be added to production and forgotten in tests, which is exactly the class of bug that makes staging behave differently from CI. Trade-offs: sharing the function means a test that *wants* different global settings must reconfigure deliberately, which needs app.useGlobalPipes to be idempotent or the test to call configureApp then override — slightly more ceremony, but explicit. Failure scenario: a security team asks whether a role field in a signup body is rejected; the e2e suite says yes because the test module had a pipe, while production had the pipe added in a file that no test imports, so the answer was no. Alternative: a lighter-weight guard against the same class of bug is an e2e assertion that boots the real entry point (import('../src/main')) behind a flag, or a contract test that generates the OpenAPI doc from the real app and diffs it in CI."

interviewQuestions.text: What is the most common `TestingModule` bug?
What should never be mocked in an E2E test?
How do you test a guard that reads `Reflector` metadata?

topics.title: Microservices: Transports, Patterns, and Operational Cost
topics.description: @nestjs/microservices adds a second transport to a NestJS application so it can call or be called by other processes over TCP, Redis, RabbitMQ, NATS, MQTT or Kafka.
keyConcepts: The three patterns
Client registration and transports

Transport.TCP is a Nest-specific JSON-over-TCP protocol. It is fast and has no broker, but it is not interoperable, has no persistence, and needs a load balancer plus a service registry. It is a poor default for anything you intend to keep for years.
Transport.RMQ is the most feature-complete (durable queues, DLQ via deadLetterQueue, priority, publisher confirms, separate queues per event type). Use it when delivery guarantees matter.
Transport.REDIS is fast pub/sub but has no built-in delivery guarantee — a subscriber that is down misses messages.
Transport.NATS and MQTT are excellent for fan-out events; NATS JetStream adds persistence.
Transport.KAFKA (via kafkajs) is for high-throughput event streams and partitioned replay.
ClientProxyFactory.create() builds an ad-hoc client; @InjectClient('NAME') is the module-registered, lifecycle-managed way (always prefer it, so the client is connected and closed with the app).
Serialization
Retries, timeouts, and correlation
Timeouts must be enforced on both sides or a slow consumer causes an unbounded queue.
Retries need idempotent handlers — a broker redelivers. See 5.4.4 and the outbox pattern in PHASE 5 Background Processing.
commonMistakes: choosing TCP for anything you need to keep; assuming pub/sub delivery is exactly-once; forgetting the timeout on the client side; using Date or BigInt over the default JSON serializer; running microservices without a DLQ and an alert; extracting services before you have CI, migrations and on-call; sharing one database across services and calling it decomposition.
practiceTasks: stand up a TCP-based users service and an HTTP→RPC hybrid gateway, then add a Redis-pub/sub event consumer. Kill the consumer, publish an event, restart the consumer, and observe which transport lost the message. Then add a DLQ, a retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and an idempotency key in the handler, and re-run the test.

interviewQuestions.text: `@MessagePattern` vs `@EventPattern` — what is the real difference?
Which transport would you pick and why? What does each one give up?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a Node.js platform team needs to decouple order processing from the HTTP API, with at-least-once delivery and independent deploys. Decision: RabbitMQ over the TCP transport, for the RPC-ish request paths and durable event fan-out. Reasoning: my hard requirement is that a consumer that was down must still get the message after it restarts, and that I need a dead-letter queue I can alert on. RabbitMQ gives durable queues, publisher confirms, per-message priority, and a first-class DLX, and the Nest RMQ client exposes all of it. TCP is faster but has no persistence and no DLQ, so a restart silently drops in-flight work; Redis pub/sub drops messages for any subscriber that is not currently connected; NATS with JetStream is the strongest alternative but has a smaller operational footprint in most companies and requires more setup for per-message priority. Trade-offs: RabbitMQ is another stateful system to run, monitor, upgrade and page on, and a broker outage becomes an API outage unless you decouple with an outbox and a local queue. Failure scenario: I choose TCP because it benchmarked 30% faster, then a rolling deploy drops 4,000 queued order.created events, and the warehouse never learns about the orders — nobody noticed for a day because there was no DLQ to alert on. Alternative: for pure internal fan-out with high volume and replay needs, Kafka is the right answer instead; for a handful of internal services that could be functions, I would skip the broker entirely and use HTTP with a proper client library, and reserve the broker for genuinely asynchronous work."

interviewQuestions.text: What happens to an `@EventPattern` handler's error?
Why must RPC handlers be idempotent?
What does `@nestjs/microservices` not give you?
When is a microservice split actively harmful?

topics.title: Express vs Fastify vs NestJS vs Hono vs Next.js Route Handlers
topics.description: Five ways to serve HTTP from Node, differing in how much structure they impose, how they validate and serialise, and where they run. The decision is about the cost of the framework versus the cost of coordination.
keyConcepts: There is no best one. The honest conclusion
Express wins on ecosystem and total familiarity. Its weakness is that structure is a matter of discipline, so teams drift — that is the exact gap NestJS fills.
Fastify wins on throughput and on schema-first design; plugin encapsulation is a real architectural tool. Reach for it when you want Express-like freedom with a performance budget.

NestJS wins when *coordination* is the bottleneck. It costs roughly 10-30% throughput versus Fastify and adds a learning curve, and it is the wrong choice for edge runtimes and trivial services. Its real deliverables are a uniform pipeline, automatic DI, a module graph you can reason about, and first-class OpenAPI generation.
Hono wins where portability matters — the same handler runs on Node, Bun, Deno, workers and edge. Small surface, Web-standard APIs, no container.

Next.js route handlers win when the API exists to serve one frontend. You get auth helpers, cookies, and one deploy unit. They are a poor fit for a public API consumed by many clients, for long-running work, and for anything that needs streaming responses with fine control.
commonMistakes: claiming a framework is faster without measuring; choosing NestJS for an edge function; using Next.js route handlers as a public API platform; assuming Fastify's schema is only validation (it also drives serialization and docs); forgetting that decorator metadata requires specific tsconfig settings and can break some bundlers.
practiceTasks: implement the same four endpoints (list with cursor pagination, get, create with idempotency, delete) in Express, Fastify, NestJS and Hono. Compare: LOC, dependencies, time to add a new endpoint, unit-test setup, and autocannon p99 at 200 rps. Write down which you'd pick for a 3-person team and which for a 30-person team, and why the answers differ.

interviewQuestions.text: Which of these would you pick for a public API consumed by 40 internal clients, and why?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a domain API with about 60 endpoints, 40 internal consumers across six teams, an in-house generated SDK, and a requirement that the schema is enforced in CI. Decision: NestJS on Node, with a code-first OpenAPI document and a CI breaking-change diff. Reasoning: my bottleneck is not throughput — it is that six teams will each interpret 'create an order' slightly differently. NestJS gives me the things that actually reduce that cost: a module graph with enforced boundaries, one global validation pipe so every body is whitelisted and typed, one error filter so every failure is a problem+json document, and a code-first spec generated from the same DTO classes the runtime validates against, which removes the drift that hand-written docs always develop. Trade-offs: I accept roughly 10-30% lower throughput than Fastify, which is irrelevant at 400 rps, and I accept the decorator learning curve and a heavier test setup. Failure scenario: a reviewer adds a new endpoint without a DTO class, so the generated spec omits it and the client generator produces nothing for it, and the contract test does not catch it because the generator reads the spec rather than the code. Alternative: Fastify with JSON-Schema definitions as the single source of truth, which is faster and arguably more honest, at the cost of losing the container and the DI-driven test seams; if my team were smaller, that is what I would pick."

topics.title: Scale and Team Considerations: When NestJS Pays Off and What It Costs
topics.description: The question is not "does NestJS scale" but "for how many engineers, how many modules, and how much governance does this team have, and what does the framework cost per request?" Both sides of that ledger, stated concretely.
keyConcepts: Where it pays off
Many engineers touching one service. The module graph plus enforced boundaries means "who is allowed to import this" is answered by the container, not by a code-review convention.
Many similar features. A new feature is copy-structure: module, controller, service, DTOs, tests. Consistency across 40 features is the product.
Cross-cutting concerns are numerous and must be uniform — authN/authZ, validation, logging with trace ids, error format, audit, rate limits. Registering each once is a genuine win.
Generated API documentation from the same types that validate at runtime. This kills spec drift.
Mixed transports (HTTP + microservice + GraphQL) in one codebase with one DI graph.
Onboarding: a documented module layout means a new engineer knows where things go.
Where it costs you

Reflection and metadata overhead: container resolution on the request path, emitDecoratorMetadata emitting design:paramtypes for every decorated class, and decorator function-call overhead at definition time. Real but modest — measure before arguing about it.

Readability: a controller method with @UseGuards, @UseInterceptors, @UsePipes, @UseFilters and five parameter decorators is hard to scan, and IDE "go to definition" is less direct than reading a plain function.
Bundle and cold-start size — matters for serverless; less so for a long-lived container.
Learning curve — the enhancer/scope/module vocabulary is a real ramp, and the failure modes are confusing.
commonMistakes: introducing a framework to "modernize" without a named problem; letting the domain layer import Nest decorators; using request scope for convenience; assuming the DI graph is automatically a good architecture rather than just a visible one; planning a rewrite instead of a strangler; running a @nestjs/config validation that fails in one environment only.
practiceTasks: take a 3-module Express service. (1) Draw its dependency graph by hand, then with a tool. (2) Convert one module to NestJS as a hybrid mount, keeping the domain folder framework-free. (3) Import the domain use case into a plain Node test with no Nest at all and prove it works. (4) Measure cold start and p99 for both stacks.

How would you introduce NestJS into an existing Express service without a rewrite?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a 40-endpoint Express service with 25 engineers, drifting structure, and no plan for a rewrite. Decision: a strangler migration — new feature modules go into NestJS alongside the existing Express app, and existing routes stay until they are touched. Reasoning: the value of NestJS is conventions and a validated DI graph, and neither is delivered by a big-bang rewrite; a rewrite loses a quarter of delivery capacity, mixes framework-learning cost with business change, and risks a silent regression in an API that 40 clients depend on. Coexisting two frameworks is ugly for about two months and then the old surface shrinks to nothing. Practical mechanics: one repository, two main.ts entry points or one entry that mounts both an Express app and a Nest application on different prefixes, a shared packages/contracts package for DTO types and the error format, and a lint rule that forbids a Nest module from importing anything from the legacy routes/ tree. Trade-offs: two HTTP stacks, two test setups, and duplicated infrastructure code (logging, tracing, health checks) until the migration completes, so I would extract that shared infrastructure into plain libraries first. Failure scenario: the new Nest path handles orders and the legacy path handles refunds, and the shared Order model evolves in the Nest DTO only, so refunds silently read a stale shape from a different serializer. Alternative: if the pain is purely 'no one enforces boundaries' rather than 'no DI', a much cheaper fix is ESLint import-boundary rules plus Zod validation in the existing Express app, and that is genuinely enough for many teams."

topics.title: Resource naming
topics.description: A REST API models the *domain* as addressable resources. URLs name things; HTTP methods say what to do with them. A good URL is boring, predictable, and tells a developer what exists without documentation.
keyConcepts: The rules that hold up in practice
Plural nouns for collections: /orders, /users, /products. Singular is for a single instance's sub-resources: /orders/{id}.
No verbs in URLs. The method is the verb. /orders/create is wrong because the operation was already a POST to /orders.
Nesting is a last resort. One level is usually the most a human can hold in their head; two is the practical maximum.
The path identifies the resource, the body and query carry the rest. If it fits in a URL, it is probably a filter.
Lowercase, hyphen-separated (/purchase-orders). Case-sensitive in principle, inconsistent in practice.
No trailing slashes. /orders/ and /orders are different keys to a cache, an analytics funnel and a router.
Don't put secrets or PII in URLs — they end up in access logs, browser history, and Referer headers.
Nesting depth and when to denormalize
Denormalize (flatten) when
Sub-resource vs action endpoint
An action endpoint is justified when
commonMistakes: verbs in URLs; mixing singular and plural; three or four levels of nesting; PUT on a collection; casing and trailing-slash inconsistency; PII in query strings; a /doSomething catch-all; treating every business operation as a PATCH of a status field.
practiceTasks: design the URL surface for a blog (posts, comments, tags, authors, media). Then draw the nesting, then flatten half of it, and justify each choice in one sentence. Then decide for each of six operations whether it is CRUD or an action, and defend the two hardest calls.

interviewQuestions.text: Why no verbs in URLs?
When do you flatten a nested URL?
Why is `PATCH /orders/{id} {status: "cancelled"}` a bad design?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a client sets order status directly, and support reports orders in illegal states — CANCELLED after SHIPPED, SHIPPED with no payment. Decision: make status transitions action endpoints (POST /orders/{id}/cancel, /ship, /fulfil), and keep PATCH /orders/{id} for the fields that are genuinely free-form (delivery notes, tags, internal notes). Reasoning: status is not a field, it is the output of a state machine whose legal transitions depend on payment state, inventory reservation and cancellation windows. Exposing it as a settable attribute means the client is now responsible for the transition table, and the server has lost the only place where the rules live. That produces exactly the corruption we saw, and it is unrecoverable because the invalid transitions are already committed. The action endpoint names the transition, keeps the precondition checks in one place, gives the operation a first-class audit entry, and makes the request idempotent by naming. Trade-offs: you lose generic field-level updates, so a legitimate status change that is not in the enum needs a new endpoint, and the API surface grows with the state machine — which is fine, because the state machine is bounded and the domain owns it. Failure scenario: a bulk import tool that legitimately needs to set several fields and a status in one call has to make N+1 requests, so someone adds PATCH /orders/{id}/status 'just for the import' and the state machine is bypassed again. Alternative: keep PATCH but require an explicit transition object with a precondition — { from: 'PAID', to: 'CANCELLED' } — so the server can validate the from state atomically. That works, but it leaks the machine into the wire format and still needs server-side validation, so the action endpoint is clearer."
