topics.title: Apollo
topics.description: The reference server implementation (schema + resolvers + context + plugins) and the reference client (a normalised cache, a fetch policy, and an optimistic layer). Apollo is a set of defaults, not a requirement: a GraphQL server needs a schema, resolvers and a per-request context, and any library providing those works.
keyConcepts: Server (Apollo Server 4) with Express
context runs once per request. Create the loaders, the tenant's database handle, and the authenticated user there.

formatError normalizes errors into your error contract. In Apollo Server 4 the error is already { message, locations, path, extensions }, so the job is mostly mapping: set extensions.code, strip internal messages for 5xx-class errors, and never let includeStacktraceInErrorResponses be on in production.
status400ForVariableCoercionErrors: true so a malformed query or variables yields a 400 rather than a 200 with errors — a 400 is cacheable-free, alertable, and matches REST semantics.
introspection: false in production (5.5.11).
ApolloServerPluginDrainHttpServer so a deploy closes the HTTP server and lets in-flight requests finish (see PHASE 5 graceful shutdown).
persistedQueries for an allowlist (5.5.10, 5.5.11).

Plugins are the extension point: an authentication plugin, a logging plugin (with a per-request resolver count), an OpenTelemetry plugin, a complexity-validation plugin, and a response-cache plugin. This is where the cross-cutting concerns live, and it maps onto NestJS interceptors/guards (5.3.6) if you prefer one framework for both.
Fastify adapter is also supported and faster, at the cost of Express middleware compatibility.
Client (Apollo Client)

Normalized cache: every object with an id and a __typename is stored by <typename>:<id>, and objects are *normalized* — two queries returning the same Order share one cache entry, so a field-level update is visible everywhere at once. That is the feature that makes field-level updates possible and the source of the data loss bugs when id is missing or non-unique.

typePolicies / keyArgs / merge are where you teach the cache how a list is combined. Get the keyArgs wrong and you get cross-filter cache pollution (change a filter, see the old results). This is the single most common Apollo Client bug.
commonMistakes: default keyArgs on a filtered list; the default merge on an infinite-scroll list; relying on cache-first for data that changes under the user; not distinguishing loading from an error state; no errorPolicy decision for partial data; using the cache for typeahead; a merge that appends without dedupe.
practiceTasks: build a normalized-cache app: a paginated list with a filter, an optimistic mutation with rollback, and a detail view that reflects a field edited in the list. Then break it deliberately three ways — wrong keyArgs, default merge with fetchMore, no errorPolicy on a partial-error query — and observe each failure. Then fix the typeahead memory growth with no-cache and a debounce.

interviewQuestions.text: What does the normalized cache actually give you?
What breaks if you get `keyArgs` wrong?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a product list filtered by category, using useQuery with a filter variable, and users report that switching from 'Shoes' to 'Bags' sometimes shows the shoes. Decision: set keyArgs: ['filter', 'orderBy'] on the Query.orders field so each distinct argument set is cached separately, and use a merge function for pagination. Reasoning: by default Apollo Client keys a field's cache entry on the field name alone, so every query for orders — filtered, sorted, paginated differently — maps to the same list in the cache. That is the wrong default for a filtered list, and it produces exactly the reported symptom: the first render of 'Bags' reads the cache entry that the previous 'Shoes' query wrote, because the entry exists and cache-first is the default fetch policy, so no network request happens and the wrong data is displayed. Declaring keyArgs tells the cache that this field's identity includes those arguments, producing one entry per argument combination. merge is the companion piece for pagination: the default merge replaces the list, which is right for a page-numbered view and wrong for infinite scroll, where you want to append and dedupe by node id so a row that shifted between pages does not appear twice. Trade-offs: more cache entries means more memory and a lower hit rate, and a deeply nested filter object produces a key per combination, so you should keep the filter arguments flat and coarse rather than passing an entire query object. Also, keyArgs is a correctness concern only for list fields; scalar fields do not need it. Failure scenario: a team adds a keyArgs: ['filter'] to fix the pollution, and now every keystroke in a typeahead search — where filter contains the search term — creates a new cache entry, so memory grows unboundedly in a long-lived SPA tab and the tab must be reloaded to stop growing. The fix is to debounce the query and to not use the cache for typeahead: fetchPolicy: 'no-cache' or network-only for search-as-you-type."

topics.title: Caching challenges
topics.description: Reconciling a client-chosen response shape, delivered by POST, with the URL-keyed, validator-driven caching model that HTTP and CDNs provide. There are four separate caches here — CDN, server, per-resolver, and client — and confusing them is the usual failure.
keyConcepts: The core tension
Layer 1 — the CDN (the hard one)
Only GET is cached, and a GraphQL query can only be a GET if it contains no mutation/subscription and its variables are simple scalars. Even then:
The workable solution: persisted queries (APQ) + GET.

The honest conclusion: CDN caching of GraphQL is achievable but only after you give up arbitrary query text, which means you are converging towards the REST property you originally left. That is a fair argument in an architecture review.
Layer 2 — the server-side response cache

@apollo/server's in-memory response cache stores parsed results keyed on the query + variables + the current user. It is per instance and it does not know about data changes, so entries go stale until their TTL. It is a micro-optimization for hot identical queries, not a correctness layer.

Redis/KeyDB as a shared response cache works, and needs the same invalidation discipline as any cache (PHASE 6): key on the operation and the variables, include the user/tenant in the key, short TTL, and accept staleness.

A field-level cache (per resolver, keyed by arguments) is more useful than a response cache, because it survives changes to the surrounding query. This is what a DataLoader cache *would* be if it were cross-request — and it is where the invalidation pain starts.
Layer 3 — the client normalized cache

Field-level invalidation is hard. You know *which object changed* (you have its id), but not *which queries depended on which of its fields*. An evict removes the object everywhere, forcing refetches that may not be necessary. cache.modify can update one field precisely, which is why it is preferred for known changes.

Cache updates vs refetch. cache.modify is instant, surgical, and *can be wrong* if your assumption about the server's state is wrong (a computed field, an aggregate, a permission). refetchQueries is always correct and always costs a round trip. The rule: use modify for local state the client knows, and refetch for anything the server computes.
commonMistakes: expecting the CDN to cache a POST; a cache key that includes the full query text; not stripping per-user data from shared caching; relying on a per-instance response cache for correctness; refetchQueries after every mutation instead of cache.modify; an in-memory cache with no TTL; trying to normalize a response you also need in raw form.
practiceTasks: enable automatic persisted queries, then measure the CDN hit rate for one public query with (a) full text in the body, (b) full text in the URL, and (c) a hash in the URL. Add a server-side Redis response cache for authenticated queries keyed by user + operation + variables, and a cache.modify-based list update versus refetchQueries — measure the latency difference and the staleness risk of each.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is a GraphQL response hard for a CDN to cache?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a GraphQL API behind a CDN, and we are paying full origin cost for every request, while the equivalent REST list endpoint was 95% cache hits. Decision: accept a GET-only, hash-keyed, persisted-query path for a specific set of public read queries, and stop trying to make the rest cacheable. Reasoning: a CDN caches by URL, and a GraphQL response has no URL. The response shape is determined by a document the client supplies, that document arrives in the request body of a POST, and even converted to a GET it becomes part of the URL — so two clients that send the same query with different whitespace, different field order, or differently ordered variable keys produce different keys and both miss. On top of that, per-user data cannot be shared at all without Vary: Authorization, which functionally disables the cache, and putting variables in a URL leaks them into access logs and browser history. Persisted queries fix the key-stability problem, because the client sends a hash instead of text, so the URL is short and canonical; the cost is that arbitrary queries are no longer accepted, so I have effectively converted the flexible endpoint back into a fixed set of operations, which is an honest thing to admit in a design review. Trade-offs: two code paths to maintain, a registry of persisted queries, and a need to re-register whenever a client updates, plus allowlists break dynamic client-generated queries entirely. Failure scenario: a team turns on a CDN for /graphql, keeps full query text in the URL, and after two weeks the hit rate is under 5% with a 3 KB average URL; they conclude CDNs do not work with GraphQL, when the actual problem is that the cache key includes the entire document, including a whitespace difference introduced by a Prettier upgrade in the client build."

topics.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC vs tRPC
topics.description: Four ways to express a service boundary, differing in what the contract is (a document, a schema, a schema, or TypeScript types), how it travels, and who can consume it.
keyConcepts: The honest conclusion: there is no best
Public/third-party → REST with a published OpenAPI contract.
Web/mobile frontend → a BFF, or GraphQL when the client team genuinely needs query flexibility.
Service-to-service → gRPC, or REST if the team is small and polyglot.
Internal full-stack TypeScript → tRPC.
commonMistakes: picking one style for the whole company; using gRPC for a public API; using GraphQL for a public API with unknown clients; reaching for tRPC when non-TS consumers exist; assuming gRPC caching can be solved at the CDN; claiming GraphQL removes N+1.
practiceTasks: design the same three operations (list with pagination, get with authorization, create with idempotency) in all four styles. Then write the decision memo for a specific fictional company with two public, two internal-TS, and one Go consumer, and defend it in 200 words.

interviewQuestions.text: Which one wins on caching, and why?
Where is N+1 most likely?
What is tRPC's disqualifying limitation?
Where is gRPC the right answer?
What is the strongest "use more than one" answer?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an interview where I have to recommend an API style for a company with a public marketplace API, a React web app, a Swift app, and about fifteen internal services. Decision: a different style per boundary, and I would say so explicitly rather than picking one. Reasoning: the constraints at each boundary are genuinely different, so a single choice is a sign the analysis was not done. The public marketplace API serves unknown third-party clients who need documentation, real HTTP semantics, ETags, and CDN caching, so it is REST with a published, diffed OpenAPI contract. The web and mobile apps both render multi-source screens, so they sit behind a BFF for the web app — one team owns the composition of upstream services, and it is a simple, cacheable, cheap-to-debug contract — and, if the mobile team needs to combine screens differently, GraphQL for mobile specifically, because that is where the round-trip saving is real and where the client is first-party and its query shapes are reviewable. The internal services, mostly TypeScript with a couple of Go ones, use gRPC where latency matters and REST for the rest, because the operational cost of a protobuf toolchain is real and the latency requirement is not universal. Reasoning that a team of three should not run three API styles is fair, so I would sequence it: REST everywhere, then introduce one of the others where a measured constraint demands it. Trade-offs: multiple styles mean multiple sets of skills, tooling, and observability, and a developer has to know which is which. Failure scenario: a company adopts GraphQL everywhere 'for consistency', then discovers their public API clients cannot use it, their internal Go services now need a GraphQL client they have to write, and the CDN cache hit rate on their product catalogue drops from 92% to zero — the consistency was worth less than the specialisation."

topics.title: Why GraphQL Exists, and What It Does Not Solve
topics.description: GraphQL is a query language and runtime for an API described by a single type schema, where the client sends a document describing exactly the fields it wants, and the server returns a response shaped like that document.
keyConcepts: The problem it solves: over-fetching and under-fetching
Over-fetching: the server returns fields nobody asked for. Costs bandwidth, JSON parse time, and serialization work on the server.

Under-fetching: the client needs data that does not exist at any single REST endpoint, so it makes a second request, and if the second request is slow the screen arrives in two pieces. Costs round-trip latency and creates waterfall rendering.
Multiple round trips are the real cost, not payload size, on a high-latency network. This is the actual argument for GraphQL, and it is strongest on mobile.
What GraphQL does NOT solve

Authorization. Every field is a separate authorization decision. A field you forgot to guard is a data leak. A guard applied per row is an N+1 (5.5.5, 5.5.11). GraphQL has no opinion on authN/authZ; see PHASE 7.
Caching at the CDN. A POST is not cached by default. Every CDN in the world caches GET by URL. See 5.5.10.
N+1 queries. Field resolvers run per parent object, so 100 posts × 1 author query = 101 queries. It is *easier* to write N+1 in GraphQL than in REST, and DataLoader is mandatory, not optional.
Query cost. A client can ask for a query that is exponentially more expensive than any REST endpoint you would have designed. Depth, complexity and cost limits are required.
Operational simplicity. It is a new protocol with a schema registry, code generation, a resolvers layer, query analysis, and a client cache that has its own invalidation model.

Partial failure semantics. GraphQL returns 200 with data containing nulls and an errors array. That is a new contract for clients, proxies, and monitoring — and 200 means your alerting will not fire unless you parse the body.
Stable, cacheable URLs. A REST resource is a URL. A GraphQL query is a document; making it cacheable requires persisted queries and GET (5.5.10).
commonMistakes: adopting GraphQL for over-fetching alone (bandwidth is cheap; latency is the real issue); believing DataLoader is optional; thinking a 200 with errors is the same as a REST 4xx; expecting CDN caching to keep working; assuming one GraphQL endpoint is one database query; treating the schema as an implementation detail rather than a published contract.
practiceTasks: take one screen in an app that makes three REST calls. Write the equivalent GraphQL query and a BFF route that does the server-side composition. Then instrument both: count queries, bytes, and p95 latency. Then try the same thing *without* DataLoader and record how the query count scales with the page size.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem does GraphQL actually solve?
Why is multiple round trips worse than large payloads?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a mobile app on a 200ms round-trip network needs the user's profile plus their recent activity. With REST that is three endpoints, so the screen renders in about 600ms of pure latency plus payload, and the waterfall is visible in the network tab. Decision: this is the strongest case for GraphQL, and I would consolidate those reads into one query. Reasoning: the cost structure of a mobile network is dominated by round-trip latency, not by bytes. A response of 4 KB and a response of 40 KB both arrive in roughly the same time on a high-latency link, because the transfer is one or a few packets; what costs 200ms is the request/response handshake plus the server's own time. Three sequential requests therefore cost roughly three times one request, no matter how small each one is. The other half is client complexity: with three endpoints the client has to join the results, handle partial failure where the profile loaded but the activity did not, and implement a waterfall that a single request removes by construction. GraphQL fixes both — one round trip, and the server returns all three shapes in one atomic response, so there is no partial state. Trade-offs: I have traded a fixed, cacheable, cheap contract for a flexible, non-cacheable, potentially expensive one. The server now has to solve the join efficiently (batching, DataLoader), guard every field, and enforce query cost limits, and the CDN stops helping because the request is a POST. Failure scenario: a team moves a mobile screen to GraphQL for one round trip, then discovers that the resolver for the activity list is N+1 with a per-row permission check, so the single query is now 200ms *slower* than the three REST calls, and they have lost CDN caching and gained a schema to govern. Alternative: keep REST for the reads and add a BFF endpoint — one server-side endpoint that composes the three REST calls and returns one response. That gets the round-trip win with none of the schema, cache, or cost-analysis problems, which is why a BFF is the answer far more often than a full GraphQL adoption."

interviewQuestions.text: Name four things GraphQL does not solve.
When is GraphQL slower than REST?
What is the trade GraphQL makes?

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
REST, a profile screen needs name, avatar, and the last 5 posts' titles
  GET /users/42                     → 4 KB, 3 of 40 fields used
  GET /users/42/posts?limit=5       → 5 KB, 20 fields per post, 2 used
  = 2 round trips, 9 KB transferred, 89% wasted

GraphQL, one request
  query { user(id: 42) { name avatar posts(first: 5) { title } } }
  = 1 round trip, ~1 KB, 100% used
```

topics.title: Schema Design: SDL, Scalars, Nullability, Inputs, and Error Types
topics.description: The schema is the contract: every type, field, argument, and enum, defined in SDL. It is the most important artifact in a GraphQL system, because clients generate against it and every field is a permission boundary.
keyConcepts: Scalars
Custom scalar (DateTime, Money, JSON, URL): parsed and serialized in one place with a GraphQLScalarType, with validation. Best for primitives that are genuinely scalar (a timestamp, a decimal).

Wrapper input/output types (Money as an object): self-documenting, allows adding formatted or currency without a breaking change, and gives you a place to hang validation. Prefer this for money, because it lets you add fields later and it forces the currency along with the amount.
Never Float for money or identifiers. Float is a double. Money as integer minor units, ids as ID (which is serialized as a string).
ID is opaque to the client: you may return a base64-encoded internal id, and clients must not parse it.
A JSON scalar is convenient and dangerous — it is an untyped hole in the schema with no validation and no documentation. Restrict it.
Nullability is a design decision with a real cost

String! (non-null) means the server *must* have a value, or the whole containing chain nulls out and the error propagates to the nearest nullable parent. A non-null field that throws takes the entire query's data to null for that subtree.
String (nullable) means "no value is a legitimate, expected outcome", and it gives you somewhere for errors to land without destroying the response.

Rule of thumb: non-null for things the system guarantees and can always produce (an id, a computed total); nullable for things that legitimately may not exist (a user's displayName, a resource that may be gone). Then reserve non-null for fields whose computation is guaranteed to succeed, and nullable for fields that hit a boundary (an external service, a permission check, an optional relation).
[String!]! vs [String!] vs [String]! encode three different promises: no list, no nulls in the list, vs an empty list. Choosing deliberately prevents a whole class of client null-handling bugs.

The trap: making everything non-null looks tidier and produces catastrophic failures — one flaky dependency nulls the entire page and the client shows nothing, with no partial data. This is a common and expensive production lesson.
commonMistakes: all-non-null schemas; Float for money; reusing output types as input types; a JSON scalar as an escape hatch; client-parsing error messages instead of using a code; enums for open sets; positional arguments instead of a single input object; forgetting __resolveType for a union or interface.
practiceTasks: design a schema for a bookstore: Book, Author, Review, with search returning a union, money as a wrapper type, dates as a custom scalar, order lookup as a connection, and a placeOrder mutation with a payload and a typed error union. Then write schema-level tests that resolve every field against fixtures, including a case with a missing author and a case with a null displayName, and confirm the failure mode is a field-level error rather than a null data.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is nullability a design decision and not a detail?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a schema where every field is non-null, and one flaky third-party enrichment call now nulls the entire product page for a few percent of requests. Decision: non-null only for values the system guarantees, nullable at every boundary, and treat nullability as part of the API contract that clients code against. Reasoning: non-null is a promise with a large blast radius. When a non-null field's resolver throws — an unexpected null from a database, a serialization failure, a downstream timeout — GraphQL cannot return a partial value, so it propagates the error upward: the field becomes null, and if its parent is also non-null the parent becomes null, all the way up. One failure in one field of one item can therefore reduce the whole data to null, and the client shows an empty screen with no context. Making the field nullable gives the error somewhere to land: the field is null, the error appears in errors with its path, the parent stays intact, and the client renders the rest of the page. That is the difference between a degraded page and a broken page. Nullability also has a design dimension: User.displayName should be nullable because a user genuinely may not have set one, and making it non-null would force the API to invent an empty string, which is a lie the client cannot distinguish from a real name. Trade-offs: nullable means every client has to handle null, which is annoying in TypeScript, and it is easy to under-apply and end up with everything optional and no guarantees. Failure scenario: a team makes Order.customer non-null because in the database it is a required foreign key, and then an order created through a legacy import path has a dangling customer reference, so one order's customer field errors and, because Order is non-null in a list, the entire orders connection becomes null — the customer's whole order history disappears because of one bad row. Alternative: make the field nullable *and* fix the data integrity, so the schema tells the truth about the possibility of absence. And enforce it in tests: a resolver for a non-null field should never return null, which is exactly what a schema-level test that resolves every field against fixtures will tell you."

topics.title: Queries, Mutations, Subscriptions, and Document Features
topics.description: The three root operation types, the document features that shape a request (fields, arguments, variables, aliases, fragments), and the execution rules that distinguish them.
keyConcepts: Operation types
Operation name and variables
Aliases
Fragments
Named fragments reduce duplication; inline fragments (... on Type) are the only way to select fields on a concrete member of a union or interface.
Conditional fragments use directives:

@include(if:) includes when true; @skip(if:) omits when true. Both are static-ish: they are resolved during query planning based on variables, so the runtime knows before execution which fields to resolve. That means @skip/@include are a *client* optimization, not a *server* permission control — a hostile client just omits the directive. Never use a directive to hide data you must not expose. Use field-level authorization that applies regardless of the document.

Custom directives (@auth(requires: ADMIN), @cost(complexity: 5), @rateLimit(weight: 10)) are a schema-definition-extension feature, supported by Apollo Server, GraphQL Yoga and Hive, and implemented in your resolvers. They are a good way to make cross-cutting rules declarative and machine-visible.
Query complexity and cost
Fragments on the client
Queries may be GET-able
Naming conventions that survive contact with clients
commonMistakes: treating @skip as access control; sending variables by string interpolation; using aliases to smuggle 1,000 requests past a per-request limit; putting a mutation behind GET; assuming depth limits stop list amplification; renaming a field because the code is cleaner; not capping first/last per field in the schema.
practiceTasks: write a static cost estimator for a schema: walk the selection set, multiply by first/last for list fields, count unions, apply per-field multipliers, reject over a budget, and separately reject over a depth limit. Then write three abusive queries that pass a naive field-count limit and confirm your estimator rejects them, and three legitimate queries that must not be rejected.

interviewQuestions.text: Why do mutations execute serially?
What are aliases good for, and what is the risk?
Why is `@include`/`@skip` not a security control?
When can a query be sent as `GET`?
Why is naive field-counting the wrong complexity measure?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a public GraphQL API with a depth limit of 7 and a field-count limit of 500, and someone still ran a query that took 40 seconds and held a connection pool for its whole duration. Decision: replace field counting with a static cost estimator that multiplies list sizes, driven by schema-level hints plus the arguments actually supplied, and combine it with a depth limit and a per-operation token bucket. Reasoning: the cost of a GraphQL query is multiplicative through lists, so a flat field count is measuring the wrong quantity. { orders(first: 100) { items(first: 100) { variants(first: 100) { price } } } } has about eight fields, well inside any field limit, and represents up to a million rows. Conversely a query with 400 fields that fetches scalars one at a time is cheap. So the estimator walks the selection set and, for each list field, multiplies the current cost by the effective page size, which comes from the first/last argument the client actually sent, capped by a schema-level maximum. That is the important detail: using the client's argument means first: 1000 is priced at 1000, and the schema can cap what is allowed. Depth is a cheap separate heuristic that catches the recursive parent { parent { parent ... } } pattern regardless of list multiplication. The token bucket then converts a cost estimate into an actual budget, so a client that repeatedly sends expensive queries is throttled by cost rather than by request count, which is the same idea as the weighted route costs in REST. Trade-offs: a static estimator is approximate — it does not know actual row counts, and a join-heavy field can cost far more than its list multiplier suggests — so it over- or under-prices, and I accept that in exchange for a decision made before execution starts, because the runtime alternative (an observed-cost baseline from a sample of real queries) is much better calibrated but only catches abuse after it has been seen. Failure scenario: a team relies purely on an observed baseline, a new query shape appears that is not in the sample, it is under-priced by an order of magnitude, and it fans out into a database read that exhausts the connection pool, taking down every other query on the instance for the duration."

topics.title: Resolvers and Context
topics.description: A resolver is the function that produces a value for a field. The resolver map is organized by type name; the runtime picks Query.<field>, Mutation.<field>, Subscription.<field>, or Type.<field> for a field resolver.
keyConcepts: The context is request-scoped state and the place DI happens

Create the DataLoaders here, per request. This is the mechanism that makes batching and caching request-scoped and therefore correct (5.5.5). A module-level loader leaks data across users and across tenants — a security bug, not just a performance one.

Create the database handle (or the transaction) here too, and put it on the context. If a mutation needs a transaction, create it in the context for mutations and commit/roll back in the resolver — or, better, use a per-request unit of work so a mutation and its reads see a consistent snapshot.
context is where authN happens (the whole request is authenticated once), and the user/permissions go on the context. authZ is per field, which is the part that is easy to forget (5.5.11).
The context is also the right place for tracing, feature flags, the request id, and the i18n locale, so resolvers can reach them without importing globals.
Field resolvers: the powerful trap
Resolvers should stay thin
Root-level Query resolvers are your only entry points
commonMistakes: module-level DataLoaders (a cross-user data leak); a database call in a field resolver without a loader; business logic in resolvers; creating a new database connection per field; trusting extensions from the client; authN inside a field resolver (it runs per object); no per-request unit of work so a mutation reads uncommitted data.
practiceTasks: stand up an Apollo Server with a context that carries user, tenant, a request-scoped loader set, and a per-request database handle. Write Query.order plus field resolvers for Order.customer, Order.total, and User.displayName. Instrument resolver count per request, then show Query.orders(first: 100) issuing 1 query with DataLoader and 101 without.

interviewQuestions.text: Where should DataLoaders be created, and why?
What is a field resolver, and why is it dangerous?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: code review on a GraphQL service; the resolvers all look like one-line property reads, and a query against 100 posts takes 4 seconds. Decision: the rule is that any field resolver which performs I/O must go through a DataLoader, enforced by a review checklist item and by an observability alert on resolver count per request. Reasoning: a field resolver is invoked once for every object of that type in the response, not once per request. Order.customer looks like a trivial accessor, but if it does db.users.findById(order.customerId), then a query returning 100 orders issues 101 queries. The code is identical in shape to a safe resolver, which is exactly what makes it dangerous: nothing in the file signals a problem, there is no loop to notice, and the endpoint passes review. The same thing happens one level deeper — User.orders on a list of users, or an isAdmin field that checks a permissions table per object. The blast radius scales with the page size the *client* chooses, so a client can take a 30ms endpoint and turn it into a 4-second one by asking for first: 1000. Trade-offs: the rule adds a layer, and lazy computation genuinely solves real over-fetching — a computed totalWithTax that nobody asks for costs nothing, which is the property that makes GraphQL attractive. The mitigation is not to avoid field resolvers but to constrain what they may do. Failure scenario: a team adds a canEdit boolean field for a UI, it checks a permissions table per order, and with a 50-item list the endpoint goes from 40ms to 2.5s, with no code change and no error — just a slow endpoint that appears only on large pages, so it is attributed to a bad database plan. Alternative: expose authorization as a *list-level* concern — return viewerPermissions { canEdit } computed once for the request and cached on the context — or batch it with a single WHERE order_id = ANY($1) query through a loader, so 1,000 rows cost one extra query instead of 1,000."

interviewQuestions.text: Where does authentication belong, and where does authorization belong?
How much logic belongs in a resolver?
What goes in the context?

topics.title: Relay Connections
topics.description: The Relay Cursor Connections specification defines a paginated list shape that is stable, extensible, and usable by infinite-scroll clients.
keyConcepts: Why the shape is edges-and-nodes and not a bare list
A bare list cannot express page metadata. Where do you put hasNextPage? You need either a wrapper object or a header, and a header is awkward for GraphQL clients.

A cursor belongs to an edge, not a node, because in a list with duplicates or a sorted-by-something-else view, the same node can appear at several positions. The cursor is a *position in a sort*, so it is edge metadata. This is also why a cursor must encode the sort order it was created for.
It is extensible: you can add totalCount, an aggregate, or a pageInfo field later without changing how clients read the list.
It is a shared convention. Every GraphQL client library understands edges/cursor/pageInfo, so an infinite-scroll component works against any connection.
Cursor encoding
connectionFromArraySlice, done correctly
Why offset pagination is wrong for GraphQL specifically
The client usually does not know the offset. Infinite scroll has no page number, so it needs a cursor regardless.

A GraphQL client cache is normalized and additive. If page 2 re-returns an item already on page 1, the client merges it and the list shows a duplicate; if it returns an item that scrolled off, the count is wrong. Offsets make that normal; cursors make it impossible.
Cursors encode the filter and sort, so a client that changes the filter cannot accidentally reuse a position from a different list. Offsets are just a number and are happily reused.
Cost. OFFSET 5000 in a GraphQL list is the same database problem as in REST, but GraphQL clients ask for deep pages more often because scrolling is the primary interaction.
commonMistakes: guessing hasNextPage from edge count; slicing in the database layer and losing the extra-row signal; no cap on first; cursors that are just offsets; reusing a cursor across a changed filter; eager totalCount; a bad cursor silently resetting.
practiceTasks: implement connectionFromArraySlice with the limit+1 convention, HMAC-signed versioned cursors, and the full first/last/after/before truth table. Write tests for: an empty list, exactly limit items, limit+1 items, a cursor in the middle, an expired/foreign/tampered cursor, first: 0, first: -1, both first and last, and both cursors. Then wire it into a resolver and confirm the SQL is LIMIT first + 1 with a composite index matching the sort.

interviewQuestions.text: Why do cursors belong to edges rather than nodes?
Why is `hasNextPage` subtly easy to get wrong?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an infinite-scroll feed where the last page occasionally repeats the last item, and users see a duplicate row at the bottom. Decision: always fetch limit + 1 rows, use the presence of the extra row as hasNextPage, and slice to limit; then test the truth table exhaustively. Reasoning: hasNextPage is a question about data you do not have. If you fetch exactly limit rows, you cannot distinguish 'this is the last page' from 'there is more but you did not ask for it', so servers are tempted to guess — and every guess is wrong in some case. Asking for one extra row converts the question into something the database already answered. The subtlety is that this only works if the resolver *knows* it over-fetched, and the common mistake is to apply slice(0, limit) inside the database layer and hand the resolver exactly limit rows, losing the signal. The second subtlety is the direction: for a forward page, hasNextPage is the extra row; for a backward page (last/before), hasPreviousPage is the extra row and hasNextPage is simply whether the page is non-empty. And the third is combining after and before — a window between two cursors — where the extra-row logic has to be applied after filtering by both, not before. The reference implementation in graphql-relay gets the combined first+last semantics wrong, which is why libraries have patched it. Trade-offs: one extra row per page is a small waste, and it is only free if the extra row is genuinely cheaper than the count query it replaces — which it very much is, because COUNT(*) on a large filtered table can cost hundreds of milliseconds while one extra indexed row costs microseconds. Failure scenario: a team returns hasNextPage: edges.length === first, which is correct until the final page happens to contain exactly first items, at which point the client fetches one more page, gets zero edges with hasNextPage: false, and the UI shows an empty loading state or a spinner that never resolves — a bug that only appears for users whose page boundary lands on an exact multiple, so it survives testing for months."

interviewQuestions.text: Why is offset pagination worse in GraphQL than in REST?
How do you cap `first`?
What does `totalCount` cost, and how do you make it optional?

topics.title: Mutations: Validation, Error Semantics, Optimistic Updates, Idempotency
topics.description: How a GraphQL write is designed end to end: one logical effect per mutation, a payload type that can carry typed errors instead of returning null, a client that updates optimistically and rolls back cleanly, and a server that can safely receive a duplicate.
keyConcepts: Shape and execution
Input validation happens in three layers

Schema-level coercion — types, required-ness, enums, first caps. Rejected before any resolver runs. Return 400 (status400ForVariableCoercionErrors) rather than a 200 with errors, because this is a malformed request.
Resolver/business validation — does the SKU exist, is the order still cancellable, is the user allowed. Throw, or return a payload with typed errors.

Database constraints — unique violations, foreign keys, check constraints. Never rely on a pre-check for concurrency; a check-then-insert has a race. Let the constraint be the arbiter and map the error code (5.3.9).
Error semantics: the choice you must make explicit
The honest recommendation
Partial success
Optimistic updates with the Apollo Client cache
The optimistic response must have the same shape and __typenames as the real one, or the cache writes a fragment the normalized cache cannot merge and the UI flashes.
A temporary id must be unique and impossible to collide with a server id.

Rollback on error is manual unless you use errorPolicy carefully; errorPolicy: 'all' gives you partial data plus errors, which is what you want for field-level business errors, and errorPolicy: 'none' (the default) throws.
commonMistakes: throwing new Error('Invalid SKU') and letting clients match the string; no clientMutationId; an optimistic response with a different shape than the real one; a refetch after every mutation; a mutation that creates an entity in a state the business does not recognise; a pre-check for uniqueness instead of relying on the constraint; no per-argument authorization.
practiceTasks: implement a mutation with a three-layer validation chain, a payload type with errors, per-item results for a bulk case, and clientMutationId idempotency with a unique constraint. Then write a client test for the optimistic path: assert the item appears immediately, assert it disappears on a server error, and assert the cache is not left with a temp object after success.

interviewQuestions.text: What are the three validation layers for a mutation?
Thrown errors vs union payload?
What is partial success, and when do you want it?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a bulk 'create order' mutation takes a list of line items, and line items sometimes reference SKUs that no longer exist. Decision: the mutation is explicitly non-atomic — it creates the order with the valid lines and returns a per-line result array, with the invalid lines reported as typed errors — and the payload states that the order was created. Reasoning: there are two defensible designs and the important thing is that I chose one deliberately rather than discovering it from a support ticket. An atomic design is a single transaction: if any line is invalid, nothing is written and the whole request fails. That is right when partial success is meaningless or dangerous — a payment, an inventory reservation, a ledger entry — because a half-created order has no useful interpretation. A non-atomic design writes what it can and reports the rest, and that is right when the operation is an import or a bulk creation where a human needs to fix three rows out of five hundred and re-submit, not start over. The cost of non-atomic is that the client must understand a state where 'the order exists' and 'two lines are missing' are both true, which is more complex, and the order may be in a state that has no business meaning — an order with no lines cannot be paid, so the payload should say so and probably the order should be created in a DRAFT_INVALID state rather than DRAFT. Trade-offs: atomic needs a transaction and locks, and a large import in one transaction is a long transaction that holds locks and bloats the WAL. Non-atomic needs a per-item error array, a partial-order state, and a recovery story for the client. Failure scenario: a team implements bulk order creation with per-item try/catch and no transaction, the database rejects the fourth line on a check constraint, the request returns 200 with three items created, and the client's UI shows 'order created' — so the customer believes all four items are on order and only three ship."

topics.title: Subscriptions over WebSockets
topics.description: A subscription is a long-lived GraphQL operation over a persistent connection, where the server pushes a result whenever something relevant changes. It is the only way a GraphQL client receives server-push data.
keyConcepts: Transports

graphql-ws (the graphql-ws library, previously subscriptions-transport-ws under the subscriptions-transport-ws name) is the current protocol for graphql-transport-ws. It defines a small message protocol: connection_init → connection_ack → subscribe → next/error/complete, plus ping/pong. Use it.
The older subscriptions-transport-ws protocol (graphql-ws subprotocol string) is deprecated; Apollo Server 4 dropped its built-in support in favour of graphql-ws.

SSE (Server-Sent Events) is now a legitimate option for *unidirectional* server-push: it works over plain HTTP, reconnects automatically, passes through HTTP proxies, and is trivial to consume. It cannot be a general GraphQL transport, but graphql-sse provides a compatible protocol for queries and subscriptions. For "notify me when my order ships", SSE is often the better engineering choice (see PHASE 5 Real-Time Systems and 3.4.4 WebSocket vs SSE).
WebSocket (graphql-ws) is the general choice, and the only one that supports a multiplexed bidirectional protocol.
Auth over WebSockets
Send credentials in the connection_init payload ({ authToken } or { Authorization }) and validate it in onConnect; throw to reject the connection. This is the recommended pattern.
Or rely on the upgrade request's cookies — but then your auth middleware must run on the upgrade, and SameSite=Lax/Strict may not send the cookie for a cross-site WebSocket. Do not assume.
Validate on connect, and re-validate per subscription. A token can expire on a long-lived connection; close the socket with a close code when it does, or reject the next subscribe.
Never trust the connection for authorization after connect: store the principal on the connection context and check object-level permission *per subscription event*, exactly as you would for a field.
Use TLS (wss://) and reject origins (WebSockets are not protected by the same-origin policy; an allow-list of Origin headers is mandatory).
Connection lifecycle
commonMistakes: sending the auth token in the URL query string; no connection_init timeout; no keepalive; not cleaning up on disconnect; assuming ordering across instances; trusting authorization from the time of connect; relying on a subscription as the only source of truth; unbounded connections per user.
practiceTasks: implement a subscription server with graphql-ws: token in connection_init, a connectionInitWaitTimeout, ping/pong keepalive, a per-tenant AsyncIterator that cleans up on return(), and per-event authorization. Then test: rejection with a bad token, a client that never sends connection_init, a disconnect mid-stream (assert the listener count returns to zero), a permission revoked mid-stream, and two server instances with a Redis fan-out so an event published on A reaches a subscriber on B.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is auth over WebSockets different from auth over HTTP?
How do you keep an idle connection alive through a proxy?
What must you clean up when a client disconnects?
Why must a client re-sync after reconnecting?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a mobile client on a flaky network, a subscription for order status, and support reports that some customers' order screens freeze on 'Processing' indefinitely. Decision: treat subscriptions as an optimization over polling, never as the source of truth, and make re-sync cheap and automatic. Reasoning: a subscription has no delivery guarantee and no replay. While the client is disconnected — underground, on a plane, a network handover — every event is simply lost, and nothing tells the client how many it missed. So a reconnecting client is holding a view of the world that is not just stale but silently stale, and the UI looks stuck because there is no new data arriving and no error either. The fix is not a better transport; it is a protocol: on reconnect, the client subscribes again and *also* re-queries the current state, or passes a cursor so the server can replay from its last delivered event if the transport is durable. Then the UI converges regardless of what was missed. Cheap re-query is what makes this acceptable, and it argues for a connection endpoint that returns both the current state and a streamCursor in one round trip. Trade-offs: this means a reconnect costs one extra request, and if the state is expensive to compute you have a performance problem during mass reconnects — which is a real event, so it needs a cached read path. Failure scenario: a team implements subscriptions as the only delivery mechanism, a deploy drops all WebSocket connections, clients reconnect and re-subscribe but the screen is now bound to the subscription only, so a user who was mid-checkout never sees their order update, and there is no error because the re-subscription succeeded. The support answer is 'refresh the page', which is a terrible answer for a mobile app."

interviewQuestions.text: How do subscriptions work with more than one server instance?
When is SSE better than a WebSocket for this?

topics.title: Apollo Server and Apollo Client
topics.description: The reference server implementation (schema + resolvers + context + plugins) and the reference client (a normalised cache, a fetch policy, and an optimistic layer). Apollo is a set of defaults, not a requirement: a GraphQL server needs a schema, resolvers and a per-request context, and any library providing those works.
keyConcepts: Server (Apollo Server 4) with Express
context runs once per request. Create the loaders, the tenant's database handle, and the authenticated user there.

formatError normalizes errors into your error contract. In Apollo Server 4 the error is already { message, locations, path, extensions }, so the job is mostly mapping: set extensions.code, strip internal messages for 5xx-class errors, and never let includeStacktraceInErrorResponses be on in production.
status400ForVariableCoercionErrors: true so a malformed query or variables yields a 400 rather than a 200 with errors — a 400 is cacheable-free, alertable, and matches REST semantics.
introspection: false in production (5.5.11).
ApolloServerPluginDrainHttpServer so a deploy closes the HTTP server and lets in-flight requests finish (see PHASE 5 graceful shutdown).
persistedQueries for an allowlist (5.5.10, 5.5.11).

Plugins are the extension point: an authentication plugin, a logging plugin (with a per-request resolver count), an OpenTelemetry plugin, a complexity-validation plugin, and a response-cache plugin. This is where the cross-cutting concerns live, and it maps onto NestJS interceptors/guards (5.3.6) if you prefer one framework for both.
Fastify adapter is also supported and faster, at the cost of Express middleware compatibility.
Client (Apollo Client)

Normalized cache: every object with an id and a __typename is stored by <typename>:<id>, and objects are *normalized* — two queries returning the same Order share one cache entry, so a field-level update is visible everywhere at once. That is the feature that makes field-level updates possible and the source of the data loss bugs when id is missing or non-unique.

typePolicies / keyArgs / merge are where you teach the cache how a list is combined. Get the keyArgs wrong and you get cross-filter cache pollution (change a filter, see the old results). This is the single most common Apollo Client bug.
commonMistakes: default keyArgs on a filtered list; the default merge on an infinite-scroll list; relying on cache-first for data that changes under the user; not distinguishing loading from an error state; no errorPolicy decision for partial data; using the cache for typeahead; a merge that appends without dedupe.
practiceTasks: build a normalized-cache app: a paginated list with a filter, an optimistic mutation with rollback, and a detail view that reflects a field edited in the list. Then break it deliberately three ways — wrong keyArgs, default merge with fetchMore, no errorPolicy on a partial-error query — and observe each failure. Then fix the typeahead memory growth with no-cache and a debounce.

interviewQuestions.text: What does the normalized cache actually give you?
What breaks if you get `keyArgs` wrong?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a product list filtered by category, using useQuery with a filter variable, and users report that switching from 'Shoes' to 'Bags' sometimes shows the shoes. Decision: set keyArgs: ['filter', 'orderBy'] on the Query.orders field so each distinct argument set is cached separately, and use a merge function for pagination. Reasoning: by default Apollo Client keys a field's cache entry on the field name alone, so every query for orders — filtered, sorted, paginated differently — maps to the same list in the cache. That is the wrong default for a filtered list, and it produces exactly the reported symptom: the first render of 'Bags' reads the cache entry that the previous 'Shoes' query wrote, because the entry exists and cache-first is the default fetch policy, so no network request happens and the wrong data is displayed. Declaring keyArgs tells the cache that this field's identity includes those arguments, producing one entry per argument combination. merge is the companion piece for pagination: the default merge replaces the list, which is right for a page-numbered view and wrong for infinite scroll, where you want to append and dedupe by node id so a row that shifted between pages does not appear twice. Trade-offs: more cache entries means more memory and a lower hit rate, and a deeply nested filter object produces a key per combination, so you should keep the filter arguments flat and coarse rather than passing an entire query object. Also, keyArgs is a correctness concern only for list fields; scalar fields do not need it. Failure scenario: a team adds a keyArgs: ['filter'] to fix the pollution, and now every keystroke in a typeahead search — where filter contains the search term — creates a new cache entry, so memory grows unboundedly in a long-lived SPA tab and the tab must be reloaded to stop growing. The fix is to debounce the query and to not use the cache for typeahead: fetchPolicy: 'no-cache' or network-only for search-as-you-type."

topics.title: Security
topics.description: The controls required because a single endpoint now executes arbitrary selection over a whole graph: per-field authorization, query cost limits, introspection policy, batching limits, and depth limits.
keyConcepts: Query depth and complexity

Depth blocks the recursive pattern (parent { parent { parent ... } }) and cycle exploitation. A max depth of 7-10 for internal apps, 5-6 for public ones. It is cheap, and it catches the obvious abuse.
Complexity is what actually costs you; measure list sizes, not field counts (5.5.3). A static estimator with per-field multipliers plus a per-operation budget is the practical answer.
Timeout: a hard server-side query deadline (AbortSignal or a driver statement timeout) so a query that slipped under the cost budget still cannot run forever.

Also cap: aliases per query, fragment count, introspection depth, the number of variables, and the total request body size. Alias-batching is the most under-appreciated vector — 10,000 aliases of one field is 10,000 units of work in one HTTP request.
Disable introspection in production
Persisted queries / allowlists
Automatic (APQ) — clients may register new queries at runtime. Convenient; still lets an attacker run *any* query your type system allows, subject to depth/complexity limits.

Allowlist — only pre-registered hashes are served. This is genuinely strong: the endpoint becomes a fixed set of operations. It does mean a client with a dynamically-built query needs a registration step, and every client update requires re-registration, so it suits first-party clients and published APIs with managed consumers.
Field-level allowlists per role (a "whitelist graph" of what each role may query) are powerful and brittle; treat them as defence in depth, not the primary control.
Field-level authorization

Defense in depth, in order: database row-level security (or a mandatory tenant predicate in the repository) is the backstop; a directive or a resolver check is the readable layer; a gateway-level field allowlist is the outer layer. Any one of them can be forgotten.
commonMistakes: a per-row authorization query in a field resolver; hoisting one check for the whole list; trusting @skip for access control; believing introspection-off is a security control; no first cap; allowing HTTP batching of operations without per-operation cost limits; interpolating variables into SQL inside a resolver; a GET query in a cookie-authenticated API without CSRF protection.
practiceTasks: add depth and complexity limits, disable introspection, and enable both APQ and allowlist modes (switchable by env) to a GraphQL API. Then attempt, in a test suite: a depth-20 recursive query, a 1,000-alias query, a first: 1000000 query, an orders { canEdit } query on 1,000 rows (count queries before and after batching), an un-registered query under allowlist, a query with a variable from another tenant, and a GET query without a CSRF token.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is a field count a bad complexity measure?
Does `introspection: false` actually secure the API?
What is the N+1 authz trap, and what is the tempting-but-wrong fix?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a GraphQL API where the team added a canEdit field to Order so the UI could hide an Edit button, and each check was a per-row permissions query. Decision: two changes — batch the check with a DataLoader so it is one query per request, and, more importantly, express the permission as a row filter in SQL rather than a post-filter, so unauthorized orders never leave the database. Reasoning: a per-row authorization check is a database query inside a field resolver, which is the N+1 pattern wearing a security costume. With first: 100 it is 101 queries, and the endpoint is slow for large pages while looking fine in development with five orders. The tempting fix, and the one I have seen in production code reviews, is to hoist the check: fetch the permission once for the current user, then return that single value for every order in the list. That is a data-leak vulnerability, not an optimization — the user is authorized to view *some* orders, so the list is authorized, and now the field reports the same capability for orders they must not touch. The UI would show an Edit button on an order they cannot edit, and any client could act on it. So the rule is: authorization must be evaluated per object, and the cheap way to evaluate it per object is batching, not memoizing. Trade-offs: batching a permission check needs the key to be the object and the value to be a boolean, so you need a well-indexed permissions(order_id, principal_id) table and a query that returns exactly one row per requested id — if the table is missing rows, "absent" must mean "denied", which is an easy thing to get backwards. Failure scenario: a team batches the check correctly, then later optimizes the query with SELECT order_id, bool_or(...) and forgets the tenant_id predicate, so ids from another tenant resolve to false and users see orders they should not see at all — a batching optimization that quietly became a tenant boundary."

topics.title: Federation Awareness
topics.description: Apollo Federation splits one graph schema across independently deployed subgraphs. A gateway composes the subgraphs into a supergraph and a router executes queries across them.
keyConcepts: The mechanism
Each subgraph is an ordinary GraphQL service that owns some types. It declares @key (the entity's identity) and, with @shareable, which fields multiple subgraphs may resolve.
A subgraph can resolve a field for an entity it does not own, using an entity resolver:

The router (@apollo/router) holds the supergraph schema, produced by composition with rover dev / @apollo/composition. _service { sdl } on each subgraph is what composition reads; _entities and _Any are the runtime entity-fetch interface.

Composition errors are the real work: duplicate @key definitions, incompatible field types across subgraphs, a field resolved by two subgraphs without @shareable, and version mismatches. Every subgraphs' CI should run rover supergraph compose and fail on error, and ideally run rover supergraph diff against the currently deployed supergraph so an incompatible change is caught before deploy.
What it buys and what it costs
Buys: independent team ownership and deploys; a single endpoint for clients; the ability to reorganize a service boundary without changing the client contract.

Costs: composition in CI and a router as a new component to operate; entity resolution is a network hop per cross-subgraph field, so a query spanning four subgraphs can be several round trips (and the *router* can hide N+1 across services the same way resolvers do — entity resolvers need care); a debugging model that spans router + every subgraph (distributed tracing is mandatory); query cost analysis now spans services you may not own; and a schema-level coupling that reappears at the boundary, which is the thing microservices were supposed to avoid. Federation is not a way to avoid a domain boundary; it makes the boundary explicit and tooled.

Federation 2 adds: @shareable and @inaccessible (composition-time ownership rules), @requires/@provides for field-level dependencies, and @interfaceObject. Federation 1's rule that every subgraph could resolve any field is a major source of the accidental-coupling problems 2 was designed to prevent.
The honest evaluation
commonMistakes: federation without real team boundaries; no rover supergraph compose in CI; skipping rover supergraph diff; N+1 entity resolvers across subgraphs; @shareable used to silence a composition error instead of fixing ownership; no distributed tracing; the router as a single point of failure with no HA.
practiceTasks: split a schema across two subgraphs (users, orders) with a @key on User, implement __resolveReference in the users subgraph, and extend User with an orders field in the orders subgraph. Run composition, fix the two composition errors you will create on purpose, then query across both and count the network hops. Then convert the same API to a BFF and compare latency and operational surface.

interviewQuestions.text: What does a router add, and what does it cost?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an organisation with five teams, each owning a domain, all serving the same web and mobile clients, and the clients are making six calls per screen. Decision: adopt federation, but only after the teams are already independently deployable and the boundaries are real. Reasoning: the router solves a genuine problem — one endpoint, one schema, clients stop composing — and it solves it without a central team owning every field, which is what a hand-rolled BFF forces. The cost is a new runtime component in the request path, composition in every subgraphs' CI (a shared-schema change must be composed against all of them, so a change in one service can fail another service's build), and a debugging model that now spans the router and N services. The failure mode I care about is latency: a query that touches four subgraphs becomes several sequential hops, and a naive field resolver in the router or an entity resolver in a subgraph turns that into an N+1 across the network, which is far more expensive than a local N+1 because each miss is a real round trip. That means the DataLoader discipline from 5.5.5 becomes a distributed-systems problem, and latency observability across subgraph boundaries becomes mandatory rather than nice to have. Trade-offs: I give up the ability to inspect a subgraph's database directly from a query, and I add a schema-level coupling that shows up at the federation boundary — so a poorly chosen boundary is now a permanent, visible contract rather than something a migration script can quietly fix. Failure scenario: a team adopts federation to solve over-fetching, splits User across three subgraphs without clear ownership of the @key, every query that touches a user fans out to three services, and the p95 for the home page goes from 180ms to 1.2s with no single service showing a problem — because the latency is in the router's fan-out and each individual service looks fast in its own dashboard. Alternative: a BFF, where one team owns the composition of six upstream REST services into one endpoint. It is a central contract, but it is a *simple* one, its latency is one hop, its debugging is one service, and the ownership problem it creates is a known and manageable organizational cost rather than a distributed query planner."

topics.title: Where GraphQL Is the Wrong Choice
topics.description: The situations where a different tool is strictly better, stated as concretely as the reasons to adopt it. A candidate who can only argue for GraphQL is not demonstrating judgement.
keyConcepts: Honest reasons to say no

Bandwidth-constrained clients. A metered 2G device, a low-end Android in a market with expensive data, or an IoT device paying per kilobyte. GraphQL optimizes for round trips, not bytes — a client can request exactly what it needs, but the schema design tends toward rich objects, and there is no built-in sparse fieldset enforced for mobile. A gzip'd REST list is often smaller than the equivalent GraphQL response.

Simple CRUD with cacheable GETs. If the API is mostly reads of whole resources, GET /orders/42 with an ETag is faster and cheaper than a POST to a GraphQL endpoint that goes to origin every time. If you do not need multiple round trips to collapse, GraphQL's central benefit is absent.

A public API with untrusted, unknown clients. The flexibility that makes GraphQL great for first-party clients makes it a liability for public ones: query cost is client-controlled, the schema is a large surface, and the allowlist you need to make it safe removes much of the flexibility. This is the strongest argument for REST on a public API.

A team without schema governance. GraphQL's central artifact is a shared schema. Without an owner, a review process, deprecation discipline, and a breaking-change gate, a schema with 40 teams' worth of fields becomes a graph nobody can reason about — worse than 40 REST resources, because the *combinations* are unbounded even when the types are stable.
The data is a graph but the operations are not. GraphQL shines on traversals. If the real work is a few heavy analytical queries, a warehouse query engine or a purpose-built endpoint is better.

You need strict HTTP semantics — status codes, ETag/If-Match, Cache-Control, standard retries, CDN caching, POST-to-GET semantics. GraphQL returns 200 with a body, which breaks every tool that reasons about status codes.

Operational maturity is low. GraphQL needs persisted-query or allowlist management, cost analysis, resolver-level observability, a client cache policy, and a composed supergraph if federated. None of that is free.
What to pick instead

REST + a BFF: the highest-value alternative. One server-side endpoint per screen, composing several REST services, returning exactly what the screen needs. You get the round-trip win without the schema, the cost analysis, the cache problem, or the query planner. The cost is a central composition layer, which is an organizational cost rather than a technical one.

tRPC: end-to-end type safety with a procedure-per-endpoint model, no schema language, no resolver map, no client cache. Ideal for a TypeScript monorepo where the server and every client are TypeScript and deploy together (5.5.15).

gRPC: when the primary requirement is low latency and typed contracts between *services*, with strongly typed clients in other languages, and HTTP caching is irrelevant (see PHASE 7 for the wire details).
commonMistakes: adopting GraphQL because "REST is old"; measuring only latency and not bytes; ignoring schema ownership; forgetting that 200-with-errors breaks standard tooling; no fallback plan if the schema spawls; treating a BFF as uncool rather than as the right-sized answer.
practiceTasks: take one real screen from an app you have built. Write the GraphQL query, the BFF route, and the plain REST-plus-client-composition version. Then score each on: round trips, bytes, cacheability, implementation effort, and the number of places a bug can hide. Pick one and defend it in 150 words.

interviewQuestions.text: Name four situations where GraphQL is the wrong choice.
What is a BFF, and when is it the better answer?
Why is GraphQL a poor fit for an unknown public API?
How do you decide, in an interview, without a bias?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an interview question about whether we would adopt GraphQL, and the interviewer is watching for a balanced answer. Decision: I would ask three questions and let the answers decide, because there is no universal answer. Reasoning: first, does the client's screen actually need more than one round trip to render? If a page needs three data sources that live in three services, GraphQL or a BFF both collapse three round trips into one, and that is the whole benefit. If a page needs one resource, the benefit is zero and the cost is not. Second, can we afford the query planner and the schema governance? GraphQL hands the client control over the query, which means cost analysis, depth limits, a persisted-query or allowlist story, resolver-level observability, and a client cache with its own invalidation semantics. That is a real ongoing commitment, and if the team does not have a named owner for the schema, the schema will sprawl and no client will be able to predict what a field returns. Third, who are the clients? If they are our own TypeScript and Swift clients that we deploy alongside the server, we control the query shapes and can review them; if they are unknown third parties, a POST endpoint that accepts arbitrary documents is a liability, and a REST API with a stable contract, real status codes, ETags, and CDN caching is simply the better tool. Trade-offs: I am aware that the balanced answer is sometimes read as indecision, so I follow it with a concrete recommendation for the situation in front of me, and I say what I would measure to be wrong. Failure scenario: a team adopts GraphQL for a mobile app on a 3G network, and the flexibility means every screen pulls eight fields deep across four services, so the p95 time-to-content improves slightly but data usage doubles, and the product metric that mattered — engagement on a metered plan — goes down. The GraphQL decision was evaluated on latency alone and never on bytes, which is the measurement failure, not the tool."

topics.title: tRPC: End-to-End Type Safety
topics.description: tRPC is a TypeScript RPC framework where the *server's* types are the contract. A client calls client.user.byId.query({ id }) and the input type, the output type, and the error type are all inferred from the server implementation. No schema language, no resolver map, no codegen step.
keyConcepts: Routers and procedures
Client
Adapters
createExpressMiddleware({ router: appRouter, createContext }) — mount on Express/NestJS.
createHTTPHandler / fetchRequestHandler — mount on Hono, a Next.js route handler, Fastify, or anything with a Request.
wsLink + createWSClient — subscriptions.
Node standalone server, or a Next.js App Router integration where the server router *is* the type source for client components.
experimental_standaloneClient style setups let the server type live in a package shared with a separate client app.
Honest trade-offs

It needs TypeScript on both ends. There is no generated SDK for Java, Python, or Go. You *can* call the underlying HTTP endpoint by hand (tRPC's wire format is documented: GET/POST /trpc/<path>?input=<json>), but you lose everything that makes it tRPC. So: not viable as a public or third-party API. This is the disqualifying limitation and you should say it out loud in an interview.

It is HTTP + JSON, so wire overhead and browser/devtools support are the same as REST. No binary encoding, no HTTP/2 multiplexing from the framework's perspective, no schema registry, no grpcurl-style reflection, no cross-language tooling.

Caching is limited. Batching uses POST. Without batching, queries can be sent as GET, which is cacheable, but you do not get REST's ETag/Cache-Control story for free and CDNs need configuring for tRPC's URL shape.
commonMistakes: exposing tRPC procedures to non-TypeScript clients; using it for a public API; expecting tRPC's batching to be CDN-cacheable; hand-writing a wire-format client and calling it supported; forgetting superjson and then debugging Date serialization; not applying tenant scoping in createContext; no rate limiting because tRPC "is type safe" (types do not protect a runtime endpoint).
practiceTasks: stand up tRPC with four procedures (list with a cursor, get, create with clientMutationId idempotency, and a subscription), superjson for dates, a public and a protected procedure with router-level middleware, and rate limiting in middleware with TOO_MANY_REQUESTS. Then mount it three ways — Express, a Next.js route handler, and a fetch adapter — and write a hand-written JavaScript client against the wire format to see exactly what tRPC's non-TS story looks like.

interviewQuestions.text: What is tRPC's core idea, and what does it remove?
What is tRPC's disqualifying limitation?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a marketplace with a public API for third-party sellers, a React web app, a Swift iOS app, and a Node BFF. Decision: tRPC for the React app and the BFF only; OpenAPI REST for the public API and a generated or hand-written client for iOS. Reasoning: tRPC's entire value is that the client and the server share TypeScript types, so the contract is the compiler rather than a document or a schema. That value evaporates the moment the other end is not TypeScript, because there is no artifact to consume: tRPC has no schema, no code generation, and no language-agnostic client story, and the type inference is the contract. An iOS team would have to hand-build a client against tRPC's documented wire format — a GET /trpc/order.byId?input={...} with a JSON envelope — and that client gets none of the benefits: no autocomplete, no compile-time checking against the server, and a hand-maintained path that will drift silently the first time a field is renamed. Worse, the drift is invisible from the server side, because the server believes its contract is enforced by types when in fact it is only enforced for the callers that happen to share a language. So I scope tRPC to the boundary where both ends are TypeScript and deploy together, and I use a real interface, a published OpenAPI contract with a CI breaking-change diff, for everything else. Trade-offs: two API styles in one codebase, and a team that learns two sets of conventions. I mitigate that by keeping the boundary crisp: tRPC inside the web app's own surface, OpenAPI at every organizational edge, and no procedure is ever exposed directly to a non-TS caller. Failure scenario: a team adopts tRPC across a polyglot company, the Swift team hand-writes clients against the wire format, and a schema change that is a compile error for the web app ships silently as a runtime decoding error on iOS, where the field arrives undefined and a force-unwrap crashes. The Swift team's tests covered the old shape, so nothing fails until a user hits the new code path in production."
