topics.title: At-least-once vs exactly-once
topics.description: At-least-once vs exactly-once within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: What "exactly-once" really means
It is scoped to a system boundary. Kafka EOS covers "read from topic, write to topic, commit offset atomically". It does not cover a Postgres insert or an HTTP call.

Distributed transactions across a broker + database are theoretically possible (2PC) and practically avoided because of blocking, latency, and the coordinator being a new failure mode. The industry answer is to *avoid needing* cross-system atomicity: make the operation idempotent and retry until it converges.
Effectively-once is the honest goal: at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing + a dedupe table + reconciliation for anything money or count related.
The mechanics of effectively-once
Idempotency key — the caller (or the event) supplies a stable key: payment_intent_id, order.id + ':fulfilled', event.id. It must be derived from *intent*, not from attempt time.
Dedupe table with a unique constraint, inserted in the same transaction as the side effect:

Provider-side idempotency for anything that leaves your system: Stripe accepts an Idempotency-Key header (and stores the response for 24 hours), so a retry of the same charge returns the original result instead of a second charge. Use it on every create/capture/refund.
Natural convergence: design the side effect as a set-state operation (status = 'fulfilled', SET n = GREATEST(n, ?)) so a repeat is a no-op.
commonMistakes: assuming unique constraint alone gives exactly-once (it stops double-insert but not double-charge); server-generated idempotency keys; not storing the *response* so retries cannot return a consistent answer; forgetting that idempotency keys have retention windows.
practiceTasks: implement withIdempotency with a unique-constraint race test (fire 50 concurrent identical calls), a key-reuse-with-different-payload test, and a simulated crash-and-retry test with a provider that charges unless it sees the same idempotency key.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Define at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once.
🟡 Why is at-least-once the default in every mature queue?
🟡 What is "effectively-once" and what are its ingredients?
🟡 Why is a client-supplied idempotency key better than a server-generated one?
🔴 Explain why Kafka's exactly-once does not protect a Postgres write, and what you do instead.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a consumer reads card-payment events from Kafka, charges a customer through a REST API, and writes the order row in Postgres. The requirement is 'exactly once'. Decision: I would not claim exactly-once. I use Kafka transactions for the Kafka→Kafka hop if I produce derived events, but the actual charge goes through the provider's idempotency key (order.id as the key), and the Postgres write is guarded by a unique constraint on (order_id, event_id) plus a state-precondition update. Reasoning: exactly-once is only well-defined inside a single transactional store. The moment the side effect crosses a network boundary to a provider, the best you can do is at-least-once attempts plus a provider-side idempotency guarantee, plus a dedupe table so your own writes don't double-apply. Trade-offs: this means my correctness story is a composition of three mechanisms instead of one, and each has a failure mode to test: provider idempotency window expiry, dedupe table retention, and constraint violations under concurrency. Failure scenario: the charge succeeds, then the process dies before the DB write; the redelivered message retries the charge with the same key, the provider returns the *original* charge instead of a second one, and then the DB write succeeds. That works only because the key was derived from intent. If the key had been random per attempt, the customer is charged twice. Alternative: an orchestrating saga in 5.6.13 with compensating refunds, which is more code but handles the multi-step case."

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 Design idempotency for "increment a user's referral count" when duplicates are possible.
🔴 What breaks if you reuse an idempotency key with a different request body? How do you detect it?
🔴 When is at-most-once actually the right choice?
⚫ Explain why 2PC is avoided in modern architectures despite being "correct".

topics.title: Dead-letter queues
topics.description: Dead-letter queues within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: Retry taxonomy — the first thing to get right
Backoff formulas
Retry budgets
DLQ vs park vs drop
DLQ triage and replay tooling

Never replay to production without a filter and a rate limit. Build a small CLI/service: dlq list --queue billing --reason timeout --since 1h, dlq replay --ids ... --rate 50/s --dry-run, dlq inspect <id> (full payload + headers + failure reason).
Record the failure *reason and attempt count* on the DLQ entry, otherwise triage means reading payloads blind.
Alert on DLQ depth and age, and also on DLQ growth *rate* (a rising slope is the early signal, days before the depth is scary).
After the fix, replay oldest-first, at a controlled rate, while watching the DLQ drain and the success rate.

Poison detection: a job that failed maxAttempts times with the same error signature in the last hour is a poison source; quarantine it and, if the source is a batch, split the batch so one bad row does not kill 999 good ones.
commonMistakes: retrying validation errors; exponential backoff with no jitter; capping attempts but not elapsed time (or vice versa); replaying a DLQ at full rate; DLQ entries with no reason metadata.
practiceTasks: build a retry wrapper with permanent/transient/rate-limited classification, full jitter, attempts + elapsed-time caps, and a retry budget that sheds load. Test it against a fault-injecting HTTP server returning 500, 429 with Retry-After, and 400.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Give three examples each of permanent and transient failures.
🟡 Why is naive exponential backoff worse than full jitter?
🟡 What is a retry budget and why does it matter?
🟡 When do you drop a message instead of DLQ-ing it?
🔴 Derive full jitter for `base = 500ms`, `cap = 30s`, and explain the shape of the distribution.
🔴 A webhook to a partner has been failing for 6 hours at a 30% rate. Walk through your retry and DLQ decisions.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a partner webhook has been returning 500s for six hours; we retry with exponential backoff up to 6 attempts and DLQ after that. Roughly 30% of attempts fail, so the partner's queue is full of our retries. Decision: three changes. One, classify by status code — 4xx other than 408/429 is permanent, fail straight to DLQ; 429 gets Retry-After honoured exactly; 5xx/timeout is the only transient class. Two, add full jitter with a 5-minute cap and a total retry-volume budget capped at 10% of normal traffic, with a per-partner concurrency limit so a struggling partner cannot consume the whole worker pool. Three, put the partner behind a circuit breaker: after 50% failures over 20 requests, open for 60 seconds and fail fast into a parking queue, so we stop hammering a service that is already down. Reasoning: retries without jitter and without a budget amplify an outage into a self-inflicted denial of service, and the useful behaviour under downstream failure is to *shed load* and preserve the backlog. Trade-offs: DLQ means the partner is out of sync with us, so I need a replay path and an eventual consistency check, and a circuit breaker risks false trips if the partner is merely slow rather than down — hence error-ratio plus latency thresholds and a half-open probe. Failure scenario: partner recovers, we replay 200k parked messages at full rate and knock them over again. So replay is rate-limited and prioritised by event age. Alternative: an outbox plus a dedicated delivery worker per partner so one partner's problems never touch the request path."

topics.title: Outbox pattern
topics.description: Outbox pattern within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: The dual-write problem
Transactional outbox
Why for update skip locked: N relay processes can poll concurrently; each claims disjoint rows, so throughput scales by adding relays and there is no thundering herd on the same rows.
Idempotent consumers are mandatory here: the relay can publish and crash before published_at is written, so the same event will be emitted again. Use the inbox pattern below.

Ordering: relay order is id order per batch, but concurrent relays and retries break global ordering. Per-aggregate ordering is preserved *only* if you route by aggregate_id and use a FIFO/partitioned broker, and even then a retry can overtake. Accept and document it.
Relay vs CDC (Debezium) vs logical decoding
Care with CDC
Inbox / dedupe pattern (consumer side)
Cleanup/archival of the outbox
published_at is not null and published_at < now() - interval '7 days' → delete (or move to cold storage / a compacted audit topic).

Keep *unpublished* rows forever, and alert if count(*) where published_at is null grows or if max(created_at) for unpublished rows is older than a few minutes. Also alert on the *oldest* unpublished row's age — that is the true outbox lag metric.
When to prefer direct publishing
commonMistakes: publishing inside the transaction; holding a DB lock across the broker call; an outbox with no cleanup so it grows forever; trimming the consumer inbox before the redelivery window expires; relying on the outbox for events that need to happen only if the transaction commits *and* then also publishing directly (you now have both).
practiceTasks: implement the outbox relay with three concurrent relay processes, a broker stub that fails 10% of the time, an inbox table, and a test that kills a relay between publish and published_at write — then assert each event produced exactly one domain change.

🟢 What makes the outbox pattern correct?
interviewQuestions.answer: the event row commits in the same transaction as the domain change

interviewQuestions.text: 🟡 Why is `for update skip locked` the right primitive for the relay?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: the relay is a poller, and I want to run three of them for throughput without them fighting over rows or double-publishing. Decision: claim rows with select ... for update skip locked, inside the same statement batch as the update that marks them claimed, then commit. Reasoning: skip locked makes each relay's select skip rows already locked by another transaction, so the result sets are disjoint by construction. It converts a queue into a set of independent claims with database-grade crash safety — if a relay dies, its rows unlock automatically and the next poll picks them up, so there is no lease to expire or reap. Trade-offs: it puts row locks on your primary database, so a slow relay or a big batch blocks vacuum and can contend with real queries; I keep batches small (100) and the transaction short, and I never hold a lock across a network call to the broker — the publish happens after the claim commits, which is precisely why the design is at-least-once and needs the inbox on the consumer side. Failure scenario: a relay publishes 100 events and is killed before writing published_at; those 100 are emitted again on the next poll. That is not a bug in the design, it is the accepted cost of not using 2PC, and consumers dedupe on message_id = outbox:<id>. Alternative: CDC with logical decoding removes the load from the primary and gives lower latency, at the cost of operating a replication slot, a CDC connector, and schema-history handling — worth it when publish volume is high enough that polling becomes measurable load."

topics.description: four escalating ways to move work off the request path, each buying durability and scale at the price of latency, ops burden, and new failure modes.
keyConcepts: The ladder
When each is right (and the failure mode you accept)
The four classic mistakes of in-process async
A Postgres queue that is actually correct
Reaper for crashed workers: update job set state='ready' where state='active' and locked_at < now() - interval '5 minutes'.
Idempotency: create unique index on job (kind, dedupe_key) where dedupe_key is your idempotency key — on conflict do nothing makes enqueue naturally idempotent.
Trade-off vs BullMQ: none of the delay/DLQ/flow/cron sugar, but one less production dependency and everything is transactional with your domain writes (which is the outbox's job anyway — see 5.6.12).
commonMistakes: calling "fire-and-forget" a pattern that survives restarts; assuming a queue gives exactly-once; enqueueing inside a transaction and publishing outside without a design; polling Postgres on a tight loop without skip locked; treating a queue as a load balancer for request-time latency.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟡 How does `for update skip locked` work, and why is it the right primitive for a Postgres queue?
🟡 When would you deliberately use in-process async rather than a queue?
🔴 Design the escalation criteria: at what volume/complexity do you move from timers to a Postgres queue to BullMQ to a broker?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: I'm designing the async boundary for a mid-size product with Postgres and Redis already available, and one Node service. Decision: three stages. Stage one is in-process async only for genuinely lossy work — analytics, prefetch — with a global unhandled-rejection handler so it can't kill the process. Stage two, the default for anything a user is waiting on indirectly (emails, thumbnails, exports), is a durable queue. Because Redis is already operated, that's BullMQ; if we had no Redis I'd use a Postgres table with for update skip locked, which gives me transactional enqueue for free. Stage three is a real broker only when two conditions both hold: fan-out to many independent consumers, and per-message routing with TTLs — or when I need a replayable event log. Reasoning is about failure semantics, not throughput numbers: timers lose work on deploy, a queue survives deploy and retries, a broker adds acks and routing, a stream adds replay. Trade-offs: each step costs latency (a queued job is asynchronous, so the request returns before the work happens), new failure modes (retries, DLQs, poison messages), and ops surface. Failure scenario I care about most: a deploy during peak means timers silently drop emails, so from day one my queue must be idempotent. The alternative I'd consider is doing it synchronously inside the request for sub-100ms work with a hard timeout — cheaper and more debuggable when it's genuinely fast."

topics.title: Job Queue Anatomy: Enqueue → Worker → Ack/Nack → Retry → Dead-Letter
topics.description: the vocabulary every queue shares. Learn it once and you can read any queue's docs.
keyConcepts: Anatomy
Job state machine (the canonical model)

Waiting → active is a *lease*, not a move: the record stays retrievable with a "visible at" timestamp. If the worker dies, the lease expires and the job becomes visible again. That is the visibility timeout (SQS) / stalled check (BullMQ) / ack timeout (RabbitMQ).
Ack means "I finished this, delete it". Nack/reject means "I failed" and may mean requeue (immediately) or route to a dead-letter exchange.
Delayed is a scheduled job; repeatable is a job template that enqueues new instances on a cron pattern.
The correctness contract

At-least-once is the default everywhere. The job can be delivered more than once because: the worker finished the side effect and crashed before acking; the lease expired while work was still running (slow handler, GC pause, network partition); the consumer was moved to a different partition/group and re-read the same offset. You must assume your handler runs twice.
Idempotent processing is the answer. The three canonical shapes:
Concurrency limits protect a downstream with limited capacity (a third-party API with 5 req/s, a single-threaded writer). Per-queue concurrency, per-group group.concurrency, per-worker rate limiter.
Rate limiting (producer-side) is about not *offering* more work than consumers can absorb — see 5.6.3 for limiter: { max, duration }.

Prefetch / batch size is about not taking more work than you can buffer. Too high and a slow consumer holds many jobs hostage (head-of-line blocking) and memory grows; too low and throughput collapses on per-job network round-trips.
Job options and the semantics that bite
commonMistakes: acking after a partially completed composite job; confusing a stalled job with a retry (a stalled job may have already had side effects); raising attempts to 100 to "fix" a poison message; setting removeOnComplete: true everywhere and losing all history.
practiceTasks: implement the full state machine above against a Postgres queue, including lease expiry reaping, attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, and a DLQ table — plus a test that kills a worker mid-job and asserts the job runs exactly twice and the side effect happens once.

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 Design the ack policy for a handler that does three side effects: send email, charge card, write DB row. Where do you ack?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: one job that must email the customer, charge the card, and mark the order fulfilled. Decision: never make it one unit of at-least-once work if the side effects have different reversibility — split it. The charge is the risky one, so it gets its own job keyed on the order id with an idempotency key sent to the payment provider, so a duplicate charge attempt is collapsed by the provider rather than by me. The DB write is inside a transaction with a state precondition, so the second run is a no-op. The email is last and keyed on order.fulfilled event id. Reasoning: acking early loses work; acking late risks re-running a partially completed composite. Ordering by reversibility means the hardest-to-undo step is the one with the strongest idempotency key. Trade-offs: more jobs, more infra to reason about, and no longer atomic across all three — I accept that, because cross-system atomicity is not achievable. Failure scenario: charged, then the process dies before the DB write; the reconciliation job in 5.8.6 finds a captured payment with no fulfilled order and repairs it. Alternative: a saga with compensating actions, per 5.6.13."

```
producer                     broker                        consumer
   │ add(job) ──────────────▶ [ waiting ]                        │
   │                            │  fetch (prefetch / poll)       │
   │                            ├───────────────────────────────▶ │ start processing
   │                            │   state: active, visibility     │
   │                            │   timer running (lease)         │
   │                            │        │                        │ commit side effects
   │                            │        ▼                        │
   │                            │   [ ack  ] ◀──────────────────── │ success → remove job record
   │                            │                                │
   │                            │   [ nack  ] ◀──────────────────── │ failure → attempts+1, backoff
   │                            │        │                        │
   │                            │        └── attempts < max ─────▶ back to waiting (with delay)
   │                            │                                │
   │                            │   [ dead ] ◀─────────────────── │ attempts == max → DLQ
   │                            │                                │
   │                            │   [ stalled ] ─────────────────▶ lease expired, worker died → requeue
```

```
        ┌──────────┐  enqueue    ┌───────────┐
        │ delayed  │────────────▶│  waiting  │◀──────┐
        │ (scheduled)           └─────┬─────┘       │ backoff delay
              ▲                       │ fetch        │
              │                       ▼              │
              │                 ┌───────────┐   fail │
              │                 │  active   │────────┘
              │                 └─────┬─────┘  lease expiry → stalled → waiting
              │                       │
              │         ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
              │         ▼             ▼             ▼
              │    ┌─────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
              │    │completed│  │  failed  │  │ dead     │  (DLQ; manual triage/replay)
```

```ts
// (a) idempotency key table — the workhorse for external side effects
await db.tx(async (tx) => {
  const ins = await tx`insert into processed_message (key, created_at) values (${job.data.idempotencyKey}, now()) on conflict do nothing returning key`;
  if (ins.length === 0) return;                 // already handled → return so we ack
  await tx`update orders set status = 'fulfilled' where id = ${job.data.orderId}`;
});

// (b) state preconditions — only act if the entity is in a state that allows it
const o = await orders.find(job.data.orderId);
if (o.status !== 'pending') return;             // duplicate run is a no-op
await orders.transition(o.id, 'fulfilled');      // transition is conditional in SQL

// (c) natural upsert — write an absolute end state, not a delta
await db`insert into counter (id, n) values (${job.data.key}, ${job.data.delta})
         on conflict (id) do update set n = counter.n + excluded.n`;
```

topics.title: BullMQ Deep
topics.description: Redis-backed job queue built for Node, with first-class delayed jobs, flows, repeatable jobs, sandboxes, rate limiters, and stalled-job detection. Bull (the original) is legacy.
keyConcepts: The four primitives
Redis structures BullMQ actually uses (and why this matters to you)
Why the stalled check can freeze your queue

BullMQ needs a globally coordinated moment to decide which workers are dead. The scheduler sets bull:<q>:stalled-check; when a worker notices the key changed, it marks its active jobs as stalled-checked and waits. If the lock cannot be taken, all workers block and throughput drops to zero. The fix is running QueueScheduler (or a modern BullMQ with the built-in scheduler) with a *dedicated* Redis connection that is never used for anything else. This is the single most common BullMQ production incident: "everything froze at 3am".

maxMemorySize per job: if set, the worker checks process.memoryUsage().heapUsed before starting the next job and *pauses itself* when the limit is exceeded. Useful for image processing where one job can allocate 500MB.
Job groups vs flows vs repeatable

Job groups (queue.addGroup('g1', [...], opts)): a soft tag on a set of jobs so you can getGroupCounts, removeGroup, or use group-level concurrency/rateLimit (throttle a whole batch, e.g. one API key's worth of jobs).

Flows: dependency DAG. Parent fails → children are *not* executed (and with removeOnFail: true, are removed). Children run in parallel. Use flows when B must happen only if A succeeded; use groups when jobs are independent but should share a throttle or be observable as a batch.
Repeatable: cron template, deduped by key = name + pattern + tz + jobId. Good for per-tenant crons: jobId: 'tenant:42:digest' with repeat.pattern.
Failure modes to know by name
commonMistakes: sharing Redis between cache and queues with an eviction policy; missing maxRetriesPerRequest: null; running without a QueueScheduler; removeOnComplete: false everywhere; using one giant queue for unrelated job types (you lose per-type concurrency, rate limits, and you can't pause one workload).
practiceTasks: stand up BullMQ with two queues, one flow, one repeatable job per fake tenant, a group with group.concurrency: 1, maxMemorySize on a job that allocates 200MB, and a test that SIGKILLs a worker mid-job. Read bull:<q>:* keys in redis-cli --scan and map each key to the structure it is.

interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a queue hosted on the same Redis instance as our session cache, deployed on a managed Redis with maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru, and jobs disappearing after memory pressure. Decision: separate the workload. A dedicated Redis instance or at minimum a dedicated non-shared instance for BullMQ, with maxmemory-policy: noeviction, so Redis returns OOM errors instead of silently deleting keys, and set removeOnComplete: { age: 86400, count: 5000 } plus removeOnFail: { age: 2592000 }. Reasoning: eviction is an *acceptable* policy for a cache and catastrophic for a queue, so the two workloads must never share a policy. I also set an alarm on evicted_keys and on used_memory crossing 80% of maxmemory, because the failure is silent by design. Trade-offs: one more instance to pay for and patch; a noeviction queue will start returning errors under memory pressure, which is the behaviour I want — jobs stall instead of vanishing. Failure scenario: even after this, a Redis failover can lose writes that hadn't been replicated, so job records need a durability story — AOF appendfsync everysec, and accept that at-most-one-second of job loss on failover, which the outbox pattern (5.6.12) removes entirely for domain events. Alternative: run the Postgres queue in 5.6.1 and keep Redis only for caching, at the cost of losing delayed-job and flow ergonomics."

topics.title: Cron in Production
topics.description: scheduled work that must run on time, exactly once per slot, without overlapping, without drift, and without a human noticing when it silently stops.
keyConcepts: The seven hard problems

Timezone. 0 3 * * * is ambiguous. Store schedules with an explicit IANA timezone, convert to UTC at write time, and run the scheduler in UTC. DST is why: in spring, 02:30 local does not exist; in autumn it happens twice. Decide explicitly — either "run at 02:30 local except on the DST transition day", or "always 02:30 UTC". cron-parser and BullMQ's repeat: { pattern, tz } both handle this if you pass tz.

Overlap prevention. A long run must not overlap itself. Every scheduler offers a "skip if running" option (BullMQ: no built-in; you add a lock; node-cron has none). If a run takes longer than its interval you must decide: skip, queue, or extend — and log which.

Missed-run policy. If the process was down at 03:00, do you run once, run N times, or skip? Almost always: run once, immediately, on startup, and skip the missed slots. That is "catch up once", and it prevents a thundering herd of 24 hourly jobs after a weekend outage.
Distributed lock. Only one instance may run the job. See 5.6-5.10 must-implement #5 for a correct SET NX PX lock with safe (compare-and-delete) release.

Per-tenant crons at scale. One setInterval per tenant does not survive 50,000 tenants. Instead: keep schedules in a DB, and run one poller per minute that asks "which tenants are due within the next tick?" — index (next_run_at) where enabled. Store next_run_at and advance it on enqueue, not on completion.

Jitter. If 10,000 tenants all have "09:00 daily", every one enqueues in the same millisecond. Add deterministic jitter per tenant: jitterMs = hash(tenant_id) % window. This is better than random jitter because it is stable across retries and restarts.

Observability. A cron that silently stops is the worst failure mode in backend engineering — no user complains about a report that never arrives. Record and alert on: last_success_at, last_duration_ms, drift_ms (now minus next_run_at at start), and a heartbeat row that goes stale. Alert on staleness, not on "job failed".
Job-queue versus cron-library split
Use a cron library (node-cron) only for sub-minute, in-process, best-effort ticks.
Use the queue's repeatable job feature for anything durable: it persists the schedule, dedupes by key, computes next run in the scheduler, and survives restarts.
Use an external scheduler (Kubernetes CronJob, AWS EventBridge Scheduler) when you want the trigger to be independent of the app, so an app outage doesn't stop the schedule.
commonMistakes: running cron in the server's local timezone; trusting a library's overlap prevention without testing a 10-minute job on a 5-minute cron; interval recomputed from completion time (drift accumulates); per-tenant setInterval; alerting on failures instead of on staleness.
practiceTasks: build a scheduler with three jobs (fast, slow-overlapping, per-tenant), run it on three processes at once with deliberately skewed clocks, and prove exactly one instance executes each slot. Add DST transition tests using cron-parser for both Europe/Berlin and America/New_York.

interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an hourly usage report job that must reach finance by 09:00 daily, currently scheduled with a repeatable queue job. Decision: I persist a heartbeat row per job in a scheduled_job_health table — job_name, last_started_at, last_success_at, last_duration_ms, last_error, consecutive_failures — updated by the job itself, and I alert on the *staleness* of last_success_at rather than on individual failures. Two alerts: one at 2× the interval (something is late or stuck) and one on consecutive_failures >= 3 (something is broken). Reasoning: a job that dies at 03:00 because the process was OOM-killed produces no error event, so failure-based alerting is structurally blind; staleness monitoring detects both crashes and silent non-execution. Trade-offs: the health table needs its own reliability — I update it with upsert inside the job and also touch it from the scheduler tick, so a stuck job is visible even if the completion write never happens. Failure scenario: the whole service is down, so no heartbeat is written at all — that is precisely the case staleness alerting catches, and the fix is a monitor that queries the table from outside. Alternative: external monitoring of the *output* artefact (did today's report exist?) which is end-to-end but only works for jobs with a visible output."

topics.title: RabbitMQ Deep
topics.description: an AMQP 0-9-1 broker built around exchanges, queues, bindings, and explicit acknowledgements. Its mental model is *topology first*: you declare a routing network, then messages flow through it.
keyConcepts: Topology
Exchange types

Unbound messages are dropped unless you set alternate-exchange on the exchange. That is the single best practice here: bind a catch-all unrouted queue as the alternate exchange, or typos in routing keys vanish silently.

Queue arguments worth knowing: x-message-ttl (per-message expiry), x-dead-letter-exchange + x-dead-letter-routing-key (where rejected/expired messages go), x-expires (delete the queue after unused for N ms), x-max-length / x-max-length-bytes (with x-overflow: drop-head or reject-publish-dlx), x-queue-type: quorum.

Quorum queues (the default recommendation for new work): Raft-replicated across 3 nodes, poison-message handling, better flow control, no data loss on node failure. Classic mirrored queues are deprecated. Classic queues are in-memory-plus-disk and lose messages if the node dies during a publish.
Producer: confirms are mandatory
mandatory: true plus a return handler turns "unroutable" into an event you can log, rather than silence.
Publishing is asynchronous by default; with confirms, publish returns false when the internal buffer is full and you must wait for 'drain' — that is your producer-side backpressure.
Consumer: acks, prefetch, poison messages

Prefetch tuning is the main throughput knob. High prefetch = more parallelism but more unacked messages at risk and worse fairness (one slow message holds a slot); low prefetch = less memory, more round-trips. Rule of thumb: prefetch ≈ concurrency, and for expensive or slow handlers, use prefetch 1 with many consumers or an ackTimeout of hours with heartbeats on (RabbitMQ 3.12+ x-consumer-timeout).

nack(requeue=true) is a hot loop. If you requeue a poison message immediately, it is redelivered instantly forever, and one bad message starves the queue. Always requeue with a delay (delayed exchange plugin), or nack(false) to the DLX.
Redelivery flag: messages that were requeued come back with redelivered: true — use it to trigger extra logging or route to a different handler.
commonMistakes: one connection per message; prefetch(0); nack(requeue=true) for a poison message; assuming durable: true, persistent: true alone means durable (disk fsync, queue type, and node count all matter); forgetting channels close on broker restart so your consumer must reconnect and re-declare topology.
practiceTasks: declare a topic exchange with an alternate exchange, a DLX, and a quorum queue; publish 10k messages with confirms; consume with prefetch(1) and measure throughput vs prefetch(100); then nack one poison message in a loop and observe the hot loop before fixing it with a delayed exchange.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What do exchanges, queues, and bindings actually do?
🟢 What happens to a message published with a routing key that matches no binding?
🟡 What is an alternate exchange and why should every exchange have one?
🟡 Why is `prefetch` the primary throughput knob for a RabbitMQ consumer?
🟡 What does `x-message-ttl` do and how does TTL + dead-letter exchange implement delayed retries?
🟡 When should you use `nack(requeue=true)` and when is it a bug?
🔴 Explain publisher confirms and what happens without them.
🔴 What are quorum queues and why are they now the default recommendation?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: we run classic durable mirrored queues for billing events, and last quarter we lost an in-flight message set when a single node was replaced during a rolling upgrade. Decision: migrate to quorum queues with x-queue-type: quorum, replicate factor 3, and set delivery-limit on the DLX policy so a message that returns to the queue more than N times is dead-lettered automatically. Reasoning: classic queues are only as durable as the node that holds them, and mirrored queues are deprecated and lack poison-message handling and Raft-based flow control. Quorum queues give a quorum of replicas to acknowledge writes, so a single node failure — including losing its disk — is survivable. Trade-offs: quorum queues need at least three nodes to be meaningful, they consume roughly 2× disk for replication, they do not support some features such as per-message priorities at the same granularity, and they have a lower peak throughput ceiling per queue than a well-tuned classic queue, which matters only at very high per-queue rates. Failure scenario: a full partition between two of three nodes — the minority side is stopped by Raft, publishes are rejected there, and clients retry; availability drops but no data is lost or duplicated. Alternative: move to a managed offering so the broker's own failover is someone else's pager, at higher per-message cost and less control."

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 How do you get per-order ordering out of RabbitMQ, and where does that stop scaling?
🔴 Your consumer processed 500 messages and the broker restarted. Walk through the ack semantics.
🔴 Compare `x-max-length` overflow behaviour: `drop-head` vs `reject-publish` and which you want for a billing queue.
⚫ A message with `persistent: true` is lost on restart. Why, and what else do you need?

topics.title: Kafka Deep
topics.description: a distributed, partitioned, replicated append-only log. It is not a queue; it is a *durable event log* that consumers read at their own pace and can replay.
keyConcepts: The mental model

Partitions are the unit of parallelism and the unit of ordering. Adding partitions is the only way to scale, and it is (depending on keying) a breaking change for ordering. You cannot decrease partitions.
Producer keys: always key domain events by the aggregate id (orderId, userId), never by timestamp or random, or you lose per-entity ordering.

Replication factor and ISR: each partition has one leader and N-1 followers. Writes go to the leader and are replicated. min.insync.replicas: 2 with acks: all gives durability at the cost of availability (if 2 of 3 replicas are down, writes fail — which is what you want). acks: 0/1 trades durability for latency.
Consumer groups and offsets
A partition is assigned to at most one consumer in a group at a time. That is why consumers in a group ≤ partitions; more consumers than partitions means idle consumers.

At-least-once is the default. With enable.auto.commit: true, the offset for the record is committed as it is consumed, so a crash between processing and the next poll re-delivers. Commit after processing (autoCommit: false, commitOffsetsIfNecessary: false, then consumer.commitOffsets([{ topic, partition, offset: nextOffset }]) after the side effect is durable) gives at-least-once you control.

Exactly-once semantics come from combining an idempotent producer (enableIdempotence: true, dedup by producer id + sequence number, at-most one duplicate per partition per session) with transactions (producer.transaction(), sendOffsetsToTransaction, consumerOffset committed atomically with the produced records). Scope: it covers *Kafka reads → your processing → Kafka writes*. It does not cover your Postgres write or your HTTP call to a payment provider. That is the sentence to say in an interview.

Rebalancing: when consumers join/leave, partitions move. *Eager* (stop-the-world) revokes everything, then reassigns — a latency spike per rebalance. *Cooperative sticky* (partition.assignment.strategy: CooperativeStickyAssignor, group.protocol=consumer) revokes only the partitions being moved and reuses prior assignments to reduce cache misses. Always use cooperative sticky for latency-sensitive consumers, and set max.poll.interval.ms high enough for your slowest batch.

Consumer lag = log-end-offset - committed-offset, per partition. It is the single most important Kafka metric. Alert on lag *age* too, because a lag of 10k on a high-throughput partition may be seconds while 10k on a low-throughput one is hours.
Backpressure in Kafka comes from consumer throughput, not queue depth. Slow consumers hold their position and lag grows. Production-rate control is a producer-side concern.
Producer tuning
commonMistakes: treating consumer groups as load balancers with more consumers than partitions; autoCommit: true while claiming at-least-once control; acks: 1 for anything financial; compaction with a non-unique key; believing transactions make your database writes atomic; adding partitions to fix lag without considering key hashing changes.
practiceTasks: run a 3-broker, 6-partition topic; produce 1M keyed events; run two consumer groups (one auto-commit, one manual post-processing commit); kill consumers mid-run; then measure lag over time and write the runbook for "lag is growing, what do you check in order".

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why is Kafka a log and not a queue?
🟢 What is the relationship between partition count and consumer count in a group?
🟡 Why key messages by aggregate id?
🟡 What is consumer lag and how do you alert on it?
🟡 `acks: 1` vs `acks: all` with `min.insync.replicas: 2`?
🔴 Why are transactions + idempotent producer called "exactly-once", and what is outside their scope?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: we need to process card payments in the same transaction as recording the outcome, and the ask is for 'exactly-once'. Decision: I would push back on the framing. Kafka's exactly-once semantics are scoped to the Kafka boundary: with enableIdempotence: true on the producer and sendOffsetsToTransaction, the read offsets and the produced records are committed atomically inside a Kafka transaction, so a Kafka-to-Kafka pipeline sees each record exactly once even across retries and failover. What that does *not* cover is a Postgres write or a call to the payment API. So for the payment path I use transactions only for the Kafka-to-Kafka hop and make the final side effect idempotent with a unique constraint on (order_id, payment_intent_id), then rely on the outbox for the database-to-Kafka direction. Reasoning: exactly-once across a distributed boundary is not achievable; what is achievable is exactly-once within one transactional store plus effectively-once everywhere else. Trade-offs: transactions cost throughput, add latency, constrain producer config, and cap transaction.timeout.ms, so I only use them where the atomicity is actually needed. Failure scenario: a consumer crashes after the provider call but before the commit — the transaction rolls back and the record is redelivered, so the provider call must be idempotent with a key the provider honours; without that, the second attempt double-charges. Alternative: skip transactions entirely, use at-least-once end to end, and spend the saved complexity budget on idempotency keys everywhere plus a reconciliation job."

topics.title: Managed Queues
topics.description: serverless queues where the vendor runs the broker, you send an HTTP-ish API call. The trade is money and control for durability, scaling, and a much smaller ops surface.
keyConcepts: Amazon SQS: standard vs FIFO

Long polling: WaitTimeSeconds: 20 with ReceiveMessage keeps one long HTTP request open and returns as soon as a message is available, which cuts empty receives and cost dramatically. Poll on all your SQS receive calls.

Visibility timeout: the message is hidden for N seconds after being received. When it expires the message reappears. Set it to ~6× your p99 handler duration, and use ChangeMessageVisibility to extend long jobs (max 12 hours) rather than setting a global 6-hour timeout. If processing exceeds it you get duplicates, not failure.

DLQ redrive: attach a DLQ to the source queue with maxReceiveCount. After N receives, the message moves to the DLQ. Alert on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible on the DLQ — the only metric that matters.

Exactly-once-ish: FIFO gives deduplication *within the window*, not exactly-once. You still need idempotent handlers because the redelivery-to-DLQ path and cross-group ordering interactions can duplicate.
Long message payloads: put big data in S3 or DynamoDB and send a pointer.
SNS → SQS fan-out
Each SQS subscriber queue is an independent consumer group with its own DLQ and lag. This is the managed replacement for a RabbitMQ fan-out exchange.
SNS also supports filter policies (JSON rules on message attributes) so subscribers only receive what they care about — cheaper and quieter than sending everything and filtering downstream.
Google Cloud Pub/Sub

Ack deadline: the server-assigned lease (10–600s, configurable, and it *extends* on pull). ack() removes it; nack() re-delivers immediately (hot-loop risk — use a delay via a dead-letter topic plus redelivery backoff).

Ordering keys: set orderingKey (e.g. orderId) and consume with an ordering-enabled client. Cost: all messages with the same ordering key go to one regional backend and are delivered serially, so throughput per key is limited and a stuck message blocks its key. Only enable ordering where you truly need it.
commonMistakes: short-polling SQS (20× the API calls for the same work); setting visibility timeout to the p50 handler time; ignoring FIFO message-group blocking; assuming FIFO means no duplicates; replaying a DLQ at full rate.
practiceTasks: create both SQS queue types plus SNS fan-out to two queues; send 1,000 messages with a handler that fails 5% of the time; prove visibility-timeout duplication by sleeping past the timeout; then redrive the DLQ with a replay rate limit and measure end-to-end lag.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What does `WaitTimeSeconds: 20` do and why does it save money?
🟢 What is the SQS visibility timeout and what happens if your handler exceeds it?
🟡 Standard vs FIFO: what is the *real* ordering guarantee, and what is `MessageGroupId` for?
🟡 What does `MessageDeduplicationId` give you and what does it not give you?
🟡 How does SNS → SQS fan-out differ from a RabbitMQ fan-out exchange operationally?
🟡 What is a Pub/Sub ack deadline, and why is `nack()` dangerous in a loop?
🔴 You must process S3 upload events for 4 tenants. Where do you put the fan-out and why?
🔴 Your FIFO queue has a poison message and one key's events have stopped. Diagnose and fix.
🔴 A DLQ has 40,000 messages after a bad deploy. What is your triage sequence?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a deploy at 14:02 added a null check that threw on historical records, 40,000 messages are in the DLQ, and the pipeline is stalled. Decision: triage in four ordered steps. One, stop the bleeding — fix the code, and roll forward before touching the DLQ. Two, sample: read the first 20 messages, group them by error signature and by MessageGroupId/orderingKey, and check whether the failure is uniform or a single poison payload. Three, classify: if it's one bad record, redrive selectively; if it's a code bug, redrive in batches behind a replay rate limit so we do not re-run 40,000 jobs at once and hammer the downstream. Four, prevent: add a circuit breaker and a dead-letter reason header so the next incident is triagable without reading bodies. Reasoning: DLQ replay is a *mass* operation on a system that already failed once; replaying at full rate recreates the incident. Trade-offs: selective redrive tooling is work, and slow replay means the backlog persists — acceptable, because the backlog is not user-visible if it is order history. Failure scenario: the fix depends on data backfilled later, so the DLQ sits for two weeks; that argues for a DLQ *age* alarm and a monthly triage ritual, not just a size alarm. Alternative: write DLQ contents to S3 and replay from a controlled worker when volume is large enough to need it."

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 How do you set a visibility timeout for a job whose duration is unknown and can be hours?

⚫ Are SQS standard queues ever exactly-once? Prove your answer.

topics.title: Redis Streams vs Lists vs Pub/Sub vs a Broker
topics.description: Redis offers four messaging shapes on the same server, each with very different guarantees. Confusing them is a classic production incident.
keyConcepts: Redis Streams consumer groups

Pending Entries List (PEL): every delivered-but-unacked id, with its idle time and owning consumer. XPENDING summary, XPENDING ... IDLE detailed form. Unbounded PELs are a real memory leak and cause slow XAUTOCLAIM walks.

Independent groups: billing and analytics groups on the same stream each read every message once. This is the pattern that makes a stream more than a queue, and it is what makes Redis Streams a credible substitute for a broker at moderate volume.

Consumer groups and the same group, two consumers: competing consumers share the load; entries pending with a dead consumer must be reclaimed (XAUTOCLAIM) or they are invisible forever — this is the #1 Streams bug.

Streams vs lists: a list gives you one message per pop with no history, no groups, no ack. Streams give you history, groups, acks, and pending tracking. Use lists/BLPOP only for trivial work distribution.

Pub/Sub: still fine when the messages are genuinely ephemeral and the failure mode of loss is acceptable — cache invalidation, "config changed", UI nudges, metrics fan-out inside one process. Never for anything a user waits on.
Choosing among the four
commonMistakes: Pub/Sub for anything durable; no PEL reaping on Streams; XREADGROUP without BLOCK (busy-loop); unbounded streams; one group reused for two workloads so they steal each other's messages.
practiceTasks: implement one stream, two consumer groups, three consumers, a DLQ stream, XAUTOCLAIM reaping, and approximate trimming. kill -9 a consumer and verify no entry is lost and no entry is processed twice by the same group.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What does Redis Pub/Sub guarantee, and what happens with no subscribers?
🟡 What is the PEL and why does it grow?
🟡 What does `XAUTOCLAIM` solve?
🟡 When is a Redis list a better fit than a stream?
🔴 Two consumers read the same stream, group `g1`. Consumer A dies holding 5 unacked entries. What happens and what do you run?
🔴 Compare a Redis stream group with a Kafka consumer group. When is the swap worth it?
🔴 Why is `MAXLEN ~` approximate trimming the right default for streams?
🔴 You use Redis Pub/Sub for "new order" events and a critical consumer misses some. Diagnose, then redesign.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: order events published on a Redis Pub/Sub channel, a fulfilment consumer occasionally misses them, and support tickets say orders sometimes never ship. Decision: two changes. First, migrate to Redis Streams with a consumer group per consumer type — fulfilment, analytics — and XACK only after the DB transaction commits; reclaim stragglers with XAUTOCLAIM every 30 seconds. Second, and more importantly, stop using the transport as the source of truth: the durable event is the outbox row in Postgres (5.6.12), and Redis is only the delivery mechanism, so even a total Redis flush is recoverable by replaying from the outbox. Reasoning: pub/sub has no durability, no replay, and no way to know what was missed, so any business-critical event published on it is lost with probability proportional to subscriber downtime. Trade-offs: streams require operating consumer groups correctly — dead consumers, PEL growth, trimming — which is more machinery than subscribe; and if the event rate goes past a few hundred thousand per second, move to Kafka rather than debug Streams. Failure scenario: a consumer group is stuck because nobody reclaimed the PEL after a crash, so its queue silently grows. Prevention: alarm on XPENDING count and on PEL oldest-idle, and treat group health as a metric you own. Alternative: Postgres outbox plus a poller, which trades latency for simplicity if the volume is modest."

interviewQuestions.text: ⚫ How do you guarantee at-least-once with `XREADGROUP` when the handler can be retried forever?

topics.title: Choosing a Queue System: The Decision Table
topics.description: Choosing a Queue System: The Decision Table within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: No universal winner
"Just use Postgres as a queue" — when it is genuinely the right call

Do use it when: you already run Postgres, volume is low-to-moderate, the job must be transactional with a domain write (outbox!), your team cannot operate another datastore, or you need exactly-once enqueue for free (unique + on conflict).

Do not use it when: you need per-job delays at scale (polling cost), long-running jobs holding connections, priority queues, huge fan-out, or you cannot tolerate analytical queries sharing the same lock/CPU budget with your workers.
Hybrid that works well in practice: Postgres for the durable domain events (outbox) + BullMQ/SQS for the execution. You get transactional enqueue and a real queue's ergonomics.
A decision procedure to say out loud in an interview
Do I need durable, guaranteed delivery? If no → in-process async, done.
Do I need replay or multiple independent consumers of the same events? If yes → Kafka/Pub/Sub-style stream; if no → work queue.
Do I need per-entity ordering? Yes → FIFO/partitioned queue, and check that a poison message cannot block the key.
Do I need complex routing (patterns, headers, TTLs, DLX)? Yes → RabbitMQ.
Am I on AWS and want zero ops? Yes → SQS (+SNS for fan-out), FIFO only where ordering is required.
Do I have zero appetite for another production datastore and modest volume? Yes → Postgres queue, or BullMQ if Redis is already operated.
commonMistakes: picking by benchmark throughput; ignoring the poison-message-blocks-the-key problem in FIFO; forgetting that SQS "unlimited" throughput still has API request and in-transit message limits; not checking per-region pricing and data residency before committing.
practiceTasks: take one real product feature and evaluate it against all six systems, writing the one-paragraph decision memo, the cost estimate at 1M and 100M messages/month, and the migration path if you outgrow the choice.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟡 When is "Postgres as a queue" the right answer?
🟡 Which system gives the strongest ordering guarantee and why?
🟡 Compare dead-letter handling across BullMQ, RabbitMQ, and SQS.
🔴 Your team has AWS, three backend engineers, and needs to send 5M notifications/day with per-user ordering. What do you pick and why?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: AWS-hosted, 5M notifications a day, ordering per user required, small team, and we already run S3 and Lambda. Decision: SQS FIFO queues sharded by a hash of userId into the MessageGroupId, one queue per message type, with SNS fan-out to per-channel queues, DLQs attached with maxReceiveCount: 5, and long-polling consumers. Reasoning: ordering per user maps directly onto FIFO message groups; managed means no cluster to page about; and per-type queues mean email backpressure does not stall push. Trade-offs: FIFO is limited to 300 TPS per API call, so I batch sends and shard across multiple queues if needed; FIFO message groups are the honest weak point — a poison message blocks all later messages for that user until it is dead-lettered, so I set a short visibility timeout, a low maxReceiveCount, and an alarm on oldest-message-age per group. Failure scenario: a handler bug causes one user's messages to dead-letter repeatedly; that user's notifications stop for minutes. I detect it with a per-queue alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage plus a per-group redrive, and I add synthetic canary messages per group so a stuck group surfaces in minutes rather than at a customer complaint. Alternative: BullMQ on our existing Redis, which removes the per-call TPS ceiling and gives cron/DLQ ergonomics, at the cost of owning Redis durability and having exactly one region."

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 When would you reject Kafka for an event pipeline?
🔴 Cost model: 8M small messages/day, 2KB average. Compare managed queue vs self-hosted Rabbit vs Kafka.
🔴 Cross-region: your primary is in Frankfurt, you must not lose jobs during a regional failover. What changes per system?
🔴 A multi-cloud requirement (data residency) — how does that constrain the choice?
⚫ You must support a 20-minute delay before a job is processed. Which of the six can do it, and how?

topics.title: Delivery Semantics: At-Least-Once vs At-Most-Once vs Exactly-Once
topics.description: Delivery Semantics: At-Least-Once vs At-Most-Once vs Exactly-Once within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: What "exactly-once" really means
It is scoped to a system boundary. Kafka EOS covers "read from topic, write to topic, commit offset atomically". It does not cover a Postgres insert or an HTTP call.

Distributed transactions across a broker + database are theoretically possible (2PC) and practically avoided because of blocking, latency, and the coordinator being a new failure mode. The industry answer is to *avoid needing* cross-system atomicity: make the operation idempotent and retry until it converges.
Effectively-once is the honest goal: at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing + a dedupe table + reconciliation for anything money or count related.
The mechanics of effectively-once
Idempotency key — the caller (or the event) supplies a stable key: payment_intent_id, order.id + ':fulfilled', event.id. It must be derived from *intent*, not from attempt time.
Dedupe table with a unique constraint, inserted in the same transaction as the side effect:

Provider-side idempotency for anything that leaves your system: Stripe accepts an Idempotency-Key header (and stores the response for 24 hours), so a retry of the same charge returns the original result instead of a second charge. Use it on every create/capture/refund.
Natural convergence: design the side effect as a set-state operation (status = 'fulfilled', SET n = GREATEST(n, ?)) so a repeat is a no-op.
commonMistakes: assuming unique constraint alone gives exactly-once (it stops double-insert but not double-charge); server-generated idempotency keys; not storing the *response* so retries cannot return a consistent answer; forgetting that idempotency keys have retention windows.
practiceTasks: implement withIdempotency with a unique-constraint race test (fire 50 concurrent identical calls), a key-reuse-with-different-payload test, and a simulated crash-and-retry test with a provider that charges unless it sees the same idempotency key.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Define at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once.
🟡 Why is at-least-once the default in every mature queue?
🟡 What is "effectively-once" and what are its ingredients?
🟡 Why is a client-supplied idempotency key better than a server-generated one?
🔴 Explain why Kafka's exactly-once does not protect a Postgres write, and what you do instead.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a consumer reads card-payment events from Kafka, charges a customer through a REST API, and writes the order row in Postgres. The requirement is 'exactly once'. Decision: I would not claim exactly-once. I use Kafka transactions for the Kafka→Kafka hop if I produce derived events, but the actual charge goes through the provider's idempotency key (order.id as the key), and the Postgres write is guarded by a unique constraint on (order_id, event_id) plus a state-precondition update. Reasoning: exactly-once is only well-defined inside a single transactional store. The moment the side effect crosses a network boundary to a provider, the best you can do is at-least-once attempts plus a provider-side idempotency guarantee, plus a dedupe table so your own writes don't double-apply. Trade-offs: this means my correctness story is a composition of three mechanisms instead of one, and each has a failure mode to test: provider idempotency window expiry, dedupe table retention, and constraint violations under concurrency. Failure scenario: the charge succeeds, then the process dies before the DB write; the redelivered message retries the charge with the same key, the provider returns the *original* charge instead of a second one, and then the DB write succeeds. That works only because the key was derived from intent. If the key had been random per attempt, the customer is charged twice. Alternative: an orchestrating saga in 5.6.13 with compensating refunds, which is more code but handles the multi-step case."

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 Design idempotency for "increment a user's referral count" when duplicates are possible.
🔴 What breaks if you reuse an idempotency key with a different request body? How do you detect it?
🔴 When is at-most-once actually the right choice?
⚫ Explain why 2PC is avoided in modern architectures despite being "correct".

topics.title: Retry, Backoff, and Dead-Letter Queues
topics.description: Retry, Backoff, and Dead-Letter Queues within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: Retry taxonomy — the first thing to get right
Backoff formulas
Retry budgets
DLQ vs park vs drop
DLQ triage and replay tooling

Never replay to production without a filter and a rate limit. Build a small CLI/service: dlq list --queue billing --reason timeout --since 1h, dlq replay --ids ... --rate 50/s --dry-run, dlq inspect <id> (full payload + headers + failure reason).
Record the failure *reason and attempt count* on the DLQ entry, otherwise triage means reading payloads blind.
Alert on DLQ depth and age, and also on DLQ growth *rate* (a rising slope is the early signal, days before the depth is scary).
After the fix, replay oldest-first, at a controlled rate, while watching the DLQ drain and the success rate.

Poison detection: a job that failed maxAttempts times with the same error signature in the last hour is a poison source; quarantine it and, if the source is a batch, split the batch so one bad row does not kill 999 good ones.
commonMistakes: retrying validation errors; exponential backoff with no jitter; capping attempts but not elapsed time (or vice versa); replaying a DLQ at full rate; DLQ entries with no reason metadata.
practiceTasks: build a retry wrapper with permanent/transient/rate-limited classification, full jitter, attempts + elapsed-time caps, and a retry budget that sheds load. Test it against a fault-injecting HTTP server returning 500, 429 with Retry-After, and 400.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Give three examples each of permanent and transient failures.
🟡 Why is naive exponential backoff worse than full jitter?
🟡 What is a retry budget and why does it matter?
🟡 When do you drop a message instead of DLQ-ing it?
🔴 Derive full jitter for `base = 500ms`, `cap = 30s`, and explain the shape of the distribution.
🔴 A webhook to a partner has been failing for 6 hours at a 30% rate. Walk through your retry and DLQ decisions.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a partner webhook has been returning 500s for six hours; we retry with exponential backoff up to 6 attempts and DLQ after that. Roughly 30% of attempts fail, so the partner's queue is full of our retries. Decision: three changes. One, classify by status code — 4xx other than 408/429 is permanent, fail straight to DLQ; 429 gets Retry-After honoured exactly; 5xx/timeout is the only transient class. Two, add full jitter with a 5-minute cap and a total retry-volume budget capped at 10% of normal traffic, with a per-partner concurrency limit so a struggling partner cannot consume the whole worker pool. Three, put the partner behind a circuit breaker: after 50% failures over 20 requests, open for 60 seconds and fail fast into a parking queue, so we stop hammering a service that is already down. Reasoning: retries without jitter and without a budget amplify an outage into a self-inflicted denial of service, and the useful behaviour under downstream failure is to *shed load* and preserve the backlog. Trade-offs: DLQ means the partner is out of sync with us, so I need a replay path and an eventual consistency check, and a circuit breaker risks false trips if the partner is merely slow rather than down — hence error-ratio plus latency thresholds and a half-open probe. Failure scenario: partner recovers, we replay 200k parked messages at full rate and knock them over again. So replay is rate-limited and prioritised by event age. Alternative: an outbox plus a dedicated delivery worker per partner so one partner's problems never touch the request path."

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 Design the alert set for a DLQ.
🔴 Your nightly import job has 2M rows and one row violates a constraint. How do you avoid losing 1,999,999 good rows?
🔴 Explain how "attempts" and "max elapsed time" caps interact, and which one prevents the hot loop.
⚫ How would you retry a message whose failure is caused by *downstream* unavailability, without making the thundering herd worse?

topics.title: The Outbox Pattern
topics.description: The Outbox Pattern within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: The dual-write problem
Transactional outbox
Why for update skip locked: N relay processes can poll concurrently; each claims disjoint rows, so throughput scales by adding relays and there is no thundering herd on the same rows.
Idempotent consumers are mandatory here: the relay can publish and crash before published_at is written, so the same event will be emitted again. Use the inbox pattern below.

Ordering: relay order is id order per batch, but concurrent relays and retries break global ordering. Per-aggregate ordering is preserved *only* if you route by aggregate_id and use a FIFO/partitioned broker, and even then a retry can overtake. Accept and document it.
Relay vs CDC (Debezium) vs logical decoding
Care with CDC
Inbox / dedupe pattern (consumer side)
Cleanup/archival of the outbox
published_at is not null and published_at < now() - interval '7 days' → delete (or move to cold storage / a compacted audit topic).

Keep *unpublished* rows forever, and alert if count(*) where published_at is null grows or if max(created_at) for unpublished rows is older than a few minutes. Also alert on the *oldest* unpublished row's age — that is the true outbox lag metric.
When to prefer direct publishing
commonMistakes: publishing inside the transaction; holding a DB lock across the broker call; an outbox with no cleanup so it grows forever; trimming the consumer inbox before the redelivery window expires; relying on the outbox for events that need to happen only if the transaction commits *and* then also publishing directly (you now have both).
practiceTasks: implement the outbox relay with three concurrent relay processes, a broker stub that fails 10% of the time, an inbox table, and a test that kills a relay between publish and published_at write — then assert each event produced exactly one domain change.

interviewQuestions.answer: the event row commits in the same transaction as the domain change

interviewQuestions.text: 🟡 Why is `for update skip locked` the right primitive for the relay?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: the relay is a poller, and I want to run three of them for throughput without them fighting over rows or double-publishing. Decision: claim rows with select ... for update skip locked, inside the same statement batch as the update that marks them claimed, then commit. Reasoning: skip locked makes each relay's select skip rows already locked by another transaction, so the result sets are disjoint by construction. It converts a queue into a set of independent claims with database-grade crash safety — if a relay dies, its rows unlock automatically and the next poll picks them up, so there is no lease to expire or reap. Trade-offs: it puts row locks on your primary database, so a slow relay or a big batch blocks vacuum and can contend with real queries; I keep batches small (100) and the transaction short, and I never hold a lock across a network call to the broker — the publish happens after the claim commits, which is precisely why the design is at-least-once and needs the inbox on the consumer side. Failure scenario: a relay publishes 100 events and is killed before writing published_at; those 100 are emitted again on the next poll. That is not a bug in the design, it is the accepted cost of not using 2PC, and consumers dedupe on message_id = outbox:<id>. Alternative: CDC with logical decoding removes the load from the primary and gives lower latency, at the cost of operating a replication slot, a CDC connector, and schema-history handling — worth it when publish volume is high enough that polling becomes measurable load."

topics.title: Ordering, Partitioning, and Guarantees
topics.description: Ordering, Partitioning, and Guarantees within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: Ordering keys are the only ordering you can have. Per-entity ordering (all events for orderId on one partition/queue) is achievable; global ordering is not, at any useful scale. "Global order" would mean one partition, i.e. one consumer's throughput.

Ordering vs concurrency: you can have per-key ordering and per-key concurrency by sharding by key and running N consumers, each handling a disjoint set of keys. You cannot have both ordering *and* the same key processed in parallel.

Sequence numbers beat timestamps. Every event for an entity carries seq (a per-entity monotonic counter, or the broker offset). Timestamps across machines are unreliable (clock skew, NTP steps); a per-entity sequence is derived from the database and therefore correct. Cross-ref Phase 12 (distributed clocks, Lamport/vector clocks) for the theory.

Gaps must be detected and repaired, not assumed away. A consumer that sees seq = 7 after seq = 5 must fetch 6 (or request a resync from 5) rather than applying 7. This is the same discipline as 5.7.7.

Compensating events, not distributed transactions. Multi-step business flows use a saga: each step commits locally and emits an event; a later step's failure publishes a compensating event (order.reservation_released) that undoes the effect. Compensations are *eventually* consistent and may themselves fail, so they need retries and, ultimately, manual repair.

Ordering hazards to state explicitly: retries can overtake (attempt 3 of event A succeeding before attempt 1's neighbour event B), partition reassignment during a broker failure, and multi-instance producers racing on the same key. All are handled by (a) idempotent handlers, (b) sequence-gap detection, and (c) treating a detected gap as a resync trigger.

Eventual consistency is a product decision. Say it plainly: "we accept that for up to 5 seconds after checkout, the fulfilment view may show pending while payment shows succeeded, because the alternative is a distributed transaction that cannot span the payment provider." Then define the user-visible consequence for each window, and put a staleness indicator in the UI if the window is user-visible.
commonMistakes: assuming per-key ordering survives retries; using wall-clock time for ordering; describing eventual consistency without a window or a user-visible story; "fixing" ordering by adding a global mutex (kills throughput).
practiceTasks: design the event set for order.created → payment.authorized → inventory.reserved → order.fulfilled, assign ordering keys and sequence numbers, define the four compensating events, and write the consumer gap-detection pseudocode.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why is global ordering not achievable at scale?
🟡 What is an ordering key and how do you choose it?
🟡 Why are per-entity sequence numbers better than timestamps for gap detection?
🟡 What is a compensating event and when is a saga the right pattern?
🔴 A retry overtakes a later event. How do you prevent a consumer applying events out of order?
🔴 Your broker reassigns partitions and two consumers briefly process the same key. What breaks and how do you contain it?
🔴 How do you describe "eventual consistency" to a product manager who is worried?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: checkout shows paid while the fulfilment dashboard still shows pending, and the product owner is asking whether we can make it atomic. Decision: no, and instead I quantify the window. I state: payment success and order fulfilment are in two systems with no shared transaction; we accept up to 5 seconds of divergence, we detect it, and we do not lose or duplicate either fact. Then I make the divergence non-surprising: the user-facing order page reads the payment state and shows Processing for that window, support has a view that flags orders stuck in the window past 2 minutes, and a reconciliation job reconciles nightly. Reasoning: the useful conversation is about the window and the user-visible consequence, not about eliminating the window, which is impossible without a distributed transaction that the payment provider cannot participate in. Trade-offs: a 5-second window means we need idempotency, gap detection and reconciliation — three mechanisms that cost complexity, and they are unavoidable given the boundary. Failure scenario: the event is lost rather than delayed, so the window becomes permanent; the reconciliation job is the backstop that converts an unbounded outage into a bounded delay. Alternative: for the small set of flows where atomicity truly matters, move the money and the order state into the same system and use a saga with compensations for the external steps only."

topics.title: Email, SMS, and Push as Background Jobs
topics.description: Email, SMS, and Push as Background Jobs within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: Why notifications are the canonical background job
Provider API semantics
The three distinct events
Accepted: the provider took the message. This is the only thing your send call confirms.
Delivered / opened: a callback or an open-tracking pixel much later.
Bounced / complained: permanent negative signal. You must act on it: mark the address invalid, unsubscribe, and stop paying to send to it.

Template versioning: store templates in the DB or a template service with a version, not in code. render('welcome', { version: 3, data }). Never mutate a version in place — a user who opens a "reset your password" email two days later must see the same body that was sent, for support and compliance. Keep the rendered output (text + HTML) stored per send.
Bounce and complaint handling: a suppressions table (email_hash, reason, at). Send jobs check it before calling the provider — that is a table lookup instead of a wasted paid API call.

Unsubscribe: every marketing email needs a one-click unsubscribe (List-Unsubscribe header plus a POST endpoint that verifies a signed token, not a raw user id). Transactional mail is exempt from opt-out requirements but must have an opt-out for marketing categories; never put marketing content in a transactional template.

Quiet hours: per-user timezone, computed at send time from the recipient's profile, not at enqueue time (which may be hours earlier). Suppress non-urgent pushes and SMS between 21:00 and 08:00 local; urgent pushes (security alerts) bypass with an explicit priority.

Batching and digests: hourly/daily digest jobs group pending notifications per user, render one email, and mark the individual rows as batched_into = digestId. This is the standard defence against a spike ("everyone signed up at 08:00") and against per-recipient provider charges.

Delivery SLOs: define and measure. Example: "95% of password-reset emails accepted by the provider within 5 seconds of the request; <0.1% hard bounce; <0.01% complaint rate; >99.9% of pushes delivered within 30s." Instrument by accepted_at, delivered_at, failed_at per channel, and alert on bounce-rate anomalies (a spike usually means list-quality damage or a spam-filter trigger, which is an incident).
commonMistakes: sending synchronously in the request; rendering from a mutable template; treating "accepted" as "delivered"; no suppression list; computing quiet hours at enqueue time; no per-hour send budget.
practiceTasks: build a notification dispatcher with three channel workers, template versioning, a suppression table, quiet hours with per-user timezones, digest batching, and a dashboard of accepted/delivered/bounced per channel.

🟢 What is the difference between accepted, delivered, and bounced?

interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a launch drove 50k signups in one minute against a provider limit of 500 sends/sec and a per-domain reputation risk. Decision: the API writes only to the DB plus an outbox row; the relay enqueues to a welcome-email queue with a per-user jobId (welcome:<userId>) so re-enqueueing is a no-op, and the worker is configured with concurrency: 40 and limiter: { max: 500, duration: 1000 } plus a per-domain-token limiter so we never exceed what the provider tolerates from one domain. Digest/batch is the second line of defence: anything unsent after 30 minutes is folded into a catch-up batch job. Reasoning: the request path must never know about provider limits, and rate limiting belongs at the queue so that multiple producers share one budget. Trade-offs: users wait up to 30 minutes for a non-urgent welcome email (acceptable, and I show a 'check your inbox' state in-product), and the extra queue hop adds one more place to lose a message — mitigated by the outbox plus queue. Failure scenario: the provider rejects a batch due to a reputation or content-policy trigger, so 500/s fails continuously. Then the limiter, the retries, and the DLQ all interact badly: I set a per-hour *sent* budget, not just a per-second rate, so a degraded provider cannot consume the day's sending quota in ten minutes, and I alert on the accepted-rate plateau. Alternative: a dedicated email microservice with its own deploy cadence and quota accounting, which is the right call once the volume makes email a business-critical dependency."
