topics.title: Backpressure and Queue Health
topics.description: Backpressure and Queue Health within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: The four metrics that matter for any queue
Depth — messages waiting (SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, BullMQ waiting count, Kafka lag). Necessary, not sufficient.
Age of the oldest message — the metric that actually predicts user pain. A depth of 10,000 that drains in 10 seconds is fine; a depth of 50 that is 4 hours old is an incident.
Throughput in vs out — if in > out for long enough, everything else follows. Plot the delta; the crossing point is your capacity ceiling and is the number to know.
Failure and retry rate — a sudden rise in retries *before* the depth rises is the earliest signal you get.
Dashboards and alarms
When a consumer is 10× slower than normal — triage in this order

Is it the consumer or the dependency? Check the consumer's own latency distribution (p50, p99) and its dependency's latency separately. A 10× jump in consumer time with a flat dependency time means CPU/GC/IO contention locally.
Is it one job or all of them? Sample slow job names/IDs from logs. One pathological payload (a 200MB image, an N+1 query over 10M rows) is a different problem from uniformly slow processing.

Local saturation: event-loop lag (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay), GC pauses, CPU, memory, connection-pool exhaustion (waiting on the DB pool), or an accidental await of a slow dependency inside a tight loop.
Dependency degradation: a downstream p99 jumped (DB plan change after a deploy, a third-party API, a cold cache). If the dependency slowed 10×, your consumer legitimately slowed 10×.

Are you the victim of your own retry storm? A DLQ-less retry loop with no backoff can saturate the consumer and starve fresh work — check whether the slow jobs are retries of the same failing dependency.
commonMistakes: alerting on absolute depth only; paging on a small non-growing DLQ; scaling consumers when the bottleneck is a downstream dependency; ignoring pool exhaustion; treating lag as a group aggregate.
practiceTasks: build a queue dashboard from Prometheus-style metrics — depth, oldest age, in/out rate, retry rate, DLQ depth and age — then write a synthetic "slow consumer" test that reduces worker throughput 10× and confirm each alarm fires with the right severity.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Which queue metric best predicts user pain, and why?
🟢 Why alert on rates rather than absolute depth?
🟡 What does consumer lag mean in Kafka and what is `records-lag-max`?
🟡 Why can a rising retry rate be an earlier signal than a rising depth?
🔴 A consumer becomes 10× slower. Give the exact triage order.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: production latency for a job type jumped from 200ms to 2s and depth is climbing. Decision: I run an ordered triage, because the answer differs completely by cause and random fixes waste the incident. First, split consumer time from dependency time using traces — if my own processing is 10× slower with flat dependency latency, it is me. Second, determine whether it is uniform or a tail: I group slow jobs by name and by payload size, which immediately separates 'one pathological payload' from 'everything is slower'. Third, check local saturation in this order: event-loop lag histogram, GC pause time, CPU, and pool wait time — a job that awaits a slow dependency while holding a DB connection looks like a consumer problem but is a pool problem. Fourth, check whether the consumer is saturated in a way replicas would fix, and whether a single-threaded worker is the ceiling. Fifth, check the retry hypothesis: if the slow jobs are all retries of one failing dependency, the queue is being consumed by doomed work and the fix is a circuit breaker plus DLQ, not more replicas. Only then do I scale out consumers. Reasoning: adding replicas to a consumer that is blocked on a connection pool or a 200MB payload multiplies the problem. Trade-offs: this triage takes ten to fifteen minutes under pressure, which is why the metrics need to answer steps one and two without me. Failure scenario: the true cause is a new index or a query plan change on the database, which looks exactly like dependency slowdown — that is why dependency latency is step one rather than step four. Prevention: latency budgets per job type, alert on p99 not p50, and a per-dependency dashboard that makes step one a one-glance check."

topics.title: Cost and Operational Reality
topics.description: Cost and Operational Reality within Background Processing and Messaging.
keyConcepts: One broker vs many. Start with one. The number of failure modes is not linear in the number of brokers, but it is linear in the number of *configurations*. Multiple brokers are justified by hard isolation needs (a customer-facing stream vs an internal batch pipeline), data residency, or blast-radius separation — not by "we might need it later". Every extra broker is a thing to patch, monitor, back up, capacity-plan, and put in a runbook.

Retention is the biggest hidden cost. Kafka retention is *per partition per replica*: 1 TB/day × 7 days × 3 replicas × 20 partitions of headroom is a number that surprises people. SQS and BullMQ are per-message. Design retention as a product decision ("do consumers ever need to replay more than 24 hours?") and cost it.

Cross-region replication triples your bill and adds a consistency story you now have to explain (active/passive with a failover runbook, or active/active with conflict resolution you probably do not need). For job queues, the honest pattern is regional queues with regional consumers, and *not* replicating the broker — replicate the *source of truth* (the DB) and re-derive.

Cost per million messages (order of magnitude, always re-check current pricing): managed SQS in the tens of dollars; a small managed Kafka cluster in the low thousands; self-hosted RabbitMQ is hardware plus your on-call; BullMQ on a small Redis is pennies to a few dollars. The implication: managed queues let you say yes to features you would otherwise not build; self-hosted wins at very high, steady volume where the utilisation is genuinely high.

"We run one queue and it's fine" — a legitimate and often correct answer. Say what makes it *stop* being fine: sustained depth growth, in > out, a p99 that needs more concurrency than the queue's parallelism allows, retention needs beyond job lifetime, more than one independent consumer of the same events, or on-call pain. Give the trigger conditions, not just the conclusion.

FinOps habits: tag resources per service/team; alert on queue cost anomalies; prefer delayed jobs over retained logs (a job queue with 7-day retention on 200M messages is a log store you did not plan for); delete completed-job payloads aggressively.
commonMistakes: replicating queues across regions for ephemeral work; running 14 job types in one queue with no per-type limits; not costing retention; multi-broker for imagined scale.
practiceTasks: write a one-page "messaging cost and capacity" note for your own project: current volumes, projected 10× growth, cost per option, and the three trigger conditions that would make you migrate.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What is the biggest hidden cost of Kafka?
🟡 Why is retention a product decision?
🟡 When is one broker the right answer?
🔴 Cost out 8M small messages/day on SQS vs a managed Kafka cluster vs self-hosted RabbitMQ.
🔴 Your jobs must survive a regional failover. Do you replicate the broker?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: our primary region is Frankfurt, and during a regional failure we must not lose queued work. Decision: do not replicate the broker; replicate the source of truth and re-derive. Concretely, the job enqueue happens in the same transaction as the domain write, and the durable record is the outbox/DB row. In the failover region I promote the read replica, spin up consumers, and run a recovery relay that republishes everything the primary's outbox says was never published. Reasoning: cross-region broker replication gives you a second copy of *transient* work — but the events that recreate that work already exist durably in the database, so replicating them through the broker duplicates a durable source of truth for no additional guarantee, at 3× the cost and with an active/active consistency problem. Trade-offs: recovery is slower — instead of failing over the broker in seconds, I replay from the outbox, which takes minutes — and I accept that trade because correctness beats switchover speed for background work. Failure scenario: a region dies mid-publish and the outbox row was written but not yet published; the failover relay picks it up because published_at is null, which is exactly the state we need to detect. Alternative: replicate the queue for low-latency failover and accept the cost, if the business genuinely cannot tolerate minutes of backlog."

topics.title: Socket.IO
topics.description: a library that provides its own protocol on top of WebSocket (with HTTP long-polling fallback), plus rooms, namespaces, acknowledgements, middleware, connection state recovery, and cluster adapters. It is not raw WebSocket, and a WebSocket client cannot talk to it.
keyConcepts: Why it is not raw WebSocket
Connection state recovery
Choosing Socket.IO vs raw ws

Socket.IO when: you need rooms, acks, reconnection-with-retry semantics, cross-instance fan-out, and a heterogeneous client team (React Native, plain JS, non-Node SDKs). Default for chat and notifications.

Raw ws when: you need protocol-level control, minimal overhead at very large scale, binary framing you own, interoperability with non-Socket.IO clients, or you do not want a dependency that must be upgraded in lockstep with your clients.
commonMistakes: using Socket.IO when raw ws is required for interop; assuming recovery survives a server restart; forgetting socket.to(...) vs socket.in(...) semantics; leaving transports: ['websocket'] for users behind restrictive proxies.
practiceTasks: build a chat server on Socket.IO with two namespaces (/chat and /admin), room fan-out, acks, middleware auth, a Redis adapter across three instances, connection state recovery, and a test that kills a client for 30 seconds and asserts zero missed messages.

🟡 How does Socket.IO's reconnection differ from a hand-rolled client backoff?
🔴 What is connection state recovery and what are its two limitations?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: users on mobile lose connectivity for 10–60 seconds constantly, and with raw WebSockets they miss every message that happened while disconnected and then have to refetch the whole conversation on reconnect. Decision: enable Socket.IO connectionStateRecovery with maxDisconnectionDuration: 120000. When a client reconnects and presents the same recovery token, the server replays the packets it sent during the disconnection window, so the client applies a normal ordered stream instead of doing a full resync. Reasoning: this is a big correctness and latency win for exactly the reconnect pattern real users produce, and it is built into the library rather than something I maintain myself. The two limitations I would state in the same breath: first, the recovery buffer must live somewhere the reconnecting instance can read, so with a Redis adapter it lives in Redis — which means real-time recovery now depends on Redis, and with a single-instance in-memory adapter a server restart loses the buffer. Second, it is best-effort within the window: if the client is gone longer than the configured duration, or the buffer has been evicted, recovery does not apply and the client must do a full resync. So I still implement the resync path as the fallback, and I do not treat recovery as a substitute for a cursor. Trade-offs: it consumes memory per disconnected socket for the window duration, and it adds a state store to operate. Failure scenario: Redis is unavailable exactly when 5,000 clients reconnect — recovery fails and the whole cohort does a full refetch, which is precisely the thundering herd I was trying to avoid; so I also rate-limit the resync endpoint. Alternative: client-side cursors over raw WebSocket with per-message sequence numbers, which is more work but has no server-side recovery state to keep."

topics.title: Scaling WebSockets (sticky sessions, Redis adapter)
topics.description: Scaling WebSockets (sticky sessions, Redis adapter) within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: The core problem: connection-local state
Patterns
Sticky sessions: the honest framing
Redis adapter fan-out
Registry-based, fully stateless fan-out
Load balancer configuration
Idle timeout above your heartbeat interval (see 5.7.2 Q8).
Connection limits per instance so one instance is not OOM-killed by a burst: a max_connections on the instance and a queue/redirect at the LB.
Disable buffering and compression on the WebSocket path; some proxies inject a 30s idle timeout of their own.
Health check must be shallow (a TCP/HTTP check on the *upgrade* endpoint), not a WebSocket-level check that breaks every connection on restart.

Drain on deploy: flip readiness to false (LB stops routing new *HTTP*, but existing WS connections stay), stop accepting new upgrades, broadcast "going away" (1001), let clients reconnect, wait up to N seconds, then exit.
Per-instance limits and capacity planning
commonMistakes: sticky sessions as the default answer; assuming the Redis adapter deduplicates; skipping the origin socket so the sender gets its own message twice; a connection registry without TTL; a health check that churns live sockets on every deploy.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why do WebSockets need special handling to scale?
🟢 What is a sticky session and when is it required?
🟡 What does the Socket.IO Redis adapter actually solve?
🟡 Why do you skip the originating socket when echoing via pub/sub?
🔴 Design a stateless, drainable WebSocket deployment with no sticky sessions.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 50k concurrent chat clients, three deploys a week, and a 30-second rollout window. Decision: no sticky sessions. Fan-out goes through Redis pub/sub, and each instance keeps only its own sockets in memory. On connection, the client authenticates over the upgrade request, then the instance claims conn:<clientId> with a 90-second TTL and renews it every 30 seconds; publishing to a room publishes to Redis and every instance forwards to its local members, skipping the originating socket. Reasoning: without sticky sessions I can scale instances independently and deploy without disconnecting anyone, and the connection registry plus TTL means a crashed instance's entries expire on their own instead of requiring cleanup. Trade-offs: every message now costs a Redis round trip, so I batch fan-out for high-traffic rooms and I accept that Redis becomes a delivery dependency — if Redis is down, sockets stay connected but messages stop, so I alert on Redis pub/sub health and have the client fall back to REST fetch of missed messages. Failure scenario: a deploy during peak. The instance flips readiness, sends close code 1001 to its sockets, and exits only after clients reconnect elsewhere; because there is no sticky routing, the reconnect can land on any instance and still receive messages. Alternative: an external realtime broker removes the Redis dependency and the socket ops entirely at a per-message cost, which I would take if real-time is becoming a product differentiator rather than a feature."

topics.title: Presence
topics.description: knowing who is connected right now — the hardest "real-time" feature, because presence is a *negative* fact (someone left) and absence of evidence is ambiguous.
keyConcepts: The core problem: liveness needs a lease

Ghost presence on crash: the SET membership outlives the per-user TTL key, so a hard crash leaves a user in the room set forever. Fix by pruning: either store presence entirely as TTL keys and let them expire (presence:<resource>:<user> with no set — then membership is SCAN/sorted-set queries), or keep a sorted set scored by last-seen timestamp and prune entries older than the lease on read. presence:zset with ZADD key now user and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf (now - lease) on read gives you both membership and pruning with one command.

Refresh loop: one EXPIRE per connected user per lease interval. At 100k users that is 100k commands per 30s — trivial for Redis (a few thousand ops/sec), but batch them with a pipeline if you want headroom.
One user, many tabs/devices: count per resource rather than boolean presence, and decide how to represent "online in 2 places" (count, device list, or last-seen device).
Last-seen: store the last activity timestamp and expose last_seen_at; it is often more valuable than a boolean and it degrades gracefully.

"Who's typing": ephemeral, not presence. Use a short TTL key (typing:<room>:<userId>, EX 3) or a socket-room membership plus a setTimeout to clear, and never persist it. Also rate-limit the event (one per user per second) because it is the easiest way to generate traffic for no user value.
Multiple resources: a user can be in 5 rooms. Presence per resource is the right granularity; a global "online" is a COUNT over the set or a global presence:<user> key with the longest lease.

Scale: presence is one of the few features that genuinely needs shared state. Redis hash (per resource: field = user, value = timestamp) or sorted set is the standard. At very large scale, presence should be approximate — a "5% of your friends are online" estimate is often enough and removes the hot key problem entirely.
Never trust the client's own presence signal. A client that reports "I'm online" when it is not is a bug or a griefing vector. Presence is derived from server-observed heartbeats.
commonMistakes: client-reported presence; SADD without pruning; storing typing indicators durably; assuming the disconnect event always arrives; presence keyed only by user with no resource, which collapses all rooms into one.
practiceTasks: implement presence with sorted sets, a 60s lease with 20s refresh, prune-on-read, room member counts capped at 100 with a total count, and a test that SIGKILLs a gateway and measures how long ghost presence lasts.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why can't you detect presence by polling a socket?
🟡 How does a TTL key turn into presence, and what sets the TTL?
🔴 Explain ghost presence and give the mechanism that prevents it.
🔴 Design presence for 500k users in 50k rooms with Redis. What are the hot keys?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 500k users across 50k rooms; every connect/disconnect must be visible to other members within a couple of seconds, and we run multiple gateway instances. Decision: one Redis sorted set per room, presence:room:<id>, scored by last-seen timestamp, with ZADD on connect, ZADD with a new score on each heartbeat refresh, and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE presence:room:<id> -inf <now - lease> executed on read. Membership query is ZRANGEBYSCORE presence:room:<id> <now-lease> +inf, which gives live members and prunes ghosts in the same round trip; count is ZCOUNT. Reasoning: a plain set plus TTL keys needs two commands and leaves ghost members behind after a crash, whereas a sorted set scored by time makes liveness a *range query* and makes staleness impossible to represent — an entry that stops being refreshed simply falls out of the range. That is exactly the property presence needs. Trade-offs: every read pays a prune write, and a hot room's sorted set is a hot key — so for the biggest rooms I cap the returned member list and use ZCARD for the count, and I accept approximate presence there. Also, ZADD on every heartbeat is 500k commands per lease interval; I pipeline them and increase the lease to 60 seconds with a 20-second refresh to cut the rate. Failure scenario: a gateway instance is killed, so its users stop refreshing. They correctly disappear from presence within the lease, which is the desired behaviour, but they also never receive a disconnect event, so clients rely on the lease expiry rather than an explicit leave. Prevention: run a sweeper that reports rooms whose member count collapsed in the last interval, which surfaces a dead gateway instance in under a minute rather than as gradual user confusion. Alternative: ephemeral pub/sub presence with client-side reconciliation, which has no Redis cost but is only eventually consistent and cannot answer 'is this specific user online' cheaply."

topics.title: Transport Comparison: WebSocket vs SSE vs Long Polling vs Polling vs gRPC Streaming vs MQTT
topics.description: the six ways to push data to a client, and the trade-offs that decide between them.
keyConcepts: The HTTP/2 SSE caveat that changes the calculus

Over HTTP/1.1, each SSE connection is a separate TCP connection, so 10,000 concurrent SSE clients means 10,000 sockets and 10,000 entries in your load balancer's connection table — the same order as WebSockets.

Over HTTP/2, many SSE streams multiplex on one TCP connection, so connection cost collapses to per-client HTTP/2 streams (a much larger limit, ~100–128 streams per connection by default) and one TLS handshake covers many streams.

Therefore: SSE is cheap only if your edge actually speaks HTTP/2 to the client and the proxy preserves per-stream semantics and enough idle timeouts. Many CDNs and LBs terminate HTTP/2 at the edge and speak HTTP/1.1 to the origin, which puts the per-connection cost straight back on your origin. Verify with a real load test; do not assume.
WebSocket, by contrast, always costs one connection per client, no matter the protocol version — and browsers will not auto-reconnect, so you must build reconnection plus resync yourself.
How to decide, in order
Does the client need to send anything other than an ack? No → SSE (simpler, auth via cookies, auto-reconnect).
Is the data volume per message large or high-frequency? Consider a WebSocket plus a binary codec (e.g. protobuf over WS) rather than JSON per message.
Is the population devices, not browsers? → MQTT.
Is it service-to-service, both ends under your control? → gRPC streaming.
Do you need to survive hostile networks with minimum client complexity? → long polling.
commonMistakes: choosing WebSocket by default; assuming HTTP/2 is end-to-end through the CDN; forgetting that EventSource reconnects and therefore needs server-side id: handling or you will silently drop messages.
practiceTasks: build the same "live count" feature three ways — SSE, WebSocket, and long polling — and load test each at 5,000 concurrent connections while watching origin file descriptors, memory, and CPU.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Which transports are server→client only?
🟡 Why does SSE reconnect automatically while WebSocket does not?
🟡 When is SSE cheaper than WebSocket at scale, and what must you verify?
🟡 Why is gRPC streaming awkward from a browser?
🔴 20,000 concurrent live dashboards showing stock prices. Which transport and what are the failure modes?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 20,000 concurrent viewers on live stock dashboards; data is one-way, updates a few times per second, and the client is a browser. Decision: Server-Sent Events, not WebSockets. Reasoning: one-way data plus browser-native reconnection means SSE removes the single largest source of real-time bugs, which is the client reconnect-and-resync loop — browsers reconnect EventSource automatically and send Last-Event-ID, so I get gap recovery almost for free. Auth also gets simpler because the request is ordinary HTTP with cookies. Trade-off I must call out: SSE is only cheap at this scale if the edge terminates HTTP/2, because over HTTP/2 thousands of streams multiplex on one TCP connection while over HTTP/1.1 each dashboard costs a socket and an LB connection slot — at 20,000 that is a real infra constraint. So my first step is a load test against my actual CDN and origin path, not an assumption. Failure scenario: the CDN silently downgrades to HTTP/1.1 and my origin starts running out of file descriptors at 12,000 clients. Mitigations: verify negotiated protocol per client, alert on origin socket count, keep keep-alive aggressive, and have a polling fallback at 30s if the socket budget gets tight. Alternative: WebSockets if the dashboard later needs client→server interactivity such as per-user subscription filters, because then I would pay the per-connection cost anyway."

topics.title: WebSockets Server-Side: Handshake, Frames, Lifecycle
topics.description: WebSockets Server-Side: Handshake, Frames, Lifecycle within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: The handshake

perMessageDeflate: false unless you have measured the need: compression costs CPU per message on the hot path and introduces the permessage-deflate CRIME-style attack surface with secrets in messages. Turn it on for text-heavy, large frames only.
maxPayload is a hard DoS control. A frame larger than it is closed with code 1009.
Frame anatomy
Masking is mandatory client→server (proxies must not see your payloads) and forbidden server→client. A correct server must reject unmasked client frames (1002 protocol error).
Control frames must be ≤125 bytes, cannot be fragmented, and may be interleaved between fragments of a data message.

Fragmentation: large messages arrive as opcode 0x1, FIN=0, then 0x0, FIN=0, ... then 0x0, FIN=1. A buggy or malicious peer can hold an incomplete message forever → cap the reassembly buffer (this is why maxPayload matters).
Close codes you must handle
Connection state machine
ws.send() with no callback does not tell you the kernel accepted the data. Use the callback to track per-socket write errors, and use bufferedAmount as the high-water mark for a slow consumer.

Heartbeats must be enforced server-side with a deadline: ping every N seconds, terminate after two missed pongs. Relying on TCP keepalive alone is a mistake (default keepalive is 2 hours and many NATs drop idle mappings silently).
Capacity planning numbers to know
commonMistakes: not sending close codes; relying on TCP keepalive; ignoring bufferedAmount; not raising ulimit -n; deploying without drain; missing the LB idle-timeout interaction.
practiceTasks: build a ws server with token auth at upgrade time, a 30s ping/terminate heartbeat, 1009 handling via maxPayload, bufferedAmount-based dropping, and a drain-on-SIGTERM path; then use a local load tool to hold 20,000 connections and record memory, FDs, and event-loop lag.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What is the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value and why must the server compute it?
🟢 Why must client frames be masked and server frames not?
🟡 What are the five opcodes and which must be ≤125 bytes?
🟡 How do you detect a dead-but-open connection, and why is TCP keepalive not enough?
🟡 What does `bufferedAmount` tell you and what is the correct response to a huge value?
🟡 Why send close code `1001` on deploy?
🔴 A client claims 4GB in a single frame. What protects you, and what happens if it is disabled?
🔴 Your LB closes connections every 60s and clients see random drops. Explain and fix.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: WebSocket clients disconnect every 60–90 seconds at random, with no error on the client, and only some deployments show it. Decision: this is the classic load balancer idle-timeout problem, and the symptom pattern — roughly one minute, only on some paths, silent — is the fingerprint. I compare the LB's idle timeout with my heartbeat interval: an LB that closes at 60s and a server that pings only every 90s guarantees the LB wins. Fix: set the LB idle timeout above my heartbeat interval, and set my heartbeat interval comfortably below the LB timeout so *I* always know first. I send a WebSocket ping every 20–30 seconds and terminate anything that misses two rounds, so dead connections are detected in under a minute by me rather than being silently reaped by the edge. I also audit every hop — CDN, LBs between the CDN and origin — because there is often more than one idle timeout, and the innermost one is the one that matters. Trade-offs: heartbeats cost a small amount of bandwidth and CPU per connection, and aggressive timeouts will drop high-latency mobile clients that take 45s to wake; the mobile case argues for a somewhat longer deadline with a separate treatment for clients that are merely idle versus unresponsive. Failure scenario: a proxy that buffers rather than closing, so pings appear to succeed but nothing reaches the client — diagnosed by a packet capture or by testing through each hop individually. Prevention: an end-to-end synthetic WebSocket client on a 5-minute cycle through the real production path, which fails long before users report it."

topics.title: Scaling WebSockets
topics.description: Scaling WebSockets within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: The core problem: connection-local state
Patterns
Sticky sessions: the honest framing
Redis adapter fan-out
Registry-based, fully stateless fan-out
Load balancer configuration
Idle timeout above your heartbeat interval (see 5.7.2 Q8).
Connection limits per instance so one instance is not OOM-killed by a burst: a max_connections on the instance and a queue/redirect at the LB.
Disable buffering and compression on the WebSocket path; some proxies inject a 30s idle timeout of their own.
Health check must be shallow (a TCP/HTTP check on the *upgrade* endpoint), not a WebSocket-level check that breaks every connection on restart.

Drain on deploy: flip readiness to false (LB stops routing new *HTTP*, but existing WS connections stay), stop accepting new upgrades, broadcast "going away" (1001), let clients reconnect, wait up to N seconds, then exit.
Per-instance limits and capacity planning
commonMistakes: sticky sessions as the default answer; assuming the Redis adapter deduplicates; skipping the origin socket so the sender gets its own message twice; a connection registry without TTL; a health check that churns live sockets on every deploy.
practiceTasks: run three ws instances behind one load balancer with Redis pub/sub fan-out, then SIGKILL one instance mid-stream and verify clients reconnect, resync missed messages, and that no registry keys leak.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why do WebSockets need special handling to scale?
🟢 What is a sticky session and when is it required?
🟡 What does the Socket.IO Redis adapter actually solve?
🟡 Why do you skip the originating socket when echoing via pub/sub?
🔴 Design a stateless, drainable WebSocket deployment with no sticky sessions.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 50k concurrent chat clients, three deploys a week, and a 30-second rollout window. Decision: no sticky sessions. Fan-out goes through Redis pub/sub, and each instance keeps only its own sockets in memory. On connection, the client authenticates over the upgrade request, then the instance claims conn:<clientId> with a 90-second TTL and renews it every 30 seconds; publishing to a room publishes to Redis and every instance forwards to its local members, skipping the originating socket. Reasoning: without sticky sessions I can scale instances independently and deploy without disconnecting anyone, and the connection registry plus TTL means a crashed instance's entries expire on their own instead of requiring cleanup. Trade-offs: every message now costs a Redis round trip, so I batch fan-out for high-traffic rooms and I accept that Redis becomes a delivery dependency — if Redis is down, sockets stay connected but messages stop, so I alert on Redis pub/sub health and have the client fall back to REST fetch of missed messages. Failure scenario: a deploy during peak. The instance flips readiness, sends close code 1001 to its sockets, and exits only after clients reconnect elsewhere; because there is no sticky routing, the reconnect can land on any instance and still receive messages. Alternative: an external realtime broker removes the Redis dependency and the socket ops entirely at a per-message cost, which I would take if real-time is becoming a product differentiator rather than a feature."

topics.title: Socket.IO Deep
topics.description: a library that provides its own protocol on top of WebSocket (with HTTP long-polling fallback), plus rooms, namespaces, acknowledgements, middleware, connection state recovery, and cluster adapters. It is not raw WebSocket, and a WebSocket client cannot talk to it.
keyConcepts: Why it is not raw WebSocket
Connection state recovery
Choosing Socket.IO vs raw ws

Socket.IO when: you need rooms, acks, reconnection-with-retry semantics, cross-instance fan-out, and a heterogeneous client team (React Native, plain JS, non-Node SDKs). Default for chat and notifications.

Raw ws when: you need protocol-level control, minimal overhead at very large scale, binary framing you own, interoperability with non-Socket.IO clients, or you do not want a dependency that must be upgraded in lockstep with your clients.
commonMistakes: using Socket.IO when raw ws is required for interop; assuming recovery survives a server restart; forgetting socket.to(...) vs socket.in(...) semantics; leaving transports: ['websocket'] for users behind restrictive proxies.
practiceTasks: build a chat server on Socket.IO with two namespaces (/chat and /admin), room fan-out, acks, middleware auth, a Redis adapter across three instances, connection state recovery, and a test that kills a client for 30 seconds and asserts zero missed messages.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why can't a plain WebSocket client connect to a Socket.IO server?
🟡 What are namespaces for and how do they differ from rooms?
🟡 What do acknowledgement callbacks buy you?
🟡 How does Socket.IO's reconnection differ from a hand-rolled client backoff?
🔴 What is connection state recovery and what are its two limitations?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: users on mobile lose connectivity for 10–60 seconds constantly, and with raw WebSockets they miss every message that happened while disconnected and then have to refetch the whole conversation on reconnect. Decision: enable Socket.IO connectionStateRecovery with maxDisconnectionDuration: 120000. When a client reconnects and presents the same recovery token, the server replays the packets it sent during the disconnection window, so the client applies a normal ordered stream instead of doing a full resync. Reasoning: this is a big correctness and latency win for exactly the reconnect pattern real users produce, and it is built into the library rather than something I maintain myself. The two limitations I would state in the same breath: first, the recovery buffer must live somewhere the reconnecting instance can read, so with a Redis adapter it lives in Redis — which means real-time recovery now depends on Redis, and with a single-instance in-memory adapter a server restart loses the buffer. Second, it is best-effort within the window: if the client is gone longer than the configured duration, or the buffer has been evicted, recovery does not apply and the client must do a full resync. So I still implement the resync path as the fallback, and I do not treat recovery as a substitute for a cursor. Trade-offs: it consumes memory per disconnected socket for the window duration, and it adds a state store to operate. Failure scenario: Redis is unavailable exactly when 5,000 clients reconnect — recovery fails and the whole cohort does a full refetch, which is precisely the thundering herd I was trying to avoid; so I also rate-limit the resync endpoint. Alternative: client-side cursors over raw WebSocket with per-message sequence numbers, which is more work but has no server-side recovery state to keep."

topics.title: Reconnection and Resync
topics.description: Reconnection and Resync within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: The two different problems people conflate
Reconnecting — establishing a new transport-level connection after a drop.
Resyncing — establishing what you missed and filling the gap without duplicating what you already have.
Client-side reconnect loop with jitter
Why jitter is mandatory here: a server restart makes every client disconnect at the same instant; deterministic backoff re-creates the same spike 500ms later, for many rounds. Jitter spreads it.

Cap the delay, add a maxRetries ceiling (then show "reconnecting…" UI), reset the attempt counter only after a connection has been stable for a while (e.g. 30s) so a flapping connection does not keep resetting to attempt 1.
Respect Retry-After-style server hints: if the server sends 10013 try again later or a custom rate-limit code, back off accordingly.
Reconnect on online/visibilitychange events — a phone regains network on online, and there is no point holding a dead socket.
Server-side resync protocol: cursors
The cursor must be an ordering position in your store, not a timestamp: Kafka offset, database sequence, or a per-conversation monotonically increasing id. Timestamps collide and skew.

Retention defines what is recoverable. If your log keeps 7 days and the client was offline 8 days, you cannot replay — you must send a fresh snapshot and say so. Handle truncated explicitly; silently sending a partial catch-up is a data-corruption bug in the UI.

Idempotent client application: every message carries an id and a seq. The client keeps lastSeq and Set of recently applied ids (bounded, e.g. last 500), drops anything with seq <= lastSeq or a duplicate id, and applies the rest in order. Without this, the same message arrives twice (once live, once in the catch-up) and the UI shows duplicates — the single most common real-time bug.
commonMistakes: timestamps as cursors; live delivery starting before catch-up completes; no bounded dedupe on the client; silently truncating when history is gone; resetting the backoff attempt counter on every connect.
practiceTasks: implement resync with a 7-day-retention store, a 500-event catch-up cap, per-room sequence numbers, client-side lastSeq plus bounded id dedupe, and a chaos test that kills the client for 60s, for 10 minutes, and for 8 days, asserting the right behaviour in each case.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why must reconnect backoff include jitter?
🟡 What is a cursor and why is a timestamp a bad cursor?
🟡 When is "resubscribe from scratch" the correct resync?
🔴 Design the resync protocol for a chat room with 7-day retention.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: chat rooms, clients disconnect for 30–300 seconds on mobile, and we must not lose or duplicate a single message. Decision: every persisted message gets a per-room monotonic seq (assigned by the room's write path, not by the broker) and an immutable id. The client keeps lastSeq and a bounded set of recently applied ids. On connect the client sends { topic, since: lastSeq }; the server replies with the ordered batch after lastSeq, then switches to live delivery, and the client only starts rendering the live stream after the catch-up batch is applied. If the requested since is older than the retention window, the server replies truncated with the earliest available seq and the client replaces its view with a fresh snapshot. Reasoning: per-room monotonic sequence numbers, not timestamps, are the only cursor that is correct across multiple gateway instances and NTP steps. Ordering application — catch-up first, then live — plus id-based dedupe on the client means an event delivered both in the catch-up batch and live is applied once. Trade-offs: a per-room sequence generator is a serialization point per room, which is fine (per-key ordering already exists, see 5.6.13) but not global; the client must buffer live messages during catch-up; and the dedupe set costs memory per client. Failure scenario: catch-up of a huge gap (client offline a week) streams tens of thousands of messages and the UI freezes. So I cap catch-up batch size, page the replay, and switch to truncated + snapshot beyond a threshold like 500 events. Alternative: full-snapshot-on-reconnect only, which is dramatically simpler and fine for dashboards, but wrong for chat because it discards scrollback and can be megabytes."

topics.title: Ordering and Gaps in Real-Time Streams
topics.description: Ordering and Gaps in Real-Time Streams within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: Per-conversation (or per-topic) ordering is the goal; global ordering across all rooms is not feasible and not wanted, because a global order serialises your whole fan-out.
Sequence numbers, not timestamps, are the ordering primitive. Assign them where the write happens so they are consistent across all gateway instances.
Gap detection is mandatory. A receiver must notice it missed seq = 104 when it has 103 and 105. Options, in increasing order of cost:
Pause and request resync for the missing range (correct, simplest).
Request only the missing range ({ kind: 'gap', topic, from: 104, to: 105 }) and splice it in.
Accept the gap and mark the stream as lossy — only acceptable for non-critical data (analytics, presence pings, cursor positions) where "latest value wins" is semantically correct.

Lossy-by-design channels: for state that is superseded (cursor position, "user is typing", slider position, presence heartbeats, video quality), the newest value is the only one that matters. For these, use a coalescing channel: keep only the latest value per key, and drop intermediate ones. This is a legitimate and valuable design decision — a typing indicator should not queue 20 updates during a network blip.

Client dedupe and ordering rules: apply only seq > lastSeq; drop seq <= lastSeq; ignore duplicate ids; buffer out-of-order arrivals briefly (e.g. 250ms) and reorder by seq before applying, so a single reordered packet does not trigger a full resync.

Why global ordering is not feasible: it requires a single serialization point (one partition/one consumer), so throughput is bounded by that consumer and any hot entity blocks every other tenant. State this explicitly in an interview, with the cost.

Broker vs application ordering: brokers guarantee per-partition order; if you have multiple producers writing to the same partition, arrival order is the order, which may differ from business order. When business order matters (state transitions), derive it from the entity's own version/revision rather than from transport order.
commonMistakes: applying events by arrival order; no bounded dedupe set; unbounded reorder buffer; treating typing indicators as lossless events; assuming broker order equals business order.
practiceTasks: build a client-side stream applier with lastSeq, an id LRU, a reorder buffer, and gap requests, then feed it a recorded stream containing duplicates, reorderings, and holes and assert the final applied state matches the source.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What is the difference between per-topic and global ordering, and what does global cost?
🟡 How do you detect a gap, and what do you do about it?
🔴 Design the client-side apply algorithm for a stream that can deliver out of order and with duplicates.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a client receives real-time events over an unreliable connection with at-least-once delivery, so events arrive out of order, duplicated, and occasionally missing. Decision: the client keeps lastSeq and a bounded LRU of recently applied ids. Each message carries seq and id. On receipt: if the id is already in the LRU, drop it as a duplicate; if seq <= lastSeq, drop it as stale; if seq === lastSeq + 1, apply immediately and advance; if seq > lastSeq + 1, push it into a short reorder buffer and start a 250ms timer, then when the timer fires, apply everything contiguous from lastSeq and send a gap request for the first missing seq through the highest received. Reasoning: the LRU handles the overlap between catch-up and live delivery, which is a designed duplicate rather than a bug; lastSeq handles reordering and staleness in O(1); and the reorder buffer with a bounded timer avoids triggering an expensive server resync for a single reordered packet, which is the common case. Trade-offs: the reorder buffer adds up to 250ms of latency in the reordering case, and it costs memory per client, so the LRU is bounded to a few hundred ids. Failure scenario: if the server cannot serve the gap — the data is outside retention — it replies truncated and the client must replace its state with a fresh snapshot rather than silently applying a hole, because a hole in a chat transcript is a visible correctness bug while a snapshot is merely a flash of the UI. Alternative: client-side cursors only, with no buffer, where every reordering triggers a resync — far simpler, and it is the right choice if reordering is rare and volume is low."

topics.title: Authentication for WebSockets
topics.description: Authentication for WebSockets within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: The constraint that shapes everything
The two authorization levels
Connection-level: the socket is authenticated once; every message inherits that identity. Simple, and correct when the whole connection is scoped to one tenant/user (chat, dashboards).

Per-message authorization: every inbound message is checked against the user's permissions *at that moment*. Required whenever a socket spans multiple resources — a user subscribing to channels, or an admin console that can act on any tenant. Practical approach: a coarse connection-level check plus an explicit subscribe message whose authorization is re-checked server-side, and an ACL cache with a short TTL plus invalidation on permission change.
Never trust client-supplied identity fields in messages ({ userId: ... }) — take identity from the connection.

Multi-tenancy: bind tenantId from the session, and validate that every subscription target belongs to it. This is the highest-risk real-time vulnerability: a client subscribing to another tenant's room by guessing an id.
Long-lived connections outlive tokens
Refresh over the socket: the client sends a new token on an auth.refresh message every few minutes; the server validates and updates socket.data. Cheap and works.

Expire and reconnect: after the token's expiry the server sends { kind: 'auth.expired', code: 4001 } and closes; the client refreshes the token over HTTP and reconnects with resync. Simplest and most robust, at the cost of a reconnect every token lifetime — which is fine if reconnects are cheap and resync works (5.7.6).
Both: refresh in place, and reconnect as the backstop when refresh fails.
Set an absolute maximum connection lifetime (e.g. 12 hours) so you have a natural point to re-verify permissions and rotate internal state.
Permission changes mid-connection: publish an invalidation event that forces affected sockets to re-subscribe or close.
commonMistakes: long-lived tokens in the WebSocket URL; trusting userId from message payloads; no Origin validation; never expiring a long-lived connection; no per-connection message rate limit.
practiceTasks: implement cookie + Origin auth at upgrade, first-message auth with a 5s deadline, single-use 30s tickets from POST /ws-ticket, in-place token refresh, a 12-hour hard cap, and a revocation channel that closes sockets on permission change.

🟡 Why are tokens in the query string dangerous?
🟡 What is the ticket pattern and why is it the safest for browsers?
🔴 Your socket lives for hours and the token expires in 15 minutes. Design the lifecycle.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: chat sockets stay open for hours; our access tokens live 15 minutes, and reconnecting on every expiry would be wasteful. Decision: refresh in place with reconnect as the backstop. The client sends a auth.refresh message every 10 minutes with a freshly obtained short-lived token obtained over normal HTTPS, and the server re-validates it and updates socket.data. If a refresh fails, or if the socket has been open for more than 12 hours, the server sends { kind: 'auth.expired', code: 4001 } and closes; the client then reconnects and resyncs from its cursor. Reasoning: refreshing in place avoids a reconnect storm every 15 minutes, but it is a mechanism that can silently stop working, so it needs a hard backstop — the absolute lifetime cap and the forced close — otherwise long-lived sessions accumulate stale permissions. Trade-offs: in-place refresh means a socket's authorization state is mutable, so permission changes must also actively reach sockets, which means an invalidation channel; that is more machinery than reconnect-on-every-expiry. Failure scenario: refresh tokens get revoked (password change, SSO logout) but existing sockets keep working for up to the 12-hour cap. Mitigation: on revocation events I publish to the user's sockets and close them immediately, so the revocation path is explicit. Also, a socket that receives a refresh it cannot validate is closed within 30 seconds rather than left in limbo. Alternative: close and reconnect on every token expiry. It is simpler, and with cheap reconnects plus a solid resync protocol — which I want anyway for 5.7.6 — it may honestly be the better trade."

topics.title: Choosing a Real-Time Backend
topics.description: Choosing a Real-Time Backend within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: Decision heuristic
commonMistakes: choosing managed because demos are easy; ignoring per-message cost at chatty volumes; self-hosting without budgeting Redis for fan-out; underestimating that client-side lock-in makes migration expensive.
practiceTasks: prototype the same chat feature on ws + Redis and on a managed SDK, and write a comparison of implementation LOC, ops steps, projected monthly cost at 1k and 100k concurrent users, and the migration plan between them.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 When is a managed realtime service the right call?
🟡 What does self-hosting `ws` actually commit you to owning?
🟡 Why can per-message pricing change the architecture?
🔴 Compare Ably-style managed vs Socket.IO + Redis for a 30k-concurrent chat product.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 30k concurrent chat users, ~5 messages per second per room, roughly 400 messages per second aggregate, and a two-person platform team. Decision: Socket.IO on our own infrastructure with a Redis adapter, not a managed service. Reasoning: at 400 messages per second the per-message cost of a managed provider is manageable, but managed presence and history are not what differentiate us — chat quality is — so I would be paying for features we would not use while taking on lock-in in our client protocol. We already run Redis and Node, so the incremental ops burden is one more deployment template and a Redis adapter we know how to operate. Trade-offs: I accept that presence, history and reconnection are my responsibility, which is real work, and I accept the horizontal scaling cost: every message crosses Redis, so our Redis bill and our p99 fan-out latency both scale with message volume. Failure scenario: a fan-out peak during a viral event overwhelms Redis, and because the fan-out is on the critical path, chat latency degrades globally. Mitigations: coalesce typing indicators and presence pings (they are lossy-by-design), batch fan-out per room per tick, and put a per-connection bufferedAmount ceiling so slow clients are dropped rather than OOM-ing the gateway. I would revisit managed at roughly ten times the volume, when per-message pricing is still lower than the Redis plus instance cost and the managed edge's global reach actually matters. Alternative: managed now, with a thin internal interface over the realtime client so a later migration is a one-component change rather than a flag day."

interviewQuestions.text: 🔴 What lock-in does a managed realtime SDK create and how do you mitigate it?
🔴 When would MQTT be right in a web product?
🔴 Your real-time service must pass an audit about data residency. How does that change the choice?
⚫ How do you migrate from managed realtime to self-hosted without a flag day?

tradeoffs: Managed buys you presence, message history, global edge PoPs, SDK coverage, and no on-call. It costs per message (which punishes chatty apps), and it puts a hard dependency between you and your users in the moment they care most. It also caps how custom you can get: if you need 200-byte messages at 50k msgs/sec, per-message pricing may exceed your infra budget.

Self-hosted ws is free per message and totally flexible, and it is also a distributed-systems project you now own: presence, fan-out across instances, connection draining, TLS termination, and 3am pages.
A middle path is Socket.IO/Centrifugo on your own infrastructure: you get the feature set (rooms, presence, history) without reimplementing it, and you keep the protocol and the cost profile.

topics.title: Real-Time at Scale Architecture
topics.description: Real-Time at Scale Architecture within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: Layer responsibilities
Broker as backbone: every meaningful client message becomes a broker event; gateways are stateless delivery engines. This is what lets you scale gateways independently and drain them on deploy.

Gateway fan-out: one instance receives one event and delivers it to its local subscribers. It must be *fast* and *bounded*: per-connection send queue, bufferedAmount ceiling, and a hard drop-and-resync policy rather than unbounded buffering.

Per-region: run a regional gateway fleet with a regional broker (or a global broker with regional fan-out channels) so a user in Frankfurt talks to Frankfurt. Cross-region fan-out is a latency and cost decision, not a default. Presence is naturally regional; message history should be globally replicated if users travel.
Presence in Redis: per-room sorted sets, regional, with a lease — see 5.7.5.

Ordering guarantees: per-topic sequence numbers assigned at the writer, per-partition ordering if a broker provides it, and client gap detection. A gateway must never reorder; it delivers in the order the broker gave it, with an out-of-order flag if it can detect it (it generally cannot, which is why the client also dedupes).
Sharding: clientId % N for gateway affinity when you do need it, with rebalancing on scale events handled by client reconnect.
Debuggability practices
commonMistakes: using connection ids as metric labels; not counting dropped messages; relying on aggregate metrics when the failure is per-instance; no synthetic canary; draining without a "going away" signal.
practiceTasks: instrument a ws gateway with the full metric set above, expose a per-connection debug endpoint, and run a chaos test that kills one instance and one Redis node while a synthetic client asserts zero silent drops.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What is each layer's responsibility in a real-time architecture?
🟡 Why must gateways be stateless?
🔴 How do you keep 1M connections debuggable? Name the metrics.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: we want to operate a 1M-connection real-time system with a small team and be able to answer 'what happened at 14:02' within minutes. Decision: I fix the metric and correlation set first, before adding any feature. Metrics: connections open per instance and fleet total; connection open/close rate, because churn explains latency spikes better than any other single signal; upgrade-to-authenticated duration; messages in and out per second, per gateway and for the broker, so fan-out amplification is directly visible as the out/in ratio; the send_duration histogram and bufferedAmount p99, which are the leading indicators of a gateway being overwhelmed; dropped messages broken out by reason; heartbeat timeouts; resync request rate; event-loop lag p99, which is the hard ceiling on everything else; and broker-side publish lag. Correlation: every connection gets an id encoding instance and sequence, and every log line carries connId, userId, roomId, and msgId, so one grep takes me from a user report to the full session history. Trade-offs: this is roughly a dozen metrics and it needs cheap high-cardinality-by-connection labels done carefully — connId as a metric label would melt the metrics backend, so connection ids belong in logs and traces, not in metric dimensions, and only aggregate dimensions go into metrics. Failure scenario: a memory leak on one instance manifests as rising resync_requests fleet-wide because that instance keeps dying; the per-instance connections_open panel plus connections_opened/closed rate is what catches it before users do. Prevention: a synthetic canary connection per region that measures round-trip time and gap count every 30 seconds, so silent data loss is detected by us rather than by users."

topics.title: Testing Real-Time Systems
topics.description: Testing Real-Time Systems within Real-Time Systems.
keyConcepts: Deterministic integration tests with an in-memory bus
Use a real WebSocket client (ws) against a real server for the protocol tests — you cannot unit-test frames.

Contract tests for message schemas: share the Zod schemas between client and server (single source of truth, see 5.10.4) and add a test that every message the server can emit validates against the shared union, plus a test that the client rejects unknown message kinds instead of crashing. Run the *client's* validation against a *recorded* server stream to catch server changes that break old clients.

Chaos tests: kill a client mid-stream (SIGKILL, not close) and assert the server reaps it within two heartbeat intervals; kill the broker and assert reconnect + resync produces no gaps; kill a gateway instance and assert clients land elsewhere and resync; run a slow consumer (a client that does not read) and assert the server drops it rather than buffering.

Clock control: inject a now() and a scheduler instead of calling Date.now() and setTimeout directly. Heartbeat deadlines, idle timeouts, JWT expiry, and backoff are all time-dependent, and tests that use real time are flaky and slow. With an injectable clock you can advance 10 minutes instantly and assert a heartbeat timeout fired.

Contract tests between client and server for reconnects: a scripted client that connects, drops, reconnects with a stale cursor, and asserts the exact message sequence — golden-file style — is the highest-value real-time test you can write.
commonMistakes: testing real-time logic only through sockets; real-time dependence in tests (flaky); no tolerance for unknown message kinds; no recorded-stream regression test.
practiceTasks: build an injectable-clock + injectable-bus test suite for a chat hub: 10 unit tests on the memory bus, 3 real-socket integration tests, a chaos test that SIGKILLs a client, and a recorded-stream regression test for message schema drift.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟡 Why make the broker injectable, and what does that buy you?
🟡 Why must you still test with real WebSocket clients?
🔴 How do you test heartbeat timeouts deterministically?
🔴 Write the chaos test for "kill a client mid-stream".
🔴 How do you catch a server-side message schema change that breaks old clients?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: the mobile app in the field is on version 3.2, our server is shipping a new message kind, and we cannot force an update. Decision: the message contract is a shared discriminated union validated with Zod, published from a single package, and I enforce it with three tests. One, a server-side exhaustiveness test that every emit site type-checks against the union, so an unvalidated new message kind is a compile error. Two, a test that replays a recorded stream of server messages through the *oldest supported* client schema and asserts every message still validates — this is what catches a removed or renamed field. Three, a test that feeds an unknown kind to the client and asserts it is ignored with a log line rather than crashing, so a newer server can safely talk to an older app. Reasoning: schema drift is the default failure mode of real-time systems because there is no compiler linking the two ends — TypeScript erases types, so the type is documentation unless something validates at runtime. Trade-offs: keeping the client tolerant means every unknown message is silently dropped, so I log an unknown-kind counter and alert if it is non-zero after a server deploy, which tells me an old population exists. Failure scenario: a field changes from string to number and the old app renders undefined — a runtime test that replays actual payloads through the old client build is the only thing that catches it. Alternative: versioned message envelopes with a v field and per-version schemas, which is more machinery but lets you support several client generations deliberately instead of by tolerance."

topics.title: File upload (multipart, presigned URLs)
topics.description: File upload is not a form field; it is a resumable, observable, retryable, cancellable transfer that a user is watching. The design problem has five parts: the UX states (idle → validating → uploading with progress → processing → done/failed), the transport (single POST vs multipart vs direct-to-object-storage), the preview, the queue (concurrency), and the failure/retry path.
keyConcepts: Why you cannot use fetch for progress
The transport decision — this is the real engineering
Previews — the part that looks easy and is not
The upload queue UX
"Why can't you get upload progress with fetch?"
"Presigned vs multipart: when and why?"
"What must the server do after a presigned upload, and why?"
"How do you make a 2 GB upload resumable?"
"How do you avoid leaking memory with previews?"
"What are the security risks of client uploads?"
commonMistakes: fetch for a progress bar (no progress events). Revoking an object URL while it is still displayed. Trusting file.type server-side. Presigning without ownership scoping or with a 24-hour expiry. Uploading through the app server for multi-GB files. No concurrency limit (20 parallel 100 MB uploads). Announcing every percent to a live region. Losing the queue on refresh.
URL.createObjectURL without revoke; unbounded concurrency; no server-side verification of the uploaded object; assuming a presigned PUT means the file is validated.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why you cannot use fetch for progress and when you would use it.
Explain the transport decision — this is the real engineering and when you would use it.
Explain previews — the part that looks easy and is not and when you would use it.
Explain the upload queue ux and when you would use it.
Explain "why can't you get upload progress with fetch?" and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Direct-to-storage saves the most money of anything in this section. A 2 GB/day video product that proxies uploads pays double egress and needs serverless with huge timeouts; presigned PUTs make the app server stateless.

Presigned URLs are capabilities: short expiry, exact key, exact content type, pinned content length, and a quarantine/ prefix that only your worker can promote. Never let the client choose the key freely (path traversal, overwriting other users' objects, serving XSS from your domain).
Timeouts and proxies: an upload through your server dies at 30–60 s on most ingress. That alone is the reason to move large uploads off your server.

Resumability requires persisting { key, uploadId, parts: [{ PartNumber, ETag }] } in IndexedDB; on resume, call ListParts and upload only what is missing. This is a real feature users notice on mobile.

Never trust File.type — it is whatever the OS reported, and on some platforms it is empty. Sniff magic bytes server-side (file-type), re-encode images, strip EXIF, and transcode video (an uploaded "video" can be a 4 GB decompression bomb).

Serving uploads: serve user content from a *different domain* than your app (so an XSS in an HTML upload cannot touch your session), with Content-Disposition: attachment for non-media, a strict Content-Type, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
Cost/UX: for large files, show an estimated time, run uploads while the user does something else, and support paste-from-clipboard (onPaste) and drag-from-Finder.
Mobile: capture="environment" for camera, accept="image/*" for the picker (accepts HEIC on iOS), and remember iOS may downscale the video before it reaches you.

topics.title: Image processing
topics.description: Image processing within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: sharp is the default image tool

Pipeline shape: original lands in S3 → DB row created → queue job → worker reads from S3 (stream), writes variants to S3, updates the DB row with the variant keys → CDN serves. The worker does not hold the original in memory and does not use the API server's CPU budget.

Responsive variants: a fixed ladder (320, 640, 960, 1280, 1920, 2560) plus AVIF and WebP and a JPEG fallback, with <picture> + srcset + sizes on the client (Phase 3 Part 3 covers the markup). AVIF encodes noticeably smaller but is slower to encode and slightly less universally decoded; WebP is the pragmatic default with AVIF for clients that support it.

EXIF stripping is a privacy requirement, not a nicety: photos from phones carry GPS coordinates, device serial numbers, and timestamps. Strip by default; keep a separate, access-controlled copy if there is a legal reason to retain the original.

Lazy generation (on-demand derivatives): do not generate 8 variants for every upload. Generate one 480px "preview" eagerly, and generate the rest on first request, caching the result — either in the app (with a lock to avoid a thundering herd) or at the CDN with a rewrite to a "resize" origin. This is a large cost saver on image-heavy products.
Content-addressed derived keys (derived/{hash-of-(sourceKey,width,format,q)}) make the cache naturally idempotent: the same request always produces the same key.

Video transcoding is a separate, heavier pipeline. Minimum viable: transcode to MP4 (H.264 + AAC) for broad compatibility and generate a poster frame; use HLS for adaptive streaming (multiple bitrate renditions plus a manifest playlist) or DASH when you need CMAF and offline/DVR features. HLS costs more to produce (many renditions) but plays everywhere and is the industry default; DASH is better on some platforms and required for some DRM workflows.

Transcode reality check: ffmpeg is CPU-heavy and slow. Use a queue with bounded concurrency (CPU count, not queue depth), per-job timeout, and a hard memory cap; consider managed transcoding services for the long tail. Codec parameters matter: two-pass for target bitrate, -movflags +faststart so the moov atom is at the front (otherwise the browser must download the tail before playing), and -g keyframe interval aligned to the HLS segment length so segments start on keyframes.
Audio/FFmpeg gotchas: shell out with argument arrays, never string interpolation (injection), set -nostdin, always capture stderr for diagnosis, and set explicit output paths.
commonMistakes: buffering the source image in memory; skipping EXIF stripping; -movflags forgotten; unbounded transcode concurrency on a CPU-bound worker; generating every variant eagerly.
practiceTasks: build a worker that takes one uploaded image and produces thumbnail/medium/large in WebP + AVIF + JPEG fallback, strips EXIF, verifies GPS is gone, and enforces a memory ceiling — then benchmark throughput at concurrency 1, 4, and 16.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why strip EXIF by default?
🟡 What does `rotate()` then removing orientation do?
🟡 What is `limitInputPixels` for?
🔴 How do you stop an upload from generating 8 × 4 derivatives and a 4K transcode for every file?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: image-heavy product, 2M uploads a month, and generating a full derivative ladder eagerly would cost more than the storage itself. Decision: two tiers. Eagerly generate exactly one 480px WebP preview plus the EXIF-stripped original; generate the rest on demand at first request. The on-demand path computes a content-addressed key from (sourceKey, width, format, quality), so the cache is idempotent, and I guard against a thundering herd with a short Redis lock per key plus the CDN caching the result. Reasoning: most images are viewed at one size by most users, so eager generation is paying for 90% of variants that are never requested, and content-addressed keys mean the second request is free and two concurrent requests produce the same artefact rather than duplicates. Trade-offs: the first request for an uncached variant is slow, which I mitigate by generating the two most common sizes eagerly (thumbnail and a 1280px "large"), so the common path is never slow; and the on-demand path needs its own lock, error handling, and metrics. Failure scenario: a viral post makes every viewer request 12 sizes and the resize workers become the bottleneck. Mitigation: a per-key lock so the work happens once, plus a fallback to the closest already-generated size when the resize queue is saturated, which degrades quality rather than latency. Prevention: track derivative cache hit rate and resize queue wait time, and if hit rate is high, promote the popular sizes to eager generation automatically. Alternative: eagerly generate everything for a plan-limited set of sizes and lazily grow the ladder based on which sizes are actually requested."

topics.title: OAuth integrations
topics.description: OAuth integrations within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: The flows
Storage

Refresh: store refresh_token, expires_at, and a scope set. Refresh proactively at ~80% of lifetime with a lock per credential so concurrent requests do not race (provider-dependent: some providers invalidate a refresh token on use, so a race revokes your access — hence the lock and keeping the *previous* token until the new one works).
Revocation: a DELETE on the provider when the user disconnects, and treat a 400 invalid_grant response as "must re-consent" — surface that in the UI rather than retrying forever.

Scopes: request the minimum, record the *granted* scopes (they can differ from requested), and re-consent when you need more. Requesting everything up front gets your app rejected by review and trains users to click "Allow" without reading.

Refresh-token rotation hazards: rotating tokens mean a crash mid-rotation can lose access permanently. Store the new refresh token transactionally and only delete the old one once the new one is confirmed working.

Webhooks from OAuth providers: verify their signature (same discipline as Stripe, different scheme), dedupe on their event id, and process idempotently. Providers' webhooks are also how you learn about *revoked* grants.

Reconnect flows: when a grant dies mid-session, do not silently retry in a loop. Queue the action that needs the integration, mark it blocked_on_reconnect, show the user a "Reconnect <provider>" action, and resume the queued work when the new token arrives. That is the pattern that makes integrations feel reliable rather than broken.
Long-running work in an integration: never hold an HTTP request open while an OAuth-protected third-party call retries; enqueue and let the worker handle reconnection.
commonMistakes: storing tokens in plaintext; no state validation; refreshing on the request path without a lock; deleting the old refresh token too early; retrying invalid_grant forever; requesting every scope.
practiceTasks: implement the authorization-code + PKCE flow with encrypted per-tenant token storage, a lock-protected proactive refresher at 80% of lifetime, revocation on disconnect, granted-scope recording, and a queued job that is blocked and resumed on reconnect.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why PKCE, and why on every flow?
🟡 What is the `state` parameter for?
🔴 How do you store per-tenant OAuth tokens securely?
🔴 What happens if two requests refresh the same refresh token concurrently?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a per-tenant token store with expires_at, and two requests race to refresh the same credential. Some providers issue single-use rotating refresh tokens, so the second request presents an already-used token and the provider responds invalid_grant — which, if we treat that as fatal, revokes a working integration because of our own race. Decision: a per-credential Redis lock (SET NX PX) around refresh, plus write-on-read semantics where the new refresh token is stored transactionally and the previous one is retained until the new one has been successfully used once. Reasoning: the provider's guarantee is single-use rotation; our guarantee must be single-flight use, and the failure mode is not a transient error but permanent revocation, so a plain mutex is not enough — I need the ability to recover. Trade-offs: a distributed lock adds a Redis dependency on the integration path, and lock handling must be careful (lease expiry mid-refresh is possible); keeping the old token temporarily means the record holds two secrets, so both must be encrypted and both must be purged on success. Failure scenario: the process dies between storing the new token and deleting the old one. That is safe, because the old token is still valid for one more use only if we have not already used it — so I record which token was last used and only retry with the newest. If the provider has already consumed it, the integration is dead and we surface a reconnect prompt rather than looping. Prevention: alert on invalid_grant rate per tenant, because a burst means a code path is double-refreshing; and set refresh at 80% of lifetime so there is time to retry before expiry. Alternative: a scheduled refresher that refreshes all credentials proactively on a cron, which removes the race from the request path entirely at the cost of a background job per credential."

topics.title: Third-party API resilience (retries, circuit breaker)
topics.description: Third-party API resilience (retries, circuit breaker) within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: 1. Timeouts at every layer
Without a timeout, one slow dependency becomes an unbounded pile-up of open sockets, and your process runs out of file descriptors — the classic cascading failure.
Propagate a deadline (a deadline header or a context field) so *your* upstream knows your remaining budget and does not start work it cannot finish.

Set a lower timeout on internal calls than on external ones, and never let a request-timeout cascade: if service A calls B with 5s and B calls C with 5s, one slow C consumes three layers of thread/connection capacity.
Always finally the timer clear. Always drain or cancel the response body (res.body?.cancel()) on early exit, or you leak a socket.
2. Retries, only where they are safe
Never retry a non-idempotent POST without an idempotency key (see 5.8.9's neighbours in 5.6.10: Stripe accepts them; most providers do not, so use a natural idempotency design or do not retry).
Jitter across *callers* too: add a small random spread so 5,000 workers do not all retry the failing dependency at the same instant.
3. Circuit breaker
Fail fast while open with a synthetic, clearly-typed error (DependencyUnavailable) so callers can degrade gracefully instead of hanging.

Per dependency, per region — a breaker is scoped to a specific dependency (and often a specific region of it), because a failure in one provider must not stop you calling another. Global breakers cause correlated outages.

Rolling window (e.g. last 20 requests, or last 60s), minimum volume before the breaker can trip (so 3 failures out of 3 requests at startup does not open it), separate thresholds for error ratio and latency (a dependency returning 200s in 30s is as broken as one returning 500s), and success threshold to close again (e.g. 5/5 successful probes).
commonMistakes: liveness checks that call dependencies; one global breaker; retrying non-idempotent POSTs; no minimum volume on the breaker; forgetting to clear/abort timers; failing the whole service when one dependency is degraded.
practiceTasks: implement a resilient HTTP client: layered timeouts, retry with full jitter + Retry-After, a per-dependency circuit breaker with half-open concurrency gate, a per-dependency bulkhead, single-flight request coalescing, and a fault-injecting server that returns 500s, 429s, and hangs — then prove no more than N concurrent upstream calls ever occur.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What are the four timeout layers on an outbound HTTP call?
🟡 When is it safe to retry?
🟡 What does `Retry-After` look like and how do you handle both forms?
🔴 Explain the three breaker states and the purpose of half-open.
🔴 Why must the breaker be per dependency and per region?
🔴 What is a bulkhead and how do you size it?
🔴 Design the degraded behaviour for a product-page enrichment service.
🔴 What is request coalescing and when does it matter most?
🔴 Your service's liveness probe starts failing when a third-party API is down. Why is that bad and what do you change?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: our liveness probe includes a call to a third-party enrichment API, and when that provider has an incident, Kubernetes restarts all our pods — turning a third-party degradation into a full outage of our service. Decision: liveness must depend only on whether *this* process can serve traffic, never on whether a dependency is reachable. So the liveness endpoint is a pure process check, readiness includes only local capacity checks (event-loop lag, memory, connection-pool headroom, queue depth), and dependency health is a separate signal used for alerting, breaker decisions, and graceful degradation. Reasoning: the purpose of a liveness probe is to detect a wedged process that cannot recover and should be restarted. A dependency outage is not a wedged process — restarting makes it worse, because we throw away warm caches, force a reconnect storm, and remove the capacity we need to serve cached or degraded responses. Failure scenario: a provider outage triggers liveness failures, every pod restarts simultaneously, the restart hammers the provider as it recovers, and our users see a total outage instead of a partial one. That is the textbook cascading failure. Prevention: a CI test that asserts the liness endpoint makes no network calls, plus a chaos drill that kills a dependency and confirms zero pod restarts while the service continues serving degraded responses. Trade-off: a dependency can then be fully down while we look healthy, so I compensate with per-dependency alerts on error ratio and latency, plus a visible degraded-mode indicator so the on-call knows without a page storm. Alternative: keep a lightweight dependency probe but mark it as a *separate* readiness gate used for draining rather than for restarts — useful when you want to stop sending new traffic to an instance that cannot serve, without killing it."
