topics.title: File Upload Deep
topics.description: File Upload Deep within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: The three upload architectures
Why multipart/form-data buffers
Presigned URLs
Conditions are the security control, not the key. A PUT presigned URL without a Content-Length and Content-Type condition lets anyone upload 10GB of anything to your bucket.
Expiry: minutes, not hours. A presigned URL in a browser tab is readable by the user and logged by the proxy; keep the window as short as the upload can tolerate.

Key must be server-generated — never let the client choose the whole key, or you get path traversal and overwrite of other users' objects. Generate a UUID key and carry the metadata in S3 object metadata, then map key → record in your DB.

Verify after the fact. The client uploading directly means your server never sees the bytes: verify with a post-upload HeadObject (size, ContentType) and a queue job that scans magic bytes, strips EXIF, and generates derivatives (5.8.3). Treat the metadata the client sent as untrusted.
Multipart uploads and resumability

Part sizing: minimum 5 MiB (except the last part); larger parts mean fewer requests but wasted bandwidth on retry. 8–16 MiB is the sweet spot for a browser uploader. Concurrency of 3–6 parallel part uploads hides latency without saturating the connection. Never upload more than 10,000 parts (S3 limit).

Resumability: persist { key, uploadId, parts: [{partNumber, etag}] } in IndexedDB (or server-side if you need cross-device resume). On resume, call ListParts to reconcile with the server's truth — the client's list can be stale — then continue from the first missing part. Parts already uploaded are never re-sent.
Etag ≠ MD5 for multipart uploads (it contains a part-count suffix), so validate integrity with your own checksum per part, or upload a checksum file with ChecksumAlgorithm: 'SHA256'.
Abort lifecycle: mark an upload pending in your DB, and have a scheduled job abort multipart uploads older than 24h, or you accumulate storage cost.
commonMistakes: client-chosen keys; long-expiry presigned URLs; multipart parts below 5 MiB; never aborting incomplete uploads; tracking progress with fetch; trusting client-declared Content-Type or size.
practiceTasks: implement multipart upload with resume in a browser (IndexedDB state, per-part presign, ListParts reconciliation, cancellation, quota check at presign time), plus the server-side 24-hour abort janitor and a corruption test using a deliberately altered part.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why does naive multipart handling buffer the whole file in memory?
🟢 Why is a PUT presigned URL without conditions dangerous?
🟡 What is the minimum multipart part size, and how do you choose the actual size?
🟡 Why must parts be sent in ascending order to `CompleteMultipartUpload`?
🟡 Why does `fetch` not support upload progress and `XMLHttpRequest` does?
🔴 Design the whole flow for a 5GB video upload with resume, progress, cancellation, and quota enforcement.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 5GB videos, flaky consumer connections, and we must show real progress, support resume, and stop over-quota users before they waste their bandwidth. Decision: multipart upload with 16 MiB parts and four concurrent part uploads, plus IndexedDB persistence of { key, uploadId, parts } so a browser refresh or crash can resume. The client asks our API for a presigned CreateMultipartUpload, then requests a presigned URL per part just-in-time from us, so URLs are short-lived and we never hand out a long-lived credential. Progress is computed from the sum of completed part sizes plus XMLHttpRequest.upload.onprogress for the in-flight parts, since fetch gives no progress events. On resume, the client calls our resume endpoint, which reconciles with S3 ListParts — the client's stored list may be stale — and returns the missing part numbers. Reasoning: presigning per part keeps the exposure window at minutes and lets us re-authorize each part, and the S3 ListParts reconciliation means we never trust client state. Trade-offs: 5GB at 16 MiB is roughly 320 parts, more requests than one PUT, and we need IndexedDB handling plus a cleanup path. Failure scenario: the user abandons the upload, so we hold an incomplete multipart upload and pay for it indefinitely. So a scheduled job aborts uploads older than 24 hours, and quota is checked at presign time and re-checked on completion. Prevention: alert on the count and total size of in-progress multipart uploads, because that number is the leading indicator of a client bug creating orphans. Alternative: the tus protocol with a resumable endpoint server-side, which gives standards-based resume and a library-managed protocol at the cost of a proxy component in front of storage."

topics.title: Storage Layout and Delivery
topics.description: Storage Layout and Delivery within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: Key naming

Prefix partitioning by tenant and date means a prefix listing is bounded (no millions of keys in one folder), lifecycle rules can target media/2024/ wholesale, and deletion by tenant is a prefix operation. Dates go in the *key*, not only in metadata, because metadata is not a prefix and listing cannot filter on it cheaply.

The uuid (not the original filename) prevents collisions, path traversal, and overwrites. Keep the user's filename in S3 object metadata (x-amz-meta-original-name) and in your DB, and sanitise it for the Content-Disposition header when serving.
Never let the key be derived from user input without normalisation. ../../other-tenant/key in a key parameter is the canonical S3 vulnerability.
Delivery options
CDN delivery
Range requests

Handle malformed ranges with 416 and a Content-Range: bytes */size header; browsers rely on this to retry correctly. Handle HEAD too. Multiple ranges (bytes=0-99,200-299) may be ignored — returning the whole body is acceptable if you signal Accept-Ranges honestly, but implementing multipart/byteranges is the correct answer.
CORS on the media origin needs Range in Access-Control-Request-Headers for cross-origin video seeking.
Content-type sniffing risks
Lifecycle policies
commonMistakes: allowing client-supplied keys; serving user content as text/html on the app origin; ignoring Range; setting immutable on non-hashed keys; no lifecycle policies.
practiceTasks: implement signed-URL download, Range/HEAD/206/416 handling, a CDN cache policy for hashed keys, and a tenant erasure job with a manifest — then verify curl with a mid-file range and an oversized range.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why put the date in the key rather than only in metadata?
🟡 Why use a UUID in the key instead of the user's filename?
🟡 When is a public bucket acceptable?
🔴 Implement `Range` handling properly, including 416 and `HEAD`.
🔴 Why do you serve user content from a different origin?
🔴 How do you serve a fresh version of an object whose key never changes?

🔴 How do you delete everything for one GDPR erasure request in a prefix-partitioned bucket?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a user requests erasure under GDPR and we have three years of media across media/{tenantId}/..., derived thumbnails keyed by their own prefixes, and an audit trail. Decision: erasure is a delete program, not a query. Our erasure service enumerates prefixes derived from the tenant id, lists objects in batches, deletes them, and records a signed deletion manifest (count, bytes, keys hashed, timestamp) in a compliance bucket with write-once retention. Derived images live under a per-object prefix keyed by the media id, so they are found by listing, not by reverse index. Audit logs are different: we do not erase them, we pseudonymise the user identifier, because an audit trail must remain attributable for security investigations while the personal data is minimised. Reasoning: prefix partitioning is what makes erasure tractable; without a tenant prefix you would need a reverse index that will inevitably drift out of sync with reality. Trade-offs: a per-tenant prefix means a hot tenant with millions of objects produces very large listings, so we list and delete in bounded batches with pagination, and we run erasure in a background job with progress rather than in the request. Failure scenario: a partially completed erasure leaves orphans that we only discover during an audit; mitigation is recording progress per prefix and alerting on any incomplete erasure job older than its SLA. Alternative: encrypt objects per tenant with a tenant key held in KMS, so erasure is a key destruction; that is much faster but only works for future objects and complicates per-object sharing and derived images."

topics.title: Image and Video Processing
topics.description: Image and Video Processing within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: sharp is the default image tool

Pipeline shape: original lands in S3 → DB row created → queue job → worker reads from S3 (stream), writes variants to S3, updates the DB row with the variant keys → CDN serves. The worker does not hold the original in memory and does not use the API server's CPU budget.

Responsive variants: a fixed ladder (320, 640, 960, 1280, 1920, 2560) plus AVIF and WebP and a JPEG fallback, with <picture> + srcset + sizes on the client (Phase 3 Part 3 covers the markup). AVIF encodes noticeably smaller but is slower to encode and slightly less universally decoded; WebP is the pragmatic default with AVIF for clients that support it.

EXIF stripping is a privacy requirement, not a nicety: photos from phones carry GPS coordinates, device serial numbers, and timestamps. Strip by default; keep a separate, access-controlled copy if there is a legal reason to retain the original.

Lazy generation (on-demand derivatives): do not generate 8 variants for every upload. Generate one 480px "preview" eagerly, and generate the rest on first request, caching the result — either in the app (with a lock to avoid a thundering herd) or at the CDN with a rewrite to a "resize" origin. This is a large cost saver on image-heavy products.
Content-addressed derived keys (derived/{hash-of-(sourceKey,width,format,q)}) make the cache naturally idempotent: the same request always produces the same key.

Video transcoding is a separate, heavier pipeline. Minimum viable: transcode to MP4 (H.264 + AAC) for broad compatibility and generate a poster frame; use HLS for adaptive streaming (multiple bitrate renditions plus a manifest playlist) or DASH when you need CMAF and offline/DVR features. HLS costs more to produce (many renditions) but plays everywhere and is the industry default; DASH is better on some platforms and required for some DRM workflows.

Transcode reality check: ffmpeg is CPU-heavy and slow. Use a queue with bounded concurrency (CPU count, not queue depth), per-job timeout, and a hard memory cap; consider managed transcoding services for the long tail. Codec parameters matter: two-pass for target bitrate, -movflags +faststart so the moov atom is at the front (otherwise the browser must download the tail before playing), and -g keyframe interval aligned to the HLS segment length so segments start on keyframes.
Audio/FFmpeg gotchas: shell out with argument arrays, never string interpolation (injection), set -nostdin, always capture stderr for diagnosis, and set explicit output paths.
commonMistakes: buffering the source image in memory; skipping EXIF stripping; -movflags forgotten; unbounded transcode concurrency on a CPU-bound worker; generating every variant eagerly.
practiceTasks: build a worker that takes one uploaded image and produces thumbnail/medium/large in WebP + AVIF + JPEG fallback, strips EXIF, verifies GPS is gone, and enforces a memory ceiling — then benchmark throughput at concurrency 1, 4, and 16.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why strip EXIF by default?
🟡 What does `rotate()` then removing orientation do?
🟡 What is `limitInputPixels` for?
🔴 How do you stop an upload from generating 8 × 4 derivatives and a 4K transcode for every file?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: image-heavy product, 2M uploads a month, and generating a full derivative ladder eagerly would cost more than the storage itself. Decision: two tiers. Eagerly generate exactly one 480px WebP preview plus the EXIF-stripped original; generate the rest on demand at first request. The on-demand path computes a content-addressed key from (sourceKey, width, format, quality), so the cache is idempotent, and I guard against a thundering herd with a short Redis lock per key plus the CDN caching the result. Reasoning: most images are viewed at one size by most users, so eager generation is paying for 90% of variants that are never requested, and content-addressed keys mean the second request is free and two concurrent requests produce the same artefact rather than duplicates. Trade-offs: the first request for an uncached variant is slow, which I mitigate by generating the two most common sizes eagerly (thumbnail and a 1280px "large"), so the common path is never slow; and the on-demand path needs its own lock, error handling, and metrics. Failure scenario: a viral post makes every viewer request 12 sizes and the resize workers become the bottleneck. Mitigation: a per-key lock so the work happens once, plus a fallback to the closest already-generated size when the resize queue is saturated, which degrades quality rather than latency. Prevention: track derivative cache hit rate and resize queue wait time, and if hit rate is high, promote the popular sizes to eager generation automatically. Alternative: eagerly generate everything for a plan-limited set of sizes and lazily grow the ladder based on which sizes are actually requested."

topics.title: Security of Uploads
topics.description: Security of Uploads within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: Threats and defences
Magic-byte validation
Only trust the first bytes for identification; a polyglot file can be valid in two formats. If you care, also parse the container fully (that is what sharp, ffprobe, and a PDF parser do).
Never trust the extension the client sent. Renaming payload.html to payload.png is the trivial attack; magic bytes plus a separate origin plus nosniff is what actually stops it.
SVG is the hard case
Quarantine → scan → promote
The quarantine prefix has no public access and a short lifecycle (delete after 24h), so an unscanned file can never be served even if the DB row is wrong.
The scan is asynchronous, so the user sees "processing" — for images, show a preview only after the scan, or at minimum never render the raw uploaded file inline.
Serving uploads safely

Separate origin (e.g. uploads-cdn.example.com with no cookies and no access to your app origin's session). This is the single most effective defence: even if a file is an HTML/SVG payload, it cannot touch the origin that holds your session.

Headers: Content-Disposition: attachment for unknown types, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin, and never Content-Type: text/html from a user-controlled source.
CSP on the upload origin: default-src 'none'; img-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; sandbox. sandbox (opaque origin) is what stops a served HTML file from running scripts against your site.
commonMistakes: trusting Content-Type from the client; serving uploads from the app origin; no pixel/byte limits; extracting untrusted archives without limits; allowing SVG unsanitised; relying on nosniff alone.
practiceTasks: implement magic-byte sniffing for six formats, an SVG sanitiser with an allowlist, a quarantine-prefix + scan + promote worker, and a CI test that asserts every upload route serves from the isolated origin with the required headers — then attempt five real attacks (double extension, HTML as .png, SVG with script, zip bomb, oversized-pixel PNG).

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why validate magic bytes rather than file extension?
🟡 What is a decompression bomb and how do you stop it?
🟡 Why is SVG the most dangerous upload type?
🔴 Describe the quarantine → scan → promote flow and why the prefix matters.
🔴 Why serve uploads from a separate origin?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: users can upload arbitrary bytes, and we serve them back. Even with magic-byte validation there is a gap: a file can be a valid image and also contain markup, and browsers render what the Content-Type says. Decision: uploads are served from a dedicated origin — uploads.example-cdn.com — with no cookies, no access to the app origin, and its own CSP. Reasoning: this is origin isolation, and it is defence that does not depend on correctly classifying every possible file. A stored XSS payload served from the app origin runs with access to the session cookie and the DOM; the same payload served from an unrelated origin runs in an opaque sandbox with no access to your app at all. That single architectural decision neutralises the whole class. The layered controls around it are: magic-byte validation so the stored type is what we detected rather than what the client claimed, an explicit Content-Type we set, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Content-Disposition: attachment for anything not on the known-safe list, and a CSP of default-src 'none'; sandbox on the upload origin so served HTML cannot run scripts or reach out. Trade-offs: a separate origin needs its own DNS, certificate, CDN configuration and CORS rules; same-origin assets like inline images in the rich-text editor need Access-Control-Allow-Origin or crossorigin handling, which is a real source of bugs; and cookies set on the app origin are not sent, which is exactly the point. Failure scenario: someone adds a proxy route that serves uploads from the app origin 'just to fix a CORS error' — that quietly removes the entire defence. Prevention: a test in CI that asserts every upload-serving route returns the uploads. host and the required headers, so a well-meaning fix cannot land. Alternative: accept only a strict allowlist of raster formats, rasterise everything else including SVG, and never serve user bytes as anything but image/png or application/pdf — simpler, at the cost of rejecting legitimate vector uploads."

```ts
const SIGNATURES: { ext: string; mime: string; test: (b: Buffer) => boolean }[] = [
  { ext: 'jpg',  mime: 'image/jpeg', test: b => b[0] === 0xff && b[1] === 0xd8 && b[2] === 0xff },
  { ext: 'png',  mime: 'image/png',  test: b => b.subarray(0, 8).equals(Buffer.from([0x89,0x50,0x4e,0x47,0x0d,0x0a,0x1a,0x0a])) },
  { ext: 'gif',  mime: 'image/gif',  test: b => b.subarray(0, 6).toString('latin1') === 'GIF8' },
  { ext: 'webp', mime: 'image/webp', test: b => b.subarray(0, 4).toString('latin1') === 'RIFF' && b.subarray(8, 12).toString('latin1') === 'WEBP' },
  { ext: 'pdf',  mime: 'application/pdf', test: b => b.subarray(0, 5).toString('latin1') === '%PDF-' },
  { ext: 'mp4',  mime: 'video/mp4',  test: b => b.subarray(4, 8).toString('latin1') === 'ftyp' },
];
export function sniff(head: Buffer): { ext: string; mime: string } | null {
  return SIGNATURES.find(s => s.test(head)) ?? null;
}
```

topics.title: Stripe and Payments
topics.description: Stripe and Payments within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: Two flows

Signature verification uses the timestamp in the stripe-signature header and rejects replays older than a tolerance (default 5 minutes), because a captured valid signature could otherwise be replayed. Always keep the webhook signing secret in a secret manager and rotate it; during rotation, both secrets are valid for a window.
Return 2xx quickly. Stripe gives you ~10 seconds; heavy work (fulfilment, emails) goes on a queue. A handler that takes 9 seconds will eventually time out and cause duplicate retries.
Verify the amount and currency you received matches what you expected, using the PaymentIntent id you stored — never the amount from the client. Mismatches are a fraud signal.
Idempotency keys on every outbound Stripe call: stripe.refunds.create({ payment_intent: id, idempotencyKey: refund:${id}:${attempt} }). Stripe caches the response for 24 hours, so a retry is safe.
Use the test clocks and test mode for time-based scenarios (failed payments, disputes, 3DS), and never hardcode an API key in a browser — the secret key stays server-side.

Refunds and disputes: refunds are your action (partial allowed); disputes are opened by the customer's bank and require evidence within a deadline, which is why the handler pages. Track evidence_due_by and alert well before it.
3DS/SCA: required in much of the EU/UK and increasingly elsewhere. Stripe's payment_intent flow triggers it automatically; your UI must handle the requires_action state. Never try to bypass it.

Saving cards: saving a payment method for future off-session charges requires explicit customer consent and, for off-session charges, authentication exemption / mandate handling. Save only if the business needs it, and treat saved cards as a PCI and compliance surface.

PCI DSS scope reduction: the single biggest lever is *not sending card data through your servers*. Using Stripe Elements/Checkout (hosted fields or iframe) means card data never touches your infrastructure, which keeps you in a much smaller PCI scope (SAQ A instead of SAQ D). Consequences: you cannot log request bodies containing payment_method_data, you must keep your integration in the provider's documented flow, and any change that moves card handling server-side expands scope.
commonMistakes: JSON-parsing the webhook body before verification; trusting the client success callback; doing fulfilment synchronously in the handler; no event.id dedupe; logging full payloads containing PII/card-adjacent fields; ignoring amount/currency verification.
practiceTasks: build the full Stripe path in test mode: create an Intent, confirm with a test card, receive payment_intent.succeeded twice, assert the order transitions once, add a charge.refunded and a dispute fixture, and write the reconciliation job that finds captured payments with no fulfilled order.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Payment Intents vs Checkout Sessions — when do you use which?
🟢 Why must the webhook route use the raw request body?
🟡 Why is the client-side payment success callback untrustworthy?
🟡 What is a Stripe idempotency key and how long does it last?

🔴 Your webhook endpoint starts returning 500 after a deploy. What happens and how do you mitigate?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: we deployed at 14:00 and the webhook handler started returning 500 within minutes. Payment webhooks are retried for up to three days, so nothing is lost — but fulfilment is now delayed and, worse, the failure is invisible unless we alert. Decision: two independent mitigations. First, make the handler fast and non-throwing: it deduplicates on event.id, inserts the event row, enqueues work, and returns 2xx within milliseconds, so no third-party call can make it time out. Second, because returning 5xx is how you ask for a retry, I monitor the endpoint itself: a synthetic check plus an alarm on 5xx rate and on the age of the oldest unprocessed row in stripe_events. I also treat a burst of retries as an incident signal rather than noise, because a provider-side pattern change can also cause it. Reasoning: the failure mode of webhooks is not loss but *silent* delay — Stripe queues and retries, so a broken handler looks like a quiet business rather than an outage, which is the worst possible shape. Trade-offs: acknowledging quickly means failures surface in the queue rather than at the endpoint, so I need end-to-end monitoring from event receipt to fulfilment, and I keep failed events in stripe_events with status = 'failed' for inspection instead of discarding them. Failure scenario: the deploy broke the handler for two hours and 4,000 payments sat unfulfilled with no page — prevented by the alarm on oldest unprocessed age rather than on error rate, since a low-volume payment day would not trip a rate threshold. Prevention: contract-test the handler against recorded Stripe event fixtures for every event type you claim to handle, run in CI, so a schema or field change is caught before deploy."

topics.title: Payment Failure Modes and Ledger-First Design
topics.description: Payment Failure Modes and Ledger-First Design within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: The catalogue
Ledger-first design

Record the intent before the charge, always. If you charge first and crash before writing, you have money taken with no record — an unrecoverable support problem. If you record first and crash before charging, you have a pending row that the reconciliation job can find and cancel.
Amounts as integers in the smallest currency unit. Never 19.99 as a float; store 1999. Never compute totals with floating point; compute in integer minor units, or use a decimal library.
Reconciliation job (the safety net that makes all of the above survivable):
Use the provider's dashboard as the authority for the sweep; the local stripe_events table is a cache, not the source of truth.
Alert on the delta between provider totals and local totals — a daily invariant like "sum of captured today == sum of local paid today" is the single best financial alarm.
Never mark an order paid from a client callback, a redirect return parameter, or a Checkout success URL. Those are UX only. The webhook is the proof.
commonMistakes: dedupe on event id without tracking completion status; floating-point money; charging before recording; trusting the events table as the authority; no oldest-pending alarm.
practiceTasks: write the ledger schema (payments, refunds, stripe_events, fulfilments) with unique constraints, the 10-minute reconciliation query, the nightly invariant check, and a chaos test that drops the queue during a webhook.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 List the payment failure modes you can name.
🟡 Why store amounts as integer minor units?
🟡 Why record the payment intent before charging?
🔴 Explain paid-but-not-fulfilled end to end, including detection and recovery.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: the payment_intent.succeeded webhook handler passed withIdempotency, so the event was recorded, but the fulfilment enqueue failed because the queue was unavailable, and the handler returned 500 so Stripe retried — except the retry hit the event.id dedupe and returned early without re-enqueueing. This is the exact bug that produces paid-but-not-fulfilled. Decision: never let dedupe short-circuit work that has not actually completed. My stripe_events row has a status, and the dedupe check only skips when status = 'processed'; a received or failed row re-runs the handler. And because relying on retries is fragile, I add a reconciliation job that finds payments rows stuck in pending for more than 10 minutes, cross-references the provider, and re-drives fulfilment idempotently, plus a nightly full sweep comparing provider charges to local records. Reasoning: at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent handler only works if "idempotent" is scoped to *completed* work, not to *received* work. The reconciliation job is the backstop for everything the event path cannot see, including webhooks that were never delivered at all. Trade-offs: the reconciliation job is real operational code with its own failure modes and needs an alert on its own staleness, and the nightly sweep costs API calls and provider rate-limit budget, so I page it for large amounts and log the rest. Failure scenario: a customer is charged and never notified for days — the fix is a staleness alarm on the oldest pending payment, not on failure rate, because nothing fails loudly in this scenario. Prevention: state-machine tests in CI that walk every legal and illegal transition, and a daily invariant check between provider totals and local totals."

```
                                   then transition to 'paid'
4. FULFIL                         → enqueue, idempotent by order
5. REFUND (on demand)            → ledger row first, then the Stripe call, then confirm by webhook
```

```sql
-- payments captured at the provider but not marked paid locally
select p.id, p.stripe_payment_intent_id, p.amount_minor, p.created_at
from payments p
where p.status = 'pending'
  and p.created_at < now() - interval '10 minutes'
  and exists (select 1 from stripe_events e
              where e.type = 'payment_intent.succeeded'
                and e.payload->'data'->'object'->>'id' = p.stripe_payment_intent_id)
order by p.created_at;
```

topics.title: Email, SMS, and Push Providers
topics.description: Email, SMS, and Push Providers within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: Templates
Retries
Bounce handling
Compliance, at a level you can talk about

CAN-SPAM: accurate headers (From, Reply-To), a physical postal address, a working unsubscribe link honoured within 10 business days, and no deceptive subject lines. Applies to commercial email regardless of consent.

GDPR/ePrivacy: for marketing email to EU residents, consent is generally required (soft opt-in from an existing customer relationship is possible under narrow conditions), and every subscriber needs an easy unsubscribe; you must be able to prove consent (consent_at, source, ip).

TCPA (SMS in the US): express written consent before sending, honour STOP immediately, and never send autodialed marketing SMS to numbers on the DNC registry. Per-country rules differ, and you need per-region send windows.
Push: platform rules require a way to opt out, and both FCM and APNs enforce content requirements; exceeding user-quota limits gets your app throttled by the OS.
Delivery vs acceptance vs bounce
commonMistakes: treating acceptance as delivery; ignoring complaints; sending marketing through transactional templates; not honouring unsubscribe promptly; no per-country SMS rules.
practiceTasks: build a provider adapter interface with SES/Postmark, Twilio, and FCM implementations, a preference store separating transactional from marketing, a bounce/complaint webhook consumer that writes to a suppression table, and a compliance checklist per channel.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟡 What is the difference between accepted, delivered, and bounced?
🟡 What must you do on a complaint, and what happens if you ignore it?
🔴 Describe the difference between hard and soft bounces and the action for each.
🔴 What are the CAN-SPAM requirements?
🔴 What does TCPA require before you send an SMS in the US?
🔴 Why do providers support per-recipient template substitution instead of you sending a batch?
🔴 How do you structure notification preferences so transactional and marketing never mix?
🔴 Your transactional email deliverability dropped. What do you check first?
🟡 Why store the rendered body and not just the template id?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a user reports that a password-reset email says 'Hi Jane' but Jane was renamed to 'Jo' two weeks ago, and support cannot tell what was actually sent. Decision: store the rendered output — subject, text part, and HTML part — alongside the template id and version on the send record. Reasoning: three reasons. Support needs to show the customer exactly what was sent, which is impossible if you re-render from current data. Legal and compliance need reproducibility: if the message contained something that later proves unlawful, you must be able to prove what was sent and to whom. And debugging needs the exact bytes, because the discrepancy might have been in the template version, the data, or the rendering, and re-rendering destroys the evidence. Trade-offs: storage cost, which is small (a few KB per send), and a privacy obligation — rendered bodies contain the recipient's data, so they must inherit the retention policy of the underlying record and be included in erasure requests. Failure scenario: a template is edited in place without a version bump, so historical sends re-render differently and support's record is wrong; versioned templates plus stored renders make that impossible. Prevention: make templates immutable by construction — editing creates version 2, never modifies version 1. Alternative: store only template id and version and accept that support cannot reproduce a historical send, which I would only accept for low-stakes transactional mail with no compliance requirement."

topics.title: OAuth Integrations with Third Parties
topics.description: OAuth Integrations with Third Parties within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: The flows
Storage

Refresh: store refresh_token, expires_at, and a scope set. Refresh proactively at ~80% of lifetime with a lock per credential so concurrent requests do not race (provider-dependent: some providers invalidate a refresh token on use, so a race revokes your access — hence the lock and keeping the *previous* token until the new one works).
Revocation: a DELETE on the provider when the user disconnects, and treat a 400 invalid_grant response as "must re-consent" — surface that in the UI rather than retrying forever.

Scopes: request the minimum, record the *granted* scopes (they can differ from requested), and re-consent when you need more. Requesting everything up front gets your app rejected by review and trains users to click "Allow" without reading.

Refresh-token rotation hazards: rotating tokens mean a crash mid-rotation can lose access permanently. Store the new refresh token transactionally and only delete the old one once the new one is confirmed working.

Webhooks from OAuth providers: verify their signature (same discipline as Stripe, different scheme), dedupe on their event id, and process idempotently. Providers' webhooks are also how you learn about *revoked* grants.

Reconnect flows: when a grant dies mid-session, do not silently retry in a loop. Queue the action that needs the integration, mark it blocked_on_reconnect, show the user a "Reconnect <provider>" action, and resume the queued work when the new token arrives. That is the pattern that makes integrations feel reliable rather than broken.
Long-running work in an integration: never hold an HTTP request open while an OAuth-protected third-party call retries; enqueue and let the worker handle reconnection.
commonMistakes: storing tokens in plaintext; no state validation; refreshing on the request path without a lock; deleting the old refresh token too early; retrying invalid_grant forever; requesting every scope.
practiceTasks: implement the authorization-code + PKCE flow with encrypted per-tenant token storage, a lock-protected proactive refresher at 80% of lifetime, revocation on disconnect, granted-scope recording, and a queued job that is blocked and resumed on reconnect.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why PKCE, and why on every flow?
🟡 What is the `state` parameter for?
🔴 How do you store per-tenant OAuth tokens securely?
🔴 What happens if two requests refresh the same refresh token concurrently?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a per-tenant token store with expires_at, and two requests race to refresh the same credential. Some providers issue single-use rotating refresh tokens, so the second request presents an already-used token and the provider responds invalid_grant — which, if we treat that as fatal, revokes a working integration because of our own race. Decision: a per-credential Redis lock (SET NX PX) around refresh, plus write-on-read semantics where the new refresh token is stored transactionally and the previous one is retained until the new one has been successfully used once. Reasoning: the provider's guarantee is single-use rotation; our guarantee must be single-flight use, and the failure mode is not a transient error but permanent revocation, so a plain mutex is not enough — I need the ability to recover. Trade-offs: a distributed lock adds a Redis dependency on the integration path, and lock handling must be careful (lease expiry mid-refresh is possible); keeping the old token temporarily means the record holds two secrets, so both must be encrypted and both must be purged on success. Failure scenario: the process dies between storing the new token and deleting the old one. That is safe, because the old token is still valid for one more use only if we have not already used it — so I record which token was last used and only retry with the newest. If the provider has already consumed it, the integration is dead and we surface a reconnect prompt rather than looping. Prevention: alert on invalid_grant rate per tenant, because a burst means a code path is double-refreshing; and set refresh at 80% of lifetime so there is time to retry before expiry. Alternative: a scheduled refresher that refreshes all credentials proactively on a cron, which removes the race from the request path entirely at the cost of a background job per credential."

topics.title: Third-Party API Resilience
topics.description: Third-Party API Resilience within Files, Payments, and Integrations.
keyConcepts: 1. Timeouts at every layer
Without a timeout, one slow dependency becomes an unbounded pile-up of open sockets, and your process runs out of file descriptors — the classic cascading failure.
Propagate a deadline (a deadline header or a context field) so *your* upstream knows your remaining budget and does not start work it cannot finish.

Set a lower timeout on internal calls than on external ones, and never let a request-timeout cascade: if service A calls B with 5s and B calls C with 5s, one slow C consumes three layers of thread/connection capacity.
Always finally the timer clear. Always drain or cancel the response body (res.body?.cancel()) on early exit, or you leak a socket.
2. Retries, only where they are safe
Never retry a non-idempotent POST without an idempotency key (see 5.8.9's neighbours in 5.6.10: Stripe accepts them; most providers do not, so use a natural idempotency design or do not retry).
Jitter across *callers* too: add a small random spread so 5,000 workers do not all retry the failing dependency at the same instant.
3. Circuit breaker
Fail fast while open with a synthetic, clearly-typed error (DependencyUnavailable) so callers can degrade gracefully instead of hanging.

Per dependency, per region — a breaker is scoped to a specific dependency (and often a specific region of it), because a failure in one provider must not stop you calling another. Global breakers cause correlated outages.

Rolling window (e.g. last 20 requests, or last 60s), minimum volume before the breaker can trip (so 3 failures out of 3 requests at startup does not open it), separate thresholds for error ratio and latency (a dependency returning 200s in 30s is as broken as one returning 500s), and success threshold to close again (e.g. 5/5 successful probes).
commonMistakes: liveness checks that call dependencies; one global breaker; retrying non-idempotent POSTs; no minimum volume on the breaker; forgetting to clear/abort timers; failing the whole service when one dependency is degraded.
practiceTasks: implement a resilient HTTP client: layered timeouts, retry with full jitter + Retry-After, a per-dependency circuit breaker with half-open concurrency gate, a per-dependency bulkhead, single-flight request coalescing, and a fault-injecting server that returns 500s, 429s, and hangs — then prove no more than N concurrent upstream calls ever occur.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What are the four timeout layers on an outbound HTTP call?
🟡 When is it safe to retry?
🟡 What does `Retry-After` look like and how do you handle both forms?
🔴 Explain the three breaker states and the purpose of half-open.
🔴 Why must the breaker be per dependency and per region?
🔴 What is a bulkhead and how do you size it?
🔴 Design the degraded behaviour for a product-page enrichment service.
🔴 What is request coalescing and when does it matter most?
🔴 Your service's liveness probe starts failing when a third-party API is down. Why is that bad and what do you change?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: our liveness probe includes a call to a third-party enrichment API, and when that provider has an incident, Kubernetes restarts all our pods — turning a third-party degradation into a full outage of our service. Decision: liveness must depend only on whether *this* process can serve traffic, never on whether a dependency is reachable. So the liveness endpoint is a pure process check, readiness includes only local capacity checks (event-loop lag, memory, connection-pool headroom, queue depth), and dependency health is a separate signal used for alerting, breaker decisions, and graceful degradation. Reasoning: the purpose of a liveness probe is to detect a wedged process that cannot recover and should be restarted. A dependency outage is not a wedged process — restarting makes it worse, because we throw away warm caches, force a reconnect storm, and remove the capacity we need to serve cached or degraded responses. Failure scenario: a provider outage triggers liveness failures, every pod restarts simultaneously, the restart hammers the provider as it recovers, and our users see a total outage instead of a partial one. That is the textbook cascading failure. Prevention: a CI test that asserts the liness endpoint makes no network calls, plus a chaos drill that kills a dependency and confirms zero pod restarts while the service continues serving degraded responses. Trade-off: a dependency can then be fully down while we look healthy, so I compensate with per-dependency alerts on error ratio and latency, plus a visible degraded-mode indicator so the on-call knows without a page storm. Alternative: keep a lightweight dependency probe but mark it as a *separate* readiness gate used for draining rather than for restarts — useful when you want to stop sending new traffic to an instance that cannot serve, without killing it."

topics.title: Python (Django, FastAPI)
topics.description: Python (Django, FastAPI) within Other Backend Languages.
keyConcepts: Goroutines are cheap (a few KB of stack, multiplexed onto OS threads by the runtime). Spawning thousands is normal and idiomatic. They have no preemption guarantee in older versions (since Go 1.14, async preemption exists via signals).

Channels are the coordination primitive. Always size the buffer when the producer can outrun the consumer, or the producer blocks; and never close from the send side if senders may still be running. Prefer errgroup for a bounded group of goroutines with automatic error propagation and Wait.

context.Context is the cancellation and deadline mechanism, threaded through every call as the first parameter. It is how you propagate a client disconnect, a request timeout, and a deadline down to the database driver — which is why context.WithTimeout plus defer cancel() on every function that creates one is the single most important Go habit.
errgroup + SetLimit gives you a bulkhead for free:

net/http: the standard library server is production-grade. http.Server has ReadHeaderTimeout (set it or you have a Slowloris vulnerability), ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout, and MaxHeaderBytes. Middleware is plain wrapping of http.Handler. Graceful shutdown is srv.Shutdown(ctx) plus closing the listener, waiting for in-flight requests.
Errors are values: no exceptions; wrap with %w for errors.Is/errors.As; a missing error is a programming error. Error strings are lowercase and without punctuation because they compose into messages.
Interfaces are implicit and small: define the interface at the consumer, keep it to one or two methods (io.Reader, error).

Single static binary: cross-compiles with CGO_ENABLED=0 to a few megabytes, no runtime, no dependency manager at deploy time. Containers start in milliseconds and images stay small — an operational advantage that shows up in cold-start scale-out and in distroless/security-scanning terms.

Compile-time safety: static typing with no null, exhaustive-ish error handling, and a language that is small enough to hold in your head. Structs are value types by default; slices and maps are reference types, which is the classic aliasing bug.
Weaknesses to be honest about
Error-handling verbosity: if err != nil everywhere is a real productivity and readability cost; the ecosystem is converging on wrapped errors and helper packages rather than on magic.

Generics are still less pleasant than TypeScript or Java: no higher-kinded types, no Stream-style pipelines, still awkward for higher-order abstractions. Go 1.18+ generics help for containers but have ergonomics complaints (no method constraints on the type-parameter set in some cases).
commonMistakes: not defer cancel()ing contexts; unbounded goroutines without SetLimit; forgetting ReadHeaderTimeout; unbuffered channels between many senders and one receiver; assuming Go's GC solves tail latency by default.
practiceTasks: write a Go service with net/http, errgroup with a concurrency limit of 8, context deadline propagation, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, and a load test at 20k rps with p99 reported; then repeat in Node and compare.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why is `context.Context` conventionally the first parameter?
🟡 What is the cost of spawning a goroutine compared to a thread?
🟡 Why must channels be buffered when a producer can outrun the consumer?
🔴 What is the loop-variable capture bug in older Go and how does Go 1.22+ change it?
🔴 Explain `errgroup.WithContext` and `SetLimit` and why the limit is a feature.
🔴 Why must you set `ReadHeaderTimeout` on an `http.Server`?
🔴 What's the equivalent of graceful shutdown, and what breaks if you skip it?
🔴 Compare `sync.WaitGroup` and `errgroup` for error propagation.
🔴 When would you choose Go over Node and over Java?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a new internal service that must handle 20k requests per second with p99 under 20ms, where the team has strong Node and Java experience. Decision: I would pick Go for the service and give a short, explicit list of reasons, while naming the real costs. Reasons for Go: goroutines and channels make high IO-bound concurrency simple without an async framework or reactive types; the single static binary means no runtime dependency and fast container starts, which matters for scale-out; context gives first-class cancellation and deadline propagation all the way to the database driver, which is genuinely excellent; and the language surface is small enough that a new engineer is productive in a week. Costs I would state plainly: error handling is more verbose than TypeScript, generics ergonomics are worse, GC tuning for extreme tail latency is less flexible than the JVM's, and the hiring pool is smaller than Java's by a wide margin, so I would only assign people who want to work in Go. Reasoning: the decision hinges on the *shape of the workload*, not on a preference. If this service were mostly blocking JDBC with complex transactional queries, Java with virtual threads would be the better fit; if the team were strongest in Python and this was an ML-adjacent service, Python would win on velocity. Trade-offs: choosing Go means the on-call rotation needs Go expertise, and if we later need complex ORM-style domain modelling we are outside Go's strengths. Failure scenario: we pick Go for throughput, then the real requirement turns out to be heavy transactional domain logic with an existing team fluent in Spring — now we are paying a language-learning tax for throughput we did not need. Prevention: state the bottleneck and the constraint that drives the choice before committing, and validate the throughput assumption with a load test on a realistic handler in week one rather than trusting a hello-world benchmark. Alternative: Node, if the service is thin and the constraint is delivery speed rather than concurrency."

topics.title: Java (Spring Boot)
topics.description: Java (Spring Boot) within Other Backend Languages.
keyConcepts: The JVM in one page

Memory: heap (-Xmx, split young/old generations by default with G1) plus metaspace (class metadata — the leak that -Xmx does not bound) plus direct/native buffers (Netty, ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, off-heap caches) plus thread stacks (-Xss). A container's memory limit must be set above -Xmx to leave room for metaspace, direct buffers, and native allocations — the standard failure is an OOM-kill at container limit with plenty of heap free.

GC: automatic, generational, mostly concurrent, with pause targets rather than zero pauses. Tune by *symptom*: high allocation rate → a bigger/appropriate heap and reduce garbage; long pauses → move from high-throughput collectors (Parallel) to low-pause (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) and shrink the live set. Reach for GC tuning only after measuring allocation profiles.
Threading: a thread-per-request model with a pooled executor, so memory scales with concurrency; each thread's stack is real memory.

Virtual threads (Project Loom, stable since JDK 21) are the headline change: instead of one platform thread (≈1MB stack, expensive context switch) you get a lightweight JVM-managed thread for blocking I/O, so millions of concurrent blocking tasks become feasible and the familiar "thread pool sizing" problem largely goes away for I/O-bound work.

What virtual threads change: blocking JDBC/HTTP calls no longer need an async framework, so you can write plain blocking code again. Pool sizing math changes — HikariCP is still a real pool because *connections* are the scarce resource, and more threads means you can hit the database's connection limit faster, so the pool (usually ~10–20 for a service, sized to the DB's max_connections divided by instance count) is the true ceiling.

What they do not change: CPU-bound work still needs a real platform thread pool (Executors.newFixedThreadPool), because virtual threads do not add CPU parallelism; synchronized pinning and native/foreign-function calls can still pin carrier threads; and GC/memory behaviour with millions of live threads needs measurement.
Spring DI/IoC
Spring MVC vs WebFlux
JPA/Hibernate pitfalls
N+1 queries: lazy associations fetched per row. Fix with join fetch, @EntityGraph, or projections/DTO queries. Measure with datasource-proxy or Hibernate statistics.

Lazy loading outside a transaction: a lazy association accessed after the transaction closes throws LazyInitializationException. This is why Open Session in View (OSIV) exists — and why it is an anti-pattern.
commonMistakes: sizing -Xmx equal to the container limit; Open Session in View in production; @Transactional on private or self-called methods; unbounded thread pools; CPU-bound work on virtual threads; reactive framework with blocking libraries inside.
practiceTasks: build a Spring Boot 3 app on JDK 21 with virtual threads enabled, a 15-connection HikariCP pool, four deliberately N+1 endpoints, and prove each of the four JPA pitfalls with datasource-proxy timings — then fix all four.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What memory regions exist outside the heap?
🟡 Why do container memory limits need to be above `-Xmx`?
🟡 What problem do virtual threads actually solve?
🟡 What is a constructor-injection preference about?
🔴 Your service is OOM-killed by Kubernetes with heap at 40%. Where is the memory?
🔴 What are the four JPA pitfalls and how do you detect each?
🔴 Why is `Open Session in View` disabled by default?
🔴 Explain the `@Transactional` self-invocation bug with its symptom.
🔴 Why is the connection pool, not the thread count, the real ceiling for an IO-bound service?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an IO-bound Spring service with HikariCP and 200 platform threads, and we were about to raise concurrency by adding threads to fix latency. Decision: the thread count is not the constraint; the pool is. With blocking JDBC, throughput is bounded by concurrent connections, not by threads: 200 threads against a 20-connection pool means 180 threads blocked waiting for a connection, and p99 is the pool wait queue. So I size the pool from the database's capacity — total max_connections divided by the number of service instances, minus headroom for migrations and admin access — which is usually 10 to 20 per instance, and I set connectionTimeout low enough that a saturated pool fails fast rather than accumulating. Adding threads beyond the pool only moves the queue from the pool to the executor. Virtual threads change this only partially: they make thread creation free and make blocking cheap, but each blocked virtual thread still needs a connection, so the same max_connections arithmetic applies — and with virtual threads you can reach the pool ceiling faster, because nothing throttles you. Trade-offs: a small pool with a low timeout means fast failures and visible errors, which requires the rest of the system to degrade well (retries on a different instance, a circuit breaker), rather than a large pool that turns a database slowdown into a total outage. Failure scenario: the database's query plan changes and p99 triples; the pool saturates, waiters queue, and every endpoint degrades simultaneously — a single dependency taking down the whole service. Prevention: alert on pool utilisation and on pool wait time, keep queries indexed, and use virtual threads with JdbcClient so the handler stays blocking and simple. Alternative: reactive JDBC with virtual threads and a reactive driver, which raises the connection ceiling but requires re-validating the entire persistence stack."

topics.title: Concurrency models compared
topics.description: Concurrency models compared within Other Backend Languages.
keyConcepts: The three axes that actually decide it
Blocking tolerance. Async models must never block; thread models block freely; actor models forbid blocking by design; processes isolate everything.
Unit cost. Goroutines and virtual threads are cheap enough to have per-request units; OS threads are not; actors sit in between; processes are expensive.

Where isolation matters. If one unit's failure must not affect others (plugin code, a parser crash, an OOM), you need processes. If you need throughput with blocking libraries, you need threads or virtual threads. If you need to avoid lock-based races, actors or the single-threaded event loop give you that by construction.
Where each fits, concretely
commonMistakes: treating a blocking call as a reason to change language; assuming threads make blocking safe *and* cheap; ignoring that worker-thread pools serialise; forgetting memory per thread when sizing a pool.
practiceTasks: implement the same I/O-bound service in Node, Python (asyncio), Go, and Java (virtual threads), load test each at 10k concurrent connections, and tabulate p50/p99, memory per 1,000 concurrent units, and CPU at saturation.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟡 What is the memory cost per goroutine vs per thread?
🟡 Why do actors avoid a whole class of concurrency bug?
🔴 Your Node service occasionally freezes for 2 seconds. Which concurrency model would have made this impossible, and what would you lose?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a Node API service intermittently freezes for two seconds under load, and we have traced it to a synchronous filesystem call plus a large synchronous JSON parse on the event loop. Decision: I would not change the concurrency model for this — I would move the offending work off the loop. A thread-per-request or goroutine-per-request model would indeed make this impossible, because a blocking call would only stall that one request. What I would lose by switching: in Node, almost nothing in throughput for IO-bound work; but if I moved to Go or Java the operational and hiring costs rise, and if I moved to a worker-thread pool within Node I keep one language while making the blocking call safe. Reasoning: the freeze is a *blocking* bug, not a *concurrency model* bug. Choosing a heavier concurrency model to tolerate synchronous I/O is treating the symptom; the correct fix is that no synchronous filesystem or CPU work belongs on the loop at all — that is a code-review and lint rule, and for genuinely blocking libraries a worker_threads pool or a to_thread-equivalent gives the isolation without changing the architecture. Trade-offs: a worker pool introduces a serialisation boundary and message copying, so it is only worth it for work that genuinely blocks or burns CPU; moving everything to goroutines would be the wrong trade because the service's actual bottleneck is the database, not the loop. Failure scenario: we switch the whole service to a thread-per-request model, the freeze moves to thread-pool exhaustion under the same load, and we now have a more complex system with the same class of bug. Prevention: event-loop lag SLO with an alert, a lint rule banning sync APIs in request paths, and a load test that reports p99 rather than throughput. Alternative: worker threads for CPU-heavy and blocking tasks, which is the 80/20 answer."

topics.title: Python: CPython, the GIL, and Concurrency Choices
topics.description: Python: CPython, the GIL, and Concurrency Choices within Other Backend Languages.
keyConcepts: The GIL, precisely
What it blocks: pure-Python CPU work. Two threads doing computation get ~no parallelism.

What it does *not* block: anything that releases the GIL — socket I/O, file I/O via the OS, time.sleep, hashlib/ssl/zlib release it for large buffers, NumPy's inner loops, and native extensions in general. So I/O-bound work *does* scale across threads in CPython.

Consequence: thread-per-request in CPython gives you concurrency (many requests in flight) but not parallelism (one CPU's worth of Python at a time). For I/O-bound services that is sufficient; for CPU-bound work it is useless without processes, multiprocessing, or a native library.

Free-threading (PEP 703): an optional build of CPython 3.13+ with the GIL removed. Availability depends on your platform, wheel, and library support (C extensions must be marked thread-safe), so treat it as something to benchmark, not something to design around.
Choosing a concurrency model in Python
asyncio and Node's event loop
FastAPI: async def vs def — the rule

A blocking call inside async def stalls the entire server, not just that request: one requests.get or time.sleep(1) or a CPU-heavy pandas operation takes down all concurrent traffic. This is FastAPI's most common production incident and it is invisible in development with a single client.

BackgroundTasks runs *after* the response is sent, in the same process. It is not a queue: it is lost on crash and it does not survive a restart. Use it for small, non-critical work; use Celery or a queue for anything that must happen.

Pydantic v2 is Rust-backed and much faster than v1: field_validator, model_config, and lazy validation of nested models. Use it for boundary validation exactly as you would use Zod in TypeScript (5.10.4), and export an OpenAPI schema from the models so the frontend can generate types.
Django: what to know
commonMistakes: blocking calls inside async def; treating BackgroundTasks as a queue; post_save signals containing business logic; N+1 queries in DRF viewsets; installing into the system Python; for loops over querysets without select_related.
practiceTasks: build the same API in FastAPI (async) and Django + DRF (sync), seed 10,000 rows, and use nplusone plus EXPLAIN ANALYZE to fix every N+1; then benchmark both under 500 concurrent clients and compare thread vs asyncio behaviour.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What does the GIL block and what does it not block?
🟡 Why can threads still help a CPython web server?
🟡 When is `multiprocessing` the right tool?
🟡 What is the equivalent of `process.nextTick` in asyncio?
🔴 A FastAPI endpoint declared `async def` calls the synchronous `requests` library. What happens?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an endpoint declared async def internally calls the blocking requests library, and under production load the service intermittently stops responding for seconds with 100% CPU in the event loop. Decision: I know immediately that the blocking call runs on the event loop thread, so the whole server is frozen for the duration of that HTTP request, and every other concurrent request waits — which is why the symptom is 'the entire service hangs' rather than 'one request is slow'. The fix is two-part. Immediately, either switch that endpoint to plain def so FastAPI runs it in its threadpool, or switch to an async client like httpx.AsyncClient, which is what I would do for a service that handles high concurrency. Structurally, I add a lint rule and a test that forbids known-blocking calls inside async def, and I alert on event-loop lag so we detect this class of bug before users do. Reasoning: the event loop gives us concurrency for free only while everything running on it is non-blocking; one blocking call converts all that concurrency into a queue, and because the loop is single-threaded there is no preemption to save you. Trade-offs: declaring an endpoint def is the minimal fix but caps concurrency at the threadpool size, so for a high-traffic endpoint I would rather use async libraries throughout and keep the handler async def. Failure scenario: this appears only under load, since a single sequential test request never overlaps the blocking call — which is exactly why it reaches production. Prevention: a load test with concurrency on every endpoint, plus a CI lint rule, plus an event-loop-lag SLO. Alternative: offload CPU-bound work to ProcessPoolExecutor and blocking libraries to asyncio.to_thread, which unblocks the loop while keeping the async signature."

topics.title: Java and Spring Boot
topics.description: Java and Spring Boot within Other Backend Languages.
keyConcepts: The JVM in one page

Memory: heap (-Xmx, split young/old generations by default with G1) plus metaspace (class metadata — the leak that -Xmx does not bound) plus direct/native buffers (Netty, ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, off-heap caches) plus thread stacks (-Xss). A container's memory limit must be set above -Xmx to leave room for metaspace, direct buffers, and native allocations — the standard failure is an OOM-kill at container limit with plenty of heap free.

GC: automatic, generational, mostly concurrent, with pause targets rather than zero pauses. Tune by *symptom*: high allocation rate → a bigger/appropriate heap and reduce garbage; long pauses → move from high-throughput collectors (Parallel) to low-pause (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) and shrink the live set. Reach for GC tuning only after measuring allocation profiles.
Threading: a thread-per-request model with a pooled executor, so memory scales with concurrency; each thread's stack is real memory.

Virtual threads (Project Loom, stable since JDK 21) are the headline change: instead of one platform thread (≈1MB stack, expensive context switch) you get a lightweight JVM-managed thread for blocking I/O, so millions of concurrent blocking tasks become feasible and the familiar "thread pool sizing" problem largely goes away for I/O-bound work.

What virtual threads change: blocking JDBC/HTTP calls no longer need an async framework, so you can write plain blocking code again. Pool sizing math changes — HikariCP is still a real pool because *connections* are the scarce resource, and more threads means you can hit the database's connection limit faster, so the pool (usually ~10–20 for a service, sized to the DB's max_connections divided by instance count) is the true ceiling.

What they do not change: CPU-bound work still needs a real platform thread pool (Executors.newFixedThreadPool), because virtual threads do not add CPU parallelism; synchronized pinning and native/foreign-function calls can still pin carrier threads; and GC/memory behaviour with millions of live threads needs measurement.
Spring DI/IoC
Spring MVC vs WebFlux
JPA/Hibernate pitfalls
N+1 queries: lazy associations fetched per row. Fix with join fetch, @EntityGraph, or projections/DTO queries. Measure with datasource-proxy or Hibernate statistics.

Lazy loading outside a transaction: a lazy association accessed after the transaction closes throws LazyInitializationException. This is why Open Session in View (OSIV) exists — and why it is an anti-pattern.
commonMistakes: sizing -Xmx equal to the container limit; Open Session in View in production; @Transactional on private or self-called methods; unbounded thread pools; CPU-bound work on virtual threads; reactive framework with blocking libraries inside.
practiceTasks: build a Spring Boot 3 app on JDK 21 with virtual threads enabled, a 15-connection HikariCP pool, four deliberately N+1 endpoints, and prove each of the four JPA pitfalls with datasource-proxy timings — then fix all four.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What memory regions exist outside the heap?
🟡 Why do container memory limits need to be above `-Xmx`?
🟡 What problem do virtual threads actually solve?
🟡 What is a constructor-injection preference about?
🔴 Your service is OOM-killed by Kubernetes with heap at 40%. Where is the memory?
🔴 What are the four JPA pitfalls and how do you detect each?
🔴 Why is `Open Session in View` disabled by default?
🔴 Explain the `@Transactional` self-invocation bug with its symptom.
🔴 Why is the connection pool, not the thread count, the real ceiling for an IO-bound service?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an IO-bound Spring service with HikariCP and 200 platform threads, and we were about to raise concurrency by adding threads to fix latency. Decision: the thread count is not the constraint; the pool is. With blocking JDBC, throughput is bounded by concurrent connections, not by threads: 200 threads against a 20-connection pool means 180 threads blocked waiting for a connection, and p99 is the pool wait queue. So I size the pool from the database's capacity — total max_connections divided by the number of service instances, minus headroom for migrations and admin access — which is usually 10 to 20 per instance, and I set connectionTimeout low enough that a saturated pool fails fast rather than accumulating. Adding threads beyond the pool only moves the queue from the pool to the executor. Virtual threads change this only partially: they make thread creation free and make blocking cheap, but each blocked virtual thread still needs a connection, so the same max_connections arithmetic applies — and with virtual threads you can reach the pool ceiling faster, because nothing throttles you. Trade-offs: a small pool with a low timeout means fast failures and visible errors, which requires the rest of the system to degrade well (retries on a different instance, a circuit breaker), rather than a large pool that turns a database slowdown into a total outage. Failure scenario: the database's query plan changes and p99 triples; the pool saturates, waiters queue, and every endpoint degrades simultaneously — a single dependency taking down the whole service. Prevention: alert on pool utilisation and on pool wait time, keep queries indexed, and use virtual threads with JdbcClient so the handler stays blocking and simple. Alternative: reactive JDBC with virtual threads and a reactive driver, which raises the connection ceiling but requires re-validating the entire persistence stack."

topics.title: "Why Node.js?" — The Honest Answer
topics.description: "Why Node.js?" — The Honest Answer within Other Backend Languages.
keyConcepts: The honest case for Node

One language across the stack. Types and validators are shared (Zod schemas infer both the API types and the React props — see 5.10.4). No context switch, no serialization boundary, one test framework, one CI toolchain, one debugging story. For a full-stack team this is a real, compounding advantage.

The workload matches the runtime. Node is excellent for I/O-bound services: many concurrent connections waiting on a database or an HTTP API, with modest CPU work. Node's event loop is genuinely good at this and it has years of production hardening.
Hiring pool and ecosystem: the largest pool of backend-capable web developers, and npm covers essentially every integration. For most product companies, being able to hire is decisive.
Real CPU escape hatches: worker_threads for CPU work and blocking APIs, native addons (N-API) for hot paths, and the option of moving a hot service to Go or Rust while keeping the rest in Node.
Developer velocity: iteration speed matters more than peak efficiency for most products, and Node has a short path from idea to production.
The honest case against

CPU-bound work: image processing, large cryptography, big JSON payloads, complex analytics — all of it blocks the loop and needs worker threads or a separate service. Worker threads add serialisation cost and lose the single-threaded simplicity.
Strict numeric work: floating-point semantics differ from Java/Go in ways that matter for money (see 5.8.6), and there is no decimal type in the language.
Memory footprint per instance: Node's baseline RSS is high relative to Go or Java at small workloads, which matters for scale-to-zero and for per-request cost models.

Stack depth and type safety: TypeScript erases types, so runtime validation is mandatory at boundaries; and callback/promise layering plus a deep transitive dependency tree means supply-chain risk is a first-order concern.
Team fit: if your team is strongest in Java or Go, the honest answer may be to use that. Rewriting a working service in Node to "modernise" is a cost with no user-visible benefit.
commonMistakes: "Node because it's popular"; rewriting working services for consistency; ignoring blocking work; assuming TypeScript types protect the boundary.
practiceTasks: take an existing Node service, profile it, find the blocking work, move it to worker threads, and record the before/after p99 and CPU — then write the extraction memo for the case where that is not enough.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What workload is Node best at and why?
🟡 What is the "one language across the stack" argument, precisely?
🟡 How does Node handle CPU-bound work and at what cost?
🔴 Give the three strongest reasons for Node and the three strongest against.
🔴 When would you extract a service from Node into Go?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: our order service started in Node and is now the slowest thing we own; p99 is 300ms, CPU is pegged, and the flame graph shows 70% of time in a synchronous JSON parse and a synchronous crypto call in the request path. Decision: I would not rewrite it. I would first move the two hot spots to worker_threads — that is a day of work and usually recovers most of the loss — and only extract the service if the remaining profile is genuinely CPU-bound after that. If extraction is justified, the shape is a new Go service owning the domain, with Node reduced to a thin BFF, and the strangler pattern so both run behind a route flip. Reasoning: extraction is expensive and risky: a rewrite carries delivery risk with no user-visible benefit, and the parts of Node that are actually causing the problem (blocking work on the event loop) are fixable in Node. Go is the right *destination* when the profile stays CPU-bound after that — goroutines handle the IO fan-out, the static binary makes deployment trivial, and p99 becomes predictable. Trade-offs: two runtimes to operate, two on-call skill sets, and a contract between the services that must be maintained; that cost is only justified by a real measured bottleneck. Failure scenario: the rewrite takes four months, the feature queue stalls, and the p99 improvement could have been had in a week with worker threads — which is exactly the failure I am trying to avoid by measuring first. Prevention: a performance budget per endpoint with an alert, so the decision to extract is driven by a trend rather than by one bad week. Alternative: keep it in Node and fix the code, which is the correct answer more often than people admit."

🔴 How does Node's memory footprint affect your cloud bill?

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
Is the workload IO-bound with modest CPU?            → Node is a strong default
Does one-language-across-the-stack dominate your cost? → Node
Is there heavy CPU, encoding, or ML inference?        → separate service in Go/Rust/Python
Is money, and do you need exact decimal semantics?    → Go/Java, or integers everywhere in Node
Is the team's existing expertise elsewhere?           → use it; polyglot is cheaper than a rewrite
```

topics.title: Multi-Language Shops
topics.description: Multi-Language Shops within Other Backend Languages.
keyConcepts: When polyglot pays

A clear, measured bottleneck: one service is CPU-bound (image/video, ML inference, encryption, compression). Running it in Go or Rust while the rest stays in Node/Java is cheaper than an expensive rewrite.
Specialised ecosystems: Python for data science and ML, R for statistics, Elixir for high-fanout stateful systems — the ecosystem is the reason, not the taste.
Organisational reality: different teams already know different languages. Forcing a rewrite to a house language is often slower and more expensive than coexistence.
Latency-critical or footprint-constrained edges: CLIs, proxies, and functions where cold start and memory dominate cost.
Risk reduction: the new thing is written in the language with the best tooling for it, while the core stays stable.
What it costs
Every language is a build, deploy, observe, secure, and on-call pipeline. Version pinning, security patching, and CI matrix all multiply.

Cross-service contracts must be explicit: schemas, versioning, and generated clients. In-process type sharing (the single biggest Node advantage) is gone across a language boundary — so you need a real API contract (OpenAPI, protobuf) plus contract tests.
Hiring and rotation: a small pool per language makes on-call rotation and team mobility harder.
Observability uniformity: one tracing standard, one log schema, one metrics format, or debugging across the boundary is miserable.
Local development: N toolchains, N dependency managers, N ways to run tests.
commonMistakes: adding a language for developer preference; no shared tracing/log schema; language boundaries inside a domain; no client codegen; assuming generated clients stay in sync.
practiceTasks: write the platform ADR for adding a second language, including the measured-bottleneck requirement, the standardisation checklist, the ownership model, and the sunset path; then inventory your own repo against the checklist.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 When does a second language pay for itself?
🟡 What is lost when you cross a language boundary?
🔴 Your platform team supports four languages. What is the minimum standardisation to make it workable?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: we have Node, Python (for ML), and Go (for two extracted CPU-bound services), with eleven engineers. Decision: I standardise the *runtime*, not the language. Everything must speak OpenTelemetry with propagated trace context, emit structured JSON logs with a shared schema and a shared correlation id, expose Prometheus metrics with a naming convention and mandatory RED metrics per service, come from the same CI template with the same security scanning and dependency policy, deploy through the same pipeline, and publish an OpenAPI contract that generates typed clients on both sides. Reasoning: the debugging cost of a polyglot shop is not the languages, it is the inability to follow a request and to alert consistently across them. If tracing, logs, and metrics are uniform, the languages themselves become an implementation detail a developer rarely notices. Trade-offs: uniform conventions require enforcement in the platform template rather than in documentation, and generated clients need a codegen pipeline and a policy for when a client is stale. Failure scenario: a service is added outside the template with its own log format and no trace propagation, and now a single user-visible failure takes three tools and forty minutes to assemble. Prevention: the CI template is the only supported deployment path, and an exception requires an ADR. Prevention for drift: a nightly job that checks every service for trace propagation and metric conformance and fails the build if it regresses. Alternative: reduce the number of languages — that is genuinely better if the Python or Go services could be rewritten in Node, and I would test that hypothesis for each one rather than assuming it is worth the coexistence cost."
