topics.title: Logging levels
topics.description: a log is a structured, timestamped event emitted to stdout for a machine to read. "Structured" means key/value pairs with a schema, not an interpolated sentence. Levels exist to make the default log volume affordable and to route urgency: a log line is either *debug information for a developer*, *evidence of normal operation*, *a warning that needs attention*, or *a failure someone is being paged for*.
keyConcepts: The levels, and what actually belongs in each
Structured beats formatted, always
The correlation id is what makes a log stream usable
Redaction is a correctness requirement, not a nicety
Volume arithmetic — do this before you ship, not after you pay
Cardinality is the other half
Request logging done right
When not to log
Anything you need to count, alert on, or graph belongs in metrics. Logs are for explaining an individual event.
Anything you need to know the *shape* of (latency distribution, dependency fan-out) belongs in traces.
Expected 4xx (a validation failure) is not an error; it is info or warn with a machine-readable reason code, so the error rate stays a signal.
PII you do not need. Log userId, not the email; log country, not the address.
commonMistakes: console.log left in production: unlevelled, unstructured, unsampled, and invisible to severity filters.
Interpolating user input into the message: log injection via newlines, and unquotable values.
Logging at info on every request *and* every DB query *and* every cache miss: 5 GB/day at 100 rps, no one reads it.
Logging the request/response body "for debugging" on an auth or payment route.
Sampling errors because "it's too noisy" — the noise was the bug.
logger.error(err.message) losing the stack, which is the only part that locates the bug.
Emitting a raw Error object into JSON and getting {} because the stack is non-enumerable.
console.log in prod; logging bodies; logging URLs with tokens; sampling errors; losing stacks; unbounded field cardinality.
practiceTasks: wire the Pino logger above, add an access-log line with the route template, write a test asserting that a POST /auth/login with a password in the body produces zero occurrences of that password in the serialised output, then generate 10,000 requests and compute your bytes/day.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the levels, and what actually belongs in each and when you would use it.
Explain structured beats formatted, always and when you would use it.
Explain the correlation id is what makes a log stream usable and when you would use it.
Explain redaction is a correctness requirement, not a nicety and when you would use it.
Explain volume arithmetic — do this before you ship, not after you pay and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Structure vs readability. JSON is unreadable in a terminal. pino-pretty in development only; never in production, where it is a per-line CPU cost and a serialization hazard.

Redaction vs debugging. Aggressive redact paths hide the field you needed. The answer is a second, tightly-scoped, time-boxed "debug sink" with its own retention and access list — not disabling redaction.

Sampling vs completeness. Sampling loses the ability to reconstruct a specific user's journey. Sample by a stable hash of user id, not randomly, so a given user's requests are all-in or all-out and you can still follow them.
Retention vs cost. 30 days of everything is expensive; 7 days of everything plus 400 days of error-and-above is usually the right split, and it is a decision you should make deliberately.

Centralised vs per-node. Centralised gives you cross-node search and one place to look; per-node is cheaper and survives the aggregator. Mature setups ship both, with aggregation as the default and node files as the fallback.

topics.title: Soft deletes
topics.description: a soft delete marks a row as deleted (deleted_at timestamptz) instead of removing it, so it can be restored and so historical foreign keys and audit trails still resolve. The cost is that every query in the system now has an extra predicate, every unique index now has a subtlety, and your data grows forever unless someone owns retention.
keyConcepts: Never rely on every developer remembering where deleted_at is null
Retention: the data you actually have to keep
Cascading policy is a decision you must make per relationship
Hard cascade inside a request is a latency and lock risk
Restore has rules, and "undo" is not one of them

deleted_at changes the shape of every index. Either a partial index where deleted_at is null (small, fast, and only usable if your queries also carry the predicate) or include it in the key ((tenant_id, deleted_at, created_at desc)), which bloats the index but is simpler. Measure with the actual query.
COUNT(*) and analytics must include or exclude deleted rows deliberately. Finance reporting that silently drops soft-deleted rows is a report that disagrees with the ledger.
Restore is a privileged operation. It needs an audit entry, a reason, and (for regulated data) an approval.
Backups contain the deleted data. A soft delete is not an erasure from a backup taken last night. Your erasure procedure must say so, and your backup retention must bound it.
Cache invalidation. A soft-deleted row still exists, so an ID-keyed cache keeps serving it. Include deleted_at in the cache key or invalidate on delete.

Autovacuum. Soft-deleted rows are updated, which creates dead tuples. High-churn soft deletes need aggressive autovacuum on that table or the table bloats and queries slow down for reasons nobody connects to a delete button.

Legal hold is per record, not per table. Implement it as a legal_hold boolean checked by the purge job (where legal_hold = false) rather than by disabling the job, because the hold is scoped to records.
commonMistakes: A non-partial unique index, so re-registration fails after a delete.
deleted_at is not null missing from one raw query.
Soft-deleting millions of rows in a migration with no batch size and a huge WAL spike.
No retention job, so the table grows without bound and index performance degrades quietly.
Restore bringing back live sessions or API keys.
Treating soft delete as GDPR erasure.
No deleted_by, so you cannot answer "who deleted this" — and the audit log cannot answer it either.
plain unique index; missing predicate; unbatched purge; restore reviving credentials; soft delete ≠ erasure; no deleted_by.
practiceTasks: add deleted_at/deleted_by to customers and orders, fix the unique index, build the repository gateway, add a retention job that soft-deletes carts older than 60 days in batches of 1,000, and prove it with a test that deletes a customer, re-registers the same email, restores, and asserts the collision is reported rather than silently overwriting.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain never rely on every developer remembering where deleted_at is null and when you would use it.
Explain cascading policy is a decision you must make per relationship and when you would use it.
Explain hard cascade inside a request is a latency and lock risk and when you would use it.
Explain restore has rules, and "undo" is not one of them and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Soft delete vs hard delete. Soft delete keeps the row: cheap reads, a small query tax, unique-index subtleties, and unbounded growth. Hard delete is simple and satisfies erasure, but destroys history and breaks FKs from audit rows. Most systems use both: soft delete for the transactional record, hard delete on a retention schedule.

Hard delete immediately vs later. Immediate hard delete is simple but irreversible; deferred purge gives users a restore window and gives you time to notice a bad bulk delete. The bad bulk delete — update customers set deleted_at = now() where tenant_id = $1 with a wrong filter — is survivable with soft delete and catastrophic without it. That alone justifies it.
Anonymous vs pseudonymise vs delete. Anonymise is legally cleaner and analytically useless; deletion is analytically clean and legally risky.

Retention job vs partition drop. DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < $1 on 900 million rows in one transaction bloats the WAL and can hold locks for minutes. DETACH PARTITION/DROP TABLE on a date-partitioned table is instantaneous and reclaims space. If you keep high-volume event data, partition it.

topics.title: Audit logs
topics.description: an audit log is an append-only, tamper-evident record of *who* did *what* to *which* object, *when*, with enough detail (before and after) to reconstruct the state and to attribute the action to a human. It is not application logging: application logs are diagnostic and disposable, audit logs are evidentiary and retained.
keyConcepts: The five questions a usable audit log answers
The shape, and why the diff is mandatory
Immutability has four levels, and they are not equivalent
The hash chain, and why the external anchor matters
Auditing that actually holds up
Attribute to a human. "Service account billing-svc" is only as good as the delegation record: which user or job authorised that service to act, at what time, with what scope. Store the delegation.
Time is a witness. Clock skew undermines "who changed what when" entirely. Use NTP/chrony, log the clock offset in the entry, and record the source (db_now, app_now) so a discrepancy is detectable.

Coverage is auditable. You need to answer "is every privileged action audited?" The way to do that is a test: privileged endpoints cannot be reached without an audit call. An audit-coverage test that fails when a route with role = 'admin' has no audit call is worth more than any amount of documentation.
Retention exceeds the dispute window. If a claim can be filed two years later, two years of retention is not enough.

🟡 "What must an audit entry contain?" 🟡 "Why before-and-after rather than field names?" 🔴 "How do you make an audit log tamper-evident?" (Permissions + hash chain + external anchor, and the limit of each.) 🔴 "An admin says they did not change a user's role. Walk me through the evidence." (Entry with actor, session, ip, diff of role, request id → application log and trace for the same id → the delegation record for the service account → the head hash anchored in WORM storage.) 🔴 "How do you audit 10,000 read requests per second?" (Separate store, async, sampled or restricted to sensitive records, no hash chain per read; chain only the privileged writes.) ⚫ "Your database was fully compromised for six hours. What can you still prove?" (Anything anchored outside the DB before the compromise window; hash-chain continuity until the first forged row; nothing after. That answer is why the external anchor exists.)
commonMistakes: Logging to the application log and calling it an audit trail (it has levels, sampling, retention, and no actor).
Recording the action name but not the values.
Recording user_id only, so a support agent impersonating a customer is indistinguishable from the customer.
No request_id, so the entry cannot be joined to anything else during an incident.
A table the application role can UPDATE, so "immutability" is a code-review promise.
Hash-chaining without an external anchor, which an attacker with DB write access defeats by rewriting the tail.
Storing audit rows in the same table as the data, so DELETE FROM users WHERE … can be made to cascade.
Auditing reads of every row, which produces cost without covering the disputes that actually happen.
practiceTasks: create the audit_log table with permissions, build a repository hook that diffs before/after and calls audit_append, verify the chain with a query that recomputes every hash and reports the first mismatch, then corrupt one row by hand as a superuser and show the verification catching it.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the five questions a usable audit log answers and when you would use it.
Explain the shape, and why the diff is mandatory and when you would use it.
Explain immutability has four levels, and they are not equivalent and when you would use it.
Explain the hash chain, and why the external anchor matters and when you would use it.
Explain auditing that actually holds up and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: In-transaction vs asynchronous auditing. In-transaction is atomic with the change (you cannot change a row without an audit row) at the cost of latency and write amplification. Asynchronous (outbox → consumer → audit table) is fast and eventually consistent, and it can lose the entry if the consumer dies after the change. For privileged and financial actions, in-transaction. For high-volume reads, asynchronous or do not audit at all.
Full snapshots vs diffs. Snapshots are complete and grow with row size; diffs are readable and can miss a field you did not capture. Snapshots for small rows, diffs for large ones.

Same database vs separate store. Same database is transactional and simple, and shares the fate of a compromise. A separate store (or a different cluster/account) is stronger and cannot be tampered with in the same transaction as the data.

Full audit vs sampled audit. Auditing every read of every document produces terabytes and is rarely required; auditing every *privileged* action plus every export plus every authentication event covers the realistic dispute surface.

PII in audit logs. before/after snapshots copy personal data into a second store with a longer retention. Apply the same erasure policy to the audit log, which conflicts with immutability — the standard resolution is to anonymise the audit entry in place (a legitimate, logged exception to immutability) and record that the erasure happened.

topics.title: Multi-tenancy
topics.description: multi-tenancy is serving many customers (organisations) from one application such that no customer can see another's data, each customer gets their own configuration and limits, and the whole thing is operable. Three storage models dominate: shared schema (one table, a tenant_id column), schema-per-tenant (one Postgres schema, same tables), and database-per-tenant (one database).
keyConcepts: The decision table
The honest conclusion most teams reach
Connection strategy — the part database-per-tenant forces you to solve
Tenant resolution — where the tenant id comes from, in order of trust
Per-tenant settings and the limits you must enforce
Migrations at scale are the real operational cost

Expand/contract is mandatory: add the new column (nullable, no constraint) → deploy code that writes both and reads new-with-fallback → backfill in batches → add the constraint NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT concurrently → deploy code that reads new only → drop the old column in a later release. Every step is independently reversible.

Per-tenant migrations need a version ledger: tenant_schema_version(tenant_id, version, applied_at, duration_ms, error). Without it you cannot answer "is tenant 4,211 on version 47?" and a fleet-wide migrate will wedge on the one tenant whose migration failed.

Long-running per-tenant migrations need a lock budget. A create index without concurrently on a large tenant database takes an exclusive lock and blocks that tenant's writes. One tenant blocked is acceptable; all tenants blocked is an outage.
Migration code must be idempotent or versioned, because a per-tenant migration can fail halfway and be retried.

🟡 "Compare the three multi-tenancy models." 🟡 "How do you resolve the tenant id, and how do you stop spoofing?" 🔴 "You have 5,000 tenants. Walk me through your connection strategy." (Router pool / bounded LRU per-tenant pools; PgBouncer transaction mode; set local; cap the total.) 🔴 "How do you run a schema change across 5,000 tenant databases?" (Expand/contract, version ledger, batched, per-tenant lockouts, resumable, with a dashboard.) 🔴 "One enterprise customer needs their own database and a data-residency guarantee. How do you add that without forking the app?" (The tenant record carries a tier and a dsn; the pooler resolves by tier; all queries go through the tenant-scoped repository, so nothing else changes.) ⚫ "A customer requests deletion of all their data. Describe the execution plan across the model you chose." (Foreign-key-ordered anonymisation, per-table jobs with a progress record, object storage and search index and analytics warehouse and sub-processors, a certificate of completion that is itself audited, and the retention exceptions you are allowed to keep.)
commonMistakes: Resolving the tenant from a client-supplied header with no gateway enforcement.
Creating a Pool per tenant with no eviction, then running out of Postgres connections at 2am.
Tenant id in the app session but not in the WHERE clause of the query that runs later.
A search_path set at session level under transaction-mode pooling.
Migrations run as one big statement across all tenants.
Per-tenant schema divergence for "customisation", discovered eighteen months later.
No tenant_schema_version, so no way to prove which tenant is on which version.
Tenant settings read per row inside a loop.
practiceTasks: build the tenant registry and the withTenant context, then implement all three storage models behind one interface and a config switch. Measure query latency, migration wall time for 100 tenant databases, and connection count at 200 concurrent tenants. Write a one-page ADR choosing a model and citing the numbers.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the decision table and when you would use it.
Explain the honest conclusion most teams reach and when you would use it.
Explain connection strategy — the part database-per-tenant forces you to solve and when you would use it.
Explain tenant resolution — where the tenant id comes from, in order of trust and when you would use it.
Explain per-tenant settings and the limits you must enforce and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Isolation vs operational simplicity. Every step up the ladder buys isolation with connection count, migration fan-out, cross-tenant queries, and onboarding latency.

Uniformity vs customisation. Schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant let you add a column for one customer. That is exactly how you end up with 3,000 subtly different schemas and no idea what the actual shape is. Customisation belongs in configuration, not in schema, and this rule is worth more than any single architectural choice.
Cost vs compliance. A dedicated database per enterprise customer is a sales requirement and an operational tax. Price it.

Aggregate analytics. Shared schema makes "all tenants" trivial; database-per-tenant makes it a data-pipeline problem. If cross-tenant analytics is a product requirement, that alone justifies shared schema.
Noisy neighbours. Shared schema means a customer's bulk import slows everyone. Mitigations: statement timeouts, per-tenant concurrency limits, queueing of heavy operations, and a resource-group tier.

topics.title: API design reviews
topics.description: an API design review is a structured critique of an endpoint contract *before* it ships, focused on the properties that are expensive to change later: naming, resource shape, error contract, idempotency, authorisation, pagination, and evolution. A code review asks "is this correct?"; a design review asks "will this still be correct in six months, for two clients, after the team that wrote it has moved on?"
keyConcepts: Naming and shape: the conventions that actually matter
The review artefact
The public API is a promise. Everything you expose, you support. If you cannot support it, do not expose it. The cost of a field is permanent; the cost of an endpoint is measured in support tickets.

Contract tests between services. Consumer-driven contract tests fail the *provider's* build when a consumer's expectations break. This catches a field rename before the deploy rather than after the incident.

Version strategy interacts with review. If you are doing additive-only changes, you rarely need a /v2. Decide the versioning strategy first (5.10.15), because it changes what "compatible" means in review.
Deprecation headers are a machine-readable promise. Deprecation: true + Sunset + a Link to docs, so automated consumers can detect it (5.10.15).

Review the failure paths explicitly. Ask: what does this return when the dependency is down, when the row is missing, when the caller lacks permission, when the request is retried? Most bad contracts are good on the happy path.
Review the cost model. What is the most expensive request a client can make? Unbounded page size, an N+1, a full-text scan, a synchronous fan-out to 40 services.

🟢 "Review this endpoint." 🟡 "Is adding an enum value backwards compatible?" (No, for strict clients.) 🟡 "How does PATCH handle clearing a field?" 🔴 "What must every API define?" (Resource shape, error envelope, pagination, idempotency, authz, versioning/deprecation, rate limits, and the additive rule.) 🔴 "Your client says a field went missing after a deploy." (Contract test, OpenAPI diff, deprecation window.) ⚫ "Design the review process for a company with 300 internal APIs and no central ownership." (Mandatory OpenAPI in-repo, a CI diff gate per repo, a platform team's design-review office hours, consumer-driven contracts, a deprecation registry with usage telemetry, and a paved-road default template so the good pattern is the easy one.)
commonMistakes: Reviewing the happy path only.
Approving a design in a comment thread with no written artefact.
No CI gate, so the additive rule is enforced only by reviewer memory.
Returning entity objects directly from the ORM, leaking columns and coupling the contract to the schema.
No Location header on 201, no Retry-After on 429.
Enums that are integers, so a client cannot tell what 2 means.
Error bodies that are HTML from a proxy or a framework default.
A review that turns into a style debate and misses the authorisation check.
practiceTasks: take an existing endpoint of yours and write a review against the blocking-class table, find at least six real issues, fix four, and add an OpenAPI diff job to CI that fails on a deliberately breaking change.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the review artefact and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Review speed vs coverage. A 30-minute design review on an endpoint that will have 40 clients is an obvious win; on an internal endpoint with one consumer it is ceremony. Match the ceremony to the blast radius: *who else will depend on this, and for how long?*
Strictness vs flexibility. .strict() everywhere makes client typos loud but breaks clients that send fields from a newer version. Strict on writes and money; lenient on reads.
Consistency vs local clarity. A uniform envelope (data/pageInfo/errors everywhere) makes clients trivial and occasionally fits an endpoint poorly. Uniformity wins because client code is written once.
REST purity vs pragmatism. Strict REST with hypermedia is elegant and rarely adopted. A pragmatic subset — resources plus a few action sub-resources — is what ships.
Ship-now vs design-first. A week of design on an endpoint whose domain model is still moving is wasted. Design when the *shape* is stable; prototype while it is not.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
Resources are plural nouns, not verbs:              /orders, /orders/{orderId}
Hierarchy implies containment:                      /orders/{orderId}/line-items
Actions that are not CRUD get sub-resources:        POST /orders/{id}/cancellations
Never a verb in the path:                            /createOrder, /deleteUser
IDs are opaque to the client:                        "ord_01H8..." not 42
Booleans read as assertions:                         {"is_active": true}
Timestamps: RFC 3339, UTC, always with an offset:   "2026-03-04T11:02:31.481Z"
Money: integer minor units + explicit currency:     {"total_cents": 1299, "currency": "USD"}
Never a float for money. Never a boolean for a state machine.
Enums are lowercase snake_case strings, not numbers.
```

```
absent (key not in the body)  -> leave unchanged
null                           -> set to null (explicitly clear it)
"value"                        -> set to it
```

```ts
// The trap: `user.name = body.name` turns an absent key into undefined, and many ORMs
// then write NULL. The correct pattern distinguishes the three states.
const patch = UpdateProfile.parse(req.body);
const data: Record<string, unknown> = {};
if ('name' in patch) data.name = patch.name;                     // present -> set (may be null)
if ('avatar_url' in patch) data.avatarUrl = patch.avatar_url;   // null clears
// absent -> untouched
```

```yaml
# openapi-diff-ci.yaml — the gate that makes the additive rule real
# Fails the build on: removed paths, removed response properties, newly required
# request properties, narrowed enums, changed status codes.
rules:
  no-removed-paths: error
  no-removed-response-properties: error
  no-newly-required-request-properties: error
  no-narrowed-enums: warn        # warn: sometimes intended, never silent
  no-changed-status-codes: error
```

topics.title: Configuration and the Twelve-Factor App
topics.description: the twelve-factor methodology is a set of twelve practices for building services that scale cleanly and deploy without code changes. The two factors that dominate day-to-day backend work are II (store config in the environment) and III (treat config as code). Factor VII (port binding) is the one that turns a monolith into a container. Factor IV (build and release) and IX (disposability) are what make a deploy boring.
keyConcepts: The twelve factors, translated into what you actually type
Layering and precedence — know who wins, and write it down
The database URL is config. The pool size is config. The name of the primary key is code. Do not make structural decisions runtime-configurable.
Config that changes per request is not config — it is feature flags (5.10.12) or tenant settings (5.10.7). Putting "is the new checkout enabled" in an env var means a deploy to change it.
Config that changes per deployment of the same artifact must be in the environment, not the image (factor V).
Secrets are not config
Fail fast at boot, not at 3am
| Situation | Decision |
| Same artifact deployed to dev, staging, prod | Environment config (factors II and V). Non-negotiable |
| Feature needs to be toggled without a deploy | Feature-flag service, not env. An env change is a restart (5.10.12) |
| Per-tenant setting (retention days, plan limits) | Tenant row/config service, read from a cache with a version (5.10.7) |
commonMistakes: Reading process.env deep inside services, so there is no schema, no validation, and no test.
|| for defaults: process.env.PORT || 3000 means PORT=0 silently becomes 3000, and RETRY=0 becomes the default. Use ??, and use Zod coercion with a schema.
Shipping .env to production, or committing .env at all. Commit .env.example with every key and a comment.
Logging the config object at boot "for debugging". That is a secret exfiltration event with a friendly message.
Treating an env var as a flag: "set ENABLE_NEW_CHECKOUT=true and restart" makes every toggle a deploy, every rollback a deploy, and every experiment unmeasurable.
One giant config object passed to every function, so every unit test needs a 30-field fixture.
Booting successfully with an unreachable database and reporting healthy (5.10.13).
unvalidated env; secrets in the image; config-as-flag; no fail-fast; drift between environments; logging the config object.
practiceTasks: build the Zod config loader above, add a redactedForLog() helper, and write a test that boots with three deliberately broken environments and asserts the error message lists all three problems.

tradeoffs: Validation cost at boot: one schema parse. Worth it. The cost is that you now have a schema to keep in sync with your infrastructure, and a mismatch between "what the app requires" and "what the platform sets" is a deploy-time failure someone else has to fix at 4am. Add a CI step that runs the service with the staging environment's variable *names* (not values).
Fail-fast vs degraded start: refusing to boot is right for a required dependency, wrong for an optional one. A missing Sentry DSN should never crash a service; a missing DATABASE_URL should.

Immutability vs runtime reconfiguration: Object.freeze plus a reload endpoint means the process cannot pick up a changed env var. fs.watch on the env file is a clever idea that breaks under a read-only container filesystem and a symlinked secret mount.
Secrets manager latency at boot: pulling 40 secrets from Vault at startup adds a failure dependency. Cache them in the image or pull them in one batch with a hard timeout and a cached fallback.

topics.title: Logging Levels, Structured Logging, and Log Hygiene
topics.description: a log is a structured, timestamped event emitted to stdout for a machine to read. "Structured" means key/value pairs with a schema, not an interpolated sentence. Levels exist to make the default log volume affordable and to route urgency: a log line is either *debug information for a developer*, *evidence of normal operation*, *a warning that needs attention*, or *a failure someone is being paged for*.
keyConcepts: The levels, and what actually belongs in each
Structured beats formatted, always
The correlation id is what makes a log stream usable
Redaction is a correctness requirement, not a nicety
Volume arithmetic — do this before you ship, not after you pay
Cardinality is the other half
Request logging done right
When not to log
Anything you need to count, alert on, or graph belongs in metrics. Logs are for explaining an individual event.
Anything you need to know the *shape* of (latency distribution, dependency fan-out) belongs in traces.
Expected 4xx (a validation failure) is not an error; it is info or warn with a machine-readable reason code, so the error rate stays a signal.
PII you do not need. Log userId, not the email; log country, not the address.
commonMistakes: console.log left in production: unlevelled, unstructured, unsampled, and invisible to severity filters.
Interpolating user input into the message: log injection via newlines, and unquotable values.
Logging at info on every request *and* every DB query *and* every cache miss: 5 GB/day at 100 rps, no one reads it.
Logging the request/response body "for debugging" on an auth or payment route.
Sampling errors because "it's too noisy" — the noise was the bug.
logger.error(err.message) losing the stack, which is the only part that locates the bug.
Emitting a raw Error object into JSON and getting {} because the stack is non-enumerable.
console.log in prod; logging bodies; logging URLs with tokens; sampling errors; losing stacks; unbounded field cardinality.
practiceTasks: wire the Pino logger above, add an access-log line with the route template, write a test asserting that a POST /auth/login with a password in the body produces zero occurrences of that password in the serialised output, then generate 10,000 requests and compute your bytes/day.

tradeoffs: Structure vs readability. JSON is unreadable in a terminal. pino-pretty in development only; never in production, where it is a per-line CPU cost and a serialization hazard.

Redaction vs debugging. Aggressive redact paths hide the field you needed. The answer is a second, tightly-scoped, time-boxed "debug sink" with its own retention and access list — not disabling redaction.

Sampling vs completeness. Sampling loses the ability to reconstruct a specific user's journey. Sample by a stable hash of user id, not randomly, so a given user's requests are all-in or all-out and you can still follow them.
Retention vs cost. 30 days of everything is expensive; 7 days of everything plus 400 days of error-and-above is usually the right split, and it is a decision you should make deliberately.

Centralised vs per-node. Centralised gives you cross-node search and one place to look; per-node is cheaper and survives the aggregator. Mature setups ship both, with aggregation as the default and node files as the fallback.

topics.title: Input Validation and Boundary Discipline
topics.description: boundary validation is the practice of converting untrusted input into a typed, trusted value exactly once, at the edge of the system, and passing only that typed value inward. "Parse, don't validate" is the sharper version: a validator that returns true/false leaves the caller to re-derive meaning; a parser that returns a Date, a number, and a narrowed string has already done the work, and the type system takes over from there.
keyConcepts: The mechanics: reusable primitives, then one schema per boundary
The middleware that composes boundaries and produces one error shape
Coercion is where boundary bugs live
Mass assignment is the canonical boundary failure
Validation does not stop injection
When to validate / when not to
Body size limit is a validation concern. express.json({ limit: '100kb' }) plus a 413. A schema with .max() on every string does not save you from a 2 GB array of 1-byte objects.
Query-string sort and order must be allowlisted. ORDER BY ${req.query.sort} is SQL injection with extra steps, even if you "sanitised" it with a regex that allows commas and parens.
Depth and breadth limits on nested JSON. A schema with unbounded recursion is a stack-overflow endpoint.

Unicode and normalisation. Zalgo text, RTL overrides, homoglyphs in slugs, and different byte lengths for the same visible string all break uniqueness assumptions. Normalise to NFC at the boundary and compare normalised forms for uniqueness.
Validation is not authorisation. A perfectly valid GET /invoices/:id for someone else's invoice is an IDOR, and no schema prevents it.
Error budget for validation failures. A sudden spike in 422s from one client version is a deploy signal for *them*; a slow drip is an abuse signal. Track it.
commonMistakes: Validating only the body and trusting params/query.
Validating in the frontend only. Client validation is a UX affordance; it is not a control.
Coercing without constraining (Number(req.query.page) → NaN reaching the query builder).
.passthrough() on a body schema, which lets unknown keys through in a nested object.
Trusting Content-Type on uploads, or trusting the file extension.
Echoing submitted values in validation errors.
Treating validation as a substitute for parameterisation and output encoding.
Skipping validation on background-job payloads "because they came from us".
practiceTasks: build validate() above plus four schemas, then write a test file with 25 hostile inputs (deeply nested array, 10 MB string, sort=1;DROP TABLE, "1e999", __proto__, unicode homoglyph slug, duplicate keys, null where a string is expected, 200-item array, a duplicate JSON key) and assert the exact status and error path for each.

tradeoffs: Reject unknown vs ignore unknown. .strict() surfaces client typos immediately but breaks forward compatibility with a client sending a field from a newer API version. Choose per resource: strict on write endpoints for money and identity, lenient on read endpoints.
Rich errors vs information leakage. A field-level error map helps legitimate clients and helps attackers enumerate your schema. Never echo the submitted *value* back in an error.

Validate-at-the-edge vs validate-everywhere. Edge-only is DRY and fast; a queue consumer that trusts its producer will be broken by a producer deployed an hour earlier. Validate at each trust boundary, and make it cheap.
One schema vs three. Body, query, and params need three schemas and three middleware calls. That verbosity is the price of a typed route handler.

Early rejection vs partial processing. Validating the whole request before doing any work is correct and occasionally wasteful when 95% of requests are valid. Keep the validation cheap enough that it is never the bottleneck.

topics.title: Pagination Contracts: Offset vs Cursor, and Stability Under Writes
topics.description: pagination is a contract, not a utility: a fixed request shape, a fixed response envelope, and a stated guarantee about what the sequence means under concurrent writes. Choosing offset or cursor without stating the guarantee is how "the list skips items" tickets get filed.
keyConcepts: Offset vs cursor
Why the cursor must be opaque, signed, and tamper-evident
The response envelope — pick one and never vary it
When offset is still the right answer
Admin tables over small, bounded, non-changing result sets where a user *needs* to jump to page 40.
Backwards compatibility with an existing offset-based public API.
Random-access search UIs where the total is small and users expect it.
Export/report generation where you will iterate a fixed snapshot anyway (better: materialise the id list once and page over it).

Cursor invalidation. Cursors break when the sort column's collation or type changes, when a cursor outlives a deploy that changed the query, and when the filter set changes. Version the cursor: encodeCursor({ v: 2, ... }) and return 400 cursor_version rather than returning wrong rows.
Cursor TTL. Expire them (a day) to bound the blast radius of a stale-but-valid cursor, and encode an issued-at timestamp so you can.

Deep-offset degradation is a real incident. OFFSET 100000 on a 5-million-row table can burn 30 seconds of CPU. Cap the offset (MAX_OFFSET = 10000) and tell clients to use a cursor beyond that, or maintain a "jump to id" endpoint.
Unstable sort column. Sorting by updated_at means an item can move between pages while you page. Accept it, or sort by the immutable creation tuple and expose updated_at as a filter.
commonMistakes: Omitting the id tiebreaker — silently losing rows with equal timestamps.
The index does not match the ORDER BY.
Exposing raw created_at as the cursor, letting clients hand-edit it.
Accepting an arbitrary ?sort= value.
COUNT(*) inside the page query.
Keyset pagination with a nullable sort column.
Assuming OFFSET results are a snapshot.
Cursor pagination on a LEFT JOIN where duplicate joined rows break the limit + 1 trick (paginate the parent ids, then fetch children).
practiceTasks: implement both paginators behind one envelope, write a test that inserts 500 rows in the middle of paging and asserts the cursor version returns each id exactly once while the offset version does not, and inspect both plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE at page 1 and page 5,000.

topics.title: Soft Deletes, Retention, and the Data You Actually Have to Keep
topics.description: a soft delete marks a row as deleted (deleted_at timestamptz) instead of removing it, so it can be restored and so historical foreign keys and audit trails still resolve. The cost is that every query in the system now has an extra predicate, every unique index now has a subtlety, and your data grows forever unless someone owns retention.
keyConcepts: Never rely on every developer remembering where deleted_at is null
Retention: the data you actually have to keep
Cascading policy is a decision you must make per relationship
Hard cascade inside a request is a latency and lock risk
Restore has rules, and "undo" is not one of them

deleted_at changes the shape of every index. Either a partial index where deleted_at is null (small, fast, and only usable if your queries also carry the predicate) or include it in the key ((tenant_id, deleted_at, created_at desc)), which bloats the index but is simpler. Measure with the actual query.
COUNT(*) and analytics must include or exclude deleted rows deliberately. Finance reporting that silently drops soft-deleted rows is a report that disagrees with the ledger.
Restore is a privileged operation. It needs an audit entry, a reason, and (for regulated data) an approval.
Backups contain the deleted data. A soft delete is not an erasure from a backup taken last night. Your erasure procedure must say so, and your backup retention must bound it.
Cache invalidation. A soft-deleted row still exists, so an ID-keyed cache keeps serving it. Include deleted_at in the cache key or invalidate on delete.

Autovacuum. Soft-deleted rows are updated, which creates dead tuples. High-churn soft deletes need aggressive autovacuum on that table or the table bloats and queries slow down for reasons nobody connects to a delete button.

Legal hold is per record, not per table. Implement it as a legal_hold boolean checked by the purge job (where legal_hold = false) rather than by disabling the job, because the hold is scoped to records.
commonMistakes: A non-partial unique index, so re-registration fails after a delete.
deleted_at is not null missing from one raw query.
Soft-deleting millions of rows in a migration with no batch size and a huge WAL spike.
No retention job, so the table grows without bound and index performance degrades quietly.
Restore bringing back live sessions or API keys.
Treating soft delete as GDPR erasure.
No deleted_by, so you cannot answer "who deleted this" — and the audit log cannot answer it either.
plain unique index; missing predicate; unbatched purge; restore reviving credentials; soft delete ≠ erasure; no deleted_by.
practiceTasks: add deleted_at/deleted_by to customers and orders, fix the unique index, build the repository gateway, add a retention job that soft-deletes carts older than 60 days in batches of 1,000, and prove it with a test that deletes a customer, re-registers the same email, restores, and asserts the collision is reported rather than silently overwriting.

tradeoffs: Soft delete vs hard delete. Soft delete keeps the row: cheap reads, a small query tax, unique-index subtleties, and unbounded growth. Hard delete is simple and satisfies erasure, but destroys history and breaks FKs from audit rows. Most systems use both: soft delete for the transactional record, hard delete on a retention schedule.

Hard delete immediately vs later. Immediate hard delete is simple but irreversible; deferred purge gives users a restore window and gives you time to notice a bad bulk delete. The bad bulk delete — update customers set deleted_at = now() where tenant_id = $1 with a wrong filter — is survivable with soft delete and catastrophic without it. That alone justifies it.
Anonymous vs pseudonymise vs delete. Anonymise is legally cleaner and analytically useless; deletion is analytically clean and legally risky.

Retention job vs partition drop. DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < $1 on 900 million rows in one transaction bloats the WAL and can hold locks for minutes. DETACH PARTITION/DROP TABLE on a date-partitioned table is instantaneous and reclaims space. If you keep high-volume event data, partition it.

topics.title: Audit Logs: Immutability, Who Changed What, and Legal Defensibility
topics.description: an audit log is an append-only, tamper-evident record of *who* did *what* to *which* object, *when*, with enough detail (before and after) to reconstruct the state and to attribute the action to a human. It is not application logging: application logs are diagnostic and disposable, audit logs are evidentiary and retained.
keyConcepts: The five questions a usable audit log answers
The shape, and why the diff is mandatory
Immutability has four levels, and they are not equivalent
The hash chain, and why the external anchor matters
Auditing that actually holds up
Attribute to a human. "Service account billing-svc" is only as good as the delegation record: which user or job authorised that service to act, at what time, with what scope. Store the delegation.
Time is a witness. Clock skew undermines "who changed what when" entirely. Use NTP/chrony, log the clock offset in the entry, and record the source (db_now, app_now) so a discrepancy is detectable.

Coverage is auditable. You need to answer "is every privileged action audited?" The way to do that is a test: privileged endpoints cannot be reached without an audit call. An audit-coverage test that fails when a route with role = 'admin' has no audit call is worth more than any amount of documentation.
Retention exceeds the dispute window. If a claim can be filed two years later, two years of retention is not enough.

🟡 "What must an audit entry contain?" 🟡 "Why before-and-after rather than field names?" 🔴 "How do you make an audit log tamper-evident?" (Permissions + hash chain + external anchor, and the limit of each.) 🔴 "An admin says they did not change a user's role. Walk me through the evidence." (Entry with actor, session, ip, diff of role, request id → application log and trace for the same id → the delegation record for the service account → the head hash anchored in WORM storage.) 🔴 "How do you audit 10,000 read requests per second?" (Separate store, async, sampled or restricted to sensitive records, no hash chain per read; chain only the privileged writes.) ⚫ "Your database was fully compromised for six hours. What can you still prove?" (Anything anchored outside the DB before the compromise window; hash-chain continuity until the first forged row; nothing after. That answer is why the external anchor exists.)
commonMistakes: Logging to the application log and calling it an audit trail (it has levels, sampling, retention, and no actor).
Recording the action name but not the values.
Recording user_id only, so a support agent impersonating a customer is indistinguishable from the customer.
No request_id, so the entry cannot be joined to anything else during an incident.
A table the application role can UPDATE, so "immutability" is a code-review promise.
Hash-chaining without an external anchor, which an attacker with DB write access defeats by rewriting the tail.
Storing audit rows in the same table as the data, so DELETE FROM users WHERE … can be made to cascade.
Auditing reads of every row, which produces cost without covering the disputes that actually happen.
practiceTasks: create the audit_log table with permissions, build a repository hook that diffs before/after and calls audit_append, verify the chain with a query that recomputes every hash and reports the first mismatch, then corrupt one row by hand as a superuser and show the verification catching it.

tradeoffs: In-transaction vs asynchronous auditing. In-transaction is atomic with the change (you cannot change a row without an audit row) at the cost of latency and write amplification. Asynchronous (outbox → consumer → audit table) is fast and eventually consistent, and it can lose the entry if the consumer dies after the change. For privileged and financial actions, in-transaction. For high-volume reads, asynchronous or do not audit at all.
Full snapshots vs diffs. Snapshots are complete and grow with row size; diffs are readable and can miss a field you did not capture. Snapshots for small rows, diffs for large ones.

Same database vs separate store. Same database is transactional and simple, and shares the fate of a compromise. A separate store (or a different cluster/account) is stronger and cannot be tampered with in the same transaction as the data.

Full audit vs sampled audit. Auditing every read of every document produces terabytes and is rarely required; auditing every *privileged* action plus every export plus every authentication event covers the realistic dispute surface.

PII in audit logs. before/after snapshots copy personal data into a second store with a longer retention. Apply the same erasure policy to the audit log, which conflicts with immutability — the standard resolution is to anonymise the audit entry in place (a legitimate, logged exception to immutability) and record that the erasure happened.

topics.title: Multi-Tenancy: Shared Schema, Schema-Per-Tenant, and Database-Per-Tenant
topics.description: multi-tenancy is serving many customers (organisations) from one application such that no customer can see another's data, each customer gets their own configuration and limits, and the whole thing is operable. Three storage models dominate: shared schema (one table, a tenant_id column), schema-per-tenant (one Postgres schema, same tables), and database-per-tenant (one database).
keyConcepts: The decision table
The honest conclusion most teams reach
Connection strategy — the part database-per-tenant forces you to solve
Tenant resolution — where the tenant id comes from, in order of trust
Per-tenant settings and the limits you must enforce
Migrations at scale are the real operational cost

Expand/contract is mandatory: add the new column (nullable, no constraint) → deploy code that writes both and reads new-with-fallback → backfill in batches → add the constraint NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT concurrently → deploy code that reads new only → drop the old column in a later release. Every step is independently reversible.

Per-tenant migrations need a version ledger: tenant_schema_version(tenant_id, version, applied_at, duration_ms, error). Without it you cannot answer "is tenant 4,211 on version 47?" and a fleet-wide migrate will wedge on the one tenant whose migration failed.

Long-running per-tenant migrations need a lock budget. A create index without concurrently on a large tenant database takes an exclusive lock and blocks that tenant's writes. One tenant blocked is acceptable; all tenants blocked is an outage.
Migration code must be idempotent or versioned, because a per-tenant migration can fail halfway and be retried.

🟡 "Compare the three multi-tenancy models." 🟡 "How do you resolve the tenant id, and how do you stop spoofing?" 🔴 "You have 5,000 tenants. Walk me through your connection strategy." (Router pool / bounded LRU per-tenant pools; PgBouncer transaction mode; set local; cap the total.) 🔴 "How do you run a schema change across 5,000 tenant databases?" (Expand/contract, version ledger, batched, per-tenant lockouts, resumable, with a dashboard.) 🔴 "One enterprise customer needs their own database and a data-residency guarantee. How do you add that without forking the app?" (The tenant record carries a tier and a dsn; the pooler resolves by tier; all queries go through the tenant-scoped repository, so nothing else changes.) ⚫ "A customer requests deletion of all their data. Describe the execution plan across the model you chose." (Foreign-key-ordered anonymisation, per-table jobs with a progress record, object storage and search index and analytics warehouse and sub-processors, a certificate of completion that is itself audited, and the retention exceptions you are allowed to keep.)
commonMistakes: Resolving the tenant from a client-supplied header with no gateway enforcement.
Creating a Pool per tenant with no eviction, then running out of Postgres connections at 2am.
Tenant id in the app session but not in the WHERE clause of the query that runs later.
A search_path set at session level under transaction-mode pooling.
Migrations run as one big statement across all tenants.
Per-tenant schema divergence for "customisation", discovered eighteen months later.
No tenant_schema_version, so no way to prove which tenant is on which version.
Tenant settings read per row inside a loop.
practiceTasks: build the tenant registry and the withTenant context, then implement all three storage models behind one interface and a config switch. Measure query latency, migration wall time for 100 tenant databases, and connection count at 200 concurrent tenants. Write a one-page ADR choosing a model and citing the numbers.

tradeoffs: Isolation vs operational simplicity. Every step up the ladder buys isolation with connection count, migration fan-out, cross-tenant queries, and onboarding latency.

Uniformity vs customisation. Schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant let you add a column for one customer. That is exactly how you end up with 3,000 subtly different schemas and no idea what the actual shape is. Customisation belongs in configuration, not in schema, and this rule is worth more than any single architectural choice.
Cost vs compliance. A dedicated database per enterprise customer is a sales requirement and an operational tax. Price it.

Aggregate analytics. Shared schema makes "all tenants" trivial; database-per-tenant makes it a data-pipeline problem. If cross-tenant analytics is a product requirement, that alone justifies shared schema.
Noisy neighbours. Shared schema means a customer's bulk import slows everyone. Mitigations: statement timeouts, per-tenant concurrency limits, queueing of heavy operations, and a resource-group tier.

topics.title: Tenant Isolation and the Bugs That Leak Data Across Tenants
topics.description: tenant isolation is the property that no request, job, query, cache read, export, log line, or search result can ever return data belonging to another tenant. It is not a feature you add; it is a property of a system, and it fails in ways that are individually rare and collectively guaranteed.
keyConcepts: The leak catalogue — audit your codebase against this item by item
The unscoped repository method. A generic findById(id) that some endpoints use. Always findById(id, tenantId).
The object-storage path without a tenant prefix. s3://bucket/avatars/{userId}.png becomes s3://bucket/{tenantId}/avatars/{userId}.png. A path without a tenant is a cross-tenant path traversal.

The cache key without a tenant. cache:get:user:{id} must be cache:get:{tenantId}:user:{id}. This is the most common leak in otherwise-correct codebases, because the cache layer has no type that requires a tenant.

The background job without tenant context. A job enqueued from a request path that lost tenant_id processes row ids in a global scope. Jobs are the #1 source because they run with system privileges and no request context.
The export/report job. A report query written by hand with WHERE status = 'x' and no tenant filter, producing a file for a tenant.
The admin endpoint. "Support can see any tenant" implemented as ?tenantId= on a public endpoint, protected only by a role check that is missing on one route.
The search index without a tenant filter. Documents carry tenant_id but the query does not filter it, or the filter is applied in application code *after* fetching.
The ORM global scope disabled. A scoped $extends query, then one .unscoped() in a "just for the cron" line.
The join without a tenant predicate. select * from orders join users on users.id = orders.user_id where users is shared and user_id can collide across tenants.
The unique constraint across tenants. A shared unique(email) prevents two tenants from having the same email, or lets one tenant claim another's email.
The soft-delete restore. Restoring row 8,412 without checking the tenant returns someone else's deleted record.
commonMistakes: Believing an ORM global scope is a security boundary.
Enabling RLS without force, or without with check.
set instead of set_config(..., true) under a pool.
Cache keys without a tenant.
Jobs without a tenant field.
Per-tenant feature flags evaluated without tenant rules.
Testing only the endpoints someone thought of.
relying on convention; RLS without force/with check; session set under a pool; cache and job leaks; no matrix test; test fixtures with null tenant.
practiceTasks: turn on RLS with force and with check, write the route-table-driven isolation test, add a tenant-prefixed cache-key helper, then audit your repo against the 20-item catalogue and report every hit. The report is the deliverable.

tradeoffs: RLS vs application filtering. RLS is correct and costs a GUC round-trip per transaction, makes "no tenant set" an error you must handle in tooling, migrations, and admin jobs, and depends on the policy column being indexed.
Shared schema vs dedicated database. Isolation strength is the whole argument, but you pay on connections, migrations, cross-tenant queries, and support.

Strictness vs developer velocity. with check and non-null tenantId make some internal tooling (a platform migration, a support query) harder, because it now needs a tenant context. That friction is the point; provide a separate, audited break-glass role rather than weakening the default.

Encryption per tenant vs per row. Row-level encryption with a per-tenant key limits the blast radius of a leaked backup but complicates every query, every index (you cannot index an encrypted column), and every search. It is a compliance feature, not a security boundary against an application bug.

topics.title: API Design Reviews: What a Good Review Actually Catches
topics.description: an API design review is a structured critique of an endpoint contract *before* it ships, focused on the properties that are expensive to change later: naming, resource shape, error contract, idempotency, authorisation, pagination, and evolution. A code review asks "is this correct?"; a design review asks "will this still be correct in six months, for two clients, after the team that wrote it has moved on?"
keyConcepts: Naming and shape: the conventions that actually matter
The review artefact
The public API is a promise. Everything you expose, you support. If you cannot support it, do not expose it. The cost of a field is permanent; the cost of an endpoint is measured in support tickets.

Contract tests between services. Consumer-driven contract tests fail the *provider's* build when a consumer's expectations break. This catches a field rename before the deploy rather than after the incident.

Version strategy interacts with review. If you are doing additive-only changes, you rarely need a /v2. Decide the versioning strategy first (5.10.15), because it changes what "compatible" means in review.
Deprecation headers are a machine-readable promise. Deprecation: true + Sunset + a Link to docs, so automated consumers can detect it (5.10.15).

Review the failure paths explicitly. Ask: what does this return when the dependency is down, when the row is missing, when the caller lacks permission, when the request is retried? Most bad contracts are good on the happy path.
Review the cost model. What is the most expensive request a client can make? Unbounded page size, an N+1, a full-text scan, a synchronous fan-out to 40 services.

🟢 "Review this endpoint." 🟡 "Is adding an enum value backwards compatible?" (No, for strict clients.) 🟡 "How does PATCH handle clearing a field?" 🔴 "What must every API define?" (Resource shape, error envelope, pagination, idempotency, authz, versioning/deprecation, rate limits, and the additive rule.) 🔴 "Your client says a field went missing after a deploy." (Contract test, OpenAPI diff, deprecation window.) ⚫ "Design the review process for a company with 300 internal APIs and no central ownership." (Mandatory OpenAPI in-repo, a CI diff gate per repo, a platform team's design-review office hours, consumer-driven contracts, a deprecation registry with usage telemetry, and a paved-road default template so the good pattern is the easy one.)
commonMistakes: Reviewing the happy path only.
Approving a design in a comment thread with no written artefact.
No CI gate, so the additive rule is enforced only by reviewer memory.
Returning entity objects directly from the ORM, leaking columns and coupling the contract to the schema.
No Location header on 201, no Retry-After on 429.
Enums that are integers, so a client cannot tell what 2 means.
Error bodies that are HTML from a proxy or a framework default.
A review that turns into a style debate and misses the authorisation check.
practiceTasks: take an existing endpoint of yours and write a review against the blocking-class table, find at least six real issues, fix four, and add an OpenAPI diff job to CI that fails on a deliberately breaking change.

tradeoffs: Review speed vs coverage. A 30-minute design review on an endpoint that will have 40 clients is an obvious win; on an internal endpoint with one consumer it is ceremony. Match the ceremony to the blast radius: *who else will depend on this, and for how long?*
Strictness vs flexibility. .strict() everywhere makes client typos loud but breaks clients that send fields from a newer version. Strict on writes and money; lenient on reads.
Consistency vs local clarity. A uniform envelope (data/pageInfo/errors everywhere) makes clients trivial and occasionally fits an endpoint poorly. Uniformity wins because client code is written once.
REST purity vs pragmatism. Strict REST with hypermedia is elegant and rarely adopted. A pragmatic subset — resources plus a few action sub-resources — is what ships.
Ship-now vs design-first. A week of design on an endpoint whose domain model is still moving is wasted. Design when the *shape* is stable; prototype while it is not.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
Resources are plural nouns, not verbs:              /orders, /orders/{orderId}
Hierarchy implies containment:                      /orders/{orderId}/line-items
Actions that are not CRUD get sub-resources:        POST /orders/{id}/cancellations
Never a verb in the path:                            /createOrder, /deleteUser
IDs are opaque to the client:                        "ord_01H8..." not 42
Booleans read as assertions:                         {"is_active": true}
Timestamps: RFC 3339, UTC, always with an offset:   "2026-03-04T11:02:31.481Z"
Money: integer minor units + explicit currency:     {"total_cents": 1299, "currency": "USD"}
Never a float for money. Never a boolean for a state machine.
Enums are lowercase snake_case strings, not numbers.
```

```
absent (key not in the body)  -> leave unchanged
null                           -> set to null (explicitly clear it)
"value"                        -> set to it
```

```ts
// The trap: `user.name = body.name` turns an absent key into undefined, and many ORMs
// then write NULL. The correct pattern distinguishes the three states.
const patch = UpdateProfile.parse(req.body);
const data: Record<string, unknown> = {};
if ('name' in patch) data.name = patch.name;                     // present -> set (may be null)
if ('avatar_url' in patch) data.avatarUrl = patch.avatar_url;   // null clears
// absent -> untouched
```

```yaml
# openapi-diff-ci.yaml — the gate that makes the additive rule real
# Fails the build on: removed paths, removed response properties, newly required
# request properties, narrowed enums, changed status codes.
rules:
  no-removed-paths: error
  no-removed-response-properties: error
  no-newly-required-request-properties: error
  no-narrowed-enums: warn        # warn: sometimes intended, never silent
  no-changed-status-codes: error
```

topics.title: Idempotency Keys and Safe Retries
topics.description: idempotency means that performing the same operation N times has the same effect as performing it once. A client-supplied idempotency key makes a non-idempotent POST idempotent: the server stores the response for that key and replays it on subsequent identical requests instead of re-executing. It is the mechanism that turns "the network timed out, so the client retried" from a double-charge into a non-event.
keyConcepts: The full server-side contract, and every clause is load-bearing
Scoping: the three things that must be in scope
TTL and expiry
Retry storms and jitter
GETs and other naturally idempotent methods.
Endpoints that are *intentionally* repeatable (adding an item to a cart is not a bug when it happens twice — the quantity is the state, not the request).
Internal calls where you can make the operation naturally idempotent: PUT /resources/{id}/status with the target status, or an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING keyed on a business key.
Places where the side effect is already idempotent by design (upsert).

Unique index and the claim. create unique index on idempotency (tenant_id, user_id, endpoint, key) — the insert is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and its RETURNING tells you whether you claimed it. This turns a race into a database-enforced invariant.

Orphaned in_progress records. A crashed worker leaves one. A reaper clears them after locked_until, but only if the operation is *not* actually still running — so set the lock generously (a payment can take 30s) and make the reaper's window larger than the longest plausible operation.
The idempotency record and GDPR. You have stored the request body, which may contain PII, in a table designed for retention. Apply the erasure policy here too.
Cache the replay. Replaying from the database on every retry is fine; do not put the replay in a CDN cache keyed only by the idempotency key.
commonMistakes: SELECT then INSERT instead of an atomic claim — the race that double-charges.
Key not scoped to the user or tenant.
Same key with a different body silently replaying the old response.
Storing the record outside the transaction that performs the side effect.
Permanent in_progress with no reaper.
Retrying non-idempotent requests without a key.
Replaying a 5xx forever.
Exposing a response body containing another user's data through an unscoped key.
practiceTasks: implement the handler above against a real database, then write a test that fires 50 concurrent identical requests with the same key and asserts exactly one side effect, one 201, and 49 replays or 409s; then a test with the same key and a different body asserting 422; then kill the process between the side effect and the record write and prove the retry does not double-charge.

tradeoffs: Storage cost vs correctness. One row per mutating request, including the response body. It is a real table with real retention. Storing only a hash and looking up the resource instead is cheaper but changes the replay semantics.

In-progress collisions vs double execution. Returning 409 on a concurrent duplicate is honest but can fail a legitimate retry; *waiting* for the in-flight request is nicer but needs a timeout and turns your process into a synchronisation point. Most APIs return 409 with Retry-After.

Storing the response vs storing the resource id. Replaying a stored body guarantees byte-identical responses (which clients like) but goes stale if the resource changed in between. Re-reading the resource is fresher but is no longer a replay. Pick one and document it.

Failure handling. A failed record lets the client retry; keeping the failure permanently returns the same error forever, which is often what a payment client wants. Decide per endpoint: transient failures retryable, permanent failures sticky.

topics.title: Background-Job Hygiene, Cron Ownership, and the "Who Runs This" Question
topics.description: background-job hygiene is the set of practices that make scheduled and queued work safe to run in a replicated system: exactly one runner, a named owner, a stated schedule with an explicit timezone, a bounded runtime, idempotent handlers, and a dead-letter queue that somebody is accountable for. The question "who runs this?" has to have a written answer for every job in the system.
keyConcepts: The problem in one paragraph
Ownership: the minimum metadata every job needs
Single execution: the three mechanisms
Concurrency policy: what if the last run is still going?
The "who runs this" question, answered properly
Clock skew between nodes. The scheduler that fires at 03:00 and the node that logs the run must agree. NTP everywhere, and log the skew.
Job state must be observable like a service. Duration, success, count, and the newest-run timestamp as metrics; the DLQ depth as an alert; the log lines correlated by run id.
Backfills are jobs too. A backfill with 50 million rows needs batching, a rate limit, a resume cursor, and a kill switch. Treat it as a first-class job with an owner.
Idempotency for every handler. A queue is at-least-once; a scheduler retries. upsert keyed by the logical run key, or a uniqueness constraint that makes the second run a no-op.
Time limits and cancelation. Every job should honour a deadline and abort cleanly rather than being SIGKILLed mid-write.
Payload versioning. Jobs outlive deploys. A job enqueued by today's code is processed by tomorrow's worker, so validate the payload at the worker (5.10.3) and version it.
One-off admin work is a run-once process (factor XII). kubectl exec into production to fix data is a violation of every factor; ship a script with an audit entry.
commonMistakes: Cron in the app with 3 replicas.
No timezone on the schedule.
Advisory lock taken on a pooled connection that is returned before the job finishes.
pg_advisory_xact_lock with a commit in the middle, so the lock disappears.
No timeout, so a hung job holds the lock forever.
No "last success" alert, so a dead cron is discovered by a customer.
No owner, so the alert pages whoever is on call and nobody knows what to do.
Backfill with no batching, no resume, and no kill switch.
practiceTasks: move your most important scheduled job to a dedicated scheduler, add the job_runs logical-period guard, add a last_success alert, register the job with an owner, and then deliberately break it (comment out the schedule) and confirm the alert fires within one interval.

tradeoffs: Dedicated scheduler vs lock. A dedicated scheduler is more infrastructure and a second deployment to keep alive; a lock is three lines and fails open if the lock function is misused (wrong connection, transaction boundary). Both together is belt-and-braces and cheap.
Skip vs queue. Skip is safe if the handler is idempotent and re-reads its scope; queue preserves work and can cascade into a backlog. Instrument the decision rather than defaulting.

Per-job process vs a shared scheduler process. A shared scheduler is efficient and one bad job can starve the others; per-job processes are isolated and cost a cold start each. Most managed schedulers (K8s CronJob, EventBridge → Lambda) give you per-job isolation for free — take it for anything heavy.

Manual re-trigger. Runbooks need a way to run a job for one account or one period. Build that in deliberately (a CLI, or an authenticated admin endpoint with a reason field, audited) rather than letting someone run raw SQL.
Runtime limits. A job with no timeout will eventually hold a lock forever. Set both a statement timeout and a wall-clock timeout.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
name                 invoice-expander            unique, greppable
owner                team-payments  or  @alice   a team or a person, not "backend"
purpose (one line)   expand usage counters at period close so billing reads a number
schedule             0 3 * * *   timezone: UTC    NEVER implicit
concurrency policy   skip  |  queue  |  replace   what happens if the last run is still going
timeout              10 minutes                    bounded, so a hang is a failure not a stall
retries              3, exponential, jittered
idempotent           yes — upsert by (period_id, account_id)
input                the period id, resolved at run time, not baked in at schedule time
on failure           page team-payments | ticket to #billing-ops | dead-letter + daily digest
DLQ owner            team-payments                named, with an alert
observability        run duration, success rate, last success timestamp, rows processed
destructive          yes/no — gates the delete confirmation
```

```
1. Dedicated scheduler role. The deployment runs with SCHEDULER_ROLE=true, or you have a
   separate Kubernetes CronJob / Lambda / Cloud Scheduler task. One object, one replica,
   visible history in the platform. This is the default for anything important.
   Verify: the schedule is defined in IaC, and the workload has replicas: 1 or a policy.

2. Distributed lock (advisory lock). Safe inside Postgres, no extra infrastructure.
   -- A session-level advisory lock is released when the connection dies, which is exactly
   -- the behaviour you want: a crashed runner's lock disappears.
   select pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext('job:invoice-expander'));   -- 0 = someone else holds it
   ...
   select pg_advisory_unlock(hashtext('job:invoice-expander'));
   -- Must be on ONE connection for the whole job: use a dedicated client, not the pool.
   -- Do NOT use pg_advisory_xact_lock if you commit mid-job: the lock ends at COMMIT.

3. Leader election. Every replica tries; one wins and runs the scheduler.
   Typically a Redis lease with TTL and a fencing token, or a Kubernetes Lease object.
   More machinery than you need for a cron job; use it for continuous schedulers where
   every pod should be able to take over instantly.
```

```ts
// The advisory-lock version, done correctly with a dedicated connection.
export async function runExclusively(jobName: string, fn: () => Promise<void>, metrics: Metrics) {
  const client = await pool.connect();                 // ONE connection for the whole run
  try {
    const { rows } = await client.query('select pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext($1)) as ok', [jobName]);
    if (!rows[0].ok) { metrics.jobSkipped(jobName, 'lock_held'); return; }
    metrics.jobStarted(jobName);
    await fn();                                        // your body, on this same client if it needs the lock
    metrics.jobSucceeded(jobName);
  } catch (err) {
    metrics.jobFailed(jobName, err);
    throw err;
  } finally {
    await client.query('select pg_advisory_unlock(hashtext($1))', [jobName]).catch(() => {});
    client.release();
  }
}
```

```
"0 3 * * *"      -> what zone? The container's TZ (often UTC, sometimes nothing at all).
"30 2 * * *"     -> on the spring-forward day, 02:30 DOES NOT EXIST. Cron behaviour varies:
                     Vixie cron skips it; some schedulers run at 03:00; some run at 01:30.
"30 1 * * *"     -> on the autumn day, 01:30 occurs TWICE. The job may run twice.
```

```ts
// The robust pattern: key the run on the logical period in the target timezone.
const key = `${jobName}:${periodKey}`;   // e.g. 'invoice-expander:2026-03-04'
const claimed = await db.jobRuns.insertOrIgnore({ key, started_at: new Date() });
if (!claimed.inserted) { log.info({ job: jobName, key }, 'already ran for this period'); return; }
```

```
skip    take the lock, find it held, log and move on. Right for: cleanup, aggregation,
        anything that will pick up the same scope anyway. Default.
queue   let runs pile up and execute serially. Right for: imports, backfills, anything where
        dropping a run loses data. Needs a visible depth metric and a cap (5 queued runs
        means something is very wrong — alert on depth, not just on the run).
replace kill the in-flight run and start a new one. Right for: sync jobs where only the
        latest state matters. Dangerous: the killed run may have half-written.
```

```
1. "It's in the code."            Someone has to read the codebase to find it.
2. "It's in a documented list."   A `JOBS.md` or a dashboard nobody has opened.
3. "It's registered."             Each job self-registers at boot into a `jobs` table with
                                  owner, schedule, timeout, and DLQ. A UI lists them. A nightly
                                  job alerts on any job with no owner.
4. "It has a dashboard and an alert."  Per-job metrics: last success, duration, success rate,
                                  rows processed, queue depth. An alert fires if
                                  last_success > 2x the schedule interval. That single alert
                                  catches "the cron silently stopped working", which is the
                                  most damaging class of cron failure because nothing
                                  downstream breaks loudly.
```

topics.title: Feature Flags, Kill Switches, and Staged Rollout Discipline
topics.description: a feature flag is a runtime boolean (or small enum) that selects between two code paths that are both deployed. A kill switch is a flag whose purpose is to stop something harmful immediately. A release flag gates a feature's availability. A permission flag grants a capability to a specific tenant or user. These have different lifetimes, owners, and removal rules, and conflating them is where teams get stuck.
keyConcepts: The taxonomy, with the rule that matters for each
Flags vs config: the difference that prevents incidents
Staged rollout: the gates, not just the percentages
Sticky bucketing
Flag debt is the real cost
The dangerous interactions
Flags that change data shape create mixed-version states: old code reading a new shape. Migrations must be backward compatible across the whole window where the flag is partially on.
Flags inside loops and hot paths add an evaluation cost per iteration; evaluate once per request and pass it down.
Flags evaluated per request without a tenant rule mean tenant A's config leaks into tenant B's experiment, or an enterprise tenant is put in an experiment they cannot exit.
Two flags that interact (newCheckout and newPayments) produce four combinations, one of which may never have been tested. Cap the number of simultaneously-changing flags per surface — ideally one.
A flag defaulting to true in a new environment turns a launch into a config change nobody reviewed. New environments inherit "off" unless explicitly enabled.

Flag evaluation must fail closed or open deliberately. If the flag service is unreachable: fail *open* (serve the stable path) for a kill switch and a release flag; fail *closed* (do not sell) for a permission flag. Decide per flag and record it in the flag's metadata.
commonMistakes: Kill switch that depends on the subsystem it disables.
No expiry, ever; the flag becomes permanent.
Random bucketing instead of a hash, so users flip variants.
Rollout percentages with no cohort comparison, only global dashboards.
A flag on a data migration with no expand/contract plan.
if (flag) { /* 400 lines */ } with no test for the false branch.
Flag service called per row in a batch job.
Two flags changing on the same surface simultaneously.
practiceTasks: implement hash-based bucketing, wire a kill switch with an env-var backstop, add a 1% → 5% → 25% rollout with cohort metrics, and set an expiry on the flag. Then delete the flag and let CI catch the stale reference.

tradeoffs: Flags vs separate deploys (blue/green). Flags give per-user targeting and instant rollback; separate deployments give code isolation and no dead branches. Flags are the standard answer for gradual rollout because blue/green cannot do "1% of users".
Branching vs trunk-based development. Long-lived branches let you keep the old code path, but they rot and they conflict. Trunk with flags keeps main releasable and the branch short-lived.

A flag service vs a database table vs an env var. A service gives streaming updates, targeting, audit, and a UI; it is another dependency. A table gives you everything except streaming, and "refresh the in-process cache every 10 seconds" covers most cases. An env var gives you a deploy.

Removing flags immediately vs later. Removing immediately loses the ability to roll back without a deploy. Removing after two weeks of 100% is the pragmatic answer, and the code path is then provably unused.
Per-tenant entitlement via flags vs a real entitlement table. Flags are faster; an entitlement table is auditable and queryable for billing. For anything you sell, it is a table.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```ts
// WRONG: the switch lives in the database the failing subsystem uses to operate.
const kill = await db.featureFlags.get('payments');      // db is the thing that is down

// RIGHT: the switch is readable without the failing dependency, and there is a
// last-resort path that does not need the application at all (env var, instance
// metadata, a gateway rule, or an infrastructure-level toggle).
function isEnabled(name: string): boolean {
  const emergency = process.env.EMERGENCY_DISABLE?.split(',') ?? [];   // deploy-time, always readable
  if (emergency.includes(name)) return false;
  return flagClient.isEnabled(name);                     // dynamic, cached, may be stale
}
```

```
Config   changes on deploy. Global. Bounded set. Reviewed in the PR. Removed when obsolete.
Flag     changes without a deploy. Evaluated per request. Unbounded set. Removed on a schedule.
```

```
0%    internal / dogfood only. Watch the logs, not the dashboards.
```
