```
1%    is the new path executed at all? Flag evaluation, code path, data written.
5%    is the data correct? Compare against the control: orders created, totals, error rate.
25%   does latency hold? p95/p99 for the flag-on cohort vs the control, not the global average.
50%   support tickets? A qualitative signal that dashboards will not show.
100%  full rollout, then the flag is removed within a stated window (two weeks, hard).
```

```ts
function bucket(key: string, flagName: string, variants: number): number {
  const h = createHash('sha256').update(`${flagName}:${key}`).digest();   // NOT Math.random()
  return h.readUInt32BE(0) % variants;                                     // deterministic, uniform
}
```

```
- Every flag has an owner and an expiry date, in the flag store, enforced by the UI.
- A weekly report of flags approaching expiry; the owner confirms or deletes.
- A CI job that greps for flag names that do not exist in the store   (deleted flag, live code).
- A CI job that greps for flags in the store that no code reads        (dead flag, live store).
- An expiry that DELETES, with a two-week warning. A flag that survives its expiry by
  being "just moved forward" every sprint is a permanent branch.
- Never flag a data migration without the expand/contract plan: a flag can stop new
  writes, but it cannot un-write rows already written by the on-path.
```

topics.title: Health Checks, Readiness, and Liveness That Do Not Lie
topics.description: health checks are endpoints an orchestrator or load balancer polls to decide what to do with a process. Three probes with three distinct meanings, and confusing them is one of the most reliable ways to turn a small dependency failure into a full outage.
keyConcepts: The three probes
The three rules that prevent cascading failure
The implementation, with the loop-liveness check that most people miss
The graceful-drain sequence, and where readiness fits in it
| Situation | /livez | /readyz |
| Stateless API, all dependencies healthy | Loop check only | select 1 + migration marker |
| Dependency is a cache | Loop check only | Record status, do not gate |
| Dependency is the database | Loop check only | Gate (with timeout) |
| Long migrations at boot | Loop check | Refuse until done |
| Consumer that drains on SIGTERM | Stays green | 503 immediately |
| External dependency with a local cache in front | Loop check only | Gate only if the cache cannot serve |
commonMistakes: Liveness checking the database, so one slow query restarts the entire fleet.
Readiness with no timeout, so a saturated pool evicts every pod at once.
Deep readiness checks on every probe, adding 100 queries/second of load.
Flipping liveness during the drain, so the orchestrator SIGKILLs you mid-request.
No propagation delay between readiness flipping and the LB noticing.
Counting in-flight requests on finish only, so an aborted request hangs the drain.
Probes behind rate limiting, so a probe storm gets 429s and looks like a failure.
A readiness endpoint that reports ok: true while migrations are half-applied.
practiceTasks: implement /livez, /readyz, and /startupz exactly as above, then deliberately block the event loop for 5 seconds and assert /livez fails; point DATABASE_URL at a blackhole and assert /readyz fails within its budget *without* restarting the pod.

interviewQuestions.text: Is the process wedged?
interviewQuestions.answer: Restart the container

interviewQuestions.text: Can this instance serve traffic right now?
interviewQuestions.answer: Remove from the load-balancer pool; no restart

interviewQuestions.text: Has boot finished?
interviewQuestions.answer: Keep waiting until failureThreshold is hit, then restart

tradeoffs: Deep vs shallow readiness. Deep checks route around a genuinely broken instance, which is good. Deep checks also add latency to every probe and can mass-evict pods when the shared dependency is slow. Rule: gate on what you cannot serve without, observe everything else.

Startup probe vs slow liveness threshold. A slow boot with a generous livenessProbe.initialDelaySeconds works, but the delay is static and must cover the slowest cold start including dependency timeouts. A startupProbe is dynamic: it disables liveness until boot succeeds, which is strictly better for slow starters.

Readiness as a load-shedding mechanism. Readiness is the cheapest way to shed load during a dependency brownout — better than a circuit breaker because it acts before requests arrive. But it is a blunt instrument: it removes capacity entirely, so pair it with a per-request deadline and a breaker so a shed instance is not the only defence.

Probe cost vs freshness. Caching readiness for 5-30 seconds cuts probe load by orders of magnitude at the price of a window where a failed instance still receives traffic. That window is normally fine; it is not fine if your failure mode is a hung process holding connections.

Exposing health publicly. /livez and /readyz must be unauthenticated (the orchestrator has no credentials) and must be excluded from rate limiting, tracing instrumentation, and access-log sampling. They must also expose nothing sensitive: a readiness endpoint listing your internal hostnames and database replicas is reconnaissance.

topics.title: Operational Readiness: Runbooks, SLOs, and the Pre-Launch Checklist
topics.description: operational readiness is the state in which a service can be run by someone who did not build it, at 3am, without the author on the phone. It has three components: instrumentation (metrics and dashboards you can read), objectives (a measurable target and the error budget it implies), and procedures (a runbook per alert and a pre-launch checklist that gates the release).
keyConcepts: SLI, SLO, and error budget — the vocabulary you must use precisely
Error budgets and release policy — a concrete example
Burn-rate alerting, and why a single threshold does not work
What to alert on, and what not to
The runbook: what one actually contains
The pre-launch checklist — the gate, not the wish list

🟡 "What is an error budget and how would you use it?" 🟡 "What makes a good alert?" (A symptom, with a threshold that means something, and a link to the runbook.) 🔴 "Define an SLI and SLO for a checkout service." (Successful valid requests excluding 429 and client errors, over 30 days; plus checkout-completion rate; target 99.9%; budget ~0.1%.) 🔴 "Your error rate is 0.4%. Do you ship?" (Only with context: current burn vs the window, whether it is a known cause, whether the change is reversible, and what the budget position is. An answer that is yes or no without that reasoning is the wrong answer.) 🔴 "Your p99 is 900 ms and your SLO is 300 ms. Why has nobody been paged?" (Wrong threshold, or alerting on the average, or a SLI that measures the wrong thing, or the alert routed to a dashboard nobody watches.) ⚫ "Your SLO is 99.9%, and a dependency pushes errors to 2% for 30 minutes. Walk me through the alert, the response, and the follow-up." (Multiwindow burn-rate alert fires on the 1h condition; the on-call runs the runbook; mitigation is the breaker plus a flag plus shedding; the postmortem asks whether the dependency should have been behind a timeout, whether the error budget policy should have frozen releases, and whether the runbook was current.)
commonMistakes: An SLO nobody agreed to, so it is not used to make decisions.
Alerting on causes (CPU, memory) instead of symptoms.
A single-threshold error-rate alert that pages for a trickle.
Runbooks that are links to dashboards rather than procedures.
No rollback rehearsal, so the first real rollback fails for a reason nobody predicted.
A launch with a technical metric and no business metric.
No named owner for the first 48 hours after launch.
Treating the checklist as paperwork rather than as gates.
practiceTasks: write an SLO and error-budget policy for one of your services, implement a two-window burn-rate alert, write a full runbook for one existing alert, then run a 20-minute game day where you kill the primary dependency and follow the runbook with someone who has never seen the service.

tradeoffs: SLIs vs raw metrics. A full user-journey SLI ("can a user complete checkout") is the most honest and the hardest; per-endpoint availability is easy and can be green while the journey is broken. Use both: per-endpoint for diagnosis, journey-level for the SLO.

Strict SLOs vs pragmatic ones. 99.99% for a hobby project means a 4-minute monthly budget and a feature freeze every month. 99.5% is often honest and sustainable. Pick the SLO you will actually defend.
Checklists vs judgement. A 60-item checklist gets skipped. Gate the top 8 items in CI and keep the rest as a review conversation.
Runbooks written before launch vs after the first incident. Before, if you can. After, if you must — but then write it the day it burns you, while the details are fresh.
Game days vs real incidents. A deliberate failure on a Tuesday is worth ten postmortems, because the runbook gets tested where you can still ask questions.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
SLI   a measured quantity: "the proportion of valid requests served successfully,
      measured over 30 days, excluding 429s" or "p99 latency under 300 ms for
      /checkout". The *measurement definition* is the hard part and the part
      most teams skip.
SLO   the target for an SLI: 99.9% of valid requests return non-5xx within 300 ms.
      An SLO is a promise to users, chosen by engineering + product together.
Budget  1 - SLO. With 99.9%, your monthly budget is 0.1% of requests. It is the
      currency you spend on releases: every risky deploy spends budget, and when
      it is exhausted you freeze features and fix reliability.
```

```
99.9% monthly SLO on the availability SLI, ~40M requests/month
  budget: ~40,000 failed requests

14:00  budget 60% remaining   -> ship normally
14:00  budget 20% remaining   -> fixes and stabilisation only, no feature flags on prod
14:00  budget exhausted       -> release freeze; the team works reliability until the
                                 budget recovers (windowed burn rate matters, not the
                                 monthly number, so recovery is measured properly)
```

```
Fast burn (page):   14.4x budget burn over 1h AND 5m     -> ~2% of budget in an hour
                     page, because this burns a month of budget in a day
Slow burn (ticket): 6x budget burn over 6h AND 30m        -> investigate during the day
                     AND 3x over 3d                      -> a week-long problem

Plus one multiwindow, multi-burn-rate rule, and a "budget remaining" dashboard.
The 5-minute-window condition is what stops you paging when the incident is already over.
```

```
ALERT: availability burn rate, latency burn rate, error-budget exhaustion
ALERT: queue depth and OLDEST MESSAGE AGE (depth alone lies: a deep queue draining
       steadily is fine; 3 messages stuck for an hour is an incident)
ALERT: job last-success age (catches the silently-dead cron)
ALERT: certificate expiry (< 14 days), secrets rotation overdue
ALERT: replication lag, disk space, connection-pool saturation
TICKET: individual 5xx from one upstream, slow growth of a queue, a single region degraded
LOG-QUERY: a new error signature appearing at all
NEVER: CPU at 80%, memory at 75%, "disk usage changed", a single request failure
```

```
1. Title + one-sentence statement of what breaks and who is affected
2. Severity and the alert that fires it (link)
3. Dashboard links (the exact panels, not the dashboard index)
4. Detection: how this looks in metrics, logs, and traces
5. Diagnosis: a decision tree or an ordered list of queries to run
     SELECT ... ;  -- copy-pasteable, parameterised, with a default time range
6. Mitigation: what to do RIGHT NOW, with the exact command, in order, with
   expected output at each step. Most mitigations are: roll back, disable a flag,
   shed load, restart, fail over.
7. Escalation: who, when to page them, after how long
8. Verification: how to confirm it is actually fixed (the query, the panel, the check)
9. Rollback/undo: how to undo the mitigation itself
10. Known gotchas and history: what has fooled you before
```

```
Design & correctness
  [ ] Error contract, pagination contract, idempotency, and authz reviewed (5.10.9)
  [ ] Every new endpoint in the API docs with an owner
  [ ] Backwards compatibility checked by the CI diff gate
  [ ] Feature flags default OFF in production, with an owner and an expiry

Data
  [ ] Migration is expand/contract, reversible, and has been run on a production-sized copy
  [ ] Backfill has a resume cursor, batching, a rate limit, and a kill switch
  [ ] Indexes created CONCURRENTLY where the table is large
  [ ] Retention/purge behaviour verified for every new table

Observability
  [ ] RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) per endpoint, per service
  [ ] A dashboard exists and someone other than the author has read it
  [ ] The SLO is defined and measured; the burn-rate alert is wired
  [ ] Structured logs with correlation ids and redaction verified
  [ ] Business metrics for the feature's success AND its failure (a launch with no
      business metric cannot be evaluated, only argued about)

Operational
  [ ] Runbook written for every new alert, and rehearsed
  [ ] On-call ownership and escalation are defined (CODEOWNERS)
  [ ] Capacity: has this been load tested at 2x expected peak with the new query pattern?
  [ ] Rollback plan exists and has been rehearsed — a rollback that has never been run
      is a hypothesis
  [ ] Deploy is progressive (canary or blue/green) with an automatic rollback trigger
  [ ] Dependency inventory is complete: what new third parties does this add?
  [ ] Security review: authz on every new route, secret handling, upload paths, injection

Communication
  [ ] Support and CS briefed on user-visible changes
  [ ] Customer-facing changes have a comms plan and a rollback comms plan
  [ ] Launch monitoring owner for the first 48 hours is named
```

topics.title: Deprecation, Versioning, and Killing a Feature Safely
topics.description: deprecation is the managed retirement of an interface or behaviour: you announce it, you measure who still uses it, you migrate consumers, you enforce a date, and you remove it. Versioning is one *mechanism* for deprecation; it is not the process, and the process is the part that actually gets skipped.
keyConcepts: Versioning strategies, honestly compared
The recommendation, and the reasoning you should be able to give
Deprecation is a five-step process, and the steps are the deliverable
410 vs 404 vs 501 is worth stating explicitly
Killing a feature safely — the order matters more than the decision
Internal deprecation: the same discipline for code, not just APIs

🟢 "How do you deprecate an API endpoint?" 🟡 "What headers do you send when deprecating?" (Deprecation, Sunset, Link rel="deprecation".) 🟡 "404 or 410 after removal, and why?" 🔴 "You need to remove POST /v1/charges. Walk me through the process." (Usage telemetry first; announce with a date and an alternative; migrate; 410 after sunset; then delete code and data. Explicitly: what about existing saved payment methods? That is a data migration, not a code change.) 🔴 "You deprecated an endpoint and a big customer broke. What did you miss?" (No per-consumer usage data; no direct notification; no migration path; a sunset date inside their freeze window.) 🔴 "Your API has v1, v2, and v3. How do you get to one version?" (Pick the newest as canonical, make v2 and v1 additive-compatible with it where possible, publish usage telemetry per version, set a sunset date, and offer a codemod. Do not announce a v4.) ⚫ "Design the deprecation of a legacy webhook for 40,000 registered endpoints." (Per-endpoint usage telemetry including last-delivery time and failure rate; tiered communication by usage; a signature-compatible shim so the migration is a URL change; a sandbox for verification; a 90-day window with weekly reminders; 410 with a signed migration guide; and a grandfathered exception process for the top ten accounts with named owners and dates.)
commonMistakes: Deprecating with a changelog entry and no measurement of who is affected.
No Sunset date, so it never actually ends.
Removing the code without migrating the data, so users lose their carts/integrations.
Responding 404 after removal, which generates support tickets instead of self-diagnosing errors.
Keeping the "off" path after removal, so the feature can be resurrected by a stale flag.
A deprecation with no alternative provided.
Internal deprecation with no build-level usage report, so nobody knows who still calls it.
Running v1 and v2 forever because nobody owns the migration.
practiceTasks: pick one endpoint in your API, add the three deprecation headers, build per-consumer usage telemetry for it, write the migration guide, and dry-run the whole thing with a fake consumer — including the 410 response.

tradeoffs: Additive-only vs major versions. Additive-only avoids version debt entirely and is the best long-term answer, but it constrains you: you can never change a shape, only add. That constraint is real and should be accepted deliberately, not discovered.

Long support windows vs a moving codebase. A 24-month deprecation window is generous to consumers and expensive for you (N-1 maintenance, doubled test matrix, security patching twice). Twelve months is a common compromise. The right number depends on your customers' release cycle, so ask, do not assume.

Silently breaking vs loudly failing. Silent breakage produces angry customers and a hard debugging session. A loud 410 with a pointer produces a self-diagnosing client error and a support ticket that takes two minutes. Loud always wins, provided the loudness is actionable.

Deleting data vs keeping it read-only. Deleting is clean and is often a compliance requirement; keeping it read-only for a defined period is kinder to users who need to migrate. Decide the retention explicitly, and honour an erasure request inside it.

Flags vs versions for a behaviour change. A flag can be turned off instantly and targeted at a cohort; a version cannot. Use a flag for behaviour and a version for shape, and do not use a version to ship a behaviour change "safely".

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
1. DECIDE   Write the reason and the alternative. "Deprecated because the v1 webhook
            cannot sign payloads; use v2." "Deprecated because of a security fix in
            the underlying library" are useful. "Deprecated" is not.
2. ANNOUNCE In the response headers (machine-readable), in the docs, and in the product:
              Deprecation: true
              Sunset: Wed, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT      (RFC 8594)
              Link: <https://docs.example.com/migrate-v2>; rel="deprecation"
            Email every registered consumer with usage numbers, not a generic notice.
            A banner in the developer dashboard showing YOUR usage of the deprecated
            endpoint is the single most effective announcement there is.
3. MEASURE  Per-consumer usage telemetry, exported to a dashboard and emailed weekly:
            who called it, how often, last call time, and their plan tier. You cannot
            migrate what you cannot see, and "we deprecated it and someone broke"
            is a support incident you chose to create.
4. MIGRATE  Provide a migration path that is easier than staying: a compatibility shim,
            a codemod, a self-serve migration tool, a migration deadline before the
            deadline. Deprecation without a migration path is an ultimatum.
5. ENFORCE  After the sunset date, respond 410 Gone with a pointer — not 404 (which
            looks like a bug and generates tickets) and not 200 with a warning body
            (which nobody reads). Then delete the code, the tests, and the docs.
```

```
404 Not Found     "I have never heard of this resource." Correct after removal.
410 Gone          "This resource existed and has been removed. Here is the replacement."
                  The only correct response to a post-sunset client, and it is
                  what makes the failure self-diagnosing in the client's logs.
501 Not Implemented  "This method/feature is recognised but not supported here." Correct
                  when you keep the path but disable the behaviour.
```

```
Step 1  STOP NEW USAGE. Set the feature flag to OFF for everyone (5.10.12). This is
        reversible and is the step that tells you how badly people depended on it.
        Watch metrics for a week. A feature nobody missed was already dead.
Step 2  COMMUNICATE WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, in the product, not just the changelog:
        what disappears, what replaces it, when, and what happens to their data.
        "This feature is deprecated" is not a product announcement; "Checkout v1 will
        stop working on 1 March; your carts will be preserved; here is the migration"
        is.
Step 3  MIGRATE DATA. Every user has something in the old shape: a saved cart, a
        configured integration, an API key, a report definition. Migrating data is a
        much larger project than removing code, and it is the step teams forget.
        It needs a backfill, a validation query ("no user has an unmigrated cart"),
        and a rollback.
Step 4  FREEZE. Set the old path read-only. No new writes. Now you can detect stragglers
        without risking data loss.
Step 5  REMOVE. Delete the code, the tables (after retention), the jobs, the flags, the
        docs, the dashboards. Then remove the "off" path so it cannot be resurrected
        by a stale flag.
```
